Sports.title: 'McLaren will be furious!' - Was Norris to blame for Piastri collision?
Sports.content:
The overtake Lando Norris attempted on Oscar Piastri that resulted in the McLaren team-mates crashing on the final lap of the Singapore Grand Prix Sprint was "not smart", according to Sky Sports F1's Martin Brundle.

Norris had narrowly trailed Piastri in a battle for fourth for most of the 20-lap race at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, where overtaking is extremely difficult.

Norris tried to go up the inside of Turn 5 on the final circuit, which led to a crash as Piastri turned in, with the Australian spun around as his rear-right tyre was struck by his team-mate's front-left.

Piastri suffered damage that took him out of the race, while Norris was able to get going again and take the chequered flag in eighth for the final point.

Speaking on commentary immediately after the incident, Brundle said: "McLaren will be furious about that, on the final lap of a Sprint.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix Sprint race

"Whether they were fourth or fifth, it would have made no difference to the team whatsoever."

The difference between finishing fourth and fifth in a Sprint is only one point. McLaren were on course to collect nine points, but instead ended up taking just one and seeing their lead over Red Bull in the battle for third in the constructors' standings cut to just 11 points.

The stewards launched an investigation into incident, which resulted both McLaren drivers being summoned for a hearing after the race.

Brundle suggested that reigning world champion Norris was largely responsible for the collision.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports F1's Karun Chandhok dissects who was at fault for the collision between the two McLaren's which saw Oscar Piastri crash out of the Singapore GP Sprint race

"That was not smart, Lando. That was not smart at all," Brundle said.

"I think Lando got on the kerb on the inside as the space pinched a little bit and that slid him even more into the side of his team-mate.

"It just wasn't worth the risk. What was Oscar going to do? I know they're racers. It just wasn't worth taking the risk just to swap the two cars around in a Sprint."

Norris insists pass was on

Norris immediately apologised to his team over the radio but insisted in his post-session interview that he thought the move was on.

The Brit said over team radio: "Sorry about that. Obviously I didn't want that to happen but I thought I was fully alongside. I just ran out of space at the apex but I was there, so..."

Image: Norris thought he was in position to pass his team-mate Piastri

Quizzed over in the incident in his post-race interview with Sky Sports F1, Norris added: "I'd rather just go back and review it."

On whether he still believed "the move was on", Norris said: ""It was."

Piastri played down the incident, claiming he wasn't "that bothered" due to the fact it was a Sprint event.

"I've not seen it properly," the Australian told Sky Sports F1. "From where I sit, I'm not...it's for fourth and fifth for a Sprint race so I'm not that bothered either way. Just obviously it's a lot of work now for the team to get both cars fixed.

"Just a shame for the team."

'A hell of a lunge'

Sky Sports F1 pundit and former world champion Jenson Button described Norris' move as "a hell of a lunge".

Reflecting on Norris' comments after the incident, Button said: "He was very bullish. Normally when you're that bullish, you're being defensive.

"It was a hell of a lunge. On your team-mate, at that moment in a race.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Max Verstappen takes the Singapore Grand Prix Sprint win

"And the problem is the corner does tighten quite a lot at the apex, and he found himself in the side of his team-mate."

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella and chief executive Zak Brown opted not to do any interviews with the media immediately after the session, but are expected to speak either before or after Singapore Grand Prix qualifying later on Saturday.

Sports.title: Bruno Guimarães completes Arsenal comeback to end Leeds’ unbeaten run
Sports.content:
Arsenal came back from a goal down to defeat strong opponents and reset their form after the lengthy international break. They were not great against Leeds, and the defence continues to look more vulnerable than last season, but the impact from their bench and the belief that roared through the team after they forced an equaliser suggested they have acquired the resilience of champions. Or as the home support put it: “we know who we are.”

Arsenal had six English players in their starting lineup, the first time that had happened since 1999. Daniel Farke, meanwhile, selected the same Leeds side as he had for the previous three matches. Some had predicted a goal-fest, others another upset for the champions. There was a real sense of uncertainty as to the outcome as this match began.

The first half was a tight affair, but one that allowed both sides to hope for more. Leeds were typically resilient, but able to get up the pitch in two touches. Arsenal were too intricate and, at times, alarmingly vulnerable, but also close to unpicking the visiting defence.

Leeds had the best chances, with deliveries from either side of the field appearing to unsettle Arsenal’s redoubtable back line. In the 25th minute, a Gabriel Gudmundsson delivery was well met by Jayden Bogle, but blocked, inadvertently, by Anton Stach.

Two minutes later, Bogle was denied again, this time picking up the loose ball from an Ao Tanaka cross and firing at Raya from a tight angle. With a minute remaining of the half, the Arsenal goalkeeper produced a carbon-copy save to deny Gudmundsson himself.

Arsenal could not have complained had they gone in a goal down at the break. There was some frustration in the crowd too. There were things that were working, such as the selection of Noni Madueke – one of four changes – who was having the better of James Justin on the left. Madueke’s crosses deserved better from his forwards, Kai Havertz especially, who directed a header straight at James Trafford from eight yards out with the goal at his mercy in the 21st minute.

View image in fullscreen James Justin (centre) fires Leeds ahead. Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/Reuters

With no changes at half-time, the second period offered an opportunity for one side to impose themselves and Leeds duly accepted the invite. For the first 15 minutes they dominated play, overpowering Arsenal in midfield and running beyond their full-backs. Justin and Tanaka had long-range efforts go narrowly wide before the visitors got the opener at last, Justin firing home after Gudmundsson had run off Ben White and delivered a low cross from the left that Raya could not cut out.

That was the 55th minute and Noah Okafor nearly doubled the lead three minutes later, but could not get the final touch to a Bogle cross. . Within three minutes, the game had snapped into a new direction.

Arsenal grabbed an equaliser in the manner Leeds had been threatening for so long. A deep cross from Madueke was met at the back post by White, whose header eluded Trafford and was bundled home by Riccardo Calafiori for his second Premier League goal of the season.

Mikel Arteta then made a triple substitution and unleashed Bruno Guimarães. If Arsenal had had a familiar look to this point, if there had been echoes of familiar weaknesses, then the Brazilian put paid to all that. Not only snapping into tackles, not only moving the ball at pace, he was desperate for everything to go faster, more aggressively, with sharper intention. Nine minutes after coming on, he scored the winner.

It reflected the best of what Arsenal had been trying to achieve. Again, play developed down the left, but here it was Saka swapping in for Madueke and playing a one-two with Odegaard. The captain then poked a short pass to Declan Rice who – with Bruno now covering him – had ventured into the opposition area. Rice backheeled the ball first time to the edge of the area and there was Guimarães waiting, poised, to steer the ball unerringly into the corner of the goal.

Further chances fell to the home side, including Odegaard from two yards out and Saka, who failed to execute a one-on-one with Trafford, but the misses did not ultimately matter, such was the transformation. Leeds, for their part, left the field looking shocked.

Sports.title: Portugal suspend Cristiano Ronaldo after walking out on national team
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo has been provisionally suspended as the Portuguese football federation opened disciplinary proceedings against the 41-year-old after his decision to walk out on the national team.

Ronaldo apologised to supporters on Tuesday while criticising the Portugal coach, Jorge Jesus, and said he would serve any “suspension that is imposed” on him.

According to Portuguese newspaper A Bola, the FPF confirmed that disciplinary proceedings had been opened.

“Without prejudice to the automatic preventive suspension to which ‌he was subject until the date of initiation, a non-automatic preventive suspension ​of the player was determined, and the proceedings were given urgent status,” the federation was quoted as saying.

Ronaldo gave his ⁠account of the dispute ⁠that prompted his ​departure from Copenhagen before Portugal’s Nations League match against Denmark last week.

Ronaldo said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would ⁠miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness. However, on the day of the Norway game, the coach told him he would play for 30 ⁠minutes.

“Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn’t called ​on,” Ronaldo said. “The manager had broken his ‌word to me.”

In the games, Ronaldo was either an unused substitute or absent, Portugal won all three and his replacement, Gonçalo Ramos, seized his chance by scoring three times.

Ronaldo ended the international break with a long post to his 679 million followers on Instagram, where he asked Jesus to acknowledge a mistake in asking him to warm up on the sidelines and then not send them on the field against Norway. The Portugal coach did not acknowledge any mistake.

Sports.title: Championship roundup: Swansea top after beating Norwich; Blues win at West Brom
Sports.content:
Adam Idah made up for three near misses in the first half to head Swansea, the Championship leaders, to a 2-1 home win over Norwich. The Republic of Ireland striker scored with a glancing header in the 59th minute to complete his side’s comeback after falling behind to Jacob Wright’s goal in the first half.

Joseph Opoku gave Idah a great chance to add to his three goals this season in the 22nd minute after winning the ball on halfway and driving to the Norwich area. Idah took a heavy touch from what looked to be a scoring pass and Vladan Kovacevic saved.

Norwich were quick on the counterattack and a great cross from the left forced Stephen Welsh to head over from under the Swansea bar to concede a corner.

The corner was cleared but Andre Brooks and Oscar Schwartau combined to rob Welsh of the ball and Schwartau passed across the area for Wright to score in the 28th minute. Idah had two more chances to level matters before the break, but again Kovacevic was up to the mark to deny him.

It took Swansea four minutes after the restart to get back on level terms when Yeo made it three goals in three games. Some neat interplay on the left touchline freed Josh Tymon and his cross was missed at the near post by Idah before being converted at the back post by Yeo.

The winner came just before the hour as Idah headed home from an inch-perfect cross from Melker Widell.

Norwich had two good chances in the dying minutes but Lawrence Vigouroux saved Sam Field’s shot and then saw Jovon Makama head over the bar from five yards out.

West Brom’s defender Nat Phillips was at fault for the second successive derby as Birmingham won 1-0 at The Hawthorns. Phillips, whose back pass let in Fer Lopez in the 1-0 loss to Wolves last time out, gave away a 41st-minute penalty scored by August Priske.

Phillips caught the forward in the air with a clumsy challenge from a cross and Priske side-footed the penalty high to Max O’Leary’s left for his second championship goal of the season. The result leaves the sides level on 14 points.

Sports.title: Sliding Doors meets Biff’s Almanac: City saga stirs up a world of alternate histories | Max Rushden
Sports.content:
It’s Wednesday afternoon (UK time) and I find myself interviewing Tony Hadley on TalkSport about his upcoming big band tour. We play a bit of Spandau Ballet, chat about the classics and his career – hanging out with Frank Sinatra and Tony Bennett. In as much as you can deduce in a 10-minute chat on Zoom, Tony seems like an absolute gent.

We do always try to bring it back to sport – Tony is an Arsenal fan, there’s a bit of Arteta, Leeds at the weekend. Tony brings up Billy Bremner and suggests that my co-host Charlie Baker and I are too young to remember him playing. We are, and how wonderful to be called young.

Right at the end I go for a slightly cumbersome question/joke about Manchester City. “And I know Manchester City are top of the league, but they’ll probably be bottom of the league by the end of the season?”

Hadley is a pro. Maybe he’s been waiting for this hardball question about the charges. “You just never know what’s going to happen – the world is a crazy place. I’ve got to add to all the big band songs we’re doing … at the end we do a Christmas catalogue which is great fun as well.” What a sidestep.

What am I doing? It’s quarter to midnight in Melbourne, I’m in my shed looking at Tony Hadley on a little box on my laptop asking what he thinks City’s punishment might be. Quick, put a call in to Boy George. What’s Midge Ure saying? Simon Le Bon has things to say, but they are embargoed until Drive Time.

Perhaps this is Enzo Maresca’s best strategy. The City manager’s only way out of answering difficult questions is to organise a 20-date big band tour of the UK so he can do the Hadley pivot and talk about how he really brings the house down with his spectacular Christmas medley.

It would certainly add to the monotony of every Premier League manager giving us their prepared “I’m a football man and all I’m interested in is football – I’ve got enough things to worry about at Coventry/Leeds/Bournemouth, etc.”

But such is the magnitude of the story that even these press conferences are interesting. For the first time since filming players walking off a bus in big headphones became part of the spectacle, I am interested in seeing players walking off a bus in big headphones on Sunday afternoon.

View image in fullscreen Enzo Maresca ponders the Hadley pivot. Photograph: Andy Hampson/PA

We couldn’t ask for a more perfect place or a perfect time for this game to take place. Liverpool away. The side City have pipped to the title by a point or two three times since the cheating began. I know two of the titles came after the cheating officially finished but don’t think I need to mention that. What if City couldn’t have afforded John Stones (height: 1.88m) and had settled for, say, Victor Lindelöf (1.87m)? How vital was that extra one centimetre of Stones in clearing that ball off the line against Liverpool at the Etihad in January 2019?

The hypotheticals never end. Sliding Doors meets Biff’s Almanac. Nicky Bandini explained on Thursday’s Football Weekly that Serie A has two histories depending on where you stand on Juventus and Calciopoli: “I think that’s the truth that English football isn’t ready for yet. Whatever happens with these decisions, whether they successfully end up appealing things or they don’t, you’re going to have one group of supporters who are absolutely certain they didn’t win these trophies legitimately, and therefore they don’t count, and you’re going to have one group of supporters who don’t care and are going to claim those trophies whether or not they get taken away from them.

“I think that’s the grim future that lies ahead for the Premier League. You’re going to have two alternate histories, the same that happens in Italy, where the number of titles that Juventus has won is constantly repeated differently by different sources because one side or another is not going to accept the judgment even after the final appeals are exhausted.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen John Stones clears off the line from Mohamed Salah in 2019, but what if City had never been able to sign the defender? Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters

I’m minded to side with those who favour stripping City of the titles but not assigning them to anyone else. Not just because it’s fun to see how many people say Asterix. Football just isn’t that simple. If City don’t sign those players, they sign other players. Those other players don’t sign for someone else. Games are different, results are different. Players train in different cities, different managers get hired and fired. People live in different places and move to different countries, meet different people. Different marriages, different children. It’s one thing telling Sergio Agüero that the goal isn’t real, but what about his whole life after 2011? Does he have to redo it all?

And then we get to the reason we fell in love with football: geopolitics. If the sanctions aren’t of the highest severity it’s impossible not to wonder whether anything has happened in the corridors of power, or on one of those benches in Spooks or Slow Horses when two people sit on a bench in Regent’s Park with identical briefcases and walk off in separate directions with the other one. Will the UAE really refuse to scrap investment in a tech hub between Cambridge and Oxford if Manchester City are relegated to League Two? It’s ridiculous that the two are even connected.

And while we all wait for the punishment to drop on a quiet Friday, perhaps during the next international break, City have football matches to play, whether they’ll ultimately mean anything or not. Pundits will say “galvanise” a lot. We will all talk about an “us against the world mentality”.

Who will be the first player to tell Erling Haaland to look forward to Salford away next year? My money would have been on Enzo Fernández until I remembered he’s probably frantically checking whether there’s a relegation release clause in the contract he signed in the summer.

I’d imagine it’ll be hard for Elliot Anderson to spend much time thinking about the possible sanctions while he’s trying to fend off Dominik Szoboszlai and Florian Wirtz. Regardless of the result on Sunday we’ll draw conclusions about what impact this news has had – and we may be wildly wrong.

I do sympathise with most City fans. Perhaps not the guy on a radio phone-in comparing this rule-breaking to Emmeline Pankhurst’s fight for female suffrage. But that complete loss of objectivity is part of the beauty of football and sport – somewhere we all lose all rational sense.

At my most pious I like to think I’d save my ire for the owners. They’ve dragged the club into this, they should go, but even that is an almighty mess to untangle. At the same time, if I were City, would I really swap the journey they’ve given me and these highs for finishing 12th every season for the past 15 years? Am I better than that? Like all moral dilemmas, it’s easy to have a strong opinion when it doesn’t affect you and you’re in a shed talking to a New Romantic.

Sports.title: The Premier League is back: welcome to the new era of post-verdict unreality | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
The internet: an apology. It turns out you were right. It was actually a simulation all along. Now, talk to me about chemtrails again. And yes, maybe Vinícius Júnior has been replaced by a handsome, baffled-looking waxwork.

Welcome to the weirdest weekend of them all. We are now post-judgment, post-statement, postlapsarian. As the Premier League prepares to snap back into what must be described, out of habit, as reality, armed with the knowledge its serial champions have been the authors of a 10-year sham supremacy, the first question is fairly simple. How is it going to feel?

There is no precedent for this. Even the state of total confusion feels brittle given City maintain their complete state of innocence and deny all charges. We await the release of Irrefutable Body of Evidence, the great lost Madonna erotic thriller sequel, presumably recast around a steamy three-year regulatory tribunal scenario.

City’s appeal defence appears to be based around the government giving them money. This may or may not be related to how you control what the high court considers admissible. But it is also implied confirmation that the club is the propaganda tool of an overseas state, that Kyle Walker, for example, has basically been a civil servant all these years. Maybe the United Arab Emirates should have six stars on the national team jersey, one for each title. They even look like asterisks.

Beyond this there is the more basic issue of how to present this spectacle as entertainment. How do you structure a Match of the Day now? What’s the balance in the edit of bus-rage, taunting banner clips, managerial evasiveness content, versus the trivial stuff on the pitch with the balls and goals and men in shorts?

Mainly the Manchester City affair has created an existential problem. The key questions in English football are no longer things such as who will win the league, or will Tottenham get relegated (although this is still an excellent question). They are instead: what is real now? What was real then? What will be real in the future? Will something that seems real now become unreal later?

View image in fullscreen Was Kyle Walker basically a civil servant during his time at City? Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty Images

The whole experience brings to mind visiting the Yas Marina Formula One track in Abu Dhabi a few years back, a pristine place, all sweeping curves, perfect surfaces, dreamy floral boulevards. At that stage exploring its far reaches, following the curve around the final corner, led to: nothing. Out of sight the hanging baskets stopped dead. The sprinklers cut out. The pavement ended. The next step took you straight into sand and dead space.

Beyond the main stage the Yas track was a set, an imitation of life. And it turns out this is basically what Abu Dhabi was doing to the Premier League in the years 2009 to 2018: creating a product, a simulacrum, a pop-up.

At the end of which we have a blurring of edges, different versions of what could be real eliding into one another, a place where an AI video of Uncle Phil from the Fresh Prince scoring the Özil goal against Ludogorets seems just as real, just as plausible as City’s 6-0 thrashing of Watford in the FA Cup final. Seen through that lens this can feel like an extinction-level problem. Being real is, in the end, all sport actually has.

It feels fitting City’s first date in the new unreality is Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, one of the great Premier League fixtures recast as a kind of ceremonial shame-event, a requiem for a dream. Liverpool have a clearer sense of grievance than most, having been deprived of league titles three times on the final day by a club that was colouring outside the lines.

In many ways the game at Anfield is a perfect snapshot of what we have lost. This should be an entirely pure and gripping sporting contest. Instead the biggest story in top-tier English football is the meaninglessness of top-tier English football. The headline product is gossip, side-eye, legal backstory.

In their next 14 league games City will play three teams who have reserved the right to sue them. How can these occasions be seen as credible acts of sport? Even the banter-culture is out of date. For the past 12 years City at Anfield has been soundtracked by the Steve Gerrard/He slipped on his arse incident, a source of public pain that has defined the late-stage career of Liverpool’s most beloved modern captain. Except, we now know the actual story is the club that finished above them were cheating.

View image in fullscreen Steven Gerrard after that mistake against Chelsea in 2014. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA

It turns out this is the first stage of football grief. Poring over the endless counterfactuals. Some are pretty stark. The five league titles won on the last day of the season. The 1-0 FA Cup final victory against Stoke, coached by a man with two contracts, the winning goal scored by a player linked, by close association, with the book-cooking regime.

There is a butterfly effect here of endless interference. What do Inter make of all this? Imagine losing a Champions League final that could have transformed your modern history, by the narrowest margin, to a club that appear to have built their own era out of cheating on their income. Two years later Inter were thrashed by another nation-state team and Simone Inzaghi was shunted off the set. He’s in Saudi now. Just get on the train.

Then there’s the wider structural stuff. City spent nine years flooding the zone with government-backed transfer funds (€1.2bn in those nine years: miles out in front), skewing the money supply in every league in Europe. The extra £20m disbursed at the last moment to drag Kevin De Bruyne out of the Bundesliga. What happens if that doesn’t happen?

At home, Spurs missed the Champions League by one spot four times, always in City’s slipstream. Would Manchester United have signed Rasmus Højlund without that steamrollering model of Erling Haaland-era success?

How to reprocess the deep cultural influence of Pep Guardiola? This was based on Guardiola’s genius as a coach, which is still real, irrespective of the gradient of the playing field. But nothing succeeds like success. Winners get to rewrite history. How does it feel now that Guardiola’s style affected so profoundly the way kids play park football, the way young coaches work, all of it based on sustained blockbusting example?

Even the Football Association’s England DNA pathway was basically a Pep document, predicated on the undeniable evidence of his winning way. The method is still good, the detail unarguable, the tactical blueprint pure. But that 10-year spell in England was also supercharged by cheating.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

We mourn too the legend of the Catalan brain trust, the hours spent studying this pure and monk-like dynamic. Yeah, fine. But also chuck vast amounts of hidden cash at it. Not to mention the hundreds of articles, podcasts, academic studies, fan tributes and personal tomes about purity, legacy, style, the glory that sailed above all other questions.

View image in fullscreen Pep Guardiola reminds Liverpool fans of his six titles in 2024, but how now do we assess his influence? Photograph: Ian Hodgson/AP

City’s fans are entitled to some space here, a chance to effect their own reckoning up. Elements of that support may have responded over the years with bizarre levels of aggression to any questioning of the process. But it is also normal to believe what you’re told, not least when it includes the profound transformation of the thing you love. How to process a total narrative U-turn?

The City documentary series A Beautiful Obsession is a far more interesting watch now, like The Sixth Sense when you know the ending. The project is cast by its editors as a pure passion play, Pep portrayed as a tunnel-vision obsessive, pictured most often staring at a whiteboard covered in magnets while the world turns beyond his line of vision.

It is impossible now not to see some kind of willed seclusion, Prospero on his island, rough magic starting to fray as reality crashes on to the shores. Episodes one to four are portrayed as a Viking funeral for the age of Pep. But they are now an unwitting farewell to something else too. In his final appearance Pep is shown quoting Kipling, saying triumph and disaster are both impostors. And he’s right. It turns out they were. Most notably the triumph bits.

Just before the end credits we see one of City’s club channel celebrations, with boards plastered in the usual phrases the club seems to feel drawn to. This is how it felt. We see things they’ll never see. Looking back this was always part of the dynamic, the insistence, which is usually just taken as read, that this is all real, that the feelings were feelings, that nobody can fake this away.

It is still the mantra for some. And maybe that’s true. But if so, what did it add up to in the first place? An episode of a TV show? An induced high, a snort of disposable pleasure?

View image in fullscreen Manchester City fans celebrate their 2012 Premier League title. They too are entitled to some space here. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/Getty Images

But then, this is also not the end. There is always disasterism in football, the sense the thing happening now is the thing that will always happen. But football’s enduring strength, the one thing that marks it out as indestructible, is its relentlessness. We are in the period of rupture and parallax error. But how long will it last?

Plenty of good can still come from this. The idea that English football is profoundly damaged by this may prove wide of the mark. What is happening here, and this includes the outcome of the appeal, is that rules are being enforced. Andy Burnham may have confused the process with his tone-deaf and weirdly partial comments. But for all the delay and indecision this is still the rule of law in action.

And maybe English football gets to learn something. Maybe the unregulated nature of the league can reset a little. At the very least it seems axiomatic the new regulatory powers should ensure no nation state, or state fund, however you want to semanticise it, gets to own a club again.

There are still 33 rounds of Premier League games to run in the age of whiplash. The current interlude may feel like a football version of those bits in the Terminator films where Sarah Connor drives around in a Jeep looking glazed and distant, prepping for the time of skulls and robot death-rays, disengaged from the meaningless lives of blind and foolish humans.

Football always moves on. Throw flares at a bus, taunt the deceived souls in the away end. But the future is still wide open. Perhaps we can even face it with a little hope in the time of conflict.

Sports.title: Russo’s return to form is vital but Lionesses still lack bite against low blocks | Suzanne Wrack
Sports.content:
It took a labyrinthine move from Sarina Wiegman’s team to find a way through deep-lying Greece. On the outskirts of Heraklion, the ancient city of Knossos, which is associated with the legend of the Minotaur and the labyrinth constructed by Daedalus to contain it, Laura Blindkilde Brown’s quick pass to Alessia Russo was artfully flicked first time to her Arsenal teammate Georgia Stanway and the midfielder slotted in past the goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti.

There were muted celebrations after the goal, reflective of the frustration they felt at having taken 39 minutes to get their first goal against the team ranked 54 places below them.

That was a familiar frustration because, despite two Euros wins and a World Cup final, England have struggled to completely shake free of the accusation that they struggle against low blocks. In spite of the 3-1 scoreline and their dominance in possession, the Lionesses didn’t look comfortable or particularly happy for stretches of the match.

It was the speed of thinking and inventiveness of the passing that made the difference for the opener; that is the flair England need to find in those testing moments.

“It’s tough when you come up against a low block,” said Alessia Russo afterwards. “We get it a lot at club [level] and here at England … It’s about being patient and then when you do have that moment, it’s about the quality of the pass and speeding the game up just to create half a yard for someone to get a shot off.”

It was a goal that would have usually allowed them more space but in Heraklion it didn’t. The home team remained compact, a narrow-margin loss a more favourable defeat to take to Leicester for the return leg on Tuesday night than the wider margin they would potentially have faced with a swashbuckling attempt to get back into the game. It was only as legs began to tire against the European champions that the home team left themselves more exposed.

The critical second goal, which provided a huge amount of relief, arrived in the 63rd minute. That it came from Lucy Bronze’s stand-in Maya Le Tissier was important, with Kallisti Brouksair having twice broken free of the Manchester United centre-back to whip in a cross in the first half in the rarest of forays into the final third for Greece. Le Tissier operated as a wing-back in the Pankritio stadium, still favoured by Wiegman as the best option to come in for Bronze despite playing centrally week in, week out for her club and – bar those two chances for the opposition in the first half – the goal capped a solid performance. Le Tissier said she was unfazed by switching positions for club and country and by Bronze’s weighty shadow.

View image in fullscreen Maya Le Tissier (far left) is congratulated after doubling England’s lead. Photograph: Stefanos Rapanis/Reuters

“I’ve played the position enough now to know what’s expected of me,” she said. “Every time I get on the pitch, I just want to try my best, do everything I can and do whatever Sarina wants of me. I’m not the same player as Bronzy, I try to play my own game and I love getting on the ball and creating chances even higher up as well. I looked up to her when I was younger, but people just have to realise that you’re not the same. There’s so many different players; players that play in the same position but are completely different and I don’t try to be like Bronzy, I just try to be myself and play as well as I can.”

Russo’s goal, England’s third, was also significant. It was the forward’s third goal in as many games for club and country after five games off the scoresheet.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

With Aggie Beever-Jones out of form and out of the squad, having not scored since March for Chelsea, and unconvincing experiments with Lauren James and Lauren Hemp in the No 9 role, Russo finding her goalscoring from, and staying fit, is critical to England’s World Cup ambitions.

“I’m my own biggest critic, so there’s maybe a bit of overthinking going into it,” said Russo. “I knew that stripping it back and getting back to enjoying my football and not stressing too much was important.”

It’s perhaps naive to attempt to draw too many conclusions about England’s World Cup potential from these autumn qualifiers, with Wiegman and her staff clearly still experimenting and tweaking in search of the best XI and best finishers (substitutes) that would make up her squad for Brazil. The team is also in a transition phase, at the beginning of a new cycle under Wiegman after a period laden with success.

However, the opportunities for experimentation between now and the World Cup are few and far between and the concession of a goal in Greece, one that was met with wild and slightly disbelieving celebrations from the hosts, leaves both a serious a job still to be done and provides a sliver of hope to an opposition that should have none.

Sports.title: Managers react to Manchester City’s guilty verdict: ‘Uncertainty is not good for anyone’
Sports.content:
1. Carrick ‘personally’ affected by verdict Michael Carrick has said retrospectively receiving a winner’s medal would not make up for being robbed of emotional moments of glory by Manchester City’s breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules. Manchester United’s manager was part of the squad that lost out on the Premier League title to City on the final day of the 2011-12 season when Sergio Agüero scored a last-minute winner to secure top spot on goal difference. Carrick and his United teammates were left solemn on the touchline at Sunderland while City, who have been found guilty of breaking financial rules during a nine-year-period between 2009 and 2018, celebrated. “The emotion, the feeling about winning, a lot of it is in the moment,” Carrick said. “Whether you’re successful, whether you lose, whether it goes against you, that initial [feeling], the beauty of sport and the beauty of football and the beauty of trying to win trophies here, is a little bit on the journey towards it and then the finale, and does it go for you, does it go against you. “Once that’s done, there’s no getting that back in any direction. The feeling we all crave is coming out on top – that kind of sums it up. Whatever’s done in the past tense is in the past, but in that moment is how you feel in that moment. Certainly as a participant, as a performer, and I’m sure the supporters feel the same, that’s why we love it so much because of the emotion in the moment.” Carrick was also part of United’s staff under Ole Gunnar Solskjær when they finished second, 22 points behind City, in 2021. City continue to plead their innocence and have appealed against the verdict. If they fail to overturn the independent commission’s ruling, they will probably face a serious punishment. “It’s affected me personally in different ways,” Carrick said. “But as the case is ongoing now I don’t know where that stands and how it’s going to end up, so we’ll just have to wait and see. What I will say, the sooner it gets sorted I think for everyone’s benefit is essential.” Will Unwin

2. Iraola understands Liverpool fan anger Andoni Iraola understands the anger among Liverpool supporters towards Manchester City and believes the Premier League needs a resolution to the scandal engulfing English football as swiftly as possible. Iraola avoided condemning City during his first press conference since the club were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules on an industrial scale over nine years. City have lodged an appeal against the findings and Liverpool’s head coach admitted a final, definitive verdict is essential for the good of the game. “I think it should be [concluded quickly],” he said. “There should be a moment when something comes from this, but now is not that moment. Nobody knows what is going to happen and I think this uncertainty is no good for anyone.” While refusing to be drawn on the controversy while the legal process is ongoing, Iraola acknowledged the strength of feeling that will be directed at City by Liverpool fans at Anfield on Sunday. City pipped Liverpool to the Premier League title in 2013-14, 2018-19 and 2021-22, the latter two during the fierce rivalry that developed between Jürgen Klopp’s and Pep Guardiola’s teams. Sunday’s reception for the current league leaders promises to be brutal. “We understand and I understand everything that goes above football,” said Iraola. “Every fan will have their own opinion and attitude towards that but it’s not something that I can control. I need to do my job, to give the best game we can give on the sporting side, so everyone of our supporters is happy on Sunday. I think the challenge of the game for us is big.” Liverpool’s task on Sunday, as Iraola referenced, will be complicated by the absence of leading goalscorer Alexander Isak and the in-form Cody Gakpo due to injuries sustained on international duty. The two are not long-term absentees but, with Liverpool facing four games in 10 days, they could miss several matches. He admitted: “It’s a bad thing for us, definitely, because both of them have been prolific at the start of the season but the good thing when you coach Liverpool is you still have very good players available. I trust the players we have ready to go. It’s also a good moment for those players to step up, to add good numbers and good performances while we recover Cody and Alex.” Andy Hunter

3. Kompany ‘really proud’ of City medals Vincent Kompany, the former Manchester City captain, insists he is still “really proud” of his success with the club after it was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules. The Bayern Munich manager won four Premier League titles and multiple domestic cups during his spell at City from 2008 to 2019. The former Belgium international was a key figure in City’s dominant era under their Abu Dhabi-based owners and is honoured with a statue outside the Etihad Stadium. “I played 11 years for the club. I’ve loved all of the years I played for the club and everything we achieved and [did] on the pitch – that’s something I’m really proud of,” Kompany said. View image in fullscreen A statue of the former Manchester City player Vincent Kompany’s stands outside the Etihad: ‘I’m really proud of everything we achieved.’ Photograph: Dave Thompson/AP Kompany signed for City from Hamburg just weeks before Sheikh Mansour completed a takeover that turned the club from also-rans to serial winners. Asked about the off-pitch issues at his former club, he said: “Everything else, as a player you’re not a part of that and right now as a coach of Bayern Munich I’m not too much occupied with that topic. I’m preparing the game next week and preparing the game we have tomorrow and everything I have as a coach.” Agence France-Presse

4. Arteta will wait for judgment before speaking Mikel Arteta has insisted his conscience is clear about his time as Manchester City’s assistant manager and promised to “talk with clarity” about his former club when their appeal against a guilty verdict on more than 100 Premier League’s charges has been decided. Arteta spent more than three years as Pep Guardiola’s assistant at City before moving to Arsenal in December 2019. The Spaniard, who signed a lucrative new four-year contract this week, moved to the Etihad in July 2016 and was part of Guardiola’s backroom staff as they won titles in 2018 and 2019. The first came during the period in which City breached financial regulations, according to an independent commission. Arteta was reluctant to discuss any potential punishment City could face but was asked whether his conscience was clear from his spell at City and responded: “Yes.” That was as far as he was prepared to venture after being bombarded with questions about City before Arsenal’s game against Leeds on Saturday. Arteta had been due to deliver a statement at the start of his press conference but the plan changed at the last minute. He refused to be drawn on how he felt when he heard the verdict or whether the uncertainty it had created would have a long-term impact on the Premier League’s brand. “I want to think that it doesn’t, but I don’t know,” he said. “Uncertainty is not in our control and our control is to bring everything that we can individually through the club to maintain the position that we have to be the best league in the world.” Arteta added: “The thing is that this has been going for various years. That process is still not finished. So it is very difficult to express how I feel, because it is not resolved. When it is resolved I can talk with clarity and tell you exactly how I feel.” It is understood Arsenal and other Premier League clubs are keen for the situation to be resolved as quickly as possible, although City’s appeal means it could drag on until at least the new year. Arteta also dismissed suggestions Arsenal could be the main beneficiaries should City find themselves relegated, having finished as runners up to them three years in a row before becoming champions last season. “I think we control our accelerator, and believe me, for seven years it’s been full gas in everything that we can do and take in every corner at maximum speed,” he said. Ed Aarons

Sports.title: Bruno Guimaraes rescues Arsenal off the bench to earn an unconvincing 2-1 win over Leeds - but alarm bells should be ringing for Mikel Arteta after another pedestrian display, writes RIATH AL-SAMARRAI
Sports.content:
Arsenal’s title defence might soon be spared some jeopardy by events elsewhere, but the Premier League is no place for those who would rather jog to the line than sprint. It’s a message that won’t be lost on Mikel Arteta, even in victory.

For this was an ugly, unconvincing win and the kind that owed more to the tired legs of Leeds than the quality of the team that eventually beat them.

Of course, we could make a virtue of the fighting spirit needed to retrieve a 1-0 deficit. But the truth is Arsenal were so far off the pace for long periods that it would sound a louder alarm if Manchester City weren’t facing the possibility of a massive points sanction.

An overreaction? Perhaps. But the first half against Leeds was dire. Not quite so bad as the performance against Brighton prior to the international break, but worse in the ways that they shrank from the physical battle. Worse in how willing they were to go with the flow. Worse in the means with which they then fell behind to James Justin’s goal early in the second half.

Pinpointing that moment, we could see Declan Rice is yet to return to full sharpness, despite being rested by Thomas Tuchel across the past fortnight. We can never accuse Rice of not trying, but he was easily outrun in the key phase of the attack, before Noni Madueke allowed the strike by not chasing down Justin at all.

It was a dismal goal to concede and it was almost followed by a second that would have made a real drama of this match. Arsenal survived those attempts, however, and relocated enough class to capitalise when the effort finally told on Daniel Farke’s resources.

Bruno Guimaraes came off the bench to score a crucial winner as Arsenal defeated Leeds 2-1

James Justin fired the visitors ahead in the 55th minute, threatening an upset at the Emirates

Riccardo Calafiori continued his fine form scoring Arsenal's equaliser just after the hour mark

The leveller was converted by Riccardo Calafiori, whose gifts continue to show in all areas of the pitch, and the winner soon followed from Bruno Guimaraes, whose £75million signing has been slow to justify itself. After an inauspicious beginning at the club, and having delivered an outright stinker against Brighton, his fine strike might serve as a launchpad.

For Arteta, there was doubtless some relief around the outcome and the return from injury for key personnel after a few uncertainties arose in the international break.

Christos Tzolis was unavailable with a muscular injury sustained with Greece but Kai Havertz and Ezri Konsa were passed fit, as was Rice after sitting out England duty.

Of those coming in, Havertz’s inclusion despite the niggles of a hamstring issue was interesting, primarily, for what it told us about Viktor Gyokeres’s status. Having scored four in four for Sweden across the past fortnight, the expectation was that he might find himself back in Arteta’s favour, so a place among the substitutes for the first hour was jarring.

MATCH FACTS Arsenal (4-2-3-1): Raya 6; White 7 (Timber 63, 7), Konsa 7, Gabriel 6, Calafiori 8 (Hincapie 82); Rice 6, Lewis-Skelly 5 (Guimaraes 63, 7); Saka 6, Odegaard 7 (Merino 90), Madueke 6; Havertz 5 (Gyokeres 63, 6) Subs not used: Arrizabalaga, Zubimenid, Eze, Dowman Booked: Odegaard Manager: Mikel Arteta 7 Leeds (3-4-2-1): Trafford 7; Justin 7 (Nmecha 79), Elvedi 7 (Bijol 86), Muharemovic 7; Bogle 7 (Bahoya 86), Ampadu 6, Tanaka 7 (Wilson 71, 6), Gudmondsson 7; Stach 6, Okafor 6 (Aaronson 71, 6); Calvert-Lewin 7 Subs not used: Zetterer, Bard, Gruev, Longstaff Booked: Tanaka, Ampadu, Justin Manager: Daniel Farke 7 Referee: Paul Tierney 7

Ordinarily, Arteta’s wisdom wouldn’t be questioned with any great enthusiasm and there are few volunteers willing to mount an argument for Gyokeres. But the first half here offered little vindication for Arteta – his attack was predictable and ineffective.

Madueke had a couple of moments of joy in his duel with Jayden Bogle, yielding one cross and a saved header from Havertz, but the rest of the unit were forgettable.

Bukayo Saka unpacked his sack of feints and flicks at Gabriel Gudmundsson and got nowhere. Martin Odegaard got stuck in the traffic of Leeds’s midfield. Havertz was too often isolated.

None of which happened by accident, of course. Daniel Farke has built his success this season on an excellent defence and a reliable goalkeeper in James Trafford, but there is also the benefit of calling on big men. If Brighton set a blueprint prior to the break by pressing /and hassling Arsenal out of their patterns, then Leeds showed the advantage of old-fashioned strength in the challenges. Usually, Arteta’s side can hold their own in that regard but here they found themselves being pushed around.

Occasionally, that went to ugly places – namely, Ao Tanaka and Ethan Ampadu’s bookings for clattering Myles Lewis-Skelly and Ben White.

But it is equally true that Leeds forced the best chances of the opening 45 minutes, especially those for Gudmundsson and Bogle, who both forced decent saves from David Raya. By turns, Arsenal were struggling to find the right answer to Farke’s wing backs, but they were also unable to track the clever movements of Dominic Calvert-Lewin at the tip of the spear.

Eventually, the package shaped into a Leeds breakthrough early in the second half, when Gudmundsson was able to easily outrun Rice in a race to the left-hand byline before rolling low to Justin, who had set off on his own mission up the right. Madueke had eyes on the threat but didn’t bother to pursue Justin. Poor.

It was a pivotal win for Mikel Arteta's side, who were beaten 3-0 by Brighton before the break

Leeds United suffered their first defeat of the season after an excellent start to the campaign

It might have got worse for Arteta, with his defence thrown into chaos by a long ball before Noah Okafor fell a fraction short of reaching Bogle’s cross. At 2-0, Arsenal might have been lost, but Calafiori’s equaliser reset the scale. The move, involving Odegaard, Madueke and White, was their first coherent attack in the space of an hour.

Arteta took that moment to make a decisive change, with Havertz, White and Lewis-Skelly hooked and Guimaraes among those sent in. It had the effect of pushing Rice further forward and the recalibration paid off quickly, shown by the goal for 2-1 when Saka, Odegaard and Rice were all part of the chain that opened a path for Guimaraes to stroke a low finish past Trafford from the edge of the area.

Rice’s contribution – a flicked assist – was a sublime reminder of his class even on a day when he looked lethargic. The same might be said of Arsenal as a whole.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo hit with Portugal suspension after walking out of international duty amid row with Jorge Jesus - as Portuguese FA opens disciplinary investigation
Sports.content:
Portugal have suspended Cristiano Ronaldo after he dramatically stormed out of camp following an explosive fallout with manager Jorge Jesus. Ronaldo threw his toys out of the pram last month, claiming Portugal boss Jesus 'broke promises' by leaving him on the bench during their 2-1 Nations League win over Norway. The 41-year-old icon said a plan had been drawn up for him to come off the bench for 30 minutes, but Jesus made him warm up without bringing him on because he 'didn't need Cristiano'. Before Portugal's match against Denmark, football’s all-time leading goalscorer is understood to have agreed to an eight-point statement for Jesus to deliver at his press conference, aimed at quashing speculation that Ronaldo was demanding more playing time. But Jesus veered off course, prompting Ronaldo to bail on the Portugal camp before releasing an extraordinary 1,996-word statement accusing the manager of twice backtracking on his word. Cristiano Ronaldo has been provisionally suspended by Portugal after walking out of the squad during the international window Ronaldo left the Portugal camp amid a rift with Portugal's head coach Jorge Jesus Despite apologising to his team-mates, Ronaldo now faces suspension while an investigation into his conduct takes place, and he could now miss the entire international break in November. In a statement, the Portuguese federation said: ‘Disciplinary proceedings were initiated against Cristiano Ronaldo pursuant to a decision by the Non-Professional Section dated October 9, 2026, aimed at determining whether the events reported on October 7, 2026, warrant disciplinary action. ‘Without prejudice to the automatic preventive suspension to which he was subject prior to the initiation of proceedings, a non-automatic preventive suspension of the player was ordered, and the case was designated as urgent. ‘The case was referred to the FPF Disciplinary Investigation Committee on October 10, 2026, with the proceedings remaining confidential until the conclusion of the investigation.’

Sports.title: Jamie Carragher and Piers Morgan trade insults on social media as Liverpool legend brands broadcaster an 'absolute phoney' over his staunch defence of Cristiano Ronaldo
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher and Piers Morgan have traded insults on social media after the latter took exception to being labelled 'embarrassing' over his vocal support of Cristiano Ronaldo. Ronaldo had been one of the talking points of the international break after the Portugal veteran walked out of the Portugal camp following a rift with manager Jorge Jesus. While Ronaldo has apologised for storming out of the camp, his behaviour has been defended by Morgan and Rio Ferdinand – who are both friends with the Al-Nassr striker. Morgan called Jesus, 'the Ten Hag of international football', while Ferdinand said the treatment of his former Man United team-mate was 'inappropriate', claiming the manager 'thought he was Sir Alex Ferguson or Pep Guardiola'. Speaking on the Overlap Daily on Friday, Carragher claimed their closeness to the star was problematic when analysing the situation and suggested they were 'embarrassing themselves'. 'People think it’s good to be close to people in the game, but this is where it becomes a problem,' Carragher said. Piers Morgan and Jamie Carragher traded insults on social media over the former's support of Cristiano Ronaldo Morgan took exception to being labelled 'embarrassing' by Carragher over his vocal support of Ronaldo, who walked out on the Portugal squad during the international break Morgan initially aim at Carragher over Liverpool wearing t-shirts defending Luis Suarez, who had been banned for racially abusing Patrice Evra back in 2011 Carragher responded by highlighting how he had apologised to Evra about the t-shirts years ago, as he renewed his view that Morgan's judgement is 'clouded' over Ronaldo 'People like Piers Morgan and Rio Ferdinand, who are big people in the media whether you like them or not, are embarrassing themselves with the nonsense that they’re coming out with because they know Ronaldo. 'You can know someone and try to look after them, but you cannot defend the indefensible.' Morgan responded on social media on Saturday, with the broadcaster and Carragher dragging up historical incidents as they traded insults. Morgan referenced Carragher and his Liverpool team-mates wearing shirts in support of Luis Suarez during the warm-up before a game in 2011, after the Uruguayan was banned for racially abusing Patrice Evra in 2011. 'So, @Carra23 dislikes me (and @rioferdy5) sticking up for our friend @Cristiano, or as he puts it "defending the indefensible". Here is the same Jamie Carragher supporting his friend Luis Suarez after he racially abused Patrice Evra.' Carragher responded: 'We as a team did support our teammate and we were wrong. I apologised to Patrice on tv years ago, which then prompted Liverpool to send him a letter also apologising which was the right thing to do. 'Your reaction to my slight criticism saying you & Rio are in bed with Ronaldo so it clouds your judgement when speaking about him is embarrassing. You batter people every day, when it’s the other way you storm out of a tv studio or get personal. All to get another interview you sycophant.' The Liverpool legend then added a photo of a Daily Mail column written by Morgan back in 2008 headlined 'Ronaldo is a spoiled brat, why cheer him?', with Carragher commenting 'What an absolute phoney you are.' The exchange continued with Morgan posting 'But when it comes to ‘defending the indefensible’, I do admit I have sometimes done that @Carra23.' Carragher branded Morgan an 'absolute phoney' after highlighting an old article written by the broadcaster that labelled Ronaldo a 'spoiled brat' The insults continued with Morgan referencing his support of Carragher in 2018 after the pundit was suspended by Sky Sports after spitting towards a car after being goaded Carragher claimed he questioned Morgan's sincerity as he stated Morgan had invited him on his TV show following his backing The post referenced Morgan's defence of Carragher in 2018, where the broadcaster called for the pundit to keep his job at Sky Sports after he was filmed spitting towards a car after being goaded by a fan while a 14-year-old girl was in the passenger seat. The ex-England international was suspended by Sky Sports for the remainder of that season over the incident but kept his job. Carragher, who reflected in 2021 over his embarrassment over the incident, claimed he questioned Morgan's initial support after being asked to be interviewed by the broadcaster. 'Yes I remember, I contacted you to say I appreciated your support, you then tried to get me on your tv show to talk about it, so my appreciation waned a bit as I knew it wasn’t as sincere as I first thought,' Carragher wrote. 'It was all about an interview, as is your possessive fawning over Ronaldo & [Donald] Trump. I also wouldn’t be getting personal with your history or the other two you’re defending, now that would be defending the indefensible.' The discussion could continue with Morgan having earlier posted in response to Carragher's comments about Ronaldo by promoting his upcoming talk show, writing 'I’ll deal with Mr Carragher on Monday’s Football Uncensored…'

Sports.title: Cole Palmer casually announces his new Chelsea contract on awkward mock livestream just HOURS before clash with Bournemouth - as Blues star returns to Twitch after being banned for streaming EA FC27 too early
Sports.content:
Cole Palmer casually announces his new Chelsea contract on awkward mock livestream just HOURS before clash with Bournemouth - as Blues star returns to Twitch after being banned for streaming EA FC27 too early

Cole Palmer has claimed Chelsea are 'going in the right direction' after signing a new long-term contract until 2034.

The Chelsea star announced his new deal on a mock Twitch livestream, which saw him respond to fake questions from fans.

Palmer read out the question 'How long are you staying at Chelsea then?', with the attacker responding: 'Well, I've just signed a new contract about 20 minutes ago.'

'So I'm staying for about eight more years.

'So hopefully you can sing that song a bit more that you all sing.'

The mock Twitch stream comes after Palmer was temporarily suspended from the platform last month after playing EA Sports FC 27 before the game's release, leading to the midfielder appealing for them to lift his ban.

Cole Palmer has signed a new long-term deal committing him to Chelsea until 2034

Palmer announced his new contract on a mock Twitch live stream before an official announcement

Palmer has insisted Chelsea are heading in the right direction in their pursuit of major trophies

Palmer had seven years left to run on his previous deal, but has agreed improved terms with the new contract extending his commitment by a further 12 months.

The 24-year-old expressed his belief the Blues are making progress and will be in contention to win major trophies.

'Chelsea means a lot to me and I think the club is going in the right direction, so I'm delighted to sign and I'm obviously very happy,' Palmer said.

'Speaking to the owners, to the sporting directors and obviously the manager, they gave me a lot of confidence so it was only right to sign.

'Speaking to players as well, everyone has the same ambitions. I feel like we can win major trophies here consistently and I want to be a part of that and play a big role in it too.'

Palmer has scored 58 goals and provided 34 assists in 138 appearances for Chelsea since joining from Man City in 2023.

The attacking midfielder has played a key role in helping the Blues win the FIFA Club World Cup and Conference League in 2025.

Palmer has enjoyed a strong start to the season having scored four goals and provided two assists in seven matches.

He now boasts one of the longest contracts in the Premier League, with team-mates Joao Pedro and Geovany Quenda also on deals until 2034.

Erling Haaland's long-term Manchester City contract also runs until 2034.

Despite his performances for Chelsea, Palmer has made just 14 appearances for England.

Palmer has enjoyed a strong start to the season, scoring four goals in seven matches

Palmer withdrew from the England squad during the recent international break, with Three Lions boss Thomas Tuchel stating he 'misses way too many camps' and that this was 'another missed opportunity'.

Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso defended Palmer, with his withdrawal through injury related to the groin problem which has previously plagued him

'We were cautious, and he was cautious as well, he wanted to be,' Alonso said of Palmer.

'He wouldn't have played the way he wants to play. It's sometimes better to take a step back and wait until you feel better and do it the right way.

'There is always a risk. With Morgan (Rogers), there was a risk. Nothing happened. With Jamie (Gittens), there was a risk. We've lost him for a few weeks. With Cole, it was the right decision.'

Sports.title: Max Verstappen clinches sprint race victory at Singapore Grand Prix - as George Russell misjudgement sees Mercedes star crash out
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen clinches sprint race victory at Singapore Grand Prix - as George Russell misjudgement sees Mercedes star crash out

Max Verstappen won the sprint ahead of the Singapore Grand Prix – the second Formula One event in a week to be delayed by bad weather, this time for 30 minutes.

This event was postponed when torrential rain arrived on the track some quarter of an hour before the race was due to start. This postponement came six days after the Malaysian Grand Prix was controversially deferred 90 minutes on Sunday because the half-electric engines could not run as the heavens opened.

The Dutchman’s victory around Singapore’s street circuit was achieved after George Russell crashed out while leading. ‘Sorry, sorry, sorry,’ said Russell to his team.

The British driver was in command of proceedings but he then slipped on to the white line on the final bend of the opening lap, and that was him done. He skewed over the track to the other side and glanced the wall.

Verstappen went on to triumph by 2.5 seconds ahead of Lewis Hamilton, who finished second for Ferrari, roaring up from sixth on the grid after an excellent start in which he gobbled up ground. His team-mate Charles Leclerc came third, while the McLarens of world champion Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri crashed at the end.

Russell, who shook his head disconsolately as he climbed out of his Mercedes, had made a perfect getaway, passing Verstappen, who started in pole position.

Max Verstappen claimed victory in the sprint race at the Singapore Grand Prix

George Russell made the perfect start but crashed out following a misjudgement

It was still wet on the Marina Bay Circuit at this stage, but the spray was not in Russell’s face but on those of them behind him. He made an ‘unforced’ error – and his world championship campaign is over.

Though those hopes had already withered on the vine, truth be told, and now fourth-placed Kimi Antonelli, the championship leader, heads Russell by 88 points going into qualifying later today, at 2.30pm BST, a session delayed by half an hour as a result of the earlier interruption.

There is a maximum of 175 points remaining to be won, if all the scheduled rounds go ahead, despite the war in the Middle East, with races scheduled for Qatar and Abu Dhabi in the last week of November and the first of December.

They remain on the calendar for now. Imola is an option should either or both be called off.

Sports.title: Tottenham to fly to Marbella for training camp immediately after Premier League clash with Man United - as Roberto De Zerbi hopes trip to Spain can kickstart their season following winless start
Sports.content:
Tottenham are set to head to Marbella for an early-season training camp after their Premier League clash against Man United on Saturday.

Spurs boss Roberto De Zerbi is hoping to kickstart their campaign, with his side currently bottom of the Premier League with two points from five games.

Following the encounter at Old Trafford, Tottenham have a nine-day gap until they host Coventry on Monday, October 19.

The trip to Spain will give De Zerbi's squad an opportunity to bond after a busy summer of upheaval.

Spurs added 10 players for around £250million in the transfer window, many of whom arrived late on and therefore haven't had much time to gel with their new team-mates.

The trip to southern Spain will also give De Zerbi's side the chance to train in warm weather, with expected temperatures of 25 degrees in contrast to the forecasted rain in north London.

Tottenham will head to Marbella for a training camp after today's clash against Man United

De Zerbi is hoping to use the trip to turn around his side's fortunes amid their early struggles

During pre-season, De Zerbi also expressed his frustration with the time he had to work with his new group as a result of the club's summer tour to New Zealand and Australia, along with several players returning late after the World Cup.

A team trip is nothing new to the Italian, with his squad heading to Mayfair restaurant Bacchanalia towards the end of last season for a bonding dinner to ease the pressure as they battled with relegation.

A warm-weather camp early in the season is unusual though, with these tending to happen over the winter as teams go in search of sun and recuperation during a hectic schedule.

Prior to the lengthy international break, Spurs were beaten 3-2 at home to Aston Villa, after which De Zerbi expressed his anger at his side.

'I was very disappointed, very sad, very frustrated for the performance,' fumed De Zerbi. 'We can’t lose this game in this way, absolutely.

'We can’t concede the second goal. We can’t lose balance. In the beginning of the second half I spoke with the four attackers, to use their heads, be calm.

'It was minute 51. All the second half, be calm, play, enjoy, don’t take risks. But the goal we conceded, the second goal was incredible.'

He continued: 'I don’t know if some players lost energy, but we conceded an unacceptable goal from a long goal kick, with a long ball. We knew Aston Villa are playing 86 per cent more long balls than last season. We spoke about it in many meetings.

'Then we have to explain another game like Newcastle, where we play well in the first half and then lose. For sure it’s an aspect.

'It’s my responsibility, I don’t want to leave without taking my responsibility, but in that moment of the game, when the game is different to ball possession, to playing in the last third, because we can’t play for 90 minutes in the last third like the first half, because there is an opponent.

'Aston Villa is not such a bad team. It is a good team, good players and the moment we have to defend, we have to defend compact. The leaders have to be leaders and lead the team.

The trip will give De Zerbi more time to work with some of his new signings, including Savio

'Football is like life, either you are stronger or you lose.'

De Zerbi vowed to work harder and improve in the aftermath of the defeat but accused his players of losing their way when things conspired against them.

'In the second half, we lost balance because we were losing,' added the Spurs boss. 'We forced the pass, forced the situation, lost the ball.'

Before the next international break, Spurs also face Coventry, Chelsea, Crystal Palace and Leeds in what is likely to be a crunch month for the Italian.

Sports.title: How the Premier League killed Arsenal's set-piece threat - and the fightback against winning ugly being led by referees, rulemakers... and towels
Sports.content:
Remember when set-pieces were destroying football? Remember when Arsenal scored so many goals from corners that Nicolas Jover, their set-piece coach, had his face painted on a mural outside the Emirates? Remember when dead balls were so important that Chelsea met the release clause of Aston Villa’s specialist Austin MacPhee like he was a superstar striker? Can you blame them? The Gunners, for all their creative tribulations in open play last season, scored a record 19 goals from corners and won the title for the first time in 22 years. Tottenham netted 18 of their own from them to help them survive by the skin of their teeth. But is this what football had become? Squeeze as many big blokes in the six-yard box as possible and let them wrestle it out, Royal Rumble-style, to see who can get their head on the ball first? At last summer's World Cup, analysis by FIFA found that more than 40 per cent of corners saw a member of the attacking team try to block or impede the opposition, up from less than a quarter in Qatar four years earlier. It meant that more than half of all goals scored from corners in the 2026 tournament came courtesy of a blocker. Back here, referees chief Howard Webb had threatened to clamp down on grappling the previous summer but that soon seemed to be forgotten. ‘You get the feeling now that referees really don't want to get involved in any of it,’ remarked Everton boss David Moyes last season. Now, the crackdown has begun properly, with officials encouraged to penalise any ‘holding actions that have clear material impact'. Just five weeks into this season, the change is drastic. Last season, a massive 18 per cent of goals came from corners, by far the highest percentage in Premier League history. Goals from open play, which had lingered around the 70 to 73 per cent mark for the previous eight seasons, dropped to 65 per cent. Now, under the new mandate, goals from open play are back up to nearly three quarters of the 141 we’ve seen so far. Corners have accounted for just 9.9 per cent of them this season - the second-lowest in Premier League history. Is this what football had become? Squeeze as many big blokes in the six-yard box as possible and let them wrestle it out, Royal Rumble-style, to see who can get their head on the ball first?

Your browser does not support iframes.

Your browser does not support iframes.

More than half the division are yet to score from one, including Arsenal, the masters. Neither have Spurs. Brighton, meanwhile, are embracing the best of both worlds with three goals from corners AND the best Expected Goals (xG) figure from open play in the top flight. How much of this slump is down to strict refs? According to Opta, the rate of fouls given within 10 seconds of a corner being taken this season has jumped from 6 per cent last season to 8.1 per cent, and those specifically for grappling - defined by Opta as a push or holding/pulling an opponent's shirt - up from 4.1 per cent to 5.3 per cent. None of them, though, have led to a penalty. There were 21 spot-kicks given last season within 25 seconds of a corner. The only one given so far this season for grappling at any kind of set-piece was when Arsenal defender Ezri Konsa was adjudged to have fouled Sunderland’s Dan Ballard after a long throw, but even that one was later ruled to be a mistake. Chicanery while attacking set-pieces appears to have been stamped out. But dig deeper into the numbers and referees aren’t holding as much sway as it might seem. The xG from set-pieces has dropped a little, from 0.76 per game to 0.72 - or about two goals' worth across the opening 50 matches of the season - while it’s down from 0.46 to 0.38 per game, which accounts for five fewer goals. The number of shots from set-pieces has actually gone up slightly, which suggests that teams are having to get the ball into worse positions to get shots off, away from the hustle and bustle of the six-yard box. So what has happened to Arsenal? Over the past three seasons, they ranked top for set-piece goals. This Saturday lunchtime Mikel Arteta’s former corner kings take on Leeds - the tallest team in the division - without a single set-piece goal, bar a single penalty, to their name. Hardly the easiest opponent against whom to break their duck. Despite the percentage of corners ending in a foul has gone up across the division, Arsenal’s number has actually fallen. The Gunners aren’t creating as much as they did. Last season they ranked first for xG from set-pieces and third for shots from them. This term, they're down to ninth and 14th respectively. And even the chances they are creating aren’t going in. Gabriel, so often their unstoppable force in these situations, has had three attempts on goal from them this season and hasn’t scored. From the quality of chance they have created from set-pieces, they should have a couple, and perhaps that's just luck correcting itself. Last season, they overperformed their set-piece xG by about five goals. Over the past three seasons, Arsenal ranked top for set-piece goals - but this season Arteta has already complained about a new Premier League rule that bans players from drying balls with towels before throw-ins Arteta has already complained about the impact of another new Premier League rule that bans players from drying balls with towels before throw-ins. Ben White and Declan Rice would often launch long throws into the box last season, from which Arsenal netted a couple of goals. ‘Not being able to use the towels is already a big one,’ said Arteta ahead of the season. Ahead of Leeds' visit on Saturday lunchtime, he reflected: 'You have to adjust to the rules and what is allowed and what is not. That opens other windows to do things that we want to do. We hope to score in a different way. My personal opinion is that we have done better things than last year in the first five games, but we have scored no goals. That is the reality of set-pieces. ‘Last year we had scored three goals by this time, and two of them we didn’t have to do much about and the execution it deserved wasn’t done right. There is an element of luck. I think this season we should have scored more but we haven’t. If we maintain that throughout the season, we will be in really good numbers.' William Saliba has missed all five league matches so far. His replacement Ezri Konsa will take time to get up to speed with Jover’s tricks and routines. And even he might not be fit to face Leeds. Jurrien Timber, who like Gabriel scored three goals from set-pieces last season - including two against Leeds - has missed three games through injury. Arsenal missing two of their main harbingers of chaos hasn’t helped. Webb’s clampdown is, perhaps, making teams think a little differently. Sides are taking short corners more often than last season. Goals from open play are back to the levels of previous campaigns after last season’s aberration. Maybe the beautiful game is back after all and Arsenal, this time, can’t just rely on winning ugly.

Sports.title: Man City charges LIVE: Settlement talks with Premier League as punishments agreed
Sports.content:
Man City are in the centre of a major Premier League charges storm

Manchester City are back in Premier League action for the first time since the club were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules

Hello and welcome to The Mirror's live blog on Saturday, October 10, as Premier League action returns following the extended international break.

Manchester City are set to return to the pitch for the first time since being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules. The club have already launched an appeal after an Independent Commission found them guilty of 114 out of 115 charges relating to the period between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

The allegations include claims that more than £830million in owner funding was used to inflate the club’s revenues through so-called 'sham' agreements. Speculation continues to mount over the potential sanctions City could face, with possible punishments ranging from a substantial fine and points deduction to the prospect of expulsion from the Premier League.

"Personally, I'm very calm to be honest," said Maresca. "The club has been quite clear. We trust completely the club.

"We understand the noise, but the focus for us is just what we can control and we can control just the football side."
