His track record includes pioneering solutions in mobile money, payment gatewayS, telco/fintech convergence, and marketplaces.

He actively contributes to various technology and industry advisory boards and supports non-profits advancing talent in science, technoLogy, Machine Learning, and AI.

World.title: 2027: Makinde vows one-term presidency, challenges Tinubu on fuel prices
World.content:
Gov Seyi Makinde

By Luminous Jannamike

Presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement, APM, Seyi Makinde, has pledged to serve only one four-year term if elected in 2027, promising a transitional government of national unity while challenging President Bola Tinubu to publish the Federal Government’s petroleum pricing template.

Makinde said Nigerians deserved relief from economic hardship and the right to know how fuel prices were determined, accusing the Tinubu administration of failing to deliver on key promises, including electricity supply and alternative fuel policies.

Speaking at the APM North-East town hall meeting in Yola, Adamawa State, the Oyo State governor said his party would pursue a different approach to governance, built around transparency, public participation and power-sharing.

He demanded that the Federal Government make its petroleum pricing template public, arguing that expertise in solving Nigeria’s problems was not the exclusive preserve of those in power.

“The fact that you are in government or the Presidential Villa does not make you the only Nigerians with sense. We have other citizens who can dissect issues and proffer solutions,” Makinde said.

He faulted the administration’s policies on compressed natural gas, CNG, electric vehicles and the naira-for-crude initiative, saying they had failed to deliver the expected results. He also recalled Tinubu’s pledge to fix electricity within four years.

Makinde said the 2027 election should mark a break from what he described as a culture of political deception, promising to be truthful with Nigerians about the challenges confronting the country.

“2027 will mark the end of the politics of lies and deceit. It is a time when we will all come together to establish a reset agenda and tell Nigerians the whole truth,” he said.

On concerns about the concentration of political power in one part of the country, particularly among northern stakeholders, Makinde pledged an inclusive administration that would accommodate the country’s diverse interests.

“I stand before you today to tell you that the government you will put in place from May 29, 2027, will be a transitional government of national unity. Our government will not last beyond four years. And it will be an all-inclusive government,” he said.

Makinde explained that the party had delayed releasing its manifesto to hear from stakeholders before finalising its policy proposals.

Earlier, APM National Leader and Bauchi State Governor, Bala Mohammed, declared that the party had become a force in the opposition, pointing to its governors, elected officials and growing membership.

“Whoever does not reckon with us is going to do so at his or her peril,” Mohammed said, urging supporters to rally behind the party’s presidential ambition.

He said APM was committed to national unity, mutual respect and equal opportunities for Nigerians regardless of their backgrounds.

The party’s vice-presidential candidate, Lawal Daura, said Nigeria needed a fundamental reset, describing APM as a platform for patriotic citizens determined to change the country’s direction.

“Otherwise, we will continue to be in motion but without movement,” Daura said.

World.title: Nigerian canvasser arrested by ICE after guilty plea
World.content:
A Nigerian national who worked on a Democratic congressional campaign in Pennsylvania has been arrested by United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after pleading guilty to a disorderly conduct charge arising from a public exposure incident.

The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), according to Punchng announced the arrest of Chimaobim Adedayo Igbojekwe in a statement issued on October 7, 2026.

According to the department, Igbojekwe was arrested in East Pennsboro Township, Pennsylvania, on September 27 over alleged indecent exposure and disorderly conduct. He subsequently pleaded guilty to the disorderly conduct charge.

ICE arrested him on October 1 following his conviction, the statement said.

The DHS disclosed that Igbojekwe was working as a canvasser for Janelle Stelson, the Democratic nominee for Pennsylvania’s 10th Congressional District, when the incident occurred.

Citing local media reports, the department said he was found with his trousers off and exposing himself in a residential neighbourhood near a park where residents, including children, were present.

Reacting to the incident, ICE Deputy Director Charles Wall criticised Stelson for having Igbojekwe on her campaign team.

“It’s unbelievable that Janelle Stelson would employ an illegal alien to work on a Congressional campaign, let alone a pervert who exposed himself in public,” Wall said.

He said DHS personnel were working to identify and remove undocumented immigrants considered dangerous to American communities.

“The Trump Administration will always put the safety of the American people first,” Wall added.

The DHS said Igbojekwe was lawfully admitted to the United States in June 2017 but remained in the country after his authorised period of stay expired in November 2019.

According to the department, he was granted deferred action by the administration of former President Joe Biden in September 2021.

The statement did not provide further details about the status of his immigration proceedings.

World.title: Three Nigerian sisters who drowned in UK sea took own lives – Inquest Rules
World.content:
Three Nigerian sisters who drowned in the sea off Brighton, southern England, have been ruled to have taken their own lives following an inquest into their deaths.

The sisters, Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, lived together in Greenford, west London. They had become increasingly withdrawn following the death of their mother in 2010.

The inquest heard that the sisters visited an area of Birmingham close to where their mother died on May 11 before travelling to Brighton the following day.

According to BBC, they were later seen on the town’s eastern seafront in the early hours of May 13, when they entered the sea in difficult conditions. None of the sisters could swim.

Their father, Joseph Jacobsen, described the loss of his three daughters as heartbreaking.

Coroner Penelope Schofield said the court could not speculate on the reasons behind the sisters’ actions.

Evidence presented at the inquest showed that a taxi carrying the sisters arrived in Brighton at 10.21pm on May 12. The driver reportedly noticed that they were quiet during the journey.

Closed-circuit television footage later showed the sisters on Brighton’s eastern seafront. They were last seen alive at 2.42am on May 13.

The inquest also heard that police examining Christina’s laptop found 227 references to water and 179 references to suicide. Christina had reportedly experienced anxiety and depression following their mother’s death.

Rebecca’s medical records contained no significant information relevant to the inquest, while Jane was not registered with a doctor.

Toxicology tests found no evidence of drugs or alcohol in the sisters’ systems, and investigators found no evidence of violence.

Jane was brought ashore by the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) and pronounced dead. Christina was recovered by an RNLI lifeboat, while Rebecca’s body was later washed ashore. Both were pronounced dead by paramedics.

The inquest examined the circumstances surrounding the deaths and the sisters’ movements in the hours before they entered the water.

World.title: 2027: ‘We’ll campaign with projects, not insults’ — Aliyu
World.content:
By Musa Ubandawaki, Sokoto

SOKOTO — Sokoto State Governor, Ahmed Aliyu, has challenged opposition parties in the state to present their records of achievements to voters ahead of the 2027 general elections, saying his administration will campaign on the strength of its projects and development initiatives.

Aliyu said the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the state would focus on its performance in office rather than engage in personal attacks or campaigns of calumny against political opponents.

The governor spoke at Government House, Sokoto, on Friday, shortly after observing the Jumu’at prayer, where he called for issue-based campaigns and responsible political conduct ahead of the elections.

“We will ensure decorum in our campaign language and refrain from insulting anyone,” he said, adding that political competition should focus on achievements, policy alternatives and constructive engagement.

Aliyu maintained that his administration had executed several projects across the state, which he said would form the basis of the APC’s campaign for another mandate.

He said the government would continue to listen to residents’ concerns and respond to their needs, stressing that public office should be directed towards improving living conditions and advancing the state’s development.

Challenging opposition parties to account for their time in office, the governor urged their leaders to present their achievements and policy proposals rather than concentrate on criticising the incumbent administration.

“Rather than resorting to campaigns of calumny, opposition parties should tell the people what they achieved when they were in power,” he said, according to a statement issued by the Government House.

Aliyu also cautioned politicians and their supporters against abusing freedom of expression during campaigns, saying democratic rights should not be used to undermine the rights, dignity or personal security of others.

He reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to protecting residents regardless of their political affiliations and urged APC supporters to obey the law, respect opposing views and conduct their political activities peacefully.

“We owe it a duty to protect our dear state from anyone who seeks to destroy it,” the governor said, calling for peace, stability and mutual respect as political activities intensify ahead of the elections.

Aliyu thanked the people of Sokoto State for their continued support and prayers, urging them to sustain their cooperation with his administration.

World.title: Give mental health patients a say in decisions – WHO
World.content:
By Sola Ogundipe

As Nigeria joins the rest of the world to mark World Mental Health Day 2026, the World Health Organisation (WHO) has called on governments and health systems to move beyond listening to people with mental health conditions and give them a meaningful role in shaping the policies and services that affect their lives.

The call comes amid concerns that people with lived experience are often invited to share personal stories but excluded from decisions about their treatment, recovery and access to care.

The WHO, in its message on October 10, said the theme, “Lived experiences heard: real voices, real change,” was intended to recognise the knowledge of people who have experienced mental health conditions and make their participation central to reforming mental health services.

According to WHO, meaningful participation goes beyond hearing personal testimonies. It requires involving people with lived experience in designing services, developing policies, evaluating programmes and holding institutions accountable.

“World Mental Health Day is an opportunity to meaningfully engage with people with lived experience (PWLE) of mental health conditions and to recognize their knowledge as a vital form of expertise. This year’s campaign calls for their voices to shape the policies, services and decisions that affect their lives,” the organisation noted.

Further, WHO said: “Lived experience is what someone has experienced themselves, especially when it gives the individual knowledge or understanding that people who have only heard or learnt about such experiences do not have. Too often, PWLE are asked to share their stories but excluded from decisions. Meaningful engagement extends beyond simply being heard.

“It means creating opportunities for people to influence decisions, co-design services, strengthen peer-led approaches, challenge stigma and strengthen accountability. When PWLE are meaningfully engaged, mental health systems are likely to become more person-centred, rights-based and responsive to people’s needs and concerns.”

The WHO said their experiences could reveal barriers that health professionals and policymakers might otherwise overlook, helping services respond more closely to the needs of patients and their families.

“One important priority for PWLE is the shift away from long-stay psychiatric institutions towards community-based, person-centered mental health care. Institutions tend to be isolating and are too often associated with poor-quality care, coercion and human rights abuses.

“Deinstitutionalisation requires a carefully planned shift in funding, services and support so that people can live in their communities. Reflecting this priority, WHO will launch practical guidance on deinstitutionalisation.

“On this World Mental Health Day, let us move from listening to action – and build mental health systems with PWLE, not merely for them. Mental health systems should be built with people who have lived experience, not merely for them,” WHO noted.

The campaign also draws attention to the need for more humane, person-centred care, including a shift away from dependence on long-stay psychiatric institutions towards adequately supported community-based services.

The WHO noted that only nine per cent of countries responding to its Mental Health Atlas 2024 survey had fully transitioned to community-based mental health care, while 53 per cent remained at an early stage of the transition.

It also reported that 45 percent of responding countries had ongoing collaboration with people with lived experience and family or caregiver advocacy groups in planning, delivering or monitoring mental health services.

The figures point to a gap between recognising patients’ rights and ensuring that their experiences influence how care is organised and delivered.

For Nigeria, the message raises questions about the place of patients, survivors and caregivers in mental health policy, treatment decisions and the delivery of community services.

Nigeria has a Mental Health Act, but questions remain about implementation, the availability of services and the extent to which people experiencing mental health conditions can obtain affordable, respectful care without stigma or discrimination.

Stakeholders note that the challenge is not simply to encourage people to speak about mental illness, but to ensure that their voices carry weight when decisions are made about their lives.

World Mental Health Day is observed annually on October 10 to raise awareness, challenge stigma and promote better mental health care worldwide.

World.title: Top 10 countries that received most US Aid
World.content:
Nigeria ranked sixth among the countries that received the most United States foreign assistance in the 2025 fiscal year, with about $728.8 million disbursed to the country, according to an analysis by the Pew Research Center.

Ukraine topped the global list with nearly $6.7 billion, followed by Israel with $3.31 billion and Jordan with $1.65 billion, based on data from ForeignAssistance.gov analysed by Pew Research Center.

The findings, published by Pew Research Center on July 21, 2026, showed that Ethiopia was the fourth-largest recipient, receiving $919.2 million, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo ranked fifth with $748.7 million.

Nigeria was the sixth-largest recipient, ahead of Sudan, Kenya, Mozambique and Uganda, which completed the top 10.

The figures cover US foreign assistance disbursed during fiscal year 2025, which ran from October 1, 2024, to September 30, 2025. They measure funds actually disbursed rather than amounts pledged, budgeted or approved.

According to Pew Research Center, the United States disbursed approximately $47.3 billion in foreign assistance worldwide during the fiscal year, about $26 billion less than in fiscal 2024. Adjusted for inflation, the amount was the lowest annual total since fiscal 2004.

## Full list of the 10 countries that received the most US aid in 2025

The following ranking is based on total US foreign assistance disbursements reported by ForeignAssistance.gov and analysed by Pew Research Center.

1. Ukraine — $6.70 billion

Ukraine received approximately $6.70 billion in US foreign assistance, making it the largest recipient for the fourth consecutive fiscal year.

The country received about $5.69 billion in nonmilitary assistance and $1.01 billion in military assistance. Much of the support was linked to the continuing consequences of Russia’s invasion and Ukraine’s need for economic, humanitarian and security support.

However, the amount was approximately 34.1 per cent lower than the country received in fiscal 2024, according to Pew Research Center.

2. Israel — $3.31 billion

Israel received approximately $3.31 billion, ranking second worldwide.

Almost all the assistance was military-related, with about $3.31 billion classified as military assistance and approximately $5.2 million recorded as nonmilitary aid.

Pew Research Center reported that US assistance to Israel in fiscal 2025 was 51.4 per cent lower than in the preceding fiscal year.

3. Jordan — $1.65 billion

Jordan ranked third, receiving approximately $1.65 billion in US assistance.

The country received about $1.22 billion in nonmilitary aid and $428.8 million in military assistance. The support covered different areas, including economic programmes and security-related assistance.

According to Pew Research Center, the total was 5.2 per cent lower than Jordan received in fiscal 2024.

4. Ethiopia — $919.2 million

Ethiopia was the fourth-largest recipient, receiving approximately $919.2 million in US foreign assistance.

The entire amount was classified as nonmilitary assistance in the data analysed by Pew Research Center.

The figure placed Ethiopia ahead of every other African country in the ranking, reflecting the scale of US assistance recorded for the country during the period.

5. Democratic Republic of the Congo — $748.7 million

The Democratic Republic of the Congo received approximately $748.7 million, placing it fifth globally.

About $741.1 million was classified as nonmilitary assistance, while approximately $7.6 million was recorded as military assistance.

The country was the second-highest African recipient in the ranking, ahead of Nigeria.

6. Nigeria — $728.8 million

Nigeria received approximately $728.8 million in US foreign assistance, making it the sixth-largest recipient worldwide and the third African country on the list.

The data showed that about $727.4 million, or nearly 99.8 per cent of Nigeria’s total, was classified as nonmilitary assistance. Military assistance amounted to approximately $1.44 million.

The figures indicate that US assistance to Nigeria during the period was overwhelmingly directed towards nonmilitary programmes rather than military support.

The ranking does not, on its own, specify how much of the nonmilitary assistance went to individual sectors. It should therefore not be interpreted as a breakdown of funding for healthcare, education, humanitarian relief or other specific programmes.

7. Sudan — $709.1 million

Sudan received approximately $709.1 million in US foreign assistance, placing it seventh worldwide.

The entire amount was classified as nonmilitary assistance in the data published by Pew Research Center.

Sudan’s position among the leading recipients places it alongside several African countries receiving substantial support through nonmilitary programmes.

8. Kenya — $651.1 million

Kenya received approximately $651.1 million, ranking eighth globally.

Of the total, about $624 million was nonmilitary assistance, while approximately $27.1 million was military assistance.

Nonmilitary programmes accounted for 95.8 per cent of Kenya’s total, according to the figures analysed by Pew Research Center.

9. Mozambique — $582.1 million

Mozambique ranked ninth after receiving approximately $582.1 million in US foreign assistance.

The country received about $575 million in nonmilitary aid and approximately $7 million in military assistance.

Nonmilitary assistance accounted for 98.8 per cent of its total allocation.

10. Uganda — $512 million

Uganda completed the top 10, receiving approximately $512 million in US foreign assistance.

About $503.9 million was classified as nonmilitary assistance, while approximately $8.1 million was recorded as military assistance.

The figures placed Uganda among the five African countries featured in the global top 10, alongside Ethiopia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Nigeria and Kenya, as well as Sudan and Mozambique.

World.title: Bayelsa police arrest 23 cult suspects, recover firearms
World.content:
…Lauds community partnership

By Samuel Oyadongha, Yenagoa

The Bayelsa State Police Command has arrested 23 suspects in connection with cult-related violence, attempted murder and unlawful possession of firearms in Yenagoa and its environs, recovering several weapons and suspected illicit substances.

The Commissioner of Police, Bayelsa State Command, CP Ajao Saka Adewale, disclosed this on Saturday during a press briefing at the command headquarters in Yenagoa.

Adewale said the arrests followed intelligence-driven operations and visibility patrols conducted between September 23 and October 8, 2026, in identified flashpoints, including Igbogene, Onopa, Ovom, Agudama, Amarata, Swali and Akenfa communities.

He said the operations were prompted by attacks and reprisals involving rival cult groups, which resulted in deaths and life-threatening injuries.

Giving details of the operations, the commissioner said operatives of the Anti-Cultism Unit arrested Tarimie James, 24, of Ovom community, near St. Anglican Church in the area.

According to him, James confessed in a video recording to being a member of the Icelanders Confraternity, while a locally fabricated Beretta pistol was recovered from him. He added that the suspect was on remand awaiting trial.

Adewale said Ezeikiel Joel, 24, of Igbogene community, was also arrested, with an automatic pump-action gun, other light weapons and a drum allegedly used during meetings recovered from him.

He said Joel confessed in a video recording to being a member of the Kue Klux Klan (KKK) Confraternity.

The commissioner further disclosed that the command’s Violent Crime Response Unit arrested five suspects on October 5 in connection with attacks and reprisals involving cult groups.

The suspects were identified as Zaidamun Paul, Anthony Okorie, Gods gift Angel, Richman Kudi and Victor Kelsy. Exhibits recovered from them included a Beretta pistol, axes, cutlasses and knives.

On October 6, operatives acting on intelligence recovered a locally made revolver pistol and three live 9mm ammunition at Igbogene.

Adewale said the suspect fled through a nearby swamp upon sighting the police, adding that efforts were ongoing to apprehend him.

He said eight more suspects were arrested between October 7 and 8 in Akenfa, Igbogene and Swali communities.

Among them was Baratua-Pre Bara, 30, from Ogbia Local Government Area, who allegedly confessed to being the number two member of the Icelanders Confraternity in Yenagoa. The commissioner said he would be arraigned on Monday, October 12, 2026.

Other suspects were identified as Funkuro Bereh, 25, from Ekeremor LGA; Kelvin Adamu, 28, of Igbogene community; Vincent Ikieye, 20, from Gbarain, Southern Ijaw LGA; Benjamin Akeno, 26, from Okpoma, Brass LGA; Esuaye Ikeclear, 30, a musician from Famgbe, Yenagoa LGA; Gift Torie, 23, from Ikolo community; and Job Simon, 32, a businessman from Gbarain, Southern Ijaw LGA.

Adewale said the suspects confessed to being members of the Bobos Confraternity, adding that some were scheduled for arraignment on Monday.

The commissioner said the command recovered firearms and other exhibits during the operations, including locally fabricated pistols, Beretta pistols, revolver pistols and an automatic pump-action gun.

Other items recovered were nine rounds of live 9mm ammunition, five cutlasses, two battle axes, a drum, two cans of nitrous oxide, also known as laughing gas, 17 bottles containing a codeine substance, a large bag of dried leaves suspected to be cannabis and 20 cartridges.

He said the activities of the cult groups had resulted in the deaths of four persons.

Adewale commended officers and men of the command, particularly personnel of the Doo Akpo Joint Task Force and other tactical teams, for their vigilance and commitment to the operations.

He also praised community stakeholders, including tricycle unions, the National Union of Road Transport Workers (NURTW) in Bayelsa State, traditional rulers, Community Development Committees and youth leaders across Yenagoa, for their cooperation with the police.

He said the arrests demonstrated the importance of collaboration between law enforcement agencies and residents in tackling crime.

“The Command will not allow criminals to dictate the atmosphere in our communities. We will pursue offenders within the bounds of the law, wherever they may seek refuge. We shall continue to deepen intelligence-driven policing, visibility patrols, and strengthen community partnerships,” Adewale said.

He urged residents to remain vigilant, provide timely and credible information to the police, and resist attempts by criminals and their collaborators to undermine peace in the state.

World.title: Arsenal hit back to beat Leeds and draw level with Man City
World.content:
Arsenal’s Brazilian midfielder #39 Bruno Guimarães (R) celebrates with fans after scoring the team’s second goal during the English Premier League football match between Arsenal and Leeds United at the Emirates Stadium in London on October 10, 2026. (Photo by Adrian Dennis / AFP) / RESTRICTED TO EDITORIAL USE. No use with unauthorized audio, video, data, fixture lists, club/league logos or ‘live’ services. Online in-match use limited to 120 images. An additional 40 images may be used in extra time. No video emulation. Social media in-match use limited to 120 images. An additional 40 images may be used in extra time. No use in betting publications, games or single club/league/player publications. /

Arsenal roared back to beat Leeds 2-1 and pull level with Manchester City at the top of the Premier League on Saturday, hitting the ground running after the three-week international break.

Mikel Arteta’s champions struggled to impose themselves against well-organised opponents in the first half but found their mojo after half-time to make it five wins from six games this season.

Defender James Justin gave Leeds a deserved lead early in the second half at the Emirates, silencing the home crowd in the October sunshine.

But Arsenal were level minutes later through Riccardo Calafiori, and substitute Bruno Guimaraes scored what turned out to be the winner after a finely crafted team goal.

The focus returned to the pitch on Saturday after the bombshell announcement that City had been found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules.

But Arsenal, who had a perfect record before their 3-0 defeat by Brighton last month, struggled to break down Daniel Farke’s physical team in the first half.

Noni Madueke, overlooked by Thomas Tuchel for England’s most recent squad, was handed a rare start on the left of the Gunners’ attack in place of the injured Christos Tzolis.

But neither he nor Bukayo Saka on the other flank had much joy against a defence that had conceded just three league goals all season.

Leeds had a couple of half-chances late in the first half.

First, Jayden Bogle and Anton Stach got in each other’s way as Stach struck the ball against his teammate, and Bogle was denied from close range by Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya, who was out quickly to smother his shot.

Then Raya got down smartly to keep out a shot from Leeds defender Gabriel Gudmundsson from a tight angle.

Arsenal managed just one shot on target in the whole of the first half but the game opened up after the break, with chances at both ends.

Impressive Leeds midfielder Ao Tanaka forced Raya to tip over before Justin put his side ahead in the 55th minute, finishing sweetly from just inside the box after a Gudmundsson cross following a well-worked move down the left.

Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhaes got a touch with his head but failed to keep the ball out of the net.

But the Gunners were back level just seven minutes later when the unmarked Calafiori finished past England international goalkeeper James Trafford after being set up by Ben White.

Worse was to come for Leeds when Guimaraes finished powerfully after some neat play down the Arsenal left, with Saka, Martin Odegaard and Declan Rice all involved.

The win takes Arsenal to 15 points, behind leaders City on goal difference.

Enzo Maresca’s City, with a game in hand, are braced for a hostile reception at Liverpool on Sunday following the announcement of their guilty verdict last week.

World.title: EKSU Chancellor Commends Ekiti Over Six Technical Colleges, Calls for Further Investment
World.content:
Gbenga Sodeinde in Ado Ekiti

The Chancellor of Ekiti State University (EKSU), Dr. Tunji Olowolafe, has commended the Ekiti State Government for establishing six technical colleges across the state, describing the initiative as a strategic investment capable of equipping young people with practical skills needed for the future economy.

Olowolafe, however, stressed that the initiative would require sustained investment in infrastructure, modern equipment, curriculum development and manpower to maximise its impact and meet the growing demand for technical education across the state.

He spoke while delivering the lead paper at the Ekiti at 30 Future Summit, where Governor Biodun Oyebanji declared that Ekiti must move beyond merely identifying its opportunities and begin translating them into tangible prosperity through innovation, technology and productivity.

Delivering the keynote address, Oyebanji said the state must embrace new approaches to knowledge, enterprise and development as it prepares for the next phase of its growth. He described the Ekiti Knowledge Zone as a landmark initiative capable of breaking international barriers in knowledge, technology and business, while positioning the state to compete more effectively in the global economy.

In his lecture entitled, “The Path to Ekiti’s Greatness: Opportunities, Choices, and Imperatives for the Next 30 Years,” Olowolafe also commended successive administrations, traditional rulers, community leaders and other stakeholders for their contributions to the development of Ekiti over the last three decades, particularly in the education sector.

The Are-Ekiti-born academic said the state’s longstanding reputation as a centre of educational excellence had given it a comparative advantage that should now be deliberately converted into technical skills, entrepreneurship, employment and sustainable wealth creation.

While acknowledging the establishment of six technical colleges by the state government, the EKSU Chancellor said the institutions should be expanded and strengthened to serve young people across the 16 local government areas.

He advocated the modernisation of their curricula, improved infrastructure, acquisition of contemporary equipment and sustained investment in manpower development to ensure that the colleges remained relevant to the demands of a rapidly changing global economy.

According to him, specialised training in areas such as solar installation, welding, fabrication, machinery maintenance, food processing and other technical trades would prepare young people for productive careers while reducing unemployment and creating wealth.

Olowolafe also advocated the engagement of master vocational instructors from countries renowned for technical education, including Switzerland, Germany, Canada and South Africa, to strengthen teaching capacity and expose students to international best practices.

“We must expand this capacity by modernising the curriculum and directly hiring master vocational instructors from nations with elite technical education systems, such as Switzerland, Germany, Canada and South Africa, to train our faculty and connect our colleges digitally to clients and employers everywhere,” he said.

The Pro-Chancellor of Miva Open University also pledged to partner with the state government to establish upgraded, modern and solar-powered ICT centres in the six government-owned technical colleges while supporting the introduction of foreign expertise into vocational education.

He further proposed strategic partnerships with leading international mining institutions to transform the Department of Geology of Ekiti State University into a world-class centre of excellence within the next five years.

Olowolafe said Ekiti’s educational advantage must now be complemented by deliberate investment in emerging technologies, identifying artificial intelligence, robotics, biotechnology, automation and renewable energy as sectors that would shape future economic growth.

He described the Ekiti Knowledge Zone as a transformational project capable of connecting technology entrepreneurs in the state to opportunities across the world.

According to him, the project, conceived under former Governor Kayode Fayemi and currently being implemented by Governor Oyebanji, would enable young innovators to establish globally competitive technology businesses without leaving Ekiti.

“On the digital side, the Ekiti Knowledge Zone is now under way. Conceived under former Governor Kayode Fayemi and being implemented by His Excellency, Governor Biodun Oyebanji, once complete, it will give our young people a place to build technology ventures without leaving Ekiti, serving clients in Lagos, London and Singapore, and bringing that income home to Ekiti. That is how education becomes wealth,” he said.

The renowned entrepreneur also identified reliable electricity as a critical driver of education, healthcare, manufacturing and small-scale enterprises.

He proposed the establishment of renewable-energy-powered microgrids across the state’s 177 wards to provide uninterrupted electricity for schools, hospitals, workshops and businesses, adding that collaboration with the Rural Electrification Agency would accelerate implementation.

He also challenged scientists, engineers and skilled artisans to develop solar-powered cocoa-drying equipment capable of modernising cocoa processing, increasing productivity and boosting foreign exchange earnings.

Olowolafe identified the Ekiti Agro-Allied International Cargo Airport as one of the state’s most strategic assets, describing it as evidence of the benefits of continuity in governance and long-term planning.

He, however, emphasised that improved road infrastructure would be essential to maximise the airport’s economic potential, facilitate industrial development and attract greater investment into the state.

The Chancellor also advocated stronger collaboration between government and communities in identifying and addressing local development priorities.

He cited the Gbemisola Olowolafe Memorial Community Secondary School in Are-Ekiti as an example of successful community-driven intervention, noting that plans were underway to transform the institution into a world-class secondary school with a capacity for 600 students and a curriculum built around science, technology, languages, arts and sports.

According to him, the adjoining GOMTECH ICT Centre is already providing training in artificial intelligence, coding, graphic design and Mandarin, thereby exposing young people to globally competitive digital skills.

Highlighting ongoing reforms at EKSU, Olowolafe said the university had launched Project Digi-Teach EKSU, an initiative aimed at equipping all 650 lecturers with digital teaching competencies.

“The same thinking drives our work at Ekiti State University, where His Excellency appointed me Chancellor in 2024. Through Project Digi-Teach EKSU, we are bringing all 650 lecturers to full digital teaching proficiency, and our Trading Room has grown into a Senate-approved diploma programme in financial markets,” he said.

He added that high-speed Starlink internet had also been deployed at 12 strategic locations across the university campus to enhance digital learning, research and innovation.

World.title: FRSC Cautions Commercial Vehicle Drivers Against Over Speeding On Federal Highways
World.content:
Segun Awofadeji in Bauchi

The Bauchi State Sector Commander of the Federal Roads Safety Corps (FRSC), CC Caleb Luka has appealed to drivers, particularly commercial vehicle drivers plying the ever-busy Bauchi-Jos highway to avoid over speeding in major highways in order to avoid crashes.

He made the appeal yesterday, while speaking with Journalists on the sideline of the 2026 International Customers’ Week celebration held at Yankari Express Hall, Bauchi.

“The challenges I’ve observed so far since I reported to Bauchi as Sector Commander is that drivers in Bauchi, especially the drivers driving along the Bauchi – Jos Road, are seriously over speeding and the best journey is to arrive destinations safely not so fast.”

He also observed that some tipper truck drivers within the town are careless in driving. So they should be cautious in driving within the town in order to avoid unnecessary crashes leading to death of innocent people who also have the right to use the roads.

He said that the traffic situation in Bauchi State is enormous because of the number of vehicles plying the road been the link State to three sub-regions of North-east, North-central and North-west.

” There is a very good road network that warrants a good driving culture in Bauchi State. So I will expect the drivers to take advantage of the good road network and the enlightenment to work in favour of the good driving environment that we have,” he said

Speaking on the Customer Service Week celebration, the Sector Commander Caleb Luka said, it is an international occasion that gives an opportunity for the Corps to interact with our customers. It also gives an opportunity for the Corps to strengthen our relationship with our stakeholders and customers generally.

World.title: Group Calls for Evidence-based Assessment of Surveillance Contracts for Pipelines in Niger Delta
World.content:
The Coalition of Civil Society Organisations for Good Governance (CCSOGG) has called for an evidence-based assessment of surveillance contracts for pipelines in the Niger Delta, as it called on stakeholders to avoid claims that are not verified, which are capable of undermining critical national security operations.

The coalition kicked against allegations surrounding the value and performance of

the Pipeline Infrastructure Nigeria Limited (PINL) and its Project Director, Osahon Okunbo, as it relates to the company’s pipeline surveillance contract.

A statement issued by the group’s spokesman, Comrade Declan Ihekaire, said legitimate questions about government contracts should be addressed through official documents and verifiable evidence rather than unsubstantiated claims.

According to the coalition, it has followed with serious concern the renewed controversy surrounding pipeline surveillance contracts in the Niger Delta, particularly the allegations being circulated against Pipeline Infrastructure Nigeria Limited (PINL) and its Project Director, Mr. Osahon Okunbo.

“We consider it necessary to speak at this time, not because legitimate questions about public contracts should be suppressed, but because public accountability must be based on facts, documents and verifiable evidence, not sensational allegations capable of damaging reputations, destabilising communities and undermining critical national security operations.

“The Coalition therefore rejects, in its entirety, the attempt to portray PINL and Mr. Osahon Okunbo as beneficiaries of some fictitious ₦2.7 trillion personal pipeline surveillance arrangement.

The group said further, “If there are questions about government expenditure, the appropriate response is for the relevant authorities to publish the contracts, payment schedules, scope of work and performance records and allow Nigerians to interrogate them. What is unacceptable is the circulation of figures without documentary evidence and the subsequent use of such figures to blackmail individuals”, the group said.

“We are particularly concerned that a figure of ₦2.7 trillion has been publicly associated with PINL and Mr. Osahon Okunbo.” It said.

“As at today, no credible documentary evidence has been publicly produced establishing that PINL receives ₦2.7 trillion annually for pipeline surveillance. Indeed, recent reports on the controversy have equally noted the absence of publicly presented contract or payment records supporting that allegation.

“The Coalition is therefore demanding a simple standard:

If the allegation is true, let the document be produced.

If it is not true, those responsible for spreading it must have the courage and responsibility to correct the record”, it said.

It is dangerous to casually attach such an enormous figure to a named individual, particularly when that individual is involved in a sensitive national security assignment. Such allegations can expose the person, his family, employees and communities associated with the operation to unnecessary hostility and security risks.

“We have also examined available information surrounding the PINL arrangement and wish to make clear that the figure being bandied about in the public space should not be confused with the actual value of the contract attributed to PINL.

“The Coalition’s understanding is that the PINL contract is in the region of ₦150 billion, and certainly not the ₦2.7 trillion figure being irresponsibly attributed to the company or its leadership. We challenge anyone who has documentary evidence to the contrary to publish it”, the coalition said.

It further noted that “This distinction is important because a government contract is not automatically the personal income of the individuals managing the company. A contract value covers personnel, equipment, logistics, security operations, technology, subcontractors, community engagement and other operational obligations.

“It is therefore intellectually dishonest to take a corporate contract figure, whatever it may be, and present it as money personally collected by an individual.”

The coalition said available information suggested that the figure being circulated should not be confused with the actual value of the contract attributed to PINL, which it put at about N150 billion.

It stressed, however, that contract values should not be equated with personal income, noting that such agreements typically cover personnel, equipment, logistics, security operations, technology, community engagement and other operational expenses.

The group urged the federal government and relevant agencies to assess pipeline surveillance contractors based on measurable performance, including reduction in vandalism, protection of crude oil production, community relations, technology deployment and value for money.

It said PINL is responsible for surveillance operations along the Eastern Corridor of the Trans Niger Pipeline, covering parts of Rivers, Bayelsa, Abia and Imo states.

The coalition cited figures attributed to the company indicating a significant reduction in pipeline infractions and vandalism attempts compared with previous years.

It also referred to reports by PINL that there had been no reported pipeline vandalism on sections of the Trans Niger Pipeline in Bayelsa and the wider corridor during a period under review, attributing the development to collaboration among the company, security agencies and host communities.

The group said such claims should be independently assessed by relevant government authorities.

It also highlighted the reported involvement of traditional rulers, youth leaders, women and other community stakeholders in pipeline surveillance activities.

According to the coalition, PINL’s operations cover about 215 communities along the Eastern Corridor, while the company has also reported engaging thousands of youths in surveillance and related activities.

The group said community participation was important to the protection of oil and gas infrastructure, particularly in areas characterised by difficult terrain and extensive waterways.

The coalition also commended the reported deployment of technology in pipeline surveillance, including drones, surveillance stations, security vessels, mobile response units and round-the-clock monitoring.

It said Nigeria needed to strengthen the use of technology and intelligence alongside conventional security arrangements to protect critical oil and gas infrastructure.

The coalition further urged the federal government to conduct independent assessments of all contractors before deciding whether existing arrangements should be retained, reviewed or expanded.

World.title: Ogun 2027: Everywhere You Go, It’s Yayi
World.content:
Femi Ogbonnikan

In the unfolding political contest for Ogun State, Senator Solomon Olamilekan Adeola of the All Progressives Congress (APC), popularly known as Yayi, appears to be building his campaign around a simple but compelling message: “Yayi ni, Yayi ni jọ̀ọ́.”

Beyond its catchy rhythm, the slogan projects confidence, reinforces his political identity and seeks to communicate a sense of widespread acceptance.

From okada riders and transport union members to traders, artisans, professionals and civil servants, the campaign message is designed to resonate across different segments of the state.

Yet beyond the excitement surrounding the slogan lies a more fundamental question: what has Yayi done to earn the goodwill he is banking on as he positions himself for the governorship? For a politician seeking to govern a state as politically conscious, enlightened and economically diverse as Ogun, goodwill is rarely built on slogans alone.

It grows from relationships, accessibility, perceived performance and the ability to demonstrate that political influence can translate into tangible benefits for the people.

In Adeola’s case, his legislative journey, political network and growing visibility in Ogun State constitute important elements of his appeal, but it is his record on the ground that gives weight to the chant.

Adeola’s political career has taken him through the Lagos State House of Assembly and the House of Representatives before his election to the Senate, where he represents Ogun West Senatorial District.

This experience across different legislative levels provides him with an understanding of lawmaking, public finance, constituency representation and the workings of government.

For his supporters, that background is an important qualification for a governorship contest that will demand not only political leadership but also administrative competence and the capacity to navigate competing interests.

Perhaps the most significant institutional advantage he brings to the political equation is his position as chairman of the Senate Committee on Appropriations.

The committee occupies a pivotal place in Nigeria’s budgetary process, overseeing the consideration of the federal budget and playing a major role in scrutinising proposed expenditure and coordinating legislative work on appropriations.

At a time when public resources are stretched and the demand for development continues to rise, that experience is critical because budgeting determines how public funds are allocated among infrastructure, education, healthcare, security and other priorities.

For Ogun State, Adeola’s familiarity with federal budget negotiations and public expenditure provides a platform from which he could advocate for projects and initiatives that benefit the state, while also helping him understand the relationship between federal allocations, state finances and the practical demands of development planning.

However, the real measure of effective representation must ultimately be found in verifiable outcomes, and this is where the Yayi narrative moves from politics to evidence.

In just over three years as Senator for Ogun West, Adeola has facilitated what independent observers describe as an infrastructure revolution.

Speaking at the Iganmode Cultural Festival in Ota in December 2025, he disclosed that about 300 projects had been completed across the district, a figure that has continued to grow.

The breakdown is revealing and touches every critical sector. It includes over 115 road construction and rehabilitation projects, 30 school buildings comprising more than 150 new classrooms, 32 primary healthcare centres, two intensive care units, 25 modern markets including the landmark Agbara and Igbesa Ultramodern Markets and the Obada Ultramodern Market in Imeko-Afon, 13 town halls including the Omidokun Ultra Modern Hall in Ayetoro, 10 ICT centres, two libraries and eight police stations including the Idiroko border station to strengthen security in border communities.

Strategic corridors that had been abandoned for decades have been opened, including the Imasayi-Ayetoro Road, the Ilashe-Koko-Alari Road, the Ilara-Ilashe 25-kilometre border corridor linking agrarian communities to markets, the Ilaro-Owode Road, the Atan-Agbara Road, the Kajola and Iboro network, Baba Emili Road in Ilaro, Isale Araba Road, Ebute Igbooro Road and Palace Roads in Imeko and Afon. These are not just projects; they are responses to the systemic neglect that Ogun West had suffered for over 50 years, where dilapidated roads and institutional abandonment were the norm.

In the power sector, his intervention has been equally deliberate. Over 200 electric transformers have been donated and installed, 250 solar streetlight projects comprising about 26,000 poles have been deployed, and personal intervention to repair 10 major electricity infrastructures affecting about 100 communities, including the Ilaro to Ibeshe 33KV line, has restored hope to businesses and households.

In early 2026, to mark his 56th birthday, he donated transformers to Ijebu Imushin, Ishagunse and Itele in Ogun East, signalling an expansion of his developmental reach beyond Ogun West and demonstrating a statewide outlook that is crucial for a governorship ambition.His approach to representation goes beyond concrete and mortar.

Constituency representation also involves maintaining contact, identifying needs and ensuring communities do not feel abandoned after elections, and Adeola’s empowerment architecture is perhaps his most direct connection with the people.

The flagship is the “Oloja Yayi” Market Support Fund. What started on February 6, 2023, with N25,000 grants to 5,000 traders during his Senate campaign has evolved into a statewide micro-financing scheme in partnership with the National Productivity Centre.

On January 28, 2024, another 5,000 traders across the five local governments of Ogun West received N50,000 each. By April 27, 2025, the grant had been increased to N75,000. In July 2026, 4,000 traders in Ogun West received N75,000 each at the Asade Agunloye Pavilion, Ilaro, after similar exercises for 3,000 traders in Ogun Central at Ake Palace, Abeokuta, and thousands in Ogun East in Ijebu-Ode, thereby covering all three senatorial districts. Cumulatively, over 15,000 market men and women have benefited from direct grants, while over 50,000 constituents have been empowered through skill acquisition, equipment support and cash grants.

This is designed to complement Governor Dapo Abiodun’s “Okowo Dapo” and the Federal Government’s TraderMoni schemes, but with larger ticket sizes that protect traders from loan sharks and help them restock in an era of high inflation. In agriculture, where Ogun West serves as the food basket of the state, about 6,000 farmers have received support including tractors, power tillers, improved seedlings and N100,000 cash grants per farmer, while artisans across the district have received tricycles, mini-buses, grinding machines, sewing machines and vulcanizing machines that translate directly into daily income.

Beyond markets and roads, human capital development has been central to his model.

In education, apart from the more than 150 classrooms across 25 locations including 12-classroom blocks at Ansar Ur Deen Primary School, Igbogila and Technical College, Joga-Orile, Ayetoro, his most monumental intervention is legislative and structural, playing a pivotal role in the transition of the Federal Polytechnic, Ilaro, into a Federal University of Technology, thereby giving Ogun West its first federal university and expanding access to higher education for thousands of young people.

He has also instituted a N200 million scholarship and bursary scheme for over 1,600 tertiary students across Ogun State, easing tuition pressure for families affected by subsidy removal and ensuring that financial constraints do not cut short academic dreams. The 10 ICT centres he facilitated are equipped to train young people for digital jobs, while mini-stadiums and vocational centres provide platforms for skills acquisition and sports development.

In healthcare, the 32 primary healthcare centres and two ICUs are complemented by free medical outreaches, health insurance enrolment for vulnerable constituents and upgrading of internal roads in state hospitals in Ilaro and Imeko, bringing care closer to those who need it most.

This blend of philanthropy and development, from scholarships to health support, reinforces the perception of accessibility and responsiveness that underpins the Yayi brand.

Nevertheless, the distinction must be made between holding an influential legislative office and demonstrating the capacity to govern.

A senator’s role in federal appropriations is different from a governor’s responsibility for managing a state’s finances, supervising the civil service, implementing policies and delivering public services.

Adeola’s next level challenge, therefore, is to show how his legislative experience and constituency model can translate into an effective, transparent and people-centred administration for all of Ogun.

Political goodwill remains an important currency in Ogun’s governorship race, and Adeola’s campaign slogan seeks to turn name recognition into a broader movement, presenting him as a candidate whose appeal extends beyond established political circles.

His immediate concern is to sustain that appeal across Ogun West, Ogun Central and Ogun East, while addressing the distinct expectations of communities across the three senatorial districts. What is clear, however, is that “Yayi ni Jọ̀ọ́” did not emerge from a billboard.

It emerged from markets where traders have received grants, from communities where transformers now hum after years of darkness, from roads where dusty tracks became asphalt, and from classrooms where children now sit under new roofs.

Ultimately, the Yayi project will be judged not simply by the volume of campaign enthusiasm it generates but by the strength of its policy agenda, the credibility of its promises and the evidence supporting its record.

His legislative experience, his strategic position as Chairman of the Senate Committee on Appropriations, his infrastructure footprint spanning roads, power, health and education, and his empowerment and philanthropy touching over 50,000 lives provide a foundation on which he can build his case.

For Ogun State, the stakes in 2027 go beyond slogans and sentiment.

The state needs a leader who understands its diversity, who can balance the industrial power of Ogun Central and Ogun East with the developmental yearnings of Ogun West, and who can convert federal leverage into state advantage.

Adeola’s trajectory suggests he has built more than name recognition; he has built a political economy of goodwill anchored on visible projects, direct empowerment and sustained presence.

From roads that reconnect farm settlements to markets, to transformers that revive small businesses, to grants that keep traders afloat and scholarships that keep students in school, his interventions speak to a model that prioritizes people over rhetoric.

Yet the governorship demands more than constituency touchpoints. It demands a statewide blueprint for industrial growth, for agro-processing, for youth employment, for healthcare and for fiscal discipline. If Yayi can translate the momentum of “Yayi ni jọ̀ọ́” into a coherent agenda that assures every part of Ogun that their interests will be protected and their potential unlocked, then the goodwill he has banked may indeed become the capital that delivers the Government House.

The slogan has done its job of opening ears. What remains is to present the plan that will win hearts and secure the future.

*Ogbonnikan writes from Okeagbede, in Imeko-Afon LGA of Ogun state.

World.title: Aiyedatiwa’s Education Award: When Destiny Comes Full Circle
World.content:
By Olukayode Ajulo

Yesterday, as I watched Governor Lucky Orimisan Aiyedatiwa receive a national award for his contribution to education, I found myself reflecting on the remarkable journey that brought him to that moment. For me, it was more than an award. It was a moment of destiny coming full circle. I remember, with some disbelief, when questions were raised in certain political quarters about the Governor’s educational qualifications. As his Attorney-General, I found the insinuations particularly surprising.

Public officers are, of course, subject to scrutiny. But I knew there was a much deeper story behind the certificates, a story of humble beginnings, perseverance, learning, work, service and faith. I had heard that story from the Governor himself, and on occasions, quite emotionally. He spoke of his humble beginnings in the riverine community of Obe-Nla; his unplanned journey to Lagos; his education at the Jakande school; his studies at the College of Education, Ijanikin; and how that journey eventually led him into the classroom as a teacher. It was not a story fashioned retrospectively to fit the office he occupies today. It was a life actually lived.

Then came the controversy. What had been made to appear complicated was resolved by something remarkably simple: a scratch card and the WAEC verification platform. The records spoke for themselves. But something far more powerful happened afterwards. His former classmates and, more profoundly, his former students, rallied around him. They came to see their teacher.

Men and women who had once sat before him in a classroom returned years later to testify to the man who had taught them, encouraged them and helped shape their lives.

I listened to them. I watched their emotions. I heard their testimonies, not merely about his competence or erudition, but about his character, his humanity and, above all, his faith in God. It was from those encounters that I began calling him “Bro Lucky.”

That moment remains with me. For there are forms of evidence that no certificate can fully capture. The testimony of those whose lives one has touched is one of them. A teacher may leave the classroom, but he never truly leaves the lives of his students. That, perhaps more than anything else, is why yesterday’s recognition moved me deeply.

Here was a man who once stood before a classroom as a teacher being honoured by the nation’s education establishment for his contribution to education. There was something almost poetic about it. The teacher had returned to the classroom, not this time as a teacher, but as a Governor being recognised for helping to shape the future of education. The honour therefore transcends the individual. It speaks to a larger truth about public service: sometimes, the journey of a man’s life becomes the most compelling testimony to his character.

Governor Aiyedatiwa’s journey has taken him from a modest beginning and the classroom through professional life, public service and ultimately to the highest elective office in Ondo State. Yet education has remained a constant thread. As Governor, he has shown that his commitment to education is not merely rhetorical. He has treated it as a strategic investment in the future of our State, understanding that the strength of any society is ultimately measured by what it does with the minds and potential of its young.

I saw this commitment even in the care with which he chose his Commissioner for Education. He would not politicise the portfolio or treat it as another appointment to be dispensed as patronage. He insisted on a tested professional and seasoned administrator, Professor Igbekele Ajibefun, a former Rector and Vice-Chancellor. That decision spoke volumes about his priorities.

His administration has recruited over 2,100 teachers, constructed 43 new classroom blocks, renovated 75 schools and provided furniture and learning materials across the State.

It committed millions of Naira towards the 2026 WAEC registration fees of 23,048 public-school students, sponsored NABTEB examinations and continued interventions in bursaries, scholarships, teacher development and educational infrastructure. These are not merely budgetary figures because, behind every figure is a child, behind every classroom is a future, and behind every examination fee paid is a young person whose opportunity to advance may otherwise have been lost. In the end, these numbers are really about lives.

Education is the bridge between the circumstances into which a child is born and the possibilities that child may ultimately attain. Perhaps that is why the Governor’s personal history as a teacher matters so much. A man who has stood before a classroom understands that every child represents an unfinished story. He knows that behind a school uniform is a future doctor, lawyer, engineer, teacher, scientist, entrepreneur or public servant. And sometimes, the difference between potential and achievement is simply a teacher who refuses to give up on a child, or a government that refuses to give up on education.

The education that gave a young Lucky Aiyedatiwa the foundation upon which he built his life eventually led him into the teaching profession. Decades later, that same former teacher now occupies a position from which he can influence the educational destiny of an entire generation. This is why I regard yesterday’s honour as more than a ceremonial recognition. It was a reminder of how a personal experience can become a public responsibility.

And perhaps the most beautiful part of the story is that those who once called him “Teacher” never forgot, they came back. When his credentials were questioned, they did not need political appointments, official positions or government machinery to speak for him. They simply testified: “This man taught us.”

And yesterday, the nation gave its own testimony. It was therefore a great moment, not only for Governor Aiyedatiwa, but for every teacher who has ever wondered, where lies their reward? And whether the lives they touch will remember them; for every child who has been told that their circumstances define their destiny; and for every public servant who believes that, ultimately, service should speak louder than noise.

Governor Aiyedatiwa’s story is a reminder that destiny does not always announce itself at the beginning. Sometimes it begins quietly, in a classroom; sometimes it takes an unexpected turn to Lagos, through professional life and public service; sometimes it is questioned, sometimes it is misunderstood. But when the foundation is real, time has a way of revealing the truth. Yesterday, that journey received a national acknowledgement.

And as his Chief Legal Adviser, privileged to have heard him personally recount that journey, I watched with a profound sense of satisfaction and, I must confess, emotion. For a man who once taught others to be honoured by the nation for advancing education is not merely an award. It is a circle completed. It is a reminder that the seeds planted in a classroom can, decades later, grow into institutions, policies and opportunities for an entire generation.

For Governor Lucky Orimisan Aiyedatiwa, yesterday was one of those rare moments when a man can pause, look back upon the road travelled and recognise that, through all its twists and turns, destiny was quietly preparing him for this moment.

Congratulations, Your Excellency. May this honour inspire even greater service to the children and young people of Ondo State. And may history remember not only that a teacher became Governor, but that the teacher in the Governor never left.

*Dr. Ajulo, SAN, OON, is the Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Ondo State.

World.title: FRC, Housing Ministry Fret over Poor Pace of Work at Delta Renewed Hope Housing Project
World.content:
Ndubuisi Francis in Abuja

The Fiscal Responsibility Commission (FRC) and the Federal Ministry of Housing and Urban Development have expressed concern over the slow pace and quality of work at the Renewed Hope Affordable Housing Programme (RHAHP) project located in the Asaba-Uvwie-Ekpan axis of Delta State.

The concern was raised when the FRC South-South Verification Team on Selected Federal Government Projects inspected the 96-unit housing project as part of its ongoing physical verification exercise across the South-south region.

During the inspection, the team observed that only four of the 96 housing units were nearing completion, while several aspects of the project, including roofing and other infrastructure, remained either incomplete or unattended to.

The Team Lead and Head of the Strategic Communications Directorate of the FRC, Mr. Bede Ogueri Anyanwu, expressed concern over the quality and pace of work at the site.

According to him, the Renewed Hope Affordable Housing Programme was conceived as part of the federal government’s efforts to improve living conditions and expand access to affordable housing and other essential services for Nigerians.

He noted that the level of work observed at the site did not reflect the objectives of the programme, stressing the need for contractors to return to the site and complete their respective assignments to the required standards.

Anyanwu specifically called for M/s Goodnews Creative Ideas Limited and M/s First Class Capital Project Limited to return to the site and address outstanding works, particularly the roofing of the buildings.

The verification team observed that wind had already damaged some of the roofing sheets used on completed sections of the buildings, raising concerns about the quality and durability of the materials and workmanship.

The team also sought explanations for the non-commencement of several components of the project, despite the contracts reportedly having been awarded since 2024.

The affected contractors and consultants include M/s Gozcon Investment, responsible for electricity works; M/s Blue Sea Investment Limited, handling road and drainage infrastructure; M/s Goodnews Creative Ideas Limited, also handling road and drainage works; and M/s Ecosphere Consulting Limited, engaged as consultant for the Environmental and Social Impact Assessment of the Renewed Hope Estate project in Delta State.

The representative of the Controller, Federal Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, Delta State, Uche Nwati, was invited to provide clarification on the status of the project and the reasons for the limited progress recorded.

Nwati attributed some of the challenges to what he described as inadequate feasibility studies conducted before the contracts were awarded. He also expressed dissatisfaction with the level of work executed at the project site.

The FRC verification team stressed the importance of ensuring that contractors engaged for Federal Government projects deliver according to approved specifications, timelines and quality standards, particularly on projects designed to provide critical social infrastructure to Nigerians.

FRC is currently undergoing physical verification of select federal government projects across the South-South geopolitical zone, aimed at assessing project implementation, value for money and compliance with approved standards and specifications.

World.title: Politicians and Amupitan’s 103 Million Voter Register
World.content:
By Mobolaji Sanusi

“It’s not the voting that’s democracy; it’s the counting.”

—-Tom Stoppard(1937-2005).

The first ballot of the 2027 general election is now less than 100 days away, and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) is using every opportunity to restate its preparedness to organise a credible election next year.

On two separate occasions this week — at the strategic workshop organised in collaboration with the Nigerian Guild of Editors and at the World Press Conference it convened, its Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan, personally reiterated to a listening audience and a sceptical public the Commission’s readiness for the polls. A credible election, and nothing less, is all that millions of Nigerians expect from the INEC helmsman in what is his first major assignment.

Organising general elections in a diversely multi-ethnic and multi-religious country of over 220 million people like ours cannot be described as a tea party. A cursory look at INEC’s released operational data confirms this. The Commission’s operations cover 176,846 polling units, 8,838 Registration Area Centres in 36 states plus the FCT, and 774 local government offices across the country. Its other logistical requirements include 57,000 new Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) devices and more than 100,000 vehicles and 4,000 boats for the movement of personnel and election materials.

This looks herculean but not insurmountable with steady preparation and sincerity of purpose on the part of the Commission’s leadership. With less than 100 days to the first ballot, Amupitan, during his global media briefing, assured the nation and the international community of INEC’s “total commitment to neutrality, operational excellence, and the sacred integrity of the ballot box.”

His voice is loud enough to be heard, and until his promise becomes reality, it is only fair to give him the benefit of the doubt.

But a particular aspect of Amupitan’s speech that caught yours sincerely’s attention was his revelation that the national voter register now stands at 103,428,715. According to him, this follows the completion of the three phases of the Continuous Voter Registration (CVR) exercise, which produced an additional 10,772,421 fresh registrations. This could cautiously be interpreted as a reflection of Nigerians’ commitment to performing their civic responsibility in 2027, even though the reality of the 2023 elections suggests otherwise.

Expectedly, Lagos, the former federal capital, leads with 7,488,633 registered voters, followed by Kano with 6,570,276 and Kaduna with 4,662,640. Katsina has 3,876,051 voters, Rivers has 3,736,434, Oyo has 3,588,111, Delta has 3,525,988, Benue has 3,057,225, Ogun has 3,037,981 and Bauchi has 3,012,547.

At the bottom of the table are Ekiti, Bayelsa and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) with 1,055,708, 1,200,691 and 1,732,043 voters, respectively. The demographic breakdown shows that male voters constitute 53.53 million, representing 51.75 percent, while female voters account for 49.90 million, representing 48.25 percent. Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) captured in the register, according to INEC, amount to 232,658.

Obviously, these top ten states with the highest voter registration will remain the focal points of the battle for votes between the ruling and opposition parties. Curiously, five of the ten are from the northern part of the country, and the implication of this cannot be lost on the politically discerning. Also, Lagos leading other states in voter numbers is a reminder that the 2006 national population census is now obsolete, while also bringing to the fore the long-overdue call to accord the Centre of Excellence a special status in the federation.

The significant role of a credible voter register in any election cannot be ignored, which is why yours sincerely is particularly interested in it. A well-prepared voter register serves as a verification instrument for identifying eligible voters in order to prevent multiple voting or impersonation on election day. It also helps political parties to establish eligibility for nomination and to maintain a credible membership register. It further aids in the determination of polling unit locations, among other things. In view of all this, one would presuppose that INEC, before announcing the voter registration figures, must have done the requisite due diligence that is the hallmark of a credible register. Amupitan should not be found wanting in this regard.

More importantly, it is necessary to interrogate why, despite high voter registration figures, turnout on election day has hitherto remained particularly low. For instance, the 2023 register had 93.5 million voters, but turnout was put at 27 percent, believed to be the lowest ever recorded for a presidential election in this Fourth Republic. President Bola Tinubu, GCFR, of the All Progressives Congress (APC), who won the election, polled 8,794,726 votes, or 36.61 percent of the total votes cast. Atiku Abubakar of the PDP polled 6,984,520 votes, or 29.07 percent, while Peter Obi of the Labour Party scored 6,101,533 votes, or 25.4 percent. Rabiu Kwankwaso of the NNPP scored 1,496,687 votes, representing 6.23 percent of the total votes cast.

This low turnout might not be unconnected to the shenanigans that preceded the 2023 elections, where foot soldiers of former President Muhammadu Buhari did everything to frustrate the wishes of eligible voters by creating serious socio-economic distortions with dire consequences.

Even in 2015, total voter turnout was 43.65 percent. That year, according to INEC, there were 68,833,476 registered voters.

Muhammadu Buhari scored 15,424,921 votes, amounting to 53.96 percent, while Goodluck Jonathan scored 12,853,162 votes, amounting to 44.96 percent. This result was achieved largely because opposition parties came together to wrest power from the then-ruling PDP under President Jonathan. Genuine voter interest was evident in the declared results. Can we expect a re-enactment of this in 2027? This is seriously in doubt because most eligible Nigerians believe that their votes will not count. Nigerians are also more concerned about how to weather the storm of economic hardship currently ravaging the country today.

Hitherto, electoral records show that the highest voter turnout of 69.1 percent recorded during former President Olusegun Obasanjo’s second-term re-election in April 2003 cannot be relied upon because the election itself, conducted under Professor Maurice Iwu as INEC Chairman, was replete with rigging, violence and electoral fraud. Obasanjo’s handpicked successor, the late President Umaru Musa Yar’Adua, failed the same electoral integrity test in 2007. Yar’Adua was adjudged to have recorded a similar 69.1 percent turnout — a result that he himself publicly acknowledged to be flawed. So, those two records are highly unreliable and discredited.

The high voter registration figures recorded by INEC under Amupitan are quite inspiring, but will they translate into massive turnout on election day? Will eligible Nigerians turn out in large numbers to let their votes speak for them? The turnout at political rallies, campaigns and marches has proved unreliable, judging by antecedents. We have seen several instances across the federation of orchestrated five-million-man marches for different high-profile candidates that evaporated to less than 500,000 votes on election day.

This same time-wasting political strategy by top politicians and their supporters has led to the wastage of hundreds of millions of naira through hiring crowds for such misleading rallies, marches and campaigns, only to fall flat in securing anticipated votes on election day. Some of these politicians are already enmeshed in such costly but unnecessary political marketing at the moment. These politicians and their supporters learn nothing from history.

Yiaga Africa’s National Voting Intentions Survey, NVIS 3.0, in its recently released report titled: “Willing but Wary: How Nigerians Intend to Vote in 2027,” gave this issue a scientific dimension. It indicated that Nigerians willing to vote have only a vague commitment, with the proportion of those “very likely” to vote dropping from 52% to 47%. It further stated clearly that only 41% are likely to vote and are very certain of their choice. If this report is indeed true, it already makes mincemeat of the freshly compiled INEC voter register regarding voter turnout. Indeed, the voters’ test of will lies ahead as the 2027 general election draws closer.

The final questions: Come 2027, can the genuine over-50 percent voter turnout of 2015 be replicated? If the coming together of the opposition 11 years ago made it possible, can the mass defection of governors to the ruling APC re-enact that credible 2015 turnout feat? Are the defectors sincere with the ruling party or just seeking temporary political refuge from the EFCC nightmare? The answer to especially the second question is complicated because the circumstances of the two periods are not the same. I rest my case for this week.

•Sanusi, former MD/CEO of Lagos State Signage and  Agency, is currently Managing Partner at AMS RELIABLE SOLICITORS. (WhatsApp only: 07011117777).

World.title: Fuel Price Discount: Atiku Asks FG, ‘What Happens on Day 31?’
World.content:
*Says Tinubu wrongly copied policy he once mocked

*Keyamo: Former VP’s attack on president sign of political depression

*Oyedele insists 30-day discount is commercial decision, not subsidy



*Declares politicians using populism to move country in wrong direction

Chuks Okocha, Ndubuisi Francis, Linus Aleke in Abuja, Chinedu Eze, Peter Uzoho and Dike Onwuamaeze in Lagos

Former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar has challenged the federal government to explain what will happen after the expiration of its 30-day petrol price discount, accusing President Bola Tinubu of adopting his proposed petroleum pricing policy but stripping it of the measures he said were necessary to deliver lasting relief to Nigerians.



Atiku raised the question while inaugurating the African Democratic Congress (ADC) Presidential Campaign Council ahead of the 2027 general election, arguing that a temporary reduction in petrol prices would not address the persistent pressure on households, transport operators and businesses. He said the President embraced his policy prescription that the government once mocked.



The former vice-president insisted that his proposed production subsidy was designed as a lasting, targeted intervention to support locally refined petroleum products and lower fuel costs, unlike the government’s 30-day discount at Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) retail outlets.
