World.title: Liberia: The Mark Quiah PUzzle: Named in Drug Indictment, Missing From All 11 Counts
World.content:
MONROVIA – For months, Mark Egon Kuiah’s name has hovered over Liberia’s cocaine scandal without ever quite landing.

By Rodney D Sieh

He ran operations at Roberts International Airport, the country’s main gateway, where 198 plates of cocaine were found in June hidden in cargo declared as Maggi cubes and lappas. That seizure, valued at more than US$19 million, opened the first of this year’s drug cases. Weeks later, President Joseph Boakai dismissed Kuiah “with immediate effect” in a July 30 purge of security officials.



Now, the State has named him a defendant in its 55-page indictment in the far larger US$317 million case. But a FrontPageAfrica review of the document shows an unusual gap. Each of the 11 counts opens by listing the defendants it accuses. Kuiah’s name is in none of those lists, even though eight counts describe what he allegedly did.

What the indictment says he did

The State’s account of Kuiah is short and repeated almost word for word across eight counts. Caycee Nelson, the man prosecutors say managed the cartel’s front airline, “Afri-Connect Airlines,” recruited him. Kuiah allegedly asked for US$250,000 to help the operation through the airport and received US$50,000 up front. He was given two phones “for communication.”

He is also said to have recruited two aviation colleagues: F. Augustine Claudius Tamba, Deputy Director General of the Liberia Civil Aviation Authority, and Abner Wanah Yonly, Sr., manager of James Spriggs Payne Airfield. The indictment adds, in one paragraph, that the two “did not provide any support.” Neither is charged.

The State says Kuiah “knew and had reasons to know” the cartel planned to move cocaine through Liberia to Europe, and “accepted to provide the required assistance.”

What it does not say

The indictment never describes a single thing Kuiah did at the airport for the cartel. The cartel’s aircraft, bought in August 2025, landed at Spriggs Payne, not at Roberts International. The indictment does not allege it ever carried drugs. The cocaine seized at Cement Road, by the State’s own account, came in by sea and canoe up the Po River.

The sums are muddled too. One paragraph says Nelson handed Kuiah the US$50,000. The money-laundering count says it was paid by Jammel V. Jallah, through Christian L. Nyantee.

Even his job shifts. The caption calls him a former Deputy Director of Operations at the Civil Aviation Authority. Other paragraphs place him at Roberts International Airport. One calls him “Deputy Manager for Operations.” His name is spelled both Quiah and Kuiah. Government statements at the time of his dismissal described him as Deputy Director for Operations at RIA.

Then there is the charging language itself. Each count opens with a list of the defendants the grand jury finds probable cause against. Nikola Ivancic, Jewel Howard Taylor, Gerald Folley Smith, and others appear there, count after count. Kuiah’s name does not appear in any of those lists.

A defendant the counts leave out

Kuiah is a defendant. The caption names him, General Allegation 18 calls him “The Defendant Mark Quiah,” and the October 7 writ from Criminal Court “C” orders his arrest. The indictment’s closing clause applies to all the “hereinabove named defendants.”

But each count is meant to tell a defendant exactly what he is accused of. Here, eight counts describe Kuiah’s conduct while leaving him off the list of those the grand jury finds committed the offence. Defense lawyers can be expected to argue that he was indicted without being clearly charged in any count, and to seek to quash on that ground. Prosecutors are likely to answer that the caption, the general allegations and the closing clause are enough to put him on notice.

Whether the omission is a drafting slip, like the other errors FrontPageAfrica has documented in the indictment, or something more deliberate is an open question. It comes after weeks of talk that Kuiah has been helping investigators. In August, FrontPageAfrica reported that he had been giving investigators a considerable amount of information since his dismissal, and that he had not been arrested.

The Ministry of Justice has not said publicly whether Kuiah is a cooperating witness. He is not among the witnesses listed in the indictment, which names only three police officers and “documentary evidence.” FrontPageAfrica could not confirm whether he has been taken into custody since the writ was issued.

Kuiah’s July 29 appearance on an earlier police charge sheet followed a similar pattern. That document described a “Mark Quiah” as a friend brought in to help with aircraft operations in 2024. It did not list him among its 12 defendants.

The letter not in the file

One episode is absent from the indictment altogether. On July 13, while still at the airport, Kuiah signed a letter to the Liberia Maritime Authority as “registered agent” for Madris Group of Companies Incorporated. It asked that a cargo ship, the Comoros-flagged IB Atlantic IV, be allowed into the Freeport of Monrovia because it was “in distress at sea due to loss of engine performance.”

The Maritime Authority declined. The ship was later pursued by Liberian forces off Rivercess, amid unconfirmed reports that a smaller boat had approached it at sea. No link between the letter and any crime has been established, and Kuiah has not been charged over it.

The indictment makes no mention of the letter, the ship or Madris Group.

Kuiah has not commented publicly. He is presumed innocent, as are all those named in the indictment.

The bar owner who disappeared from the case

If Kuiah is a defendant, the counts leave out George Wah Harris, a man the government charged who is missing altogether.

Harris, also known as Leroy Harris, owns Private Bar Entertainment Center in Paynesville. In early August, the government announced at a Ministry of Information briefing that he had been charged in the US$317 million cocaine probe. The listed offences were possession, importation, trafficking, economic sabotage, money laundering, conspiracy, facilitation and solicitation.

Security forces searched his bar three times. Management said they found nothing illegal on any occasion. Harris was arraigned at the Monrovia City Court and sent to Monrovia Central Prison. On August 13, the Bureau of Corrections said he was still there and had been granted no judicial relief.

Yet the October 7 indictment in the US$317 million case does not mention Harris anywhere. Not in the caption, not in the counts, not in the narrative.

Instead, Harris turned up in the other case. On August 27, Criminal Court “C” issued a writ in the June airport seizure, the 198 plates found at Roberts International Airport. That indictment accuses Harris of offering US$100,000 to two Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency officers at the airport to recover the seized cocaine. It says he handed US$5,000 to one of them, Moses Jallah, at his bar.

The shift raises a question the government has not answered. Did investigators drop their claim that Harris was tied to the US$317 million haul, or is a separate charge still to come?

Readers should not confuse two other names in the new indictment. “Harris Ward” is a community in Royesville Township where prosecutors say the cocaine was stored, not a person. And the bar the indictment does mention is Private Bar in Paynesville, where the cartel allegedly held an introductory meeting for its airline. A man named there as the airline’s “Ground Handler,” Franklin Harberg (also spelled Herbert and Harbert), is not charged either.

One airport, two gaps

The two names point to the same weakness. Roberts International Airport sits at the center of Liberia’s drug crisis this year. It was the site of the June seizure, and it is the airport the cartel allegedly paid an insider to smooth its path through.

Yet in the case that names the airport’s own operations chief as a defendant, the counts themselves leave him out. And in that same case, a man the government publicly charged in August does not appear at all.

World.title: Liberia: Former Vice President Howard-Taylor among 19 indicted, six Defendants currently held at Monrovia Central Prison
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia’s most prominent drug trafficking and money laundering prosecution entered a new phase this week as several defendants, including a former senior security official, were arrested and sent to the Monrovia Central Prison to await trial.

By Willie N. Tokpah

The arrests followed a writ issued on October 7, 2026, by Criminal Court “C” at the Temple of Justice, ordering Montserrado County Sheriff Major Austine Seinavula, or his deputy, to arrest the 19 defendants named in a grand jury indictment and bring them “forthwith” before the court. Former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor is among those defendants.



Who is in custody

The first arrest came late Wednesday, October 7, when Mark Quiah, former Deputy Director for Operations at the Liberia Civil Aviation Authority (LCAA), was taken into custody and sent to the Monrovia Central Prison.

Others followed, including Gerald Foley Smith, former Deputy Director for Administration at the National Security Agency (NSA), along with Jammel V. Jallah, Christian L. Nyantee, Cayce L. Nelson, Albenigo Janior and a defendant identified only as Sekou. They were brought before Criminal Court “C” before being jailed.

None of the defendants has been arraigned. They are being held pending further proceedings. The writ also requires the sheriff to file an official return showing how each defendant was served.

The scale of the charges

The indictment, handed up by the Grand Jury of Montserrado County, lists 11 offenses. Five relate directly to controlled drugs: unlicensed possession, importation, exportation, and sale, distribution and transportation, as well as illicit trafficking. Three are inchoate offenses: criminal conspiracy, criminal facilitation and criminal solicitation. The remaining charges are money laundering and two counts involving physical objects for lethal use, covering both possession and sale.

Taken together, the charges allege far more than simple possession. They describe an organized operation that moved drugs into and out of Liberia, laundered the proceeds and had access to lethal weapons.

Why the defendants matter

The names on the indictment give the case its weight. The NSA is among the agencies charged with protecting the state from organized crime. The LCAA oversees the airports through which drugs can cross borders. Allegations that former senior officials from both institutions took part in a trafficking network raise uncomfortable questions about whether state institutions were compromised, regardless of what the courts ultimately decide.

The inclusion of Howard-Taylor adds a political dimension. She served as Vice President from 2018 to 2024 and was former President George Weah’s running mate in the 2023 election. The prosecution of a former vice president on charges of this kind has little precedent in Liberia, and supporters and critics alike will watch closely for signs of either political motive or political protection.

A test for the justice system

For the government, the arrests signal that the indictment will be enforced rather than left to stall. Making the case stick will be harder. Drug and money laundering prosecutions depend on financial records, seized evidence, intercepted communications and often cooperating witnesses. They are complex, and in Liberia such cases have frequently been slowed by delays, adjournments and disputes over evidence. How the prosecution handles disclosure, how quickly arraignment follows and whether bail is contested will offer early signs of the case’s strength.

The courts will also be judged on fairness. With high-profile defendants and intense public interest, the pressure for a swift conviction will be considerable. So will the demand that the process be seen as impartial.

What comes next

The defendants are expected to be arraigned before Criminal Court “C,” where they will enter pleas. Defense lawyers are likely to seek bail and may challenge the indictment. Attention will also turn to the remaining defendants, including the former vice president, and whether they will be taken into custody.

The indictment contains allegations only. All 19 defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction, and they are entitled to legal representation and a fair trial under the Liberian Constitution.

World.title: Liberia: MCSS Teachers Defy Return-to-Class Call, Vow to Sustain Go-Slow Until Demands Are Met
World.content:
Teachers at a mass meeting

Public school teachers across Monrovia and its environs under the banner of the Monrovia Consolidated School System Teachers Association (MCSS-TA) are embarking on a strike action until their four-count demands are met by the system.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Members of the Association say their demands have been overdue without tangible response from the authorities of MCSS headed by Dr. Augurie E. Stevens.



The Four-count Demand

In count one of their demands, the Monrovia-based public-school teachers are calling on the Ministry of Education to immediately replace missing instructional staff and place all active volunteer teachers onto the official government payroll.

They are also demanding salary upgrades, wanting compensation structures to be adjusted to reflect higher academic qualifications earned by teachers, with payments processed prior to verification delays.

Furthermore, MCSS-TA is craving payroll reinstatement and welfare, urging the Civil Service Agency (CSA) and the Ministry of Education to unconditionally reinstate omitted employees, increase salaries for all educators and support personnel – including janitors, security officers, and administrative staff—and provide adequate operational funding for schools.

The Teachers Association, at the same time, called for leadership accountability, with a call on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to immediately dismiss the MCSS Superintendent, Dr. Augurie E. Stevens, and introduce structural reforms to restore operational oversight.

‘Don’t Be Deterred’

As they remained steadfast with a united front, the Teachers Association held a mass meeting on Wednesday morning, October 7, 2026, at the Williams V.S. Tubman High School with the President of the Association, Mr. Augustine N. Nyormui, re-echoing the position of the group to each member.

At the well-attended meeting, President Nyormui called on members to remain unbending and stick to the mandate.

“We caused the problems in the past because we have not been rising against them. But from today, the mandate is simple: please, let’s stick to the go slow. Don’t be intimidated, don’t be deterred. President Boakai is a human being, and he will listen to us,” Nyormui ordered.

“Our main goal is that we are not teaching now. Go and sit down until you hear from us. You can go to your school of assignment and just sign in the log, but don’t teach.”

Action Starts Now

Asked by a member, Madam Rebecca Krubo Korward, an instructor at A. Glen Tubman Memorial as to when the action begins and ends, he responded: “This takes effect now and no one should betray us. Don’t be afraid; no one will dismiss you. Go and sign in daily and sit down. The go slow will continue as long as government does not attend to our demand.”

No Political Undertone

Nyormui told members that the entire process is germane and ill-political, as such, it should not be misconstrued by the public.

“I am a born Liberty Party child, a party that is collaborating with this government, but this is not about party issue; it’s void of politics. Let’s stick together. This is not about political issue.”

Nyormui also clarified that this is not in any way an attempt to thwart the pending electoral process of the Association slated for December, announcing that he would not, in fact, re-contest the position.

“Don’t let no one lie to you that we are doing this to stall the pending electoral process. Election will hold, and it will hold on the date announced. In the first place, I am stepping down and will not contest. So, this is not about delaying so that issue won’t be held. Anyone saying this is just another lazy propaganda,” he, among other things, added amid cheers in the Tubman High Cafeteria meeting hall.

MCSS Rejects Report of Widespread School Closures, But Acknowledges Teachers’ Go-Slow

When contacted, authorities of the Monrovia Consolidated School System (MCSS) rejected claims that 20 of its 26 schools have been shut down as a result of a go-slow action by teachers.

In an exclusive interview with this paper while the meeting of the Teachers Association was ongoing, MCSS Communications Director Samuel Nyenuh explained that several schools have not yet fully resumed regular academic activities, and that they are shut down.

He said the reason is based on the fact that there are ongoing renovation works at some of the institutions, while at the same time student orientation is ongoing this week.

“We don’t have 20 out of 26 schools that are shut down as a result of the MCSS Teachers Association’s announced go-slow action. This is not true,” Nyenuh told this writer.

He named the institutions that are carrying renovations as G. W. Gibson High School, Botswein Junior and Senior High School, and Matilda Newport Junior and Senior High School.

This, he indicated, is being implemented by the MCSS administration in collaboration with the Ministries of Public Works and Finance and Development Planning.

Teachers’ Go-Slow Confirmed

In what stemmed out to be a sharp contradiction, the MCSS official acknowledged that teachers have raised concerns and that the leadership of the teachers’ association has confirmed a go-slow action.

He stated that the MCSS’ leadership is aware of the teachers’ grievances and is working to address them.

He, however, urged teachers to return to their classrooms while the issues are being resolved through the appropriate government channels.

“We don’t want to go that route. We are expecting our teachers in the various classrooms,” he further referring to possible disciplinary measures under the Civil Service Standing Orders.

Nyenuh narrated that MCSS teachers, as civil servants, are guided by the Civil Service Standing Orders, which provide procedures for addressing neglect of duty.

Salary Adjustments Remain a Major Concern

Among the major concerns raised by teachers is salary adjustment based on academic qualifications.

Nyenuh noted that the MCSS administration is fully aware of the issue, including concerns from teachers who have obtained additional qualifications but continue to receive salaries based on their previous credentials.

But maintained that the administration is working with the relevant government institutions to address the matter.

The MCSS Communications Director referenced provisions of the Education Reform Act of 2011, which he interpreted as providing for teachers to be compensated in accordance with their qualifications.

He acknowledged that teachers who were initially employed with lower-level qualifications may have subsequently obtained university degrees or master’s degrees without receiving corresponding salary adjustments.

Despite the acknowledgement, Nyenuh stated that resolving the issue requires government funding and must be reflected in the national budget.

Communications Chief Defends Superintendent

Accordingly, Director Nyenuh defended his boss, Dr. Augurie E. Stevens, saying she inherited several longstanding challenges when she assumed office in July 2025.

“This would be very unrealistic to expect the superintendent to resolve all of the school system’s problems within approximately one year and two months. One of the challenges she inherited was a large number of volunteer workers, and this is being addressed step by step.”

“More than 600 volunteers were initially identified, but a reverification exercise involving the Civil Service Agency, the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning and other relevant institutions reduced the number to 459. Government resources had to be identified to accommodate the volunteers, which affected the availability of funding for other salary-related adjustments.”

2027 Budget Expected to Address Salary Concerns

In the pending budget, Nyenuh is hopeful for a better outcome as he revealed that MCSS has been lobbying the government for funding to address salary adjustments based on teachers’ qualifications.

He emphasized that MCSS is not an income-generating institution and cannot independently increase salaries unless it is done by the central government.

“General salary increases come from the national government based on available resources. MCSS depends on the national government for salary adjustments for its employees.”

Call For Teachers to Return To Classrooms

Meanwhile, MCSS through its communications chief has sounded a passionate appeal for teachers to resume teaching while the government works through the budgetary process.

“The way forward is for our teachers to be in the classroom. Teachers belong in the classroom.”

Admitting that while the teachers have legitimate concerns about compensation, Nyenuh added that they also have a responsibility to perform their duties.

World.title: Liberia: Inflation Eases to 4.5% as Central Bank Moves to Tighten Grip on Dollarized Economy
World.content:
Monrovia – The Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) has kept its benchmark Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) unchanged at 16.0 percent but has raised the share of US dollar deposits commercial banks must keep in reserve, a move aimed at chipping away at the country’s heavy reliance on the greenback.

Rodney D. Sieh

The decision came out of the bank’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting held on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, and was announced in Communiqué No. 28, signed by Executive Governor and MPC Chairman Henry F. Saamoi.



Dollar reserves go up

The committee increased the reserve requirement ratio on US dollar deposits by two percentage points, from 10 percent to 12 percent. The requirement on Liberian dollar deposits stays at 25 percent.

The CBL also narrowed its interest-rate corridor. The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), the rate banks earn when they park money with the CBL, moves from 6.5 to 6.0 percentage points below the policy rate. The Standing Credit Facility (SCF), the rate at which banks borrow from the CBL, moves from 1 to 0.5 percentage points above it. At the current 16 percent policy rate, that puts the deposit rate at 10 percent and the lending rate at 16.5 percent.

The bank said the changes are meant to strengthen how its policy decisions pass through to the economy, improve liquidity management and gradually reduce what it called the structural vulnerabilities tied to Liberia’s high level of financial dollarization.

Inflation falls, growth picks up

Headline inflation dropped to an estimated 4.5 percent in the third quarter, down from 5.4 percent in the previous quarter. The committee credited a more stable exchange rate, prudent monetary management and favorable domestic prices. Inflation is projected at about 4.6 percent in the fourth quarter, within the bank’s medium-term tolerance range.

Real GDP growth is projected at 5.5 percent for 2026, up from 5.1 percent in 2025, driven mainly by mining, manufacturing and services. The CBL’s Composite Index of Economic Activity gap widened from 0.8 percent to 2.7 percent, which the bank said points to greater use of productive capacity.

Broad money supply (M2) declined modestly during the quarter, which the CBL linked to the appreciation of the Liberian dollar.

Banks strong, but bad loans persist

The committee described the banking sector as stable and highly liquid. The Capital Adequacy Ratio stood at 38.64 percent, far above the 10 percent regulatory minimum, while the liquidity ratio rose to 58.71 percent against a 15 percent minimum.

But non-performing loans remain a worry at 13.38 percent, above the 10 percent prudential benchmark. The CBL warned that bad loans pose a significant medium-term risk to financial stability and limit banks’ ability to lend to productive sectors. It reaffirmed support for the National Strategy for Non-Performing Loan Resolution and related legal and judicial reforms.

The committee also noted that bank credit remains concentrated in trade, services and personal lending, and called for more financing for agriculture and manufacturing.

Debt, trade and reserves

Public debt fell from 49.6 percent to 43.3 percent of GDP, according to the communiqué. The external sector, however, showed strain: export earnings improved, but higher import payments widened the trade deficit.

Gross international reserves stood at 3.3 months of import cover, down from the previous quarter but still above the ECOWAS benchmark of three months.

Risks ahead

The CBL said risks are broadly balanced but tilted toward higher inflation. External risks include geopolitical tensions, rising global energy prices — Brent crude rose significantly during the quarter — commodity price swings and tighter global financing. At home, the bank pointed to bad loans, high dollarization, possible fiscal slippages and structural constraints on domestic production.

The committee said it stands ready to take further action if needed. Its next meeting is scheduled for Wednesday, January 20, 2027.

World.title: When repentance is merged with a party: why the State got the prayer day wrong
World.content:
When repentance is merged with a party: why the State got the prayer day wrong

By Amb Emmanuel Mwamba

Some days a nation keeps because they are holidays, and some it keeps because it needs them. The 18th of October was the second kind. Government has now erased it from the calendar and folded what was left of it into the 29th of December, as if fasting and feasting were the same act on different dates.

The decision was announced by Secretary to the Cabinet Patrick Kangwa, the most senior civil servant in the land and the official voice of Government on such matters. In a statement issued in Lusaka, he said Statutory Instrument Number 78 of 2015 had been revoked and replaced by Statutory Instrument Number 73 of 2026, and that the merger followed consultations with the church mother bodies.

The two days are not the same, and anyone who has ever prayed knows it.

Consider what the 18th was for. Its full name was the National Day of Prayer, Fasting, Repentance and Reconciliation, and every word in that name points inward and downward. People fast to empty themselves and repent because they have done wrong. They reconcile by going to the person they have wounded and asking for forgiveness. It was a day for sackcloth, not for a stage.

The 29th of December is a different occasion. It marks the day in 1991 when President Frederick Chiluba declared Zambia a Christian Nation, a declaration later written into the preamble of our Constitution. It honours a heritage that runs back through the churches that walked with this country from Kaunda’s time. It is a day of thanksgiving, choirs and ceremony, a day to rejoice.

So where, in a day of prayer and reconciliation, do celebration and commemoration come in? No one can fast on their knees in repentance while marching in a ceremony for a historic declaration. No one can weep for the nation’s sins and toast its heritage in the same breath. Reverend Godfridah Sumaili said it plainly: “I am wondering how a day of weeping and repentance could be combined with a day of celebration.” Government has yet to answer her.

If the real concern was the cost of another public holiday, the solution was simple and in plain sight: keep the day and drop the holiday. When the 18th falls on a Thursday, observe it on the Saturday or Sunday that follows, when churches are already full and offices already closed. The nation would keep its altar and the Treasury its working day, and nobody would lose anything.instead Government chose to remove the day altogether, and that choice tells us something.

Look at what was cut. The commemoration survived and so did the heritage. What disappeared were the repentance and the reconciliation, and the timing makes that hard to ignore.

This country has just come through a bitter election. Constituencies such as Mandevu are going back to the polls because the 13 August vote there was inconclusive. Opposition leaders sit in maximum-security prisons while churches plead for a national round table. Many Zambians still carry questions about how the counting ended, and about the elder statesmen this nation has buried along the way.

That is the atmosphere the 18th would have arrived in, with a whole nation gathered around one word: reconciliation. And reconciliation is exactly what our own official record now demands.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia stopped counting, and the reason it gave the nation was violence. Yesterday the President stood before Parliament and declared that the same elections were “peaceful, free and fair”. One arm of the State says there was violence, while the Head of State says there was peace.

Both cannot be fully true. If counting had to stop because of violence, the polls were not entirely peaceful. If the polls were entirely peaceful, the nation is owed a different explanation for why the counting stopped. Either way, Zambians have been handed two official accounts of one election, and a nation holding two truths is a nation split down the middle.

That is precisely what a day of prayer and reconciliation exists for. It is the one day on the calendar built to bring the two sides of a divided country to the same altar, to name what went wrong and to ask for healing. This year, of all years, the country needed the 18th of October more than ever.

Yet this is the year it was abolished. A day of national repentance would have carried those contradictions onto every pulpit in the land, and perhaps that is exactly what someone did not want. Removing the day instead of facing it is not reform. It is cowardice dressed up as administration.

There is one more fair question. The 18th of October was declared under Statutory Instrument Number 78 of 2015, during the time of the late President Edgar Lungu. Does the day simply remind this administration of a political rival it never made peace with? Zambians are entitled to wonder whether a sacred observance has been treated as part of an old regime’s furniture and cleared out with the rest.

It would fit a pattern, because this administration treats everything as a first. Free education, we are told, is a first. Yet Zambians remember free basic education long before 2021. Many of us remember the school milk and biscuits, the free exercise books and the pencils handed out in classrooms when we were growing up.

School feeding is also called a first, and it is not. The Constituency Development Fund is called revolutionary, yet it existed for years before this Government arrived. The President himself told Parliament the fund stood at K1.6 million when his administration took over.

Raising that figure to K40 million on paper is welcome. Zambians, however, judge a fund by what they can touch. In too many constituencies the classrooms, clinics and teachers’ houses that K40 million should have built are still missing, and announcing big numbers is not the same as building with them.

A government that respected the past would have built on the 18th of October rather than buried it. Imagine what the day could have become: the nation’s annual moment of healing after a divisive election. The President, the opposition and the churches could have knelt in one cathedral, with the families of prisoners in the front pews, before the God named in the preamble of our Constitution. No budget line can buy that kind of national cohesion.

The Ministry of National Guidance and Religious Affairs, however, was dissolved soon after this Government took office in 2021, and the day of repentance has now gone the same way. Each step can be explained away on its own. Taken together, they suggest that the Christian character of this nation, written into our founding law, is being emptied out one quiet decision at a time.

It is the no-look pass of football: the ball moves while the player looks elsewhere, and by the time the crowd notices, the goal has gone in. Zambians do notice. They have been watching since 2021, and a merger announced in a Friday evening statement does not fool them.

That brings me to the church. Government says it consulted the church mother bodies, so let the mother bodies speak.

Where is Dr Nevers Mumba on this? Where are Bishop Joe Imakando and Bishop H.K. Banda? Where is Bishop Mususu, and where is Billy Mfula? Where is the United Church of Zambia? What is the position of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, whose members keep the Sabbath and understand better than most what it means to set a day apart? Where are the traditional churches that were praying in this land long before any political party existed?

And who exactly was consulted? Name them. If the decision is sound, publish the minutes of the consultation and let the faithful judge. If it cannot survive being explained, it should never have been made.

Above all, what does the ordinary Zambian think? Nobody asked the woman who fasted every 18th of October for her family and her country.

A nation that declares itself Christian in its Constitution cannot quietly retire its day of repentance and expect neither God nor the people to notice. Zambia’s Christian identity seems to make some in power uncomfortable, because repentance demands that the powerful be humbled too.

Restore the 18th of October. Keep it as a day even if it is no longer a holiday. Let the nation fast, pray and reconcile, and let those in authority kneel alongside everyone else.

World.title: Mushitala Secondary School receives water system
World.content:
Tauro Mining has handed over a water system to Mushitala Secondary School in Solwezi District of North-Western Province drilled at a cost of K242,440 to provide clean and safe water to 1,680 learners at the school.

Tauro Mining Marketing and Business Development Manager, Marriam Diaby, says the water system comes with a 100 metres borehole, 10,000 litres elevated tank and an industrial submissive pump.

Ms Diaby has assured that the company remains committed towards ensuring access to safe, clean and reliable water that supports a healthier learning environment and allows learners to have more learning time.

She states that the project is not only meant to provide water, but also promote good health and dignity among learners and teachers as well as the surrounding community.

“This project is more than water, it is health, dignity and opportunity to the community. We do understand that access to reliable water supports a healthier learning environment and allows more time to focus on education,” she notes.

Ms Diaby was speaking in Solwezi yesterday during the handover of the borehole to Mushitala Secondary School management and Parent Teachers Committee.

She said the company will continue investing in projects that improve the well-being of learners and the surrounding community.

Speaking at the same event, District Education Standards Officer, Felix Luputa, thanked the company for helping in the provision of safe and clean water to the school which he said will create a conducive learning environment.

Mr Luputa pointed out that provision of quality education is not a responsibility of the government alone, but that all stakeholders have an important role to play.

“We commend you for ploughing back into the community by donating this borehole to the community, this is a great investment that will contribute to the provision of quality education that the government is striving for,” Mr Luputa said.

World.title: Access to safe water in Kasempa’s Mpundu Ward boosted
World.content:
Kasempa District Commissioner, Benson Malipenga, says the first community solar-powered water pump project in Mpungu Ward will ease the burden of water shortage and improve access to reliable water for households.

Mr Malipenga adds that the facility marks an important development milestone for the community in Mpundu and demonstrates the value of collective action in improving rural livelihoods.

Mr Malipenga said this during the commissioning of the Mashelo Community Solar-Powered Water Pump in Mpungu Ward in Kasempa.

“Today is an important day for Mashelo and Mpungu Wards as we celebrate the commissioning of the first community solar-powered water pump in the ward,” he added.

Mr Malipenga stated that improved water access will reduce the time residents spent looking for the commodity, ease queues and support household activities.

He added that reliable water access will also create opportunities for agriculture and small-scale business activities, contributing to improved livelihoods.

Mr Malipenga commended the community for contributing labour, materials and finances towards the project, saying local participation is essential for sustainable development.

“This achievement demonstrates what can be accomplished when communities take ownership of development,” he said.

Mr Malipenga also recognised the partnership with the Peace Corps and the support provided by donors in making the project possible.

He said the project aligns with the Government’s commitment to improving water and sanitation services, promoting rural development and supporting climate-friendly solutions.

Mr Malipenga assured residents that the district administration will continue working with communities and cooperating partners to advance development.

“This project should be the beginning of more development in Mpungu Ward. Let us continue working together as Government, traditional leadership, communities and cooperating partners to improve the lives of our people,” he urged.

Mr Malipenga congratulated the people of Mashelo on the achievement and encouraged them to protect the facility for the benefit of present and future generations.

World.title: Govt. to continue prioritising children’s safety- Acting Solwezi DC
World.content:
Acting Solwezi District Commissioner, Anthony Fulwe, says government will continue prioritising children’s safety, well-being, education and development in all its policies and programmes.

Mr Fulwe says this is because protection of children is of national importance and a responsibility that must be reflected in all actions that government takes at all levels.

He adds that the government will ensure that it works with other stakeholders in providing an environment in which every child is protected from abuse, exploitation, neglect and all forms of physical or digital violence.

“We must create an environment in which children feel confident to speak out without fear of being blamed, ridiculed, punished or further victimised, “Mr Fulwe stresses.

Mr Fulwe was speaking in Solwezi yesterday during the celebration of Child Justice Week under the theme: “Protecting children in digital spaces: confronting online exploitation, harmful exposure and strengthening child justice responses”.

He called for strengthened child friendly reporting mechanisms that will ensure that children who are abused have access to appropriate psychosocial support, healthcare, legal assistance and other necessary services.

The Acting District Commissioner said the justice system must be responsive to the needs and vulnerabilities of children by ensuring that children are treated in a manner that respects their dignity and rights either as victims, witnesses or have come into conflict with the law.

Mr Fulwe said there is a need to promote justice responses that are child sensitive, timely and appropriate and ensure children are protected, offenders are held accountable and prevent further harm.

“We must never lose sight of the fact that the best interests of the child should guide decisions affecting children in accordance with applicable law,” Mr Fulwe said.

He urged traditional, faith and community leaders to use their influence in promoting positive attitudes towards child protection and to challenge harmful practices that expose children to abuse, exploitation or neglect.

Speaking at the same event, District Child Justice Forum Chairperson, Namate Simakumba, called on all stakeholders to work together in ensuring children are protected from online abuse and exploitation.

Ms Simakumba, who is also Solwezi Resident Magistrate, said protecting children is not the responsibility of one institution or individual but that it is a collective obligation that requires commitment from government, law enforcement agencies, the justice system, parents, teachers, traditional leaders and the wider community.

“While digital technology presents numerous benefits, it also exposes children to serious risks that require our urgent and sustained attention,” she said.

World.title: “Govt Has Betrayed Christians,” Sumaili Says As October 18 Holiday Ends
World.content:
Government has abolished the 18 October National Day of Prayer, Fasting, Repentance and Reconciliation as a public holiday and merged it with the 29 December commemoration of Zambia’s declaration as a Christian Nation. Former National Guidance and Religious Affairs Minister Reverend Godfridah Sumaili has condemned the change, calling it a serious betrayal of Christians and an affront to God.

Secretary to the Cabinet Patrick Kangwa announced the change in a statement issued in Lusaka. He said Government has revoked Statutory Instrument Number 78 of 2015, which declared 18 October a public holiday every year. Government has also issued Statutory Instrument Number 73 of 2026, which makes 29 December a public holiday to be known as the National Day of Prayer and Christian Heritage.

Mr Kangwa said the merger was agreed after consultations between Government and the church mother bodies. The first combined commemoration will be held on 29 December this year, which means the holiday that would have fallen in eight days’ time will not be observed.

“Accordingly, the 2026 public holidays in Zambia have been amended. Subsequently, 18th October, 2026 will not be observed as a public holiday,” Mr Kangwa said.

Rev Sumaili rejected both the decision and the way it was reached. She said the day was a sacred occasion on which the nation humbled itself before God, not simply a day off work, and that removing it for any reason amounted to telling God that Zambia no longer needs Him.

“The cancellation of the 18th October National Day of Prayer, Fasting and Reconciliation by government in consultation with some church mother bodies is a serious betrayal to Zambian Christian believers,” she said.

She also questioned the consultation Government relied on. Rev Sumaili asked which churches the mother body leaders had consulted before recommending the change, and said Government should have acted with the utmost responsibility on a matter of such public interest.

“We do not know who those church mother body leaders consulted, which is why Zambia’s identity, values and aspirations have been taken away,” she said.

At the heart of her objection is the difference between the two occasions. Rev Sumaili said 18 October was a solemn day of repentance, fasting and seeking forgiveness, while 29 December is a day of celebration marking Zambia’s declaration as a Christian Nation. Merging the two, she said, was misleading because they serve completely different spiritual needs.

“I am wondering how a day of weeping and repentance could be combined with a day of celebration. This move shows a lack of spiritual understanding by those involved,” Rev Sumaili said.

She urged citizens to condemn the decision, saying it affects every Christian believer in the country.

The October holiday was created under Statutory Instrument Number 78 of 2015 and has been observed every year since. It was set aside for national prayer, fasting, repentance and reconciliation, with churches and Government leaders gathering for services across the country.

Government’s position is that the two observances belong together. Under the new instrument, 29 December will carry both the prayer element of the old October day and the commemoration of the Christian Nation declaration, under the single name National Day of Prayer and Christian Heritage.

The statement did not name the church mother bodies that took part in the consultations, and it did not say what the merged commemoration will involve. Those details are expected as Government prepares for the first combined observance.

Workers and employers now have formal notice that 18 October will be a normal day this year, and that the 29 December holiday is now part of the official calendar under the new statutory instrument.

World.title: Kampyongo Says Peace And Unity Key To Hichilema’s Growth Targets
World.content:
Opposition lawmaker Stephen Kampyongo says the development goals President Hakainde Hichilema set out in his address to Parliament can be reached if Zambians embrace peace and unity. Britain has pledged to back the Grow Zambia Agenda, but has also said opposition parties must have room to operate.

The reactions followed the President’s speech opening the First Session of the 14th National Assembly in Lusaka. He closed the address with a call for patriotism, peace and national unity, telling MPs that “without unity, there can be no shared future.”

Mr Kampyongo welcomed the President’s recognition that divisions must be addressed and a less hostile political environment created. He said meaningful development depends on citizens living together despite their differences.

He added that unity and peace are essential if the country is to make progress and meet its development objectives. His remarks are among the first from the opposition benches since the new House sat.

The President had earlier told the chamber that the election period is behind the country. “Whatever our political choices were, we remain one law-abiding people, bound together by Zambia, and a common destiny,” he said, repeating a line from his inauguration.

British High Commissioner Rebecca Terzeon said the United Kingdom is ready to work with Government to promote growth, strengthen trade and attract investment. She said the address made clear that economic growth will be the main focus of the next five years, and that Britain is prepared to support initiatives aligned with the agenda.

“The United Kingdom has been a close partner to Zambia for many years. Zambeef has received support from British investment. There are also UK-backed companies and traders active in sectors such as energy,” Ms Terzeon said.

She pointed to the recent visit by UK Trade Commissioner for Africa Alastair Long as evidence of that commitment. Mr Long held talks with Government officials, businesses and investors on trade and investment in mining, energy, finance and infrastructure.

The High Commissioner also welcomed the larger number of women and young people in Parliament, calling it an important step towards inclusive governance. Alongside her support, she stressed that opposition parties need enough space to operate and hold Government accountable.

She said democratic institutions should remain independent, transparent and effective, and she underlined the importance of a free media in strengthening democracy.

Vice-President W.K. Mutale Nalumango made a similar appeal from the Government side. She said the nation must now look beyond political differences and unite to advance the interests of Zambia.

Mrs Nalumango said the country’s democratic maturity will be measured by how far its institutions are respected and how well citizens work together to improve lives.

Moving the vote of thanks, nominated MP Mubita Anakoka urged all members to study the speech closely so that their response to it on the floor is informed.

The new seats in the House drew their own response. Mixed-member proportional representation MP Lazarus Hakalebula, a visually impaired gospel musician and businessman, welcomed the plan to set up a structured talent-identification programme for the creative sector.

He said many people with disabilities have skills, creativity and abilities that have never been properly recognised or developed. The programme, he said, is timely because it could give talented citizens from every background a chance to benefit from the Grow Zambia Agenda.

First Lady Mutinta Hichilema said in a statement on her Facebook page that Zambia’s leadership is becoming more inclusive because of the constitutional reforms. Those reforms brought 20 more women, 15 youths and five persons with disabilities into Parliament.

“A Zambia where women are empowered, children are protected and everyone has the opportunity to thrive,” she said of the goal.

The United Nations Population Fund also welcomed the address. Its Zambia country representative, Anna Holmstrom, said she was pleased by the President’s emphasis on building a strong supply chain for medical supplies.

In his closing remarks, the President said the future the country wants cannot be delivered by Government alone. He called on the private sector, civil society, traditional and religious leaders and every citizen to take part, and acknowledged what he called “the toxicity around here” in the domestic political environment.

MPs will now take up the President’s policy pronouncements in the House. That is the first chance for the opposition to respond formally to the call for unity.

World.title: “If you engage in corruption, you are on your own”: Hichilema puts civil servants and MPs on notice
World.content:
“If you engage in corruption, you are on your own”: Hichilema puts civil servants and MPs on notice

President Hakainde Hichilema has told civil servants that clocking in and out no longer counts as work and warned MPs that every extra allowance is money that could keep a child in school. He also repeated that there will be no sacred cows in the fight against corruption. The President delivered the warnings as he opened the First Session of the 14th National Assembly in Lusaka on Friday.

“We reiterate our position that there will be no sacred cows in the fight against corruption. None. None at all,” he said.

“As we have stated before, if you engage in corruption, you are on your own.”

Eight to five is not delivery

The President called an efficient, results-oriented public service a cornerstone of national development. He said it will be judged by what it produces, not by time spent at a desk.

“The value of the public service can no longer be measured by reporting at 8 hours and knocking off at 17 hours, without measurable deliverables and benefits to our people,” he said.

He went further from the floor. “That does not constitute work. It does not constitute delivery.”

He acknowledged that the approach makes some people uncomfortable, but insisted it must happen. He said hard and smart work has placed a high premium on service delivery.

Delivery units brought into line

Government created the Presidential Delivery Unit and the Public Private Dialogue Forum to improve the delivery of public services. The President said both will now be streamlined so that they help meet the Grow Zambia targets.

“After all, they are born out of public resources, so they must be accountable to the public,” Mr Hichilema said.

Parastatals and other quasi-government bodies will be held to the same standard. He said the aim is to create savings for investment rather than consumption.

More services will be added to ZamPortal and the Government Service Bus to make them easier and cheaper to reach. The President also promised fewer administrative barriers, more transparency and a lower cost of dealing with Government.

A word to the House on allowances

Some of the President’s sharpest words were for the MPs in front of him. He reminded them that they too are public officers, created and funded by the people.

“When we put pressure on the Speaker for more allowances, remember we could use those allowances to keep more kids in school,” he said.

“Maybe we are already comfortable ourselves. Let’s release resources to those who need them the most.”

CDF: more money, better use

The Head of State described the rise in the Constituency Development Fund from K1.6 million to K40 million per constituency as revolutionary. He also admitted that the fund is not always used well.

“All of us in this House must agree that we can do better in effective utilisation of this tool, and it has got no partisanship in it,” he said.

His written address committed Government to strengthening how the fund is used, so that it responds to local development needs. Protecting the CDF was one of the reasons Government gave for restoring excise duty on fuel this month, along with free education, school feeding and the Social Cash Transfer.

The same message is going out to councils. At the installation of Livingstone Mayor Bright Hanakamba, Local Government and Rural Development Permanent Secretary Gabriel Pollen urged local authorities to turn their revenue into better services through strict financial discipline and accountable spending.

“Local Government is an engine for development because of its proximity to communities. The Government has continued providing substantial financial support through the Constituency Development Fund,” Dr Pollen said.

He said a council’s ability to meet residents’ expectations depends on raising enough revenue and spending it on critical activities within its approved budget. He also called for Ward Development Committees so that residents have a greater say in decisions.

“They cry isms”

Departing from his text, the President took aim at people who claim discrimination once they are charged.

“When people get prosecuted, they cry isms. Whatever isms are convenient,” he said.

“Public resources belong to the public. Full stop. We must not quarrel about this issue.”

He said oversight institutions have had their autonomy restored and law-enforcement agencies have been strengthened, with progress made against corruption, economic crimes and financial misconduct. Technology, he added, is now helping to detect the abuse of public resources early.

He called on every citizen to join the fight. “Corruption undermines development, weakens public institutions and deprives our people of essential services,” he said.

The ACC at work

The Anti-Corruption Commission made an arrest the same week. ACC head of corporate communications Joseph Mwenya said a 25-year-old Lusaka taxi driver had been charged with one count of corrupt practices.

He is alleged to have sent K5,000 by mobile money to officers of the Department of National Parks and Wildlife in Nakonde. The commission says the money was an inducement to release 56 vulturine guineafowl the officers had intercepted at Nakonde Bus Station. The birds are valued at more than K200,000.

“The birds were being transported to Lusaka, and the suspect had no authority to import or possess them,” Mr Mwenya said.

Order in public spaces

The President linked accountability to the rule of law. He said negative cadreism has been curtailed and markets and bus stations reclaimed, making them safer, more orderly and open to all.

“No lawlessness shall be tolerated, regardless of political or other affiliation,” he said.

He also promised that legal aid, alternative dispute resolution and legal services closer to communities will make justice more timely and affordable, whatever a person’s income or location.

What comes next

Moving the vote of thanks, nominated MP Mubita Anakoka urged all MPs to study the speech closely so that they can respond to it from an informed position.

The House now takes up the President’s policy pronouncements. The streamlining of the delivery units, and any legislation needed to enforce results across the public service, will be the first measures to come before MPs.
