World.title: Hundreds of thousands lose power as Hurricane Isaias batters Florida, Alabama
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hundreds of thousands of people in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle were without power early Saturday after Isaias crashed into the U.S. Gulf Coast as a dangerous hurricane and left flooded roads and downed trees in its wake as it moved inland.

The storm made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane, then quickly moved north through Alabama as its wind speeds dropped sharply.

But the possibility of life-threatening storm surges still loomed for parts of the Florida Panhandle, along with heavy rain and potential flooding for much of the region over the weekend and into Monday.

Isaias was about 40 kilometres south-southwest of Montgomery, Ala., and nearly 170 kilometres south of Birmingham, Ala., with maximum sustained winds of 55 km/h, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said Saturday.

Forecasters also warned that conditions could stir up tornadoes across parts of the Florida Panhandle and into Georgia and the Carolinas.

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season.

The storm's rapid intensification was fuelled by record-warm waters in the Gulf of Mexico. The Gulf has seen substantial warming over the past few decades, and experts say the current marine heatwave was made far more likely due to human-caused climate change.

While the warm waters provided the abundant energy that Isaias needed, its formation was also made possible by favourable atmospheric conditions, including weak upper-level winds that would otherwise have disrupted the burgeoning storm.

But just before landfall, upper-level wind shear increased, causing the storm to weaken slightly, dropping it back to Category 2 and making it more disorganized, expanding the area hit by damaging winds.

Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white-sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars and seafood shacks.

"The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference Friday.

Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola, police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways. While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.

Some Panhandle counties temporarily suspended emergency response Friday night because of dangerous conditions.

Parts of southern Alabama also were flooded, with officials in Mobile reporting downed trees and power lines. Roads in Houston County, which is in the southeastern corner of the state, were closed because of similar conditions.

More than 726,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.

A man tries to push a car as waves wash over the road on Friday ahead of the arrival of Hurricane Isaias, in Englewood, Fla. (Facebook/Reuters)

Tim Mowry, who rode out the storm from his home in Pensacola, said the wind was so intense it sounded like a train whistle as it whipped through a crack in his patio door. He lost power around 4:30 p.m. but was able to rely on a generator. Standing water also covered his backyard, and parts of his fence were ripped down, but overall he said the storm wasn’t as bad as he expected.

"As far as Pensacola-wise, we really got fortunate," Mowry said.

Mowry said his son, who lives about 15 minutes away, tried to drive to his home after losing power but had to turn around because downed trees and power lines blocked the roads.

Weakened storm threatens region with floods

Despite weakening, heavy rain is forecast as Isaias moves inland, with 10 to 20 centimetres or even more expected through the weekend from southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend, and southwest Georgia.

The last hurricane to hit the eastern U.S. was Milton, which tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024.

Isaias also grounded most Friday flights at several airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. U.S. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday’s football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn’t want to disrupt emergency response efforts.

In the Pacific, meanwhile, Simon strengthened into a Category 4 hurricane as it approached Mexico’s coast.

Tropical Storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.

World.title: Trolling or part of a larger plan?: Why Elon Musk waded into the separatism debate
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Elon Musk called for Quebec, Alberta and Saskatchewan to separate from Canada earlier this week, it may have been nothing more than the trillionaire engaging in some anti-Canadian trolling.

But it's also possible, according to one Musk observer, that the Tesla and Space X CEO had something else in mind.

"I think with Musk, there's often usually another game being played at the same time," said Quinn Slobodian, a professor of international history at Boston University who co-authored the book: Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed.

Earlier this week, Musk took note of a post on X that stated Parti Québécois premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon had declared his dream of independence "will be realized one day."

'Would be better off'

Musk responded: "Good. Quebec should separate."

He followed up in another post: "They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too."

Cross Country Checkup is asking: What conversations are you having about the Alberta referendum with friends and family? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for next Sunday's show

Canadian tech journalist Paris Marx, host of the Tech Won't Save Us podcast and a regular critic of Musk, said people probably shouldn't read too much into Musk's posts.

It may be nothing more than Musk being a " right-wing troll who has a problem with countries he perceives as being more progressive or left-leaning relative to his personal politics or that he feels aggrieved by," Marx said in an email to CBC News.

@Polymarket Good. Quebec should separate. —elonmusk

Musk's remarks were quickly rejected by Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and Prime Minister Mark Carney. On Friday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre also dimissed Musk's calls for separation.

WATCH | 'Tweets and memes do not affect Canada': Poilievre: 'Tweets and memes do not affect Canada': Poilievre responds to Elon Musk separatism comments | Duration closed caption 1:27 Asked whether he is concerned about foreign interference from the U.S. on separatist movements in Canada, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says 'we need to spend less time worrying about silly tweets by people who have no power over what Canadians do' and instead focus on things like affordability. He says memes do not affect Canada, but the decisions made by Canadians do.

Marx said Musk sees separatist movements in Canada as an opportunity to weaken the government's legitimacy.

Yet Marx said he doesn't believe these posts were part of any calculated move on Musk's part and that Musk likely hasn't given much thought to the ramifications of the provinces separating from Canada.

Instead, Marx said the post about Quebec independence likely appeared on Musk's timeline and he simply fired off a response.

"Many people reply to posts online with knee-jerk reactions," Marx said. "Elon Musk's replies just get news articles written about them because he's incredibly rich and powerful."

Musk, the world's richest man and first-ever trillionaire, is a South African-born Canadian-American.

'Canada is not a real country'

Musk's mother Maye Musk is from Saskatchewan. Musk moved to Canada in 1989 and attended Queen's University for two years before transferring to the University of Pennsylvania. Musk's grandfather Joshua Haldeman was the leader of the Social Credit Party of Saskatchewan.

This isn't the first time Musk has weighed in on Canadian issues.

In 2025, Musk posted on X that "Canada is not a real country" following a petition calling for his passport and citizenship to be revoked over his ties to U.S. President Donald Trump. The petition received more than 375,000 signatures.

Musk also commented on Canadian politics earlier last year when he criticized then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, referring to him as an "insufferable tool." Meanwhile, he praised and endorsed Poilievre.

WATCH | Carney responds to Musk: Carney responds to Elon Musk's support for Quebec sovereignty | Duration 0:48 Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada prioritizes living 'free from interference from foreign governments and large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do,' in response to comments from Elon Musk that called for multiple Canadian provinces to separate.

Slobodian said Musk has a reflexive dislike of Canada and what he perceives as its excessively progressive policies.

So when it come to separatism, "it's like any enemy of Ottawa is a friend of mine," Slobodian said.

But Musk has also shown a keen interest in political movements abroad, particularly in Europe. For example, he has been vocal in his supprt of the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

A Feb. 2025 NBC News report said Musk had been encouraging right-wing political movements, policies and administrations in at least 18 countries as part of a global push to slash immigration and curtail regulation of business.

Connection with far-right politics

Slobodian said he believes there is a connection between Musk's recent comments on separatism and his affiliation with far-right politics in Europe.

With legacy parties across the European continent facing disruption from agile newcomers, Slobodian said Musk has a "pretty reasonable strategy" to create a bonds or affiliations with them.

"Then when they are the ruling parties, you've got an automatic buy-in or partner," Slobodian said.

He said Musk sees the EU and Canada in their present forms as obstacles to his accumulation strategy, and that any disruption could open new opportunities for him and his products.

"I think his idea is to jump on the secessionist train early, and if it does come to pass, then he's got kind of [a competitive] advantage," Slobodian said. "And if it doesn't, then so what? It just fades off into the background again."

World.title: He was ready to fight in the 'war on terror.' This post-9/11 veteran looks back at his decision to enlist
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault first met Barry Sward in the months after 9/11 when he was a young military recruit ready to fight in the ‘war on terror.’ Twenty four years later, she tracked him down to find out if he got what he signed up for.

He went to war after 9/11. It changed him forever

On Sept. 11, 2001, Barry Sward, a high school senior in Woodbridge, Va., watched the collapse of the twin towers on TV and knew he had made the right decision.

He had already enlisted to become a U.S. marine. Emboldened by a national tragedy, he now had an enemy to fight.

"There was a spike of revenge … and I did want to get the people that did this and hurt them really bad. I don't know why they're doing it," he told CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, who at the time was reporting on post-9/11 military recruitment.

In July 2002, he would start basic training at Parris Island, S.C., and just months later was part of the first units to enter Iraq as part of U.S. President George W. Bush's so-called "war on terror."

After Sept. 11, 2001, U.S. veterans are about twice as likely as those who signed up before them to have served in a combat zone, according to a 2019 Pew Research survey that polled 1,284 veterans. As a result, they are more likely to have been scarred by the battle wounds of war — not only physically, but mentally, too.

In that same survey, half of the respondents said they had emotionally traumatic or distressing experiences, yet only a third sought help to deal with what they faced.

CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, left, sits with U.S. marine vetreran Barry Sward, who shares photos and mementoes he saved from his time serving in Iraq in 2003, including a half pack of cigarettes, cassettes and his service cap. (Roxanna Woloshyn/CBC News)

In August of this year, Arsenault tracked down an almost unrecognizable Sward in Falmouth, Va., 24 years after their first interview.

She asked him: "Are you the same person you were when you went in?"

"No, definitely not," said Sward, now facing the effects of that deployment to Iraq — a resulting back injury and a PTSD diagnosis.

The post-9/11 patriotic recruits

In the days and months after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, media reports described long lines at military recruitment offices made up of young people who wanted to fight for their country.

"Post-9/11, you have a burst of patriotism and a need to serve, and there are plenty of stories of people who immediately left their jobs, went down to a recruiting station, or finally decided that they were gonna join," said Jason Dempsey, a scholar of American civil military relations at Columbia University.

"But that was not the majority of folks entering service. And in the grand scheme of things was a very temporary blip."

Sward, seen here in 2002, participated in basic training at Parris Island, S.C., as part of his preparations in the U.S. marine corps beginning in July 2002. (CBC News)

Numbers provided by the four primary branches of the military don't show a dramatic rise in enlistment immediately following Sept. 11 compared to other years.

Dempsey said the most common reasons for someone to join the military is a history of service in their families, a desire for financial security or educational opportunities and enlisting during a period of high unemployment.

Regardless of their reason for signing up, that generation of post-9/11 fighters would go on to participate in long-lasting wars in Afghanistan and Iraq — the latter of which saw U.S. foces officially withdraw just last month.

Serving in Iraq was 'frustrating'

In March 2003, as part of the global war on terror, U.S. President Bush announced forces would be invading Iraq if then-president Saddam Hussein did not leave.

Days later, Sward's unit, the 2nd Battalion, 8th Marines, crossed into the country. Their mission was to secure bridges in a highly defended enemy territory so troops could ultimately make their way to Baghdad.

March 23, 2003, is a day that haunts Sward. It was the beginning of a deadly fight known as the Battle of Nasiriyah.

Eighteen of his fellow marines died, including a friend he met in basic training.

"It was tough. There was a lot of screaming, obviously, and we could hear it happening," said Sward. "And that was the frustrating part — knowing that something else was going on, not too far away from you, but can't do anything about it."

U.S. marines from Task Force Tarawa duck as a helicopter fires a missile that destroys a building during a deadly gun battle on March 23, 2003, in the southern Iraqi city of Nasiriyah. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

While there, his unit was tasked with patrolling inside the city and looking for leadership and evidence of weapons of mass destruction.

Bush rationalized the invasion of Iraq on unverified U.S. intelligence that the country's leadership was harbouring destructive devices that would cause massive damage to populations if deployed. In the years since, no evidence was ever found that those weapons existed.

During the interview in August, Arsenault asked Sward what it was like knowing this in hindsight.

"It's frustrating. Still proud to have served, but maybe there were some political aspects that were at play in the background," said Sward.

More than 7,000 troops died in post-9/11 wars, according to research from Brown University's Costs of War project, and four times as many U.S. military personnel have died by suicide in the years since.

Since then, those wars have been looked at with a critical eye as to whether they accomplished what they set out to do.

That same Pew Research survey found that 64 per cent of veterans say the war in Iraq was not worthwhile, and similarly, 58 per cent said the same about Afghanistan.

Post-9/11 vets made progress addressing PTSD

Sward's time serving in Iraq was cut short. He suffered chronic back pain due to a spinal issue, and he returned to the base in Camp Lejeune, N.C., that same year, and was eventually processed out of the marine corps.

But it would take 14 years for Sward to get a diagnosis for the deeper pain he was struggling with: PTSD.

"Mine tends to show up as anger. I was either sad or I was pissed off and there wasn't any in-between. It took me a lot of therapy and I learned a lot from my wife," said Sward. His wife, Rebecca, is a licensed psychotherapist.

"I was either going to get help or I was going to lose my wife and my wonderful kids. I definitely made the right choice."

"As he's gotten older, I think he's been more open to unpacking trauma and trying to heal," said Rebecca, whom he met after he returned home. They’ve been married 21 years and have four children.

Sward poses with his wife, Rebecca, right, and four children. (Roxanna Woloshyn/CBC News)

According to the U.S. Department of Veteran Affairs, 29 per cent of veterans who served in Iraq or Afghanistan will have had PTSD at some point in life, compared to 10 per cent who served in Vietnam and three per cent who served in the Second World War and the Korean War.

"Back in those times, I don't think the rates were really lower if we look at actual cases, but I think a lot of people could not come forward. They couldn't say that they were still struggling with nightmares or with flashbacks or other reminders of the war," said Timothy Hoyt, chief mental health officer with the U.S. Defence Health Agency in Falls Church, Va.

"We've seen a lot of progress in addressing those stigma concerns in the last 20 years."

Despite the trauma he faced, Sward says he still takes great pride in the time he served in the marines, he just won't encourage his children to sign up.

"I have no regrets. All my choices have led me here to this moment where I have my beautiful wife and four kids."

World.title: Conrad Black: Quebec’s Gilbert and Sullivan election
World.content:
Article content

My guess for many years has been that the Quebec electorate is now composed of a nationalist bloc of around 40 per cent, of whom approximately half are outright separatists, with the other four blocs — the French-speaking Liberals, French-speaking conservatives, non-French and a floating vote — at about 15 per cent each. My best guess is that on Monday, the nationalist vote went 12 per cent to Québec solidaire, 28 per cent to Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s Parti Québécois, accounting for all of the support those two parties received. About two-thirds of the traditional French-Canadian Liberals remained Liberal and the rest went Conservative, with the traditional conservatives. The non-French speaking Quebecers remain as the core of the Liberal party, and most of the floating vote remained with the outgoing CAQ. Another oddity is that the only party leader in the race who is a straight male is the premier-elect, as the Liberal and Conservative leaders are publicly gay men and the CAQ and QS leaders are women. There is no indication that any of this had any impact on the election.

World.title: Colombia declares official start of El Niño, warns of strong impacts
World.content:
Colombia’s meteorological institute IDEAM officially declared the arrival of El Niño, and warned that the climate phenomenon could trigger water shortages and forest fires.

In a press statement, the IDEAM said that its “confirmation reflects the sustained warm conditions in the Pacific Ocean, which, according to the latest measurement, broke records, reaching a sea surface temperature anomaly of +3.49°C.”

The meteorological institute said it expected that this year’s “Godzilla El Niño” could continue to disrupt local climate patterns until March next year.

Initially, the weather phenomenon is expected to reduce rainfall between October and December, which is normally the rainy season in large parts of the country.

“Given this situation, and in light of the alerts issued since the beginning of the year, the national government launched an interagency response,.. with specific instructions for the responsible agencies to have their contingency plans formulated and activated by November 30 at the latest,” said the President’s Office in a statement.

The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) coordinates response capabilities across the country and enhances the monitoring of wildfires using satellite technology. For its part, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is taking steps to protect strategic ecosystems, water sources, and the most vulnerable areas. President’s Office

The Mining Ministry “is implementing an emergency plan aimed at ensuring the country’s energy security by strengthening thermal power generation, securing fuel supplies, and implementing efficiency and conservation measures,” according to the President’s Office.

EPM, the local utilities firm in Medellin, has been testing the effectiveness of water rations as they fear the lack of rain could affect the hydro-electric power plants that provide the northwest of Colombia much of its energy.

Before leaving office on August 7, former President Gustavo Petro ordered the mass purchase of solar panels to reduce the pressure on the electric grid.

World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: De la Espriella announces first $309M in aid for earthquake reconstruction
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella announced that his Miracle Fund received COP1 trillion ($309 million) for the reconstruction of western Colombia, which was hit by a 7.4M earthquake on August 10.

The announcement followed announcements by the press, which reported that the Finance Ministry allocated ($192 million) COP625 billion to the fund almost two months after the disaster.

Thank you for your patience, but please understand that the government’s bureaucratic inertia and the situation we’ve inherited are extremely complex. However, we’re working to resolve the issue, and the Milagro Fund is now up and running, thanks to God and the efforts of all the officials in this administration. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“In November, the government will move forward with contracting another COP2.7 trillion ($835 million),” Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo told Caracol Radio.

The money is the first of an estimated COP30 trillion ($9.3 billion) that would be needed to rebuild the damage to airports, roads, hospitals and other public works.

The fund will be managed by De la Espriella’s general secretary, Carlos Rios, and a handful of businessmen with ties to the administration.

The announcement followed increased unrest about the government’s lack of response to the earthquake, which affected more than 400,000 people in the Valle del Cauca and Choco province, and the coffee region.

The government’s initial response was delayed because De la Espriella suspended the process to transfer power a month before he took office on August 7.

World.title: Colombia seeks to expand definition of terrorism in draft “counterterrorism statute”
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella will present Colombia’s Congress with a comprehensive “counterterrorism statute,” which would give authorities enhanced powers to fight designated terrorist organizations.

A 116-page draft bill, which was leaked to Caracol Radio, would facilitate a military approach to combat illegal armed groups and organized crime groups, for example through air strikes.

The Antiterrorism Statute would additionally create a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors, which would make it easier to freeze the assets of suspected terrorists and their financiers.

Last but not least, the bill creates a presidential Terrorism Commissioner and a special prison regime for leaders of designated terrorist organizations.

Broader definition of terrorism

The bill seeks to change Colombia’s criminal law and define terrorism as any individual or collective conduct that produces “fear, panic or terror, creating risks, threats or the use of violence.”

A technical body of the National Security Council (NSC) will advise the council on the inclusion of organizations or individuals that ought to be included to its public National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors.

Anyone who believes he was falsely put on the terror list can challenge this decision before the NSC and the Council of State, Colombia’s top administrative court.

The bill additionally seeks that “the Council of State shall hear, in the first instance, constitutional protection lawsuits filed against the President of the Republic or against defense authorities for acts or omissions related to operations by law enforcement agencies to preserve national security.”

This would make the suspension of military operations more difficult for citizens, who now can seek legal support to protect their constitutional rights at lower courts.

The bill also creates new crimes and modifies the penalties for conduct related to “terrorism,” such as the use of drones, illegal mining, oil theft, the extraction and sale of gold, kidnapping, smuggling, human trafficking, drug trafficking, extortion, cybercrimes, election crimes, riots, and attacks on critical infrastructure.

In the case of riots, “the penalty shall be increased by up to double when the riot is directed against law enforcement units conducting operations; or is carried out in conjunction with listed terrorist organizations.”

The bill also allows Colombian authorities to investigate and prosecute terrorism, terrorism financing or providing material support for terrorist organizations abroad.

High Counterterrorism Commissioner

The bill additionally seeks to expand presidential powers to create the Office of the High Counterterrorism Commissioner.

The expanded power would additionally give De la Espriella six months to regulate the powers of this new advisory office and to appoint its first commissioner.

World.title: Mayor from Colombia’s north claims De la Espriella’s armed men intimidated him
World.content:
The mayor of Sincelejo claimed Sunday that armed men intimidated him during a meeting with Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a video message, Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña said that armed men positioned themselves behind him while the president accused the mayor of corruption and threatened to pull municipal funds.

The accusations were partly published on the social media pages of the president, who accused Acuña of being “a person who, like you, faces 13 corruption charges, has a video in which he explains how to embezzle funds from the PAE, and, on top of that, is set to stand trial in the Supreme Court of Justice on charges of illicit enrichment.”

So let’s see what we do with Sincelejo, but I do not work under your scheme of corruption. And if you think you can continue engaging in those practices, know that someone has arrived who is going to prevent it and that I am going to concentrate on it. This money, mister mayor, I will take care of it, and to take care of it I have to keep it away from your control. President Abelardo de la Espriella

In his response, Acuña claimed that De la Espriella’s video “has been edited and digitally manipulated.”

I ask you, please, to show the full video, where you can see how disciplinary and criminal codes are being violated in Colombia, where you can see how a mayor is being intimidated with rifles in the hands of civilians. How can a mayor be constantly flanked—for the entire duration of an event—by a person armed with a rifle, with the sole purpose of intimidating him? Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña

Investigative journalist Laura Ardila said on social media platform X that sources from the province confirmed Acuña’s allegations.

Sources from the department who were present say—fearing they might be named—that they left the scene terrified. They claim that Acuña was indeed surrounded by heavily armed men in civilian clothing, that the president’s office was recording the entire time, and that, based on details like these, they believe it was a scene staged in advance to go viral. Journalist Laura Ardila

The mayor subsequently pointed out that the investigations into his alleged corruption existed before the presidential campaign, during which the De la Espriella campaign may have violated electoral laws, according to Acuña.

Among other things, the mayor said that he had been approached by De la Espriella’s parents to support the far-right president’s campaign and that local print shops may have received unreported campaign funds.

Since this needs to be clarified, mister President, it would be a good idea for the oversight agencies to investigate whether any printing shops in Sincelejo incurred campaign expenses that have not yet been reported to the National Electoral Council, whether there was campaign financing, and where that campaign financing came from, Mister President. Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña

The mayor also pointed out that two members of the De la Espriella administration are being investigated on corruption charges and that the president had ties to the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

The president has repeatedly used corruption allegations to target political enemies.

World.title: Colombia’s top corporate lobbyist resigns over reported tensions with president
World.content:
The director of one of Colombia’s most powerful business associations, Bruce Mac Master of the ANDI, resigned amid tensions with President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a letter to the ANDI, Mac Master said that “it is time for me to step down from my role as head of the National Association of Entrepreneurs of Colombia.”

According to the former ANDI boss, “unexpected and troubling circumstances” made working for the association “particularly complex” and ‘multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously.”

In recent weeks, unexpected and troubling circumstances have arisen that have made the Association’s operating environment particularly complex, with potential adverse effects on its members and staff. Multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously. In the face of these challenges, I have sought to act with firmness and prudence, always prioritizing institutional channels and placing the interests of the ANDI above any personal considerations, in an effort to resolve this situation. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master’s resignation followed news suggesting that De la Espriella instructed his cabinet of boycotting the ANDI chief.

According to political news magazine La Silla Vacia, the rift between the ANDI and the government was because De la Espriella’s law firm was never allowed to join the ANDI and the association’s donations in response to the august 10 earthquake bypassed the First Lady’s newly founded and very controversial foundation.

“The General Board of Directors, its Executive Committee, and I did everything in our power to facilitate a solution and create conditions that would allow the Association to fully fulfill its role, seeking to keep channels of dialogue open and to continue contributing,” but “all of those attempts were unsuccessful.”

I deeply regret this, because I have always believed in collective intelligence and in the need for the government, the private sector, and institutions to work together—even in the face of differences—with respect, independence, and a sense of national responsibility. We tried, but we were unsuccessful. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master said that he hoped that his resignation would restore “collaboration between the national government and the business community—as represented by the General Board of Directors, the members, and the various divisions of the Association.”

The former ANDI chief had been trying to represent the business interests of its approximately 1,600 members since 2013.

World.title: Colombia seeks to tighten checks on public protests
World.content:
Colombia’s government published a draft decree that seeks to tighten regulations on public protests.

The draft was published weeks before labor unions and social organizations plan regional anti-government protests ahead of a national strike that is set for November.

The draft seeks to update the Decree #3 of 2021, which was issued months before a national strike that was violently repressed by the police and the military.

In an attempt to prevent another bloodbath, the decree seeks to regulate authorities’ response to protests and the coordinated use of force in response to acts of vandalism and violence.

The decree regulates dialogue between the protesters and law enforcement authorities to promote the peaceful nature of protests.

The decree additionally limits the use of police intelligence against those organizing and participating in the protests.

Last but not least, the decree seeks the effective prosecution of those arrested during protests through increased surveillance and a permanent police presence.

The decree comes amid social tensions that surged after the far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August and announced counterrevolutionary measures that seek to undo reforms by his leftist predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro.

Swelling student protests have been publicly accused of being fueled by insurgencies and De la Espriella has warned that police may enter universities if they find evidence they are used to prepare acts of vandalism or terrorism.

World.title: Colombia breaks diplomatic ties with Iran
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that it had broken diplomatic ties with Iran and designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization.

The foreign ministry made the announcements in two separate statements that were published in its website.

In the first statement, the government claimed that the decision claimed to defend “national and hemispheric security, and the fight against transnational crime.”

According to the foreign ministry, the Iranian government has “alleged ties to international terrorist groups and other narco-terrorist groups that threaten [Colombia’s] security.”

Colombia also took into account the documented human rights violations committed by the Iranian government on its territory, the verified attacks against countries not involved in the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the authorities’ obstruction of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) efforts to verify the scope of Iran’s nuclear program. Foreign Ministry

In regards to the IRGC, the foreign ministry claimed that the Iranian armed force “poses a serious threat to international peace and security” through “covert operations beyond Iran’s borders.”

“Colombia will strengthen its control and security measures to prevent individuals associated with the IRGC from entering its territory,” said the foreign ministry in a second statement.

In his 2017 book “Watch Your Backyard,” Foreign Minister Omar Bula claimed that “Iran and Islamic extremist groups such a Hezbollah and Al Qaeda have profusely penetrated Latin America.”

As part of his foreign policy, President Abelardo de la Espriella has renewed ties with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

In a response, the Iranian government said that the accusations of the De la Espriella government go “against the principles of mutual respect” and damage both countries’ “interests and benefits.”

“It is clear that none of the arguments put forward by the Colombian government to justify this decision are valid or logical, and that this measure was adopted solely under the influence of the Zionist regime and the United States,” said Iran’s foreign ministry.

World.title: Trump says Russia will supply millions of tonnes of diesel as US eases sanctions on Moscow
World.content:
Trump says Russia will supply millions of tonnes of diesel as US eases sanctions on Moscow

9th Friday, October 2026 - 22:44 UTC Full article

”Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” he wrote

US President Donald Trump announced on Friday a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply some 4.8 million tonnes of diesel to US and global markets, aiming to curb rising fuel prices. To make it possible, the Treasury Department temporarily suspended sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the American and global marketplace, another 500,000 tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. He added that, depending on the condition of its refineries, Russia would deliver a further three million tonnes “within a short period of time”.

“Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” he wrote, saying that lowering prices for farmers, ranchers and truckers was his “greatest priority”. Putin’s investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, said energy cooperation between the two countries “will continue and benefit global markets”.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal “a weak decision” and “dishonest”, made while a Ukrainian delegation is negotiating a peace agreement in Florida with Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. “I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen,” he said. “This means millions, billions. All of it goes to the war against Ukraine.”

Russia, one of the world’s main diesel suppliers, had suspended exports of the fuel because of damage caused by Ukrainian drones to its refineries. The suspension was due to expire at the end of October.

US diesel prices hit a record on September 22 and stood at US$6.27 a gallon on Friday; futures fell 4.3% after the announcement. The increase has been exacerbated by the war with Iran, which has disrupted crude flows and refining capacity. A week ago, the G7 agreed to release 100 million barrels from strategic reserves. The cost of living is one of the central issues in the November 3 midterm elections.

World.title: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake shakes Panama
World.content:
A magnitude 7.7 earthquake shakes Panama

9th Friday, October 2026 - 22:38 UTC Full article

The epicentre was about 14 kilometres southwest of Pitaloza Arriba, a sparsely populated area near the Pacific coast some 240 kilometres from the capital, at shallow depth

A magnitude 7.7 earthquake shook Panama on Friday at 12:56 local time, centred on the Azuero peninsula in Herrera province, according to the US Geological Survey. Panamanian authorities have not so far confirmed any casualties, though inspections are continuing and they have not ruled out injuries or people trapped. Damage to buildings was reported in several provinces.

The epicentre was about 14 kilometres southwest of Pitaloza Arriba, a sparsely populated area near the Pacific coast some 240 kilometres from the capital, at shallow depth. Panama’s Institute of Geosciences estimated the magnitude at 7.2. Its director, Néstor Luque, attributed the quake to the Azuero-Sona fault system, which had been accumulating stress for some time. More than 30 aftershocks were recorded.

The National Civil Protection System reported damage in Penonomé, in Coclé province, including to the cathedral of San Juan Bautista, the governor’s office and a hotel, as well as in Chitré and Venao. Its director, Omar Smith, warned that aftershocks would continue, though with decreasing intensity.

The Education Ministry cancelled afternoon classes nationwide, public offices were closed, water supply was cut in some areas because of power failures and Tocumen international airport temporarily suspended operations. The Panama Canal Authority said the waterway was operating normally.

The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center issued an alert for the coasts of Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador and Mexico, which was lifted hours later. Smith had considered a tsunami unlikely because the epicentre was on land. In Chile, the navy declared a precautionary alert for Easter Island and lifted it after the magnitude, initially estimated at 8.0, was revised. The quake was felt in the Colombian cities of Medellín and Cartagena.

President José Raúl Mulino called for calm and asked emergency agencies for a report on the effects. “What has happened must not be used to generate alarm and disorder,” he wrote.

The earthquake comes two months after a magnitude 7.4 quake that killed 335 people in Colombia’s Chocó department on August 10.

World.title: US sanctions the International Criminal Court hours after a former judge wins the Nobel Peace Prize
World.content:
US sanctions the International Criminal Court hours after a former judge wins the Nobel Peace Prize

9th Friday, October 2026 - 20:53 UTC Full article

Pillay, 85, sat on the court’s Appeals Chamber from 2003 to 2008, presided over the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and was UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014

Donald Trump’s administration on Friday imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court as an institution, hours after the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navi Pillay, a former judge of the court, “for her efforts to promote peace and international law”.

“President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” said Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate.” The sanctions cut the court off from the US financial system and extend to those who work with it. Until now, Washington had sanctioned 13 of its judges and prosecutors. Rubio said the measures were designed to give the court and its member states time to address US concerns, and warned that if allies do not “rein in” the court, the United States will continue “its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick”.

The Hague-based court called the decision “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice” and “an attack on the rule of law and the very foundations of the international legal order”, in a statement signed by its president, Tomoko Akane, sanctioned by Washington in August. The European Union called it “deeply regrettable”, said it would work with the court to ensure it keeps functioning and hoped there was room for dialogue before the sanctions take effect in six months. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, against whom the court issued an arrest warrant in 2024 for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, congratulated the United States and called the court “a political body”.

Pillay, 85, sat on the court’s Appeals Chamber from 2003 to 2008, presided over the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and was UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014. The Nobel Committee presented the award as a message to those seeking to undermine international legal institutions. Pillay dedicated it to survivors of international crimes.

Trump has repeatedly said he deserves the Nobel Peace Prize. The 2025 laureate, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, gave him her medal at the White House in January.

More than 120 states are party to the Rome Statute, including every country in South America. The United States is not.

World.title: A mudslide sweeps away cars and a bus in Santiago after the wettest October on record
World.content:
A mudslide sweeps away cars and a bus in Santiago after the wettest October on record

9th Friday, October 2026 - 20:53 UTC Full article

Las Condes mayor Catalina San Martín put the number of homes with some damage at around 2,000, 55 of them with serious habitability problems

A torrent of water, mud and rocks swept away cars and a public transport bus on Thursday in San Carlos de Apoquindo, in the Las Condes district at the foot of the Andes in eastern Santiago, Chile, after a week of record rainfall. The official toll is six injured, with no deaths or missing, and President José Antonio Kast has declared a disaster zone in the district.

Among the injured is a one-year-old child with a broken leg, according to the presidential delegate for the Metropolitan Region, Germán Codina. More than a thousand people were rescued or assisted and some 200 hectares were affected. Las Condes mayor Catalina San Martín put the number of homes with some damage at around 2,000, 55 of them with serious habitability problems. Water and mud also entered two clinics and the University of the Andes campus.

Momento en comenzó el aluvión en Las Condes. https://t.co/he8miokwcv — Vision País Chile (@visionpaischile) October 8, 2026

Authorities gave successive explanations of the cause. Police initially pointed to an overflowing canal; the national disaster prevention and response service, to the activation of ravines, mountain watercourses that are dry most of the year. Codina later attributed the emergency to the blockage of an underground channel that drains a ravine. The emergency service said it did not send an evacuation alert to mobile phones because it was “a sudden event”, and said its response would be assessed once the emergency was over.

The agency declared a red alert in ten districts of the region, where schools were closed on Friday, and Kast cancelled a ceremony to sign the reconstruction law in order to follow the emergency.

The mudslide capped a week of record-breaking weather driven by an atmospheric river intensified by El Niño. The 52 millimetres that fell on Tuesday 6 were the capital’s highest daily October total in more than a century, and the 74 millimetres accumulated in seven days make this the wettest October on record, ahead of 65 in 1987, according to specialists cited by the Chilean press.

Chile had already suffered a storm in July that left 13 dead and 7 missing, mainly in the Valparaíso, La Araucanía and Biobío regions.

World.title: US plans its first military execution since 1961, by firing squad and livestreamed
World.content:
US plans its first military execution since 1961, by firing squad and livestreamed

9th Friday, October 2026 - 07:48 UTC Full article

Hasan, then an Army major, opened fire with a semi-automatic pistol on November 5, 2009, at a medical centre on the base where soldiers were being prepared for deployment to Afghanistan

The Pentagon will livestream the firing-squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, the military psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, scheduled for December 3. It will be the first execution carried out by the US armed forces since 1961, the first by firing squad since 1945 and the first publicly broadcast in the country’s history.

“The secretary is right. It will be livestreamed. Details will be released later,” a senior Defense Department official confirmed. The secretary, Pete Hegseth, had announced the plan in an interview with the Human Events Daily programme on the conservative network Real America’s Voice. “We’ll make sure people can see it, that it’s public. Because people need to understand that there are serious consequences for this kind of thing,” he said. Asked about the condemned man’s last wishes, he replied: “I don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”

The execution will take place at Fort Hood around 1pm, at the same site and close to the time of the shooting. Military law requires presidential approval for a firing-squad execution; the Pentagon said on Monday that President Donald Trump had given it on Hegseth’s recommendation.

Hasan, then an Army major, opened fire with a semi-automatic pistol on November 5, 2009, at a medical centre on the base where soldiers were being prepared for deployment to Afghanistan. He killed 13 people and wounded 32. A military jury sentenced him to death in August 2013. He represented himself, admitted the attack and said he had “switched sides” to defend the Taliban. He was left paraplegic by police gunfire and is held at the Fort Leavenworth military prison in Kansas. The Supreme Court declined to review his case in March 2025.

The last military execution was that of Private John Bennett, hanged in 1961. In 2008, President George W. Bush approved the execution of Ronald Gray, but a federal court stayed it. The last public execution in the United States took place in 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky.

Since 1976 only six civilians have been executed by firing squad in the country, three in Utah and three in South Carolina, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The Trump administration expanded the execution methods authorised for the most serious federal crimes, partly because of difficulties obtaining lethal injection drugs.

World.title: US charges Maduro and Cilia Flores with torture and repression in Venezuela
World.content:
US charges Maduro and Cilia Flores with torture and repression in Venezuela

9th Friday, October 2026 - 07:35 UTC Full article

Maduro and Flores, held since January 3 following a US operation in Caracas and detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, have pleaded not guilty to all charges

US federal prosecutors on Thursday brought new torture and repression charges against former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, adding to the drug trafficking and narco-terrorism case both face in a New York court. The same day, the judge denied a request by Flores for house arrest on health grounds.

According to the indictment, between 1999 and 2025 Maduro, Flores and senior officials around them “created and maintained a violent system of repression” in Venezuela, in which thousands of people were detained, tortured or killed by state agents. Prosecutors allege that Maduro “presided over this system”, “ordered the unlawful detention and torture of specific individuals” and received reports on particular prisoners, and that Flores helped develop it. The filing attributes a role to the so-called colectivos — armed civilian groups aligned with chavismo — the FARC guerrilla and the Directorate General of Military Counterintelligence.

The new charges are based on testimony from at least three former senior officials of Maduro’s government, identified in the document by codes, who say they supervised or took part in torture, including of at least three US citizens. According to the indictment, victims suffered beatings, simulated drowning and electric shocks. Former military intelligence chief Hugo Carvajal, a co-defendant in the drug case, pleaded guilty in 2025 and has offered to testify.

Maduro and Flores, held since January 3 following a US operation in Caracas and detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, have pleaded not guilty to all charges. Their defence is seeking recognition of head-of-state immunity. Prosecutors respond that the United States never recognised Maduro as president and that acting president Delcy Rodríguez’s government has not sought, through diplomatic channels, either their release or their immunity. The issue will be addressed at a hearing on November 17; the trial is scheduled to begin on June 1, 2027.

Flores’s defence cited heart palpitations, epigastric pain and weight loss of around 11 kilograms, and proposed moving her to a private residence with guards and an electronic tag. Prosecutors opposed the request, citing an “extreme risk of flight” and saying she has refused some medical tests. The judge rejected the request but did not rule out revisiting it if her health deteriorates.

The UN Human Rights Council’s fact-finding mission has documented human rights violations in Venezuela committed since 2014.

World.title: How the UK's Online Casino Regulation Has Become a Global Reference Point
World.content:
How the UK's Online Casino Regulation Has Become a Global Reference Point

9th Friday, October 2026 - 00:41 UTC Full article

Image by wavebreakmedia_micro on Magnific

The United Kingdom's approach to regulating online gambling has attracted significant attention from policymakers, industry observers and player advocacy groups outside its borders. As South American countries and other emerging markets consider how to structure their own online gambling frameworks, the UK model frequently appears as a reference case, for both its strengths and its limitations.

The UK Framework and What It Requires

The UK operates one of the most detailed online gambling regulatory regimes in the world. Operators wishing to serve UK players must obtain a licence from the national regulator, meet game fairness standards, protect player funds against insolvency, and provide mandatory responsible gambling tools.

In practical terms, this means that products like the casino slots at mr Q are subject to requirements covering game certification, payment security, and the treatment of players who display signs of problem gambling. These requirements apply across the licensed market and are meaningfully stricter than those in many other jurisdictions. Licensed operators must also make responsible gambling tools available, including deposit limits, session timers, and participation in national self-exclusion schemes.

This creates a measurable quality floor for the products UK consumers encounter, though quality of experience still varies significantly across licensed operators.

Why Emerging Markets Study the UK Model

The regulatory approach has shaped market structure in ways that are visible in the behaviour of both operators and consumers. Licensed platforms compete on product quality, payment reliability, and promotional transparency rather than on the evasion of consumer protections.

The UK Gambling Commission (UKGC) is the statutory body that licenses and enforces these standards, and its published reports and licensing data are widely referenced by policymakers in countries developing their own frameworks. Countries in Latin America and elsewhere that are building online gambling regulatory structures face versions of the same core challenge the UK worked through after its major gambling legislation came into force: how to capture tax revenue from a market that exists with or without regulation, while building consumer protections that justify the legitimacy of a licensed sector.

The UK experience is relevant in both directions. On the positive side, the framework demonstrates that detailed regulation with meaningful enforcement is operationally achievable and compatible with a commercially active market. On the cautionary side, it illustrates the speed with which digital gambling markets can grow and the lag that can develop between market growth and regulatory capacity to address the harms that growth brings.

The No-Wagering Model and Its Market Significance

One development within the UK market that has attracted attention from international observers is the emergence of no-wagering operators: platforms that differentiate specifically on the transparency of their promotional terms. This segment emerged as a response to player dissatisfaction with promotional structures whose headline appeal differed significantly from their real-world value once wagering conditions were applied.

The commercial viability of the no-wagering model is a data point of interest for market design questions more broadly. It suggests that a segment of players will actively choose a less generous-appearing promotion when they believe its terms are more honest, which has implications for how markets behave when promotional structures come under regulatory scrutiny.

The Global Perspective

The online gambling market is structurally a global market that operates within national regulatory boundaries. The UK's approach to managing this tension, through requiring offshore operators to obtain local licences as a condition of serving local players, has been adopted by several jurisdictions and is under consideration in others. For observers in South America, where several countries are at different stages of establishing online gambling regulatory frameworks, the UK experience offers a well-documented case study of both the challenges and the practical tools available to regulators who want to bring digital gambling within a functioning legal framework.

World.title: Latin America's online betting rulebook is being rewritten, and compliance is now the price of entry
World.content:
Latin America's online betting rulebook is being rewritten, and compliance is now the price of entry

9th Friday, October 2026 - 00:34 UTC Full article

Brazil's regulated betting and gaming sector paid R$8.75 billion in federal taxes between January and July 2026, almost 77% more than in the same period of 2025. Across the Andes, Chile's courts are ordering telecoms to switch off unlicensed sites, while Peru is two years into a licensing regime of its own. For companies working in the region, the question is no longer whether online gambling will be regulated. It is how many different rulebooks they can afford to follow at once.

Brazil: a market built on a R$30 million ticket

Brazil opened its federal market on 1 January 2025 under Law 14.790/2023, which makes the Ministry of Finance responsible for authorising fixed-odds betting operators through its Secretariat of Prizes and Bets (SPA). A licence costs R$30 million and lets a company run up to three brands for five years. Licensed sites must use the .bet.br domain and identify players through their CPF number and facial recognition, and credit for bets is prohibited.

When the regime launched, 66 companies were authorised, but only 14 received definitive permits; most of the others were still waiting on documents such as betting-system certification. That technical hurdle is one reason a growing number of new entrants skip in-house development and launch on a turnkey casino solution that bundles the gaming platform, payment integrations, player-verification tools and back-office reporting, then adapt it to the regulator's standards.

The tax burden is also climbing. Receita Federal figures show the sector's federal tax bill rising sharply, and Complementary Law 224/2025 lifted the levy on gross gaming revenue from 12% to 13% in 2026, with further steps to 14% in 2027 and 15% in 2028.

Peru and Chile: two opposite answers

Peru chose licensing earlier. Law 31557 took effect on 9 February 2024, and within 30 days the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Tourism (MINCETUR) had received 145 operator licence applications and 184 requests to approve technology platforms and game types. Its implementing regulation, Supreme Decree 005-2023-MINCETUR, sets separate technical standards for betting platforms. Operators pay 12% on monthly net income.

Chile has no online licensing framework at all. Its Supreme Court ruled by three votes to two that online gambling is illegal unless expressly authorised by law, ordering telecoms including Claro, Entel, Movistar and WOM to block unlicensed betting sites. As MercoPress reported at the time, the Superintendency of Casinos counts more than 900 illegal betting sites, generating an estimated US$150 million a year. A regulation bill remains in the Senate, and telecoms regulator Subtel has since ordered internet providers to block 42 betting sites.

Argentina adds another layer. Licences are issued by individual provinces and the City of Buenos Aires rather than nationally, so an operator active in several jurisdictions holds several permits, each with its own reporting rules.

Why the technology stack became a regulatory matter

The common thread is that regulators now scrutinise software almost as closely as the companies that run it. Peru approves platforms and game modalities separately from operators. Brazil requires certified betting systems before a provisional authorisation becomes permanent. Chile enforces through network-level blocking, which pushes compliant operators to show clearly where their traffic and payments come from.

That explains why fewer new entrants build their systems from scratch. In regulated sectors from payments to lotteries, companies increasingly buy pre-certified infrastructure and adapt it market by market. The model mirrors banking-as-a-service in fintech, where smaller firms reach the market on infrastructure someone else has already certified.

The trade-off is control. A shared platform can shorten time to market, but the operator stays legally responsible for compliance, and one vendor's certification gap can stall several licences at once.

What changes in 2027

Three pressures will shape the next 12 months:

- Tax ratchets: Brazil's scheduled rise to 14% of gross gaming revenue will squeeze mid-sized operators already carrying the R$30 million licence.

- Enforcement by infrastructure: Domain blocking in Chile and Brazil, along with MINCETUR's power to block unauthorised websites and disrupt their payment services, makes unlicensed operation steadily more expensive.

- Legislative uncertainty: If Chile's Senate bill passes, it would open another major market with its own technical and tax requirements.

For governments in the region, regulation has become a revenue story as much as a consumer-protection one, and Brazil's licensed market is now a meaningful source of federal receipts. For operators, the arithmetic runs the other way. Entry fees, rising taxes and country-specific certification mean that growth in Latin America depends less on marketing budgets than on how efficiently one technology base can satisfy several regulators at once.

World.title: Does having dual citizenship have any downsides?
World.content:
In 2016, my wife and I embarked on a road trip together across central Mexico — starting on Jalisco’s Pacific Coast and, over a month later, ending up on the Gulf Coast of Veracruz with innumerable side quests along the way in Michoacán, Guanajuato, Querétaro, Hidalgo, Mexico City, Estado de México and Puebla.

It wasn’t our first time in Mexico. We had, after all, spent our lifetimes visiting our extended families in Mexico as the children of immigrants.

But now we were able to see it on our own terms, as independent adults with our own incomes to spend and itineraries to plan. We rediscovered the country through our own eyes.

That summer, we had a revelation: We wanted to live in Mexico.

Three years later, in 2019, we prepared a similar trek around the southern part of the country, beginning in Oaxaca’s capital, then winding our way through mountain towns en route to the coast on a colectivo. Months prior, we had left our jobs as high school teachers with the intent to live in Mexico long term. Then, COVID-19 happened while we were staying in Mexico City’s central Narvarte Poniente neighborhood.

It was an uncertain and frightening time to be traveling. We ultimately decided, as U.S. citizens with a travel visa, to return to California after nearly half a year away. As tourists, we would have violated our 180-day limit and didn’t want to risk overstaying; had we been dual citizens, we would have had less pressure to return so suddenly.

Navigating the consulate and paperwork

But we hadn’t given up on our ambitions to live in Mexico as Mexican Americans. Shortly after returning to the San Francisco region, I began my application process to become a dual Mexican citizen.

In my case, I had a major advantage: My mom never rescinded her Mexican citizenship, despite having lived in the United States for more than 30 years after immigrating as a young woman. When she eventually moved back to Mexico, it inspired me to follow her southward. Through her, my direct path to citizenship had already been laid out.

The process took me a couple of years, though it could have been completed much more swiftly. I took my time and wasn’t in a rush during the pandemic. I visited different consulates in California, and after waiting in many lines and talking to many people, I gathered all of the documents — most importantly, proof of my mother’s citizenship and birth certificate — and approvals.

Then, it happened: I had become a Mexican citizen, and I had my Mexican passport. (I would eventually get my INE, but I opted to do it in Mexico, rather than at any Mexican consulate in the U.S.).

My wife had a trickier path. Her Mexican-born father’s documents had a typo. Therefore, some of his documents didn’t exactly match. If you aren’t yet familiar with the distress an aberrant punctuation mark can trigger in the imperfect machinery of Mexican bureaucracy, I pray you never have to.

Ultimately, my wife was forced to hire a specialist who helps Mexican descendants obtain their Mexican citizenship — it was frictionless and worth the price. To date, we highly recommend it for anyone who has the funding or has experienced any complications with the process.

A historic surge in binational applicants

During that time, we weren’t alone in our journeys toward Mexican citizenship. Many of our Mexican American friends had expressed a desire to do the same, and in some cases, a few had already started their processes as well. In fact, dual citizenship applications — particularly for the U.S.-born descendants of Mexican immigrants — are reaching a historic apex. De Los, a Latino-focused branch of the Los Angeles Times, recently reported that “Between 2024 and 2025, registrations for Mexican citizenship skyrocketed by 161% at the Los Angeles consulate.”

The trend is universal throughout the U.S. In Boise, Idaho, reports indicate a rise in applicants due to Mexico’s law change in 2023, which simplified the route to dual citizenship for anyone with at least one Mexican-born parent. Combined with the ongoing pressures of xenophobic turmoil, immigration raids and other sociopolitical factors, more people are looking to gain a sense of security and connection on both sides of the border through binational citizenship.

The benefits of dual citizenship are certainly ample: Traveling as a dual citizen offers financial breaks and accessibility perks (there are fewer foreign fees to be paid at Mexican airports and museums, for example); purchasing property in Mexico involves fewer legal hurdles; and at large, it grants unrestricted freedoms on both sides of the border, which is an ultimate privilege.

The unexpected costs of double bureaucracy

But that’s where things can get a little complicated, depending on your plans and lifestyle. In my case, I don’t use my Mexican passport solely for a beach getaway once a year; I live and work in Mexico as a dual citizen, with employers and responsibilities in both countries, and the implications are different.

Vehicle registration in California expired and needs to be updated in person? Guess who’s flying back for a visit to the California Department of Motor Vehicles? Navigating Mexico’s monthly tax payments? Might require a tax accountant. Of course, each scenario comes with a cost, and many life lessons.

When I applied for dual citizenship, I wasn’t necessarily thinking about those realities, or how I would have to pay and renew double the amount of things as someone fully integrated into two federal systems. Of course, in retrospect it makes complete sense. But it’s not the sort of thing that a bright-eyed applicant has at the forefront of their mind while pursuing dual citizenship — nor is it the kind of thing that parents or friends who are encouraging dual citizenship are thinking about, either.

Political debates and balancing two worlds

The issue of dual citizenship has even caused some political strife. Just weeks ago, President Claudia Sheinbaum proposed a ban on dual citizens being able to reach the highest levels of office within Mexico’s borders. “Why have dual nationality if you’re going to represent the people of Mexico?” she rhetorically posed. The bill has been criticized by the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) as a discriminatory human rights violation.

However, for the average person who doesn’t intend to run for the Mexican presidency, dual citizens generally don’t have much to shy away from. If you plan to work in both countries as a dual citizen, be prepared to pay the taxes (literally and metaphorically). If you don’t plan to work in Mexico for Mexican-based companies, you can simply declare your non-working status in Mexico when registering for your INE, and your biggest potential taxation headaches will disappear — at least in one of the two countries.

The benefits

For all of its potential downsides, there are double the benefits. On days when I enter the U.S. through California airports and switch over to using English with my U.S. passport, it feels like I’m home. I’m just as happy and relieved as soon as I arrive back in Mexico, activate my Spanish mode, and show my Mexican passport.

As someone who grew up around many undocumented Mexican immigrants in California, I don’t take that lightly. And I use it to constantly toggle my way between both worlds, as my fullest self.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: ‘A Pilgrimage Across Cultures’: Tamanna Bembenek on finding her third space in Mexico
World.content:
A couple of decades ago, I became fascinated by the concept of the “third place,” which Howard Schultz, then CEO of Starbucks, helped make popular. The idea came from sociologist Ray Oldenburg: a gathering place outside home and work. Maybe it was all marketing, but Starbucks wanted to define its cafés as neutral ground — a place to meet a friend, study or socialize without the usual expectations of home or work. Starbucks was never quite that place for me, but I remained fascinated by the concept. At the time, I interpreted it as a judgment-free space. As I grew older, the term stuck with me but I began to discover another meaning for myself — less about a place to go and more about the freedom to simply be. That is a feeling I have come to call “my third space.” Let me explain what I mean.

In the last few years, I’ve been thinking a lot about the concept in the context of belonging. I’ve always felt fortunate to have lived and worked in multiple countries, because it let me cherry-pick the best aspects and values from different cultures — and do so in a uniquely American way. Individuality is a value I’ve fiercely cherished, yet that same fierceness has made me feel more alone in recent years.

As the political divide has grown in the U.S., I felt I had to pick a political side to satisfy a psychological need to belong with a group of friends or family. As time passed, my identity became tethered to a party rather than to the values it claimed to represent. Social media compounded this, sorting everyone into ever-narrower boxes: age bracket, income bracket, zip code, follower count, which side of a hashtag someone landed on, or generational labels — Gen Alpha, Gen Z, millennials, Gen X, baby boomers, and I’m sure I’ve missed a few. It felt increasingly claustrophobic. Instead of feeling free to choose the values and characteristics that would nurture my own identity as a good human first — regardless of any other labels — I felt I had to fit into someone else’s box, under a category they had defined. Add geopolitical craziness and the current noise around artificial intelligence (AI), including claims that there is a 10% chance that AI will “kill all humans,” and I started feeling not only alone but increasingly anxious and hopeless!

So, I started reading books and listening to podcasts to figure out the root cause of this feeling and how to remedy it. I was already dedicating quality time to pursuing art but increasingly, I also found myself drawn to ancient history — Roman, Egyptian, Indian, Mesoamerican, just to start with. I noticed that exploring stories about ancient civilizations made me feel less alone. It felt soothing. Whether I was reading history or the myths woven through it, I was searching for common themes, a connection, a sense of belonging. There’s a timeless quality to such stories that reminds us of our own mortality and, paradoxically, makes us feel less alone in facing it.

Slowly, I found myself weaving these stories into my art through the use of icons, symbols and allegory. I started visualizing and composing art in my mind — integrating these concepts with my love and knowledge of art history and modern art, my reverence for the ancient craft of handwoven textiles, and my deep interest in astronomy and life sciences.

I have to admit that my current environment is what made all of this possible. Living in Mexico gave me the space I needed: regardless of nationality, identity, or age, I could simply live and let live. Maybe it helps to be geographically so close to the country I truly love and yet not feel so boxed in. Slowly, I began to understand that I wasn’t looking for a place where I could fit in. I was looking for the freedom to belong to something purposeful as I continue to grow as a person — my Indian heritage, my American values, and my old soul that keeps drawing me towards unfamiliar, ancient worlds — and perhaps to the wisdom and spirituality within them. Living in Mexico gave me the freedom to explore those connections, and painting became a medium to express that.

Allow me to show you what I mean, figuratively.

To create is human

Through trial and error, I have discovered that the antidote to my anxiety is not a massage or a spa day or a beach vacation (though they help from time to time) — it is creativity. Creating art in this way — finding connections between ancient cultures — has made me feel whole again, like I am part of something bigger. The more I paint, the more I realize how central creativity is to being human. That’s what my art is really about. There’s a narrative, a thought, a meaning behind every piece — observations, symbolic connections, and questions drawn from books and podcasts on history, archaeology, anthropology and astronomy. There are no political messages. Just a personal journey, trying to make sense of the world I live in today. Creativity is a process, not an outcome: It is a place where I lose my sense of time, immerse myself fully, get stumped, get frustrated, and still come out energized, rooted, grounded. In that space, I stop performing for others and follow my own curiosity.

Maybe that is why creativity makes me feel whole. I don’t have to settle into a single version of my identity. Pueblo life in Mexico, my American individuality, and the ancient civilizations that shape us all can coexist instead of competing. I can keep growing, changing, transforming — staying a “work in progress.” Creativity grants me that permission when society won’t. And while each painting begins with my own vision, it is also an invitation for the viewer to make it their own. You don’t have to see what I see or arrive at the same answers. That is the freedom I have found in my third space: I can be rooted in who I am and still have room to become someone new. Today, I am enough but I am not yet done growing.
