A third space you can visit

That sense of wholeness — maybe even greatness — is exactly what I hope visitors feel walking through my upcoming show. If this speaks to you, please come see it in person: I have a collaborative exhibition with Mexican artist Miguel Cuauhtémoc called “A Pilgrimage Across Cultures,” running Nov. 1-15 at Galería Torres del Reloj in Polanco, Mexico City. Miguel grew up immersed in the symbols and rituals of ancient Mexico, and I grew up surrounded by the colors and deities of India. Separately, we both kept arriving at the same recurring image, the third eye, which we each use to explore higher consciousness. Neither of us knew the other was painting it until we saw each other’s work. That discovery felt like another kind of belonging — a connection we had painted before we had even spoken about it.

If you’re in town, please stop by and say hello. And if you’d like to browse the fuller portfolio first, here’s the link: www.tamannabembenek.com.

I’ve written about my personal journey at length elsewhere, if you want to 

Tamanna Bembenek was born in India, studied and worked in the U.S. and now lives in Mexico with her husband, Travis. They are the co-owners of Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Sheinbaum meets with US business leaders and ambassador amid controversy over US-backed police academy
World.content:
Listen to this article

During a week in which she has questioned intrusive U.S. security policies, President Claudia Sheinbaum met with U.S. business leaders at the National Palace, but avoided discussing security initiatives with U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson who was in attendance.

Sheinbaum said Thursday’s meeting with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the American Chamber of Commerce of Mexico (AmCham) addressed issues related to the investment climate in Mexico, adding that she will address her concerns with Johnson at a later date.

“We focused on responding to the companies’ concerns, explaining the controversial new revenue law, discussing requests regarding trade and promoting the favorable environment for business investment in Mexico,” she said.

Also in attendance were the president of Mexico’s Business Coordinating Council, José Medina Mora, and the coordinator of the Advisory Council for Regional Economic Development and Relocation, Altagracia Gómez Sierra.

For its part, AmCham expressed interest in broader security issues, investment and greater private sector participation.

AmCham president Óscar del Cueto said his organization is eager for greater collaboration between the Mexican government and private enterprise, while also citing issues such as security, investment and greater private sector participation.

Several investment agreements were finalized (to be announced at a later date) and the U.S. contingent was given a detailed update on Plan México, Sheinbaum’s strategy for economic development, industrialization and regional growth.

The meeting took place amid an ongoing review of the Mexico-U.S. trade relationship as outlined in the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). AmCham has publicly stated that the USMCA should be used to deepen regional integration and preserve the competitiveness of the economies of Mexico, the United States and Canada.

Del Cueto insists the trade scenario presents a key opportunity for Mexico if the United States goes through a new stage of growth and industrialization and China loses dynamism.

“I firmly believe that next year we could be returning to the topic of nearshoring as the hot topic,” he said.

While Sheinbaum preferred discussing plans to allow for increased investment and greater North American productive integration, the kerfuffle involving Ambassador Johnson was a hot topic with the media.

After participating in a groundbreaking ceremony for an International Police Training Academy in the state of Querétaro on Oct. 2, Johnson — and Governor Mauricio Kuri — have faced criticism over the apparent failure to obtain federal authorization as required by law.

Sheinbaum publicly questioned the project several times, asserting that state governments cannot forge international security agreements or launch such academies without federal and Foreign Ministry authorization.

While clarifying that Mexico is not fundamentally against international cooperation, Sheinbaum explicitly demanded “cooperation with dignity and transparency” rather than “subordination,” adding that it is imperative that federal frameworks not be bypassed.

During a meeting with legislators on Thursday, Security Minister Omar García Harfuch addressed Mexico’s concerns about foreign interference in security matters, insisting that bilateral cooperation is subject to the provisions of Mexican law.

Sheinbaum said Johnson has agreed to meet soon with Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco to discuss the police academy and other issues related to security and the border.

With reports from Informador, Milenio, El Heraldo de México and Heraldo USA

World.title: Simon, strengthening rapidly, could hit Jalisco or Colima as a major hurricane this weekend
World.content:
Hurricane Simon strengthened into a Category 2 storm Friday as authorities prepared for possible landfall in Jalisco or Colima — potentially bringing catastrophic winds, dangerous storm surge and flooding to Mexico on the heels of Hurricane Polo last week.

Forecasters expected the Pacific storm to become a major hurricane Friday evening and reach Category 4 strength Saturday, with sustained winds of 230 km/h (145 mph), according to a Friday morning advisory from the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC).

At 3 p.m. Mexico City time, the storm had maximum sustained winds of 165 km/h (105 mph) and was about 315 kilometers south of Manzanillo, Colima, moving northwest at 4 km/h (2 mph).

The eye of the storm is forecast to turn north and pass very near or over Mexico’s west-central coast late Saturday or Sunday. Tropical storm conditions are expected to carry through Saturday morning, followed by hurricane conditions Saturday evening or Sunday.

Simon could become the second hurricane to make landfall in Mexico this Pacific season, following Polo, which struck Baja California Sur on Sept. 28 and Sonora on Sept. 29.

Simon’s precise track remains uncertain. The NHC said the storm could weaken rapidly or dissipate if its center moves inland. If its core stays offshore, it could continue north as a hurricane.

A hurricane warning issued by Mexico’s National Water Commission (Conagua) remains in effect from Punta San Telmo, Michoacán, to Punta Mita, Nayarit — points roughly 475 kilometers (295 miles) apart by road. A hurricane watch extends north to San Blas, Nayarit, while a tropical storm watch extends south to Lázaro Cárdenas, Michoacán.

Dangerous storm surge could strike the coast and nearby inland areas, accompanied by large, destructive waves. Rainfall could trigger life-threatening flooding and mudslides, particularly on steep terrain.

Simon could bring 20 to 38 centimeters (8 to 15 inches) of rain across parts of southwestern Mexico through Sunday, with isolated totals of 64 centimeters (25 inches) in Michoacán, Colima, Jalisco and Nayarit, according to the hurricane center.

Laura Velázquez, Mexico’s national civil protection coordinator, said authorities Friday would establish command centers in Puerto Vallarta, Cihuatlán and Manzanillo.

Authorities began evacuations in El Rebalse, a community in Jalisco that is vulnerable to flooding from the Marabasco River. Seventy residents left on their own and 10 were moved to a shelter, Reuters reported.

Schools in 22 Jalisco municipalities suspended classes Friday and Monday.

Meanwhile, Hurricane Isaias, a Category 3 storm, was churning through the Gulf of Mexico, with landfall in the U.S. expected Friday evening, according to the hurricane center. No landfall in Mexico is forecast.

With reports from El Sol de México, Reuters and La Silla Rota

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Mariachis, murals, drainage and demolition
World.content:
This week, Puerto Vallarta announced it will host a national children’s mariachi competition to promote this iconic Mexican musical style. Additionally, the Vallarta Institute of Culture issued a call for artists interested in decorating the walls of a local cemetery, and drainage work is expected to cause traffic disruptions on one of the city’s main thoroughfares.

Meanwhile, the Punta Paraíso tourism megaproject, planned for a stretch of beach in San Pancho, is set to be demolished due to environmental concerns.

Here are some of Puerto Vallarta’s top news stories.

Children’s and youth mariachi competition to be held in Puerto Vallarta

Puerto Vallarta will host the fourth Children’s and Youth Mariachi Competition Oct. 14-16, marking the first time the event takes place outside Guadalajara.

Featuring 18 groups from various regions of Jalisco, the competition seeks to foster the training of new generations of musicians while preserving the mariachi tradition.

Ten groups will participate in the intermediate category and eight in the advanced category. Activities will begin Oct. 14 with a masterclass at the La Lija Cultural Center. In the evening, the groups will perform in the opening gala at the Arcos del Malecón.

The jury will evaluate musical execution, performance quality, ensemble, intonation and adherence to mariachi tradition to select the finalist groups.

The finals will be held Oct. 16, starting at 6 p.m., at the Teatro Vallarta. Before the awards ceremony, all 18 participating groups will perform together.

Calling all muralists to decorate a cemetery for Day of the Dead

The Vallarta Institute of Culture is inviting artists to participate in an initiative to create 10 murals on the walls of the Municipal Pantheon in the 5 de Diciembre neighborhood.

The initiative, dubbed “Recuérdame” (Remember Me), aims to transform these spaces into public art galleries that reflect local identity and contribute to revitalizing the urban environment.

Proposals must draw inspiration from figures, traditions, flora, fauna and Puerto Vallarta’s local culture reinterpreted through the symbolism of Day of the Dead.

Applicants must submit their proposals Oct. 6-19; artist selection will take place Oct. 20. A committee will select 10 artists who must work on the murals Oct. 23-29.

Candidates must also submit a digital portfolio containing a maximum of five previous works demonstrating their experience in muralism. The portfolio must be submitted in PDF format.

Selected applicants will receive a cash prize of 7,000 pesos (US $368) upon completion of the mural.

For additional information about the application process, click here.

Demolition ordered for structures at Punta Paraíso complex in San Pancho

A federal court upheld an order for the partial demolition of the Punta Paraíso real estate development along the beach in San Pancho, Nayarit, following years of legal disputes over environmental irregularities.

The company must restore 1,466 square meters (about 15,780 square feet) of land reclaimed from the sea to its original state by demolishing unauthorized structures, and pay a fine of 96,220 pesos (US $5,300). The ruling also mandates the forfeiture to the government of the buildings known as Tower 1 and Tower 2.

The case also led to allegations against Roberto Rodríguez Medrano, the acting head of the Federal Attorney General’s Office for Environmental Protection (Profepa) in Nayarit. Former legislator Ismael Duñalds Ventura claims that the official endorsed the project’s environmental studies in 2018, when he led the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources in Nayarit.

The concession permitted only recreational and ornamental activities, not commercial exploitation. A Profepa inspection launched in December 2021 confirmed the construction work that resulted in the sanctions.

Profepa head Mariana Boy Tamborrell described the ruling as a victory for the community and for the protection of the coastal ecosystem.

Drainage work at Las Palmas Park begins

The Potable Water, Drainage and Sewerage System (SEAPAL) in Puerto Vallarta has begun sanitary infrastructure rehabilitation work in the Parque Las Palmas neighborhood and along Avenida México — a project expected to last approximately six weeks and result in partial traffic closures.

The construction corresponds to the second phase of work on the area’s drainage system. It entails replacing 66 meters (about 216 feet) of pipeline, increasing conveyance capacity and creating a new alternative for wastewater discharge.

Furthermore, this project reinforces the measures SEAPAL Vallarta is taking to address and prevent issues related to sanitation infrastructure — following recent problems in the Versalles neighborhood — by increasing conveyance capacity and improving wastewater management options in this part of the city.

The construction work will cause intermittent restrictions at the intersection of México and Las Palmas avenues; therefore, motorists traveling through the area should anticipate potential disruptions. SEAPAL asked residents and drivers to take precautions, heed warning signs and follow the instructions of municipal traffic officers.

Gabriela Solís is a Mexican lawyer turned full-time writer. She was born and raised in Guadalajara and covers business, culture, lifestyle and travel for Mexico News Daily. You can follow her lifestyle blog Dunas y Palmeras.

World.title: Senate moves to crack down on spam calls with fines of up to 2.3 million pesos
World.content:
The Mexican Senate has unanimously approved a reform to the Federal Consumer Protection Law (LFPC) to penalize abusive telemarketing calls and other unauthorized commercial communications.

Although the primary issue prompting the reform is persistent commercial calls, the amendments also apply to other communication channels used to contact consumers for advertising purposes. This includes the use of digital tools and messaging apps like WhatsApp for commercial communications.

According to the bill, companies that make persistent contact through calls or other unauthorized channels to offer credit cards, insurance, loans, services or other products without the consumer’s authorization could face fines ranging from 56,570 pesos (US $3,123) to 2.3 million pesos (US $126,982).

Senator Mayuli Latifa Martínez Simón of the National Action Party (PAN), the bill’s sponsor, stated that the goal is to protect consumer privacy and let consumers opt out of advertising.

Martínez’s original initiative envisioned the creation of a registration mechanism for individuals to express that they do not wish to receive advertising, similar to the U.S. Do Not Call Registry. However, other senators argued that the problem doesn’t lie in the lack of registry — rather, they considered it stems from insufficient sanctions.

Indeed, Mexico already has two opt-out registries where consumers can sign up to avoid unwanted advertising: REPEP, for commercial calls, and REUS, for financial services.

However, the Senate considered that existing sanctions have not been sufficient to deter unwanted commercial communications.

The bill draws on data from Truecaller, a mobile app designed to identify calls and text messages from unknown numbers. Truecaller data indicates that Mexico ranks sixth in the world for most spam calls, with an estimated average of 20 to 25 spam contacts per user per month.

The bill warns that this barrage of calls not only disrupts people’s activities but can also increase their exposure to fraud attempts.

Senator María del Rocío Corona Nakamura, of the Green Party (PVEM), noted that everyone has the right not to be persistently called by companies. Now, she emphasized, “They will no longer be able to do so without our consent — whether by text message, email or any other means.”

The bill will now move to the Chamber of Deputies for consideration and final vote. If approved, it will enter into force the day after its publication in the Official Gazette of the Federation (DOF).

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Mazatlán prison riots leave at least 12 dead, including a 2-year-old
World.content:
Riots on successive days at a state prison in Mazatlán have resulted in the deaths of 11 inmates and a toddler who was part of a family visit, while another 16 inmates were injured.

According to reports from the Sinaloa Security Ministry (SSP), Thursday’s riot, which occurred during scheduled family visiting hours, began as a violent clash between inmates who managed to acquire and use firearms inside the facility.

When gunfire broke out in two contiguous units, prison officials locked down the facility and issued a red alert, but struggled to contain the fighting.

Elements of the Army, Navy, National Guard and state security forces were deployed to regain control, but not before 10 people were killed and 16 were injured.

State Security Minister Sinuhé Téllez confirmed that a 2-year-old boy was among the dead, while the injured were transferred to a medical facility for treatment.

The boy’s mother told investigators that she went to visit her husband, but left to pick up another child, leaving the boy in his father’s care. The boy’s father is reportedly among the 16 inmates hospitalized.

Inmates’ families gathered outside the prison, known as “El Castillo,” to demand information about their loved ones, while officials secured the scene inside.

State prosecutors and federal security agents have launched a formal investigation into how firearms were smuggled into the prison — two 9mm handguns were recovered after the incident — and are piecing together the exact sequence of events that triggered the confrontation.

The SSP will collaborate fully with the State Attorney General’s Office, Téllez said, in order to clarify the facts and determine if any prison employee was involved in allowing the weapons inside the facility.

The newspaper Diario de Yucatán said the shootout was allegedly aimed at assassinating Eduardo Jonathan Martínez Larios, alias “El Owen,” identified as a member of the Los Chapitos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel. He was reportedly among the dead.

Early Friday, another confrontation broke out within a single cellblock. The authorities quickly controlled the situation, but not before two inmates were killed.

In a social media post, the SSP said the rest of the prison population was safe, adding that the interinstitutional task force maintains a presence inside and outside the prison to preserve order and security.

Prison staff are in the process of establishing communication with inmates’ relatives to inform them about the situation and “will continue with follow-up to provide them with the necessary information.”

With reports from Reforma, Milenio, Diario de Yucatán and 24 Horas

World.title: El Jalapeño: US politicians viciously harangue journalist who questions their lack of civility
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

WASHINGTON, District of Columbia — A joint campaign event held on Capitol Hill descended into hostile shouting Monday after a reporter dared to ask whether candidates running in the upcoming midterm elections might consider adopting a slightly milder tone on the trail.

The campaign event, held ahead of the upcoming midterm elections, became heated when a journalist pointed out that describing political rivals in TV ads as “communist saboteurs plotting to steal your groundwater” might be hindering civil discourse.

“How dare you question my absolute, unyielding commitment to respect and decorum, you total hack?” shouted one incumbent senator, pounding a podium while gesturing aggressively toward the press pool. “I have dedicated my entire midterm campaign to promoting mutual understanding, and anyone who claims otherwise is a radical traitor who deserves to be stripped of their credentials, horse-whipped and deported.”

According to witnesses, the campaign atmosphere further deteriorated when a visiting Mexican diplomat politely noted that political leaders in her country routinely manage to address policy disputes and host elections without accusing their opponents of being existential threats to human progress. The suggestion that public servants could run for office without resorting to daily character assassination was immediately denounced by candidates from both parties as an unprovoked attack on American democratic tradition.

“Civility is the bedrock of our republic, and I will personally ruin the career of anyone who implies our campaign strategy lacks it,” added a congressional candidate, adjusting his tie while glaring directly into the camera. “We are running to lead by example, and if the press refuses to report on how overwhelmingly polite and constructive our attack ads are, then the media is the enemy of harmony.”

By the conclusion of the half-hour briefing, three separate political campaigns had issued formal press releases condemning the concept of polite dialogue as an aggressive partisan maneuver, even as several campaign aides handed out informational brochures detailing their candidates’ lifelong passion for peaceful consensus.

At press time, midterm organizers were reportedly drafting a bipartisan resolution that would officially classify any future questions regarding campaign tone, candidate manners or basic decency as deliberate acts of war.

World.title: Cameroon Geopolitics Explained 2026
World.content:
CAMEROON · GEOPOLITICS

Key Facts — The country Cameroon is a Central African state on the Gulf of Guinea, with ports at Douala and Kribi and a currency shared through the CEMAC union.

— Who decides President Paul Biya, 93, has ruled since 1982. The Constitutional Council declared him winner of the October 2025 election with 53.66 percent.

— The United States A health deal worth nearly US$400 million through 2030, about US$7 billion of possible US business, and a deal to receive third-country deportees.

— China China held 64.9 percent of Cameroon’s bilateral debt in March 2026, and Exim Bank of China financed 75 percent of Kribi port’s second terminal.

— Russia A defence cooperation pact signed in 2022, and a 2026 row after Moscow reported 16 Cameroonians killed while fighting in its army.

— Everyone else France and the EU hold history and trade ties; Gulf, Turkish and Indian partners bring loans, flights and trade. Cameroon is not in BRICS.

— Still open Who succeeds Biya, whether Cameroon pays a US$616 million iron ore award claimed by Sundance Resources, and which US deals reach financing.

Cameroon geopolitics matters to Americans because Washington, Beijing and Moscow all court this Central African state of ports, oil and minerals. China is its largest bilateral lender, US firms eye about US$7 billion of deals, and Russia signed a defence pact in 2022.

Behind them stand France, the European Union, Gulf lenders, Turkey and India, all dealing with a 93-year-old president.

Yaoundé, Cameroon’s capital, seen from the Reunification Monument. File photo, 2019. (Photo: Franco237, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Why Cameroon Matters to the Big Powers

Cameroon sits on the Gulf of Guinea, where West Africa meets Central Africa. Its ports, oil, cocoa and untapped minerals explain most of Cameroon geopolitics.

Power sits with one man. Paul Biya, born on 13 February 1933, has been president since 6 November 1982, according to the presidency.

On 27 October 2025 the Constitutional Council, which certifies national elections, declared him the winner with 53.66 percent of the vote. His main challenger, former minister Issa Tchiroma Bakary, was credited with 35.19 percent, Business in Cameroon reported.

Diplomacy runs through the presidency and the Ministry of External Relations, led by Lejeune Mbella Mbella. He delivered Cameroon’s address to the UN General Assembly on 26 September 2026 in Biya’s place, the UN debate record shows.

Joseph Dion Ngute is prime minister and head of government, as his office confirmed in September 2026. The Cameroon country guide covers domestic politics, and the neighbours explainer covers the region.

Cameroon belongs to CEMAC, the Central African economic and monetary community, and uses its CFA franc. In October 2026 that franc traded at about 585 to the US dollar; more country coverage sits on the Cameroon page.

The Unity Palace in Yaoundé, the presidential palace and seat of power in Cameroon. File photo, 2020. (Photo: Fotsingboris, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The United States: Health Money, Deportees and a US$7 Billion Pitch

Washington calls Cameroon “of vital strategic importance”, citing counterterrorism, migration and disease control. That line comes from remarks by the US chargé d’affaires published on 1 October 2026.

The occasion was a five-year health agreement. The United States aims to provide nearly US$400 million through 2030, alongside US$450 million from Cameroon’s government.

It builds on a memorandum signed in December 2025 and puts the America First Global Health Strategy into practice. The embassy says US health aid over two decades topped US$1.1 billion.

On 27 August 2026 the first US-Cameroon economic and commercial dialogue met in Yaoundé. The US Embassy listed about US$7 billion of American opportunities “at various stages of development”.

Migration and Travel Rules

Migration is the harder edge. According to Human Rights Watch, Cameroon agreed in December 2025 to accept people the United States deports from other countries.

By September 2026, 46 such deportees had arrived on five flights and were held in government-run facilities in Yaoundé, the group reported.

Washington ended Temporary Protected Status for Cameroonians on 4 August 2025, according to the Federal Register. The State Department rates Cameroon Level 2, “exercise increased caution”, and says not to travel to three regions.

The project list from the dialogue is broken down in this report on the US$7 billion pitch.

Grand Eweng: a proposed US$3.5 billion, 1,040-megawatt hydropower plant on the Sanaga River, pursued by New York investor Hydromine.

Rutile: a US$500 million project by Connecticut’s Tronox and Australia’s Lion Rock.

Nkamouna: talks by Washington-based ARM on a cobalt, nickel and manganese project, starting near US$85 million.

Douala: a proposed US$2 billion airport and a US$75 million data centre with its own power plant.

China: The Port Builder and Largest Bilateral Lender

China’s footprint is made of concrete and steel. China Harbour Engineering Company handed Kribi’s second container terminal to the port authority on 21 February 2025, Investir au Cameroun reported.

The terminal cost about CFA400 billion (about US$683 million), with 75 percent financed by Exim Bank of China. It is run by KCT, a venture of Africa Global Logistics, the Chinese builder and France’s CMA CGM.

Debt follows the concrete. Exim Bank of China alone held CFA1,560 billion (about US$2.67 billion) of Cameroon’s debt at the end of March 2026.

China as a whole held 64.9 percent of bilateral debt, or 16.9 percent of all external debt. The figures come from the CAA, the state debt agency, cited by Investir au Cameroun.

In the first quarter of 2026 alone, Cameroon paid the Chinese bank CFA121.8 billion (about US$208 million).

Trade with China passed CFA1,600 billion (about US$2.7 billion) in 2024, according to the national statistics institute cited by Investir au Cameroun. The two governments initialled a trade framework agreement in Yaoundé on 10 December 2025.

Beijing is also opening its market. China’s zero-tariff treatment for 53 African partners took effect on 1 May 2026, Shanghai’s city government reports.

What China gets is work for its builders, a market for its goods and steady loan repayments. That gives Beijing more financial weight in Cameroon geopolitics than any other single government.

Container stacks and gantry cranes at the deep-water port of Kribi, on Cameroon’s southern coast. File photo, 2022. (Photo: BACHELOR45, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Russia: A Defence Pact and a Recruitment Row

In April 2022, weeks after Russia invaded Ukraine, Cameroon’s defence minister signed a military cooperation agreement in Moscow, Africanews reported. The reported terms cover defence exchanges, joint training and counterterrorism.

Recruitment has since become the more sensitive Russian file in Cameroon geopolitics.

At the United Nations, Cameroon cast no vote on the 2 March 2022 resolution on Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. The text passed 141 to 5, the UN voting record shows.

The relationship turned awkward in 2026. A Russian embassy note dated 5 March 2026 listed 16 Cameroonian contract soldiers killed while serving Russia, StopBlaBlaCam reported.

Mbella Mbella summoned Russia’s ambassador, Georgy Todua, on 7 April 2026 to voice “vive préoccupation” (deep concern), 237online reported. A citizens’ group, Ramenez Nos Fils (Bring Back Our Sons), says it is in contact with about ten families.

For Yaoundé, the pact adds a security partner without closing doors in Washington or Paris.

France and the European Union: History, Debt and Trade

France was the colonial power in most of Cameroon, and that past still shapes the relationship.

President Emmanuel Macron wrote to Biya on 30 July 2025, in a letter made public on 12 August. He acknowledged that a war had taken place in Cameroon, Journal du Cameroun reported.

Macron wrote that colonial authorities and the French army used “repressive violence” there. He drew on a joint French-Cameroonian commission on 1945 to 1971 that reported in January 2025, France’s foreign ministry says.

France remains Cameroon’s second-largest bilateral creditor. It held 25.8 percent of bilateral debt in March 2026, behind China, according to the same debt agency figures.

Trade is the European Union’s main lever in Cameroon geopolitics. Cameroon ratified an Economic Partnership Agreement with the EU in July 2014.

Under it, all Cameroonian goods enter the EU free of duties and quotas, the European Commission says. In return Cameroon is removing duties on 80 percent of EU exports over 15 years.

The Commission says EU trade with Cameroon has grown 43 percent since the deal started in 2014. Cocoa and cocoa products make up 62 percent of Cameroon’s exports to the EU.

Cameroon also accounts for 29 percent of the EU’s trade with Central Africa, the Commission says.

The Gulf, Turkey and India: The Quieter Partners

In Cameroon geopolitics, one Gulf-linked channel is a multilateral lender. The Jeddah-based Islamic Development Bank approved €212.35 million (about US$238 million) for the Douala-Bafoussam road on 19 May 2025.

According to the economy ministry, cited by Investir au Cameroun, the bank’s active portfolio in Cameroon neared US$1 billion in June 2026. A presidential decree of 2 October 2026 authorised an instalment-sale financing agreement for the same road.

The United Arab Emirates enters Cameroon geopolitics through ports. In February 2026 Abu Dhabi’s port operator AD Ports Group joined a 30-year Douala dry bulk terminal concession, the company says.

Its share of the first phase is about AED320 million (about US$87 million). The terminal is designed to handle around 4 million tonnes a year.

Turkey has built a steady presence since Biya’s March 2013 visit, the first by a Cameroonian president, according to Türkiye’s foreign ministry. The ministry says Turkish Airlines flies to Yaoundé every day and the Turkish Maarif Foundation runs schools in Cameroon.

Two-way trade with Turkey was almost US$205 million in 2019, the ministry says. Turkish firms also sit in KOGT, which plans a CFA50 billion (about US$85 million) farm terminal at Kribi, Business in Cameroon reported.

India is a sizeable trade partner. Two-way trade reached US$1.24 billion in 2023-24, and India was the third-largest buyer of Cameroonian goods, says India’s foreign ministry.

India opened a resident High Commission in Yaoundé in 2019. Its Exim Bank lent US$93.5 million for 225-kilovolt power lines, handed over in November 2022.

Other regional powers are courting Yaoundé too. Egypt’s offer on dams and power is set out in this water and energy report.

BRICS, the UN and the Minerals Race

Cameroon is not part of BRICS, whose 11 members include Egypt and Ethiopia, according to an Indian government backgrounder of September 2026. Its 10 partner countries include Nigeria and Uganda.

Yaoundé has raised its profile in global bodies. Philemon Yang, a former Cameroonian prime minister, presided over the 79th UN General Assembly.

Yaoundé also hosted the 14th World Trade Organization ministerial conference from 26 to 30 March 2026, the WTO says. Cameroon’s trade minister chaired it.

In its 2026 UN address, Cameroon backed the African Union’s call for better African representation on the Security Council. It argued that development finance “must not be regarded as charity”.

Minerals are where the contest turns concrete. A presidential decree of 17 August 2022 gave the Mbalam iron ore permit to Cameroon Mining Company, Investir au Cameroun reported.

The earlier developer, Sundance Resources, says an arbitration tribunal ordered Cameroon to pay it US$616 million. It announced the award, made under International Chamber of Commerce rules, on 26 July 2026.

Because the arbitration sat in Paris, any bid by Cameroon to annul the award goes to the Paris Court of Appeal. The outcome is a test case for mining investors across Cameroon geopolitics.

Bauxite is the second test. Australia’s Canyon Resources has advanced about CFA4.4 billion (about US$7.5 million) to repair the railway serving its Minim-Martap mine.

In August 2026 Canyon dropped its fourth-quarter target for a first bauxite shipment, citing financing and port questions, Investir au Cameroun reported.

Debt frames every deal. The International Monetary Fund projects 3.3 percent growth and public debt of 39.6 percent of GDP in 2026.

The Fund still rates Cameroon at high risk of debt distress.

Shipping containers and cranes at the port of Douala, the gateway for much of Cameroon’s trade. File photo, 2013. (Photo: Alessandro Aceri, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What It Means for US Readers

For US companies, Cameroon is an open contest. Washington is offering commercial dialogue and health money where China already holds the largest bilateral loan book.

For investors, the Mbalam award and the IMF’s debt warning are the numbers to watch before backing Cameroonian projects.

For Cameroonians in the United States, the end of Temporary Protected Status in 2025 removed a shield against deportation. Cameroon also now receives third-country deportees from the United States.

For travellers, the State Department’s Level 2 advisory still says not to travel to the North-West, South-West and Far North regions.

Taken together, Cameroon geopolitics rewards patience. Every major power is betting on the state machinery around Biya, not on any single deal.

What Is Not Known

The precise terms of the 2022 Russian defence pact are known only from press reports. How many Cameroonians serve in Russia’s army is also unknown; the 16 deaths are only those Moscow has notified.

It is not clear whether Cameroon will pay the US$616 million Mbalam award that Sundance reports, or challenge it. Nor is it clear which of the US projects listed in August 2026 will reach financing.

Who would succeed Biya, now 93, remains the largest unknown in Cameroon geopolitics. Each foreign partner’s standing could shift with the next president.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who runs Cameroon’s foreign policy in 2026?

In Cameroon geopolitics, President Paul Biya, in power since 6 November 1982, sets the line. Lejeune Mbella Mbella is minister of external relations, and Joseph Dion Ngute is prime minister.

Is Cameroon closer to China or the United States?

In money terms, China: it held 64.9 percent of Cameroon’s bilateral debt in March 2026. The United States offers health aid and about US$7 billion of possible business, and Yaoundé works with both.

What is Cameroon’s agreement with Russia?

Cameroon signed a military cooperation agreement in Moscow in April 2022, reportedly covering training and defence exchanges. In April 2026 Yaoundé summoned Russia’s ambassador after Moscow reported 16 Cameroonians killed in its army.

Is Cameroon a member of BRICS?

No. India’s government listed 11 BRICS members and 10 partner countries in September 2026, and Cameroon is not among them. Several BRICS members, including China, India, Russia and the UAE, already work closely with Yaoundé.

Do Cameroonians still have Temporary Protected Status in the United States?

No. The Department of Homeland Security ended TPS for Cameroon with effect from 4 August 2025, according to the Federal Register notice of 4 June 2025.

Why does Cameroon geopolitics matter to investors?

Cameroon geopolitics decides who builds ports, dams and mines there. Investors watch the US$616 million Mbalam award announced by Sundance Resources, the IMF’s high debt-distress rating and Biya’s succession.

World.title: Foreign Powers and Investors in Ghana 2026
World.content:
GHANA · FOREIGN POWERS

Key Facts — The country Ghana is a coastal West African democracy led by President John Dramani Mahama, and gold made up more than half its export earnings in 2025.

— The lenders The IMF closed Ghana’s US$3 billion rescue loan on 27 July 2026, and Ghana is moving to a 36-month IMF monitoring programme that brings no new money.

— China China is Ghana’s largest trading partner, with record two-way trade of US$14.1 billion in 2025, according to its ambassador in Accra.

— Investors Provisional figures from Ghana’s investment agency show about US$2.61 billion of foreign direct investment in 2025, up from US$652 million in 2024.

— The diaspora Ghanaians abroad sent home about US$7.8 billion in 2025, roughly 6% of GDP, according to the central bank governor.

— The United States US health aid fell from US$82 million in 2025 to US$53 million in 2026, while a 2018 defence pact gives US forces access to agreed facilities.

— Still open Gold Fields’ leases at its Tarkwa gold mine expire in April 2027, and the renewal terms were still unsettled in August 2026.

Ghana’s foreign partners, from the IMF and China to gold and oil companies, shape how this West African democracy pays its debts. As of October 2026, Ghana has finished a US$3 billion IMF rescue and restructured almost all of its debt.

Each foreign player brings money or power, and each expects something back.

Haul trucks and a drilling rig inside the Ahafo open-pit gold mine, run by the New York-listed gold company Newmont in Ghana. File photo, February 2008. (Photo: The EITI, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesMarkets, currencies and the economy › RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. × Markets today The currency Rates & inflation Economy outlook Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

The Lenders Who Rescued Ghana

The International Monetary Fund (IMF), the Washington-based lender of last resort for governments, led Ghana’s rescue after its debt crisis. It approved a 39-month, US$3 billion Extended Credit Facility, a low-cost loan for poorer countries, in May 2023.

On 27 July 2026, the IMF board completed the final review and released about US$371 million, according to the IMF’s staff report. The Fund called Ghana’s performance under the programme “broadly satisfactory”.

Inflation fell to 5.4% at the end of 2025 and 5.3% in June 2026. Gross reserves nearly doubled to US$11.9 billion by end-2025, about four months of imports.

Ghana is now moving to a 36-month Policy Coordination Instrument, the Ghana News Agency reported. The IMF board reviewed Ghana’s request for it on the same day; it lends no money but signals discipline to investors.

Ghana has set itself a target of cutting public debt to 45% of GDP by 2034. The IMF says the new instrument will help anchor Ghana’s reforms after the loan.

The rescue came with a long debt restructuring, described in our account of the IMF exit. By mid-2026, US$40.2 billion of the US$41.2 billion in debt under treatment, or 98%, had been restructured, the IMF says.

Bondholders, China and France

Eurobonds, dollar bonds sold to foreign investors, made up US$13.1 billion of that debt and were swapped for new bonds in 2024. Government-to-government loans worth US$5.1 billion were handled through the Official Creditor Committee, the group of lending countries.

Ghana announced a memorandum with that committee on 29 January 2025, the Ministry of Finance said, naming “the committee’s co-chairs, China and France”. By June 2026, Ghana had signed bilateral deals with more than half of those creditor countries, the IMF says.

The World Bank

The World Bank is the other big multilateral lender. Its Ghana portfolio held US$4.17 billion of commitments across 16 national projects, its country page said in September 2026.

Recent approvals include US$500 million for market access and connectivity and US$300 million for secondary education. Both belong to the bank’s 2026 financial-year programme for Ghana.

China, Ghana’s Biggest Trading Partner

China is one of the most visible foreign powers in Ghana’s economy, through trade, loans, builders and miners.

Ambassador Cong Song said in Accra on 23 September 2026 that two-way trade hit a record US$14.1 billion in 2025. That was up 19.3%, the Ghana News Agency reported.

He called China Ghana’s largest trading partner and said hundreds of Chinese firms work in infrastructure, energy, mining, manufacturing and farming. Beijing also offers zero tariffs on goods from African countries that recognise it diplomatically.

Chinese contractor Sinohydro built the 400-megawatt Bui hydropower dam under a 2007 contract. China’s Exim Bank lent much of the money, Modern Ghana reported in 2011.

A US$2 billion road deal with Sinohydro, brokered in 2017, is repaid “in exchange for Ghana’s refined bauxite”, Graphic Online reported. Bauxite is the ore used to make aluminium.

Zijin Mining of China bought Newmont’s Akyem gold mine for US$1 billion in a sale finalised in 2025, African Mining Market reported. Our piece on Ghana-China mining partnerships looks at Accra’s push for more local processing.

Beijing’s stated aims are deeper trade and closer cooperation. Its deals also show a clear interest in bauxite and gold.

Ghana’s environment minister, Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, said at the same reception that all investment “must be undertaken in accordance with Ghana’s laws”.

The Bui hydropower dam, built by Chinese contractor Sinohydro, shortly before its official opening. File photo, November 2013. (Photo: Wtshymanski, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Gold and Oil, the Foreign Companies That Matter Most

Gold is Ghana’s biggest export, worth more than half of export earnings in 2025, according to the IMF. Most large mines are run by foreign groups that pay royalties and taxes to the state.

What Ghana Wants Back

Lease renewals give Ghana a chance to reset terms with foreign miners. Gold Fields said in August 2026 that it was still awaiting a formal reply to its July proposal on Tarkwa.

The company warned that an adverse outcome would have a material impact on the group.

Oil is calmer. Tullow has signed a rig contract for up to 10 new wells in 2027 and 2028.

Newmont, a gold giant listed in New York since 1940, runs the Ahafo South and Ahafo North mines, its operations page shows.

AngloGold Ashanti runs Obuasi, an underground mine 1,500 metres deep about 60 km south of Kumasi, and the Iduapriem open pit, according to the company.

Gold Fields, a miner with operations from South Africa to Australia, runs Tarkwa, whose leases expire in April 2027; it applied for renewal in November 2025, Mining Weekly reported.

London-listed Tullow Oil, also quoted in Accra, operates the offshore Jubilee field, which averaged 70,800 barrels a day (gross) in the first half of 2026, Africa Oil+Gas Report said.

Kosmos Energy, listed in New York and London, discovered Jubilee in 2007 and holds 38.61% of it, next to Tullow’s 38.98% and 19.69% for state oil firm GNPC, Kosmos says.

Land disturbed by small-scale gold mining at Tarkwa, the western Ghana town that gives Gold Fields’ big mine its name. File photo, published 2015. (Photo: Mozhgon Rajaee et al., CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Cocoa Money Comes Home

Cocoa is Ghana’s other famous export, sold through COCOBOD, the state board that buys beans from farmers and sells them abroad. For more than three decades it financed each harvest with syndicated bank loans, bne IntelliNews reported.

For the 2026/27 season, COCOBOD launched a GH¢16.3 billion (about US$1.38 billion) Domestic Cocoa Notes Programme, borrowing in cedis at home. All conversions here use about 11.8 cedis to the US dollar, the October 2026 rate.

The first tranche raised GH¢3.39 billion (about US$287 million), short of a GH¢4 billion (about US$339 million) target, Asaase Radio reported. Ghana-based banks and brokers such as GCB Bank, CalBank and Absa Bank Ghana ran the sale.

Most beans are still sold abroad, so world prices still shape what farmers earn. Our report on COCOBOD’s domestic financing plan explains the shift in detail.

Who Invests in Ghana, the 2025 Numbers

The Ghana Investment Promotion Centre (GIPC), the state agency that registers foreign projects, counted about US$2.61 billion of foreign direct investment in 2025. That provisional figure compared with US$652 million in 2024, Citi Newsroom reported.

By number of projects, China led with 70, ahead of India with 22 and Nigeria with 10. The United Arab Emirates followed with 9 and the UK with 8.

By value, the Cayman Islands led with US$500 million, just ahead of China with US$486 million.

The United States accounted for only US$51 million. Petroleum again led foreign investment, with 18 oil and gas projects worth US$994 million registered by the Petroleum Commission, the Ghanaian Times reported.

Nigeria added US$105 million, and joint French-Nigerian ventures another US$100 million.

A harbour development by China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC) in Jamestown, Accra. File photo, February 2023. (Photo: Matti Blume, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The United States, Aid, Security and Deportations

Washington’s ties are old: Ghana hosted the first Peace Corps volunteers sent overseas in 1961, the State Department notes. In 2026 the relationship turns on security, health money, trade and migration.

In March 2018, Ghana’s parliament ratified a defence cooperation agreement giving US forces access to agreed facilities and runways, Defense News reported.

The US embassy said at the time that Washington had not requested a military base. The deal came with about US$20 million for training and equipment.

Health aid is shrinking. US Chargé d’Affaires Rolf Olson said health funding fell from US$82 million in 2025 to US$53 million for 2026.

Washington had spent US$2.2 billion on Ghana’s health sector since 2012, Modern Ghana reported. Olson said the cuts were meant to be gradual, not a sudden cut-off.

By October 2025, Ghana had received two groups of West African deportees from the US, MyJoyOnline reported. President Mahama said Ghana “will not become a dumping ground for deportees”.

Ministers describe the arrangement as a memorandum of understanding rather than a treaty. In June 2026, rights lawyers sued Ghana at the court of ECOWAS, the West African bloc, for 27 deportees, Pulse Ghana reported.

The deportees’ lawyer, Beatrice Njeri, is a litigator with the Global Strategic Litigation Council. Democracy Hub, a Ghanaian pressure group, took a separate case to Ghana’s Supreme Court, MyJoyOnline reported.

AGOA, the US law that lets eligible African countries export many goods to the US duty-free, lapsed on 30 September 2025. A short extension followed in February 2026, and a law signed on 2 September 2026 extends it to 2028, BusinessDay reported.

The Diaspora Sends More Than Investors Bring

One of Ghana’s biggest sources of foreign money does not come from companies at all. Ghanaians abroad sent home about US$7.8 billion in 2025, up from about US$4.6 billion in 2024, Graphic Online reported.

Bank of Ghana Governor Johnson Asiama put them at about 6% of GDP at a diaspora meeting in Virginia in April 2026. GIPC’s chief executive noted at the same meeting that diaspora money was more than double the year’s foreign direct investment.

What Ghana wants from the diaspora is investment, not only cash for families. The central bank’s “Remit2Invest” campaign urges people abroad to fund investment, a theme in our look at Ghana’s geopolitics.

What It Means for US Readers

For investors, Ghana foreign exposure runs through shares traded in New York. Newmont, Kosmos Energy and AngloGold Ashanti all depend partly on Ghanaian mines and wells.

The Tarkwa lease talks are the main near-term risk to watch. A deal on fair terms would reassure other miners, while a dispute would raise doubts about Ghana’s contracts.

For US policy, Ghana is a test of how Washington mixes smaller aid budgets with deportation deals and security access. Our guide to who holds power in Ghana explains the government making those choices, and the Ghana hub tracks new developments.

Ghana’s recovery also matters for anyone holding its restructured bonds, covered in our report on Ghana’s debt recovery.

What Is Not Known

The full text of the US-Ghana deportation memorandum has not been published. Ghana’s Supreme Court ordered the attorney-general in February 2026 to show it to the challengers’ lawyers, and its legal fate remains open.

Ghana has not yet finished bilateral deals with every official creditor. Nor is it clear whether Tarkwa’s lease will be renewed on terms Gold Fields accepts.

Washington has not decided whether a final health aid instalment will follow for the 2027 fiscal year. That decision will shape clinics and programmes that depended on US money.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Ghana still in an IMF programme?

Not a lending one. The US$3 billion Extended Credit Facility ended with a final review on 27 July 2026, and Ghana is moving to a 36-month IMF Policy Coordination Instrument that brings monitoring but no money.

Who is Ghana’s biggest foreign trading partner?

China. Its ambassador said two-way trade reached a record US$14.1 billion in 2025, up 19.3%, and called China Ghana’s largest trading partner.

Does the United States have a military base in Ghana?

No declared base. A 2018 defence cooperation agreement gives US forces access to agreed facilities and runways, and the US embassy said at the time that it had not requested a base.

Which foreign companies mine gold in Ghana?

The big operators include Newmont at Ahafo, AngloGold Ashanti at Obuasi and Iduapriem, Gold Fields at Tarkwa and China’s Zijin Mining at Akyem. Gold made up more than half of Ghana’s export earnings in 2025.

How much money do Ghanaians abroad send home?

About US$7.8 billion in 2025, roughly 6% of GDP, according to the Bank of Ghana governor. That is more than double Ghana’s foreign direct investment for the year.

Why does Ghana accept deportees from the United States?

Ghana agreed in 2025 to take West African deportees under what ministers call a memorandum of understanding with Washington. President Mahama has said it does not undermine Ghana’s sovereignty, and the deal has been challenged in Ghana’s Supreme Court and at the ECOWAS court.

World.title: Morocco Culture, the Key Figures to Know in 2026
World.content:
MOROCCO · CULTURE

Key Facts — The country Morocco is a North African kingdom of 36.8 million people (2024 census) whose 2011 constitution makes both Arabic and Tamazight official languages.

— The identity The constitution names Arab-Islamic, Amazigh and Saharan-Hassani roots, enriched by African, Andalusian, Hebraic and Mediterranean influences.

— The music Gnawa, a Sufi trance music born of the slave trade, joined UNESCO’s heritage list in 2019; rappers such as ElGrande Toto play stadium stages at home.

— The writers and film Tahar Ben Jelloun (1987) and Leïla Slimani (2016) won France’s Prix Goncourt; Maryam Touzani’s Calle Málaga was Morocco’s 2026 Oscar entry.

— The sport The Atlas Lions reached the 2022 World Cup semi-finals and the 2026 quarter-finals; Morocco co-hosts the 2030 World Cup with Spain and Portugal.

— Still open The Court of Arbitration for Sport heard the dispute over the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations final on 8 October 2026; its ruling was still pending on 10 October 2026.

Morocco culture reaches Americans more often than they notice, through World Cup football, Cannes films, Goncourt-winning novels and Gnawa trance music. This guide names the musicians, writers, film-makers, artists and athletes shaping the kingdom in 2026, and what they reveal about it.

Gnawa musicians perform in the medina of Essaouira. File photo, 2019. (Photo: Elmehdi alem, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Who Shapes Morocco Culture in 2026

Morocco is a North African kingdom of 36.8 million people, according to the census taken in September 2024. The count was run by the High Commission for Planning (HCP), the national statistics office.

Its 2011 constitution describes a national identity forged from Arab-Islamic, Amazigh and Saharan-Hassani components. The same preamble adds African, Andalusian, Hebraic and Mediterranean influences.

Amazigh is the name of North Africa’s Indigenous peoples, often called Berbers in English. Article 5 of the constitution makes their language, Tamazight, an official language alongside Arabic.

The same article commits the state to preserving Hassani, the Arabic dialect of the Saharan south. Every name in this guide draws on that layered Morocco culture, part Arab, part Amazigh, part African.

Since a Royal Cabinet decision of 3 May 2023, Yennayer, the Amazigh New Year, has been a paid national holiday. In 2026 it fell on Wednesday 14 January, the third time Moroccans marked it as a day off.

Background on the country sits on the Rio Times Morocco page. Who holds political power is set out in the Morocco politics explainer.

Gnawa, Chaabi and Rap, the Sound of Morocco

Gnawa is a Moroccan trance tradition with a global following. UNESCO inscribed it in 2019 on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

UNESCO describes Gnawa as Sufi brotherhood music that grew out of the experience of slavery and the slave trade. It traces the tradition back at least to the 16th century.

Its all-night ceremonies use rhythm and trance as a form of therapy. UNESCO notes that the number of master musicians is growing in Morocco’s villages and cities.

The genre’s showcase is the Gnaoua and World Music Festival in Essaouira, an Atlantic port town. Its 27th edition ran from 25 to 27 June 2026, and organisers have set 24 to 26 June 2027 for the next.

The festival is produced by A3 Communication, whose president Neila Tazi is its producer. Since 2024 it has hosted a training programme with Berklee College of Music in Boston, as covered in the Gnaoua festival report.

Mawazine, held in Rabat and neighbouring Salé, is the mass-audience event of Morocco culture. Its organiser, the Maroc Cultures association, counted nearly 3.6 million festivalgoers at the 21st edition in June 2026, Hespress reported.

Moroccan names shared the 2026 bill with global acts such as Tiësto and Malian singer Oumou Sangaré. Rappers ElGrande Toto and Dizzy Dros and singer Douzi all performed.

Chaabi, from the Arabic word for “popular”, is Morocco’s festive popular music. Chaabi star Abdelaziz Stati and Amazigh singer Fatima Tabaamrant played the Salé stage reserved for Moroccan artists.

What the music says about the country is simple: African roots, Arab poetry and Amazigh song sit side by side. Rap now carries the same mix to a younger, urban audience.

Musicians on stage at the Gnaoua and World Music Festival in Essaouira. File photo, 2012. (Photo: Magharebia, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Writers Who Carry Morocco to the World

Two Moroccan novelists, both writing in French, have won the Prix Goncourt. The prize is awarded each year by France’s Académie Goncourt.

Tahar Ben Jelloun, born in Fez on 15 December 1947, won it in 1987 for La Nuit sacrée (The Sacred Night). In January 2026 Gallimard published Pigiste au Monde, his account of years writing for the French daily Le Monde.

Leïla Slimani won the 2016 Goncourt for Chanson douce, a novel about a nanny in Paris. She then wrote a trilogy, Le Pays des autres (The Country of Others), published from 2020 to 2025.

In June 2026 France made Slimani a knight of its National Order of Merit. The French embassy in Lisbon said the honour recognised her work for the French language and francophone cultures.

Both write in French, which shows how much of Morocco culture still travels through France. Their novels turn Moroccan and French family life into stories read far beyond North Africa.

Film and Television, From Cannes to Marrakech

Moroccan film-makers are regular guests at the Cannes Film Festival. Nabil Ayouch showed Les Chevaux de Dieu (Horses of God) in the Un Certain Regard section in 2012.

His 2024 film Everybody Loves Touda screened in the Cannes Première section. It follows a village singer who dreams of becoming a cheikha in Casablanca.

Cheikhas are traditional women singers, once admired, whose standing fell after many moved to city cabarets from the 1970s, the festival notes. The festival’s own headline says the film rehabilitates them.

Maryam Touzani, Ayouch’s wife, co-wrote Touda with him. Her own films Adam (2019) and The Blue Caftan (2022) both screened in Un Certain Regard.

Her third feature, Calle Málaga, is set in Tangier and stars Spanish actress Carmen Maura. It won the audience award in the Venice Spotlight section, and Le360 reports it was Morocco’s entry for the 2026 Oscars.

The Marrakech International Film Festival brings world cinema to the city late each year. Its 2025 jury was led by South Korean director Bong Joon Ho, according to Morocco World News.

The 2026 edition, the 23rd, is scheduled for 20 to 28 November, according to La Tribune de Marrakech. Its jury and film selection had not been announced by late September 2026.

Morocco is also a back lot for foreign crews, including American ones. Foreign productions spent 1.21 billion dirhams (about US$122 million, at 9.95 dirhams to the US dollar) there in 2025.

The figure comes from the Moroccan Cinema Centre (CCM), the state film body, as reported by Le360. Ouarzazate, a desert town south of the High Atlas, has hosted Moroccan and foreign shoots for decades.

In June 2026 work began there on an international cinema city with a budget of 240 million dirhams (about US$24 million). The culture ministry presented it as a complement to the private studios already in the town.

On television, SNRT, the national broadcaster, runs channels including Al Aoula, sports channel Arryadia and the Amazigh-language channel Tamazight.

Film sets at the Atlas Corporation Studios in Ouarzazate, a desert town used by foreign crews. File photo, 2019. (Photo: Yair Haklai, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Visual Artists, From Casablanca to London

Tate, the British national gallery group, links the Casablanca Art School to an intense period of artistic rebirth after independence. Its peak came in the 1960s and 1970s.

The school was led by Farid Belkahia, Mohammed Chabâa and Mohamed Melehi. Tate St Ives showed work by 22 artists from its circle from May 2023 to January 2024.

The pieces ranged from abstract paintings and urban murals to applied arts, typography, graphics and interior design.

The contemporary photographer Hassan Hajjaj was born in Larache in 1961 and has lived in London since his teens. He mixes fashion portraiture, documentary photography and collage.

His portraits of musicians, framed with recycled tin cans, fill My Rock Stars at the Philharmonie de Paris. The show runs from 22 September 2026 to 25 April 2027.

Both generations turn crafts, colour and street life into modern art. That habit of borrowing from everyday objects runs through Morocco culture abroad.

Sport Icons and the Atlas Lions

Football is the loudest part of Morocco culture, and the national team is nicknamed the Atlas Lions. In Qatar in 2022, they became the first African nation to reach a World Cup semi-final, Hespress notes.

At the 2026 World Cup, Morocco beat Canada 3-0 in the round of 16, then lost 2-0 to France in the quarter-finals. Morocco World News called it the first Arab and African side to reach back-to-back quarter-finals.

The team’s star is Achraf Hakimi, a defender for Paris Saint-Germain (PSG). He is the first Moroccan named African Player of the Year since Mustapha Hadji in 1998.

CAF, the Confederation of African Football, gave him the 2025 award in Rabat on 19 November 2025. Ghizlane Chebbak took the women’s prize at the same ceremony.

Hakimi, sixth in the 2025 Ballon d’Or vote, is nominated again for the 2026 prize. The winner will be named in London on 26 October 2026.

Morocco’s under-20 team won the 2025 Under-20 World Cup, beating Argentina 2-0 in Santiago, Chile, on 19 October 2025. Le360 called it the country’s first world title.

Morocco then hosted the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations, whose final against Senegal was played in Rabat on 18 January 2026. Senegal won 1-0 on the pitch with an extra-time goal by Pape Gueye.

Senegal’s players had left the field for 16 minutes in protest at a penalty awarded to Morocco. On 17 March 2026 CAF’s appeals committee recorded a 3-0 forfeit win for Morocco, and Senegal appealed.

Nawal El Moutawakel won the 400m hurdles at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics. She was the first African and first Arab woman to win Olympic gold.

She joined the International Olympic Committee in 1998 and was elected its vice-president in 2012 and again in 2024. Steeplechaser Soufiane El Bakkali won Olympic gold at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024, plus world titles in 2022 and 2023.

Morocco will co-host the 2030 World Cup with Spain and Portugal, as FIFA’s Congress decided on 11 December 2024. Three centenary matches will be played in Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.

The 2026 run is reviewed in Africa’s World Cup record run. The money behind new stadiums is covered in who runs Morocco’s economy.

Morocco supporters at the France v Morocco quarter-final of the 2026 World Cup. Photo, 9 July 2026. (Photo: Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Festivals and Media Voices to Follow

Autumn 2026 is busy for visitors who want to see Morocco culture live. Moroccan news sites Hespress and Le360 cover the big events in French and English editions.

La Tribune de Marrakech, a local news site, lists these fixtures:

Fez Festival of Sufi Culture: 17 to 24 October 2026.

Marrakech Jazz Experience: 30 October to 1 November 2026.

Visa for Music, Rabat, 13th edition: 18 to 21 November 2026.

Marrakech International Film Festival, 23rd edition: 20 to 28 November 2026.

Trans-Saharan International Film Festival, Zagora: 6 to 11 December 2026.

What It Means for US Readers

For American travellers, the festival dates above offer a planned way to see Morocco culture live. Essaouira’s Gnaoua festival in June and Marrakech’s film festival in November are the two anchors.

Musicians have a direct US link: Berklee College of Music in Boston co-runs a training programme with the Gnaoua festival.

Sports fans met the Atlas Lions at the 2026 World Cup, hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico. Hakimi plays Champions League football for PSG, which won the competition again in 2026.

The 2028 Olympics return to Los Angeles, where El Moutawakel won gold in 1984. El Bakkali’s renewed sponsorship deal is framed around those Games, Morocco World News reported.

Live events in Casablanca, the business capital, are listed in the Casablanca October 2026 guide. Morocco’s Unity Day holiday on 31 October is set out in the Unity Day explainer.

What Is Not Known

The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), the Swiss-based tribunal for sports disputes, heard Senegal’s appeal on 8 October 2026. Its ruling on who won the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations was still pending on 10 October 2026.

Senegal’s federation asks CAS to declare it the champion; Morocco’s federation and CAF are the other parties. Hespress reported on 10 October 2026 that the ruling could take days or weeks.

The jury and line-up of the 23rd Marrakech film festival had not been published by late September 2026. Whether Hakimi wins the 2026 Ballon d’Or will only be known on 26 October 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Morocco culture known for?

Morocco culture is known for Gnawa trance music, chaabi and rap, Arab and Amazigh traditions, French-language novels, Cannes-selected films and the Atlas Lions football team.

What is Gnawa music?

Gnawa is a Sufi brotherhood music that grew out of the experience of slavery and dates back at least to the 16th century. UNESCO added it to its intangible heritage list in 2019.

When is the Gnaoua festival in Essaouira?

The 27th edition ran from 25 to 27 June 2026. The organisers have set 24 to 26 June 2027 for the next edition.

Which Moroccan writers have won the Prix Goncourt?

Tahar Ben Jelloun won in 1987 for La Nuit sacrée, and Leïla Slimani won in 2016 for Chanson douce. Both write in French.

Is Tamazight an official language in Morocco?

Yes. Article 5 of the 2011 constitution makes Tamazight an official language alongside Arabic, and the Amazigh New Year has been a paid holiday since 2023.

Who are Morocco’s sport icons?

Footballer Achraf Hakimi, 2025 African Player of the Year, leads the list. Olympic champions Nawal El Moutawakel and Soufiane El Bakkali are the athletics icons of Morocco culture.

Who won the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations?

Senegal won the final on the pitch, but CAF later awarded Morocco a 3-0 forfeit. Senegal’s appeal was heard on 8 October 2026, and the CAS ruling was still pending on 10 October 2026.

World.title: Egypt Culture, the Key Figures to Know in 2026
World.content:
EGYPT · CULTURE

Key Facts — The country Egypt, an Arab and African nation on the Nile, had about 109.5 million people at home on 19 September 2026, according to the CAPMAS statistics agency.

— Why it matters Egypt culture reached US audiences in 2026: the national team played World Cup games in Seattle, Dallas and Atlanta, and singer Tul8te plans a North American tour.

— Music Classical legend Umm Kulthum died in 1975; Amr Diab and Mohamed Mounir remain active stars, and mahraganat is the electronic street sound of Cairo.

— Books and film Naguib Mahfouz won the 1988 Nobel Prize in Literature; the Cairo International Film Festival holds its 47th edition from 11 to 20 November 2026.

— Sport Mohamed Salah joined Turkey’s Trabzonspor in August 2026 after nine seasons at Liverpool; Egyptians Mostafa Asal and Amina Orfi led squash’s world rankings in September 2026.

— Who runs culture Higher Education Minister Abdelaziz Konsowa has been acting culture minister since July 2026, after Gihane Zaki resigned over an intellectual property ruling.

— Still open As of October 2026, Egypt has not named a permanent culture minister.

Egypt culture is often reduced to pharaohs, yet its living singers, writers, film-makers and athletes draw audiences far beyond the Nile. For US readers the link grew closer in 2026, when Egypt’s World Cup team played in Seattle, Dallas and Atlanta.

The new Grand Egyptian Museum near the Giza pyramids drew about four million visitors from November 2025 to August 2026.

The Grand Egyptian Museum near the Giza pyramids at dusk. File photo, 2026. (Photo: Mohamed abdelzaher, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)
