Music Stars From Umm Kulthum to Mahraganat

Any guide to Egyptian music starts with Umm Kulthum, known as the Star of the Orient. She arrived in Cairo in 1923 and gave a concert on the first Thursday of every month, broadcast by Egyptian Radio.

She died on 3 February 1975, and hundreds of thousands joined her funeral. That account comes from Ahram Online, the English site of the state-owned Al-Ahram newspaper group.

Among living stars, Amr Diab remains a headline act. On 7 August 2026 he opened the U Arena concert season in New Alamein, a new Mediterranean resort city, EgyptToday reported.

Mohamed Mounir is a veteran whose sound mixes Egyptian, Nubian, jazz and reggae influences, as the Cairo culture site CairoScene describes it. He sang the theme of the Ramadan 2026 drama Had Aqsa, according to the UAE paper The National.

Mahraganat, Arabic for festivals, is the electronic street music of Cairo’s poorer neighbourhoods. Wedding DJs began mixing chaabi folk songs with electronic dance beats around 2006 and 2007, according to the Cairo site Egyptian Streets.

In February 2020 the Musicians Syndicate, Egypt’s professional union for musicians, banned mahraganat singers from festivals, clubs, cafes and concerts. In June 2021 it let them join a section for monologists, which allowed public shows under morality rules.

The newest name is Tul8te, a masked singer who keeps his identity hidden and emerged in 2022. His breakthrough song Layalina came from the 2024 album Tesh Shabab, and he plays Cairo’s Manara Arena on 16 October 2026.

Writers, Prizes and the Cairo Book Fair

Naguib Mahfouz, born in Cairo in 1911, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988. The Swedish Academy said he had formed an Arabian narrative art that applies to all mankind; he died in Cairo in 2006.

A newer generation is winning prizes too. In April 2025 Mohamed Samir Nada won the International Prize for Arabic Fiction for his novel The Prayer of Anxiety.

The annual award, presented in Abu Dhabi, carries US$50,000. Nada was its first Egyptian winner since 2009, according to the US trade journal Publishing Perspectives.

The Cairo International Book Fair, founded in 1969, is where Egyptian readers meet the trade each winter. Its 57th edition ran from 21 January to 3 February 2026 in New Cairo, with 1,457 publishers from 83 countries.

The Ministry of Culture counted nearly 5.9 million visitors by 2 February, the day before the fair closed, Ahram Online reported. Romania was the guest of honour.

Film, Television and Ramadan Drama

Youssef Chahine carried Egyptian cinema to the Cannes Film Festival for more than five decades. He first competed there in 1952 and received the festival’s 50th Anniversary Prize in 1997.

Mohamed Diab took Egyptian talent into Hollywood television. Marvel lists him as director of Moon Knight, a series released on the Disney+ streaming service on 30 March 2022.

At home, the biggest screen season is Ramadan, the Muslim month of fasting, when channels launch a wave of new series. Daily News Egypt counted 39 series in 2026, shown on channels such as ON and CBC and on streaming platforms.

The 2026 line-up included Amir Karara in Ras Al-Afaa, Amr Saad in Efrag and Mohamed Adel Imam in El King. Theme songs matter almost as much, and Angham, Tamer Ashour and Mohamed Adaweya all sang 2026 themes.

The Cairo International Film Festival holds its 47th edition from 11 to 20 November 2026. Its president is the veteran actor Hussein Fahmi, who still led it in September 2026, the state daily Akhbar El Yom reported.

The El Gouna Film Festival, held in a Red Sea resort town, runs its ninth edition from 15 to 23 October 2026. Together the two festivals bring stars, critics and buyers to Egypt each autumn.

Visual Artists and the Grand Egyptian Museum

Contemporary art has a prominent ambassador in Wael Shawky, born in Alexandria in 1971. His film Drama 1882, sung entirely in classical Arabic, restages the Urabi revolt against British rule.

It debuted at Egypt’s pavilion at the 2024 Venice Biennale. From 20 February to 16 March 2025 it ran at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles.

The state’s flagship cultural project is the Grand Egyptian Museum near the Giza pyramids. It was inaugurated on 1 November 2025 and opened to the public on 4 November, Ahram Online reported.

The museum shows all 5,400 objects from Tutankhamun’s burial together for the first time. Its permanent galleries cover 24,000 square metres.

About four million people visited between the opening and the end of August 2026, a museum board meeting heard in September. Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy chaired it, and museum chief executive Ahmed Ghoneim reported on recent work.

From 1 November 2026, foreign visitors pay US$5 more per ticket, the tourism ministry said in April 2026. Rio Times’ guide to what to do in Cairo in October 2026 covers the visit.

Royal statues on the Grand Staircase of the Grand Egyptian Museum. File photo, January 2025. (Photo: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Sport Icons From Salah to the Squash Champions

Mohamed Salah scored 257 goals in 442 games for Liverpool between 2017 and 2026, the English club says. He won two Premier League titles and the 2019 Champions League, and left as Liverpool’s third-highest scorer of all time.

In August 2026 he joined Trabzonspor, a Turkish top-flight club from the Black Sea city of Trabzon, as a free agent. He was still in its line-up in October 2026, Ahram Online reported.

Egypt’s national team, the Pharaohs, recorded its first-ever World Cup win in 2026, beating New Zealand 3-1 in Vancouver. It drew 1-1 with Belgium and Iran in Seattle, then beat Australia on penalties in Dallas.

In the last 16, Argentina beat Egypt 3-2 in Atlanta on 7 July 2026, according to FIFA’s match records. The game drew 192.6 million viewers on the Qatar-based broadcaster beIN SPORTS, its biggest audience for any Arab team’s match.

Egypt also produces the top-ranked players in squash. In September 2026 Mostafa Asal led the men’s world rankings, Ahram Online reported.

In the same update Amina Orfi, aged 19, became the youngest women’s world No. 1 ever.

Egypt, in red, play Tunisia in a friendly in Abu Dhabi. File photo, October 2012. (Photo: Saiflee100, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Media Voices and Television Hosts

Amr Adib hosts al-Hekaya, meaning The Story, an evening talk show on MBC Masr. The channel is the Egyptian outlet of the MBC television group.

Adib announced on air in January 2026 that he had renewed his contract with MBC Masr, Egypt Independent reported. He gave no details of the new terms.

Bassem Youssef, a former cardiac surgeon, became famous with Al-Bernameg, a satirical television programme. He later moved to the United States and became a US citizen, according to Ahram Online.

In August 2026 his tour of Australia and New Zealand was postponed while he gathered documents for his visa application. Youssef said the shows had not been cancelled and would be rescheduled.

Egyptian Radio, which first went on air from Cairo on 31 May 1934, marked its 90th anniversary in 2024. It broadcast Umm Kulthum’s monthly concerts.

Festivals and the Ministry of Culture

Egypt’s cultural year follows a clear calendar, which helps visitors plan around it. These are the main dates for 2026:

Who Runs the Ministry

Egypt’s Ministry of Culture has its own theatre sector and works with state bodies such as the General Egyptian Book Organization. In October 2026 its touring project, Confrontation and Touring, reached villages in North Sinai and the Nile Delta province of Sharqiya.

The ministry’s leadership changed in July 2026, when Culture Minister Gihane Zaki resigned. The Court of Cassation, Egypt’s top appeals court, had upheld a ruling against her.

The case was an intellectual property dispute with the writer Soheir Abdel-Hamid. The government then named Higher Education Minister Abdelaziz Konsowa acting culture minister until a permanent appointment.

In October 2026 Konsowa still held both posts, the Cairo daily Youm7 reported. For the wider political picture, see Egypt Explained and who holds power in Egypt in 2026.

Cairo International Book Fair: 21 January to 3 February 2026, in New Cairo.

Ramadan drama season: the Muslim fasting month, which moves about 11 days earlier each year.

El Gouna Film Festival: 15 to 23 October 2026, ninth edition, on the Red Sea coast.

Cairo Jazz Festival: 5 to 7 November 2026, 18th edition.

Cairo International Film Festival: 11 to 20 November 2026, 47th edition.

What Egypt Culture Says About the Country

Egypt culture shows a country where the state still sets many rules. A syndicate can ban a music genre, and a court ruling led to a culture minister’s resignation.

Yet the stars who travel furthest often build their audiences outside those channels. Salah made his name in England, Shawky in international art shows, and Tul8te through hit singles.

The Grand Egyptian Museum ties both threads together. It is a state project that presents the pharaonic past to a global audience.

More news on the country is collected on the Rio Times Egypt page.

The Giza pyramids seen from inside the Grand Egyptian Museum. File photo, 2024. (Photo: Caoimheen3, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What It Means for US Readers

For American travellers, the Grand Egyptian Museum is the main new stop near Giza. Foreign tickets rise by US$5 from 1 November 2026.

October and November also bring the El Gouna, Cairo Jazz and Cairo film festivals.

The US State Department rates Egypt at Level 2, exercise increased caution, in an advisory issued on 15 July 2025. It says not to travel to northern and middle Sinai or to Egypt’s border areas.

Tul8te’s November 2026 tour lists Washington, New York, Miami and Los Angeles, according to Ahram Online. US fans who followed Salah at Liverpool now follow him in Turkey’s top league.

Egyptian talent already works inside American culture. Moon Knight premiered on Disney+ in 2022, and Shawky’s Drama 1882 played in Los Angeles in 2025.

What Is Not Known

Egypt has not named a permanent culture minister, and the timing of an appointment is unclear. The acting minister also runs higher education.

The Grand Egyptian Museum has not published a full-year visitor total; the four million figure covers November 2025 to August 2026. Venues for Tul8te’s North American dates were not part of the tour announcement in September 2026.

How long Salah stays in Turkey, and how mahraganat rules evolve under future syndicate leaders, remain open questions. The 2020 ban and the 2021 reversal show how quickly such rules can change.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Egypt culture best known for?

Egypt culture is best known abroad for its pharaonic heritage, now shown at the Grand Egyptian Museum near Giza. Its modern stars include singers Umm Kulthum and Amr Diab, Nobel laureate Naguib Mahfouz and footballer Mohamed Salah.

Who are the most famous Egyptian singers?

Umm Kulthum, who died in 1975, is the classical giant. Amr Diab and Mohamed Mounir remain active stars, and the masked singer Tul8te is the newest name, with a North American tour planned for November 2026.

Which Egyptian writer won the Nobel Prize?

Naguib Mahfouz won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988. He was born in Cairo in 1911 and died there in 2006.

Which club does Mohamed Salah play for in 2026?

Salah joined Trabzonspor, a club in Turkey’s top league, in August 2026 as a free agent. He had spent nine seasons at Liverpool, scoring 257 goals in 442 games.

When is the Cairo International Film Festival in 2026?

The 47th Cairo International Film Festival runs from 11 to 20 November 2026. The El Gouna Film Festival on the Red Sea coast comes first, from 15 to 23 October 2026.

When did the Grand Egyptian Museum open?

The museum was inaugurated on 1 November 2025 and opened to the public on 4 November 2025. It drew about four million visitors by the end of August 2026.

Who is Egypt’s culture minister?

As of October 2026, Higher Education Minister Abdelaziz Konsowa is acting culture minister. He took over in July 2026 after Gihane Zaki resigned.

World.title: Foreign Powers and Investors in Kenya 2026
World.content:
KENYA · FOREIGN PLAYERS

Key Facts — The country Kenya is an East African republic on the Indian Ocean, home to the UN’s African headquarters, led by President William Ruto, with elections due in August 2027.

— The lenders In June 2026 the World Bank’s IDA held 29.9% of Kenya’s foreign public debt, Eurobond investors 23.9%, China 10.9% and the IMF 7.8%.

— The investors Foreign direct investment hit a record US$3.2 billion in 2025, UNCTAD figures show. A court voided the state’s Safaricom sale to Vodacom in September 2026; appeals are pending.

— The diaspora Kenyans abroad sent home US$5.04 billion in 2025, 54% of it from the United States, central bank data show.

— Security US forces use Manda Bay near Somalia, Britain keeps an army training unit near Nanyuki, and Nairobi hosts the UN’s headquarters in Africa.

— What it means for you American taxpayers, garment importers and tech firms all have money riding on Kenya, including a US$1.6 billion health deal.

— Still open A new IMF programme, the Safaricom appeal and the 2027 election could shift who holds sway in Kenya.

Kenya’s foreign partners, from the World Bank to US troops and Kenyans abroad, shape a country Washington treats as a key ally. This guide maps who lends, invests, trains soldiers, gives aid and sends money home, as of October 2026.

It also sets out what each of them wants in return.

A Kenya Railways locomotive on the Standard Gauge Railway between Mombasa and Nairobi, the best-known project financed by China (file photo, 2017). (Photo: Erasmus Kamugisha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Who Brings Money Into Kenya

Kenya’s public debt stood at KSh13.01 trillion (about US$100.5 billion) in June 2026, or 68.5% of GDP, the National Treasury says. Foreign lenders held KSh5.68 trillion (about US$43.9 billion) of it.

This guide converts at KSh129.50 to the US dollar, the Treasury’s own end-June 2026 rate. The shilling traded close to that level in October 2026.

Foreign direct investment, money that builds or buys businesses, hit a record US$3.2 billion in 2025, up 37.7% on 2024. The figures come from UNCTAD, the UN trade agency, as reported by Business Daily, a Nairobi paper.

Kenyans living abroad sent home even more: US$5.04 billion in 2025, according to the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK). That makes the diaspora a bigger source of dollars than all foreign direct investment.

President William Ruto’s government deals with Washington, Beijing, European capitals and the Gulf at the same time. Under the constitution, his term runs to the general election due in August 2027.

For the diplomatic side of this story, see Kenya Geopolitics Explained. For the domestic players, see who runs Kenya’s economy and the Kenya news page.

The Lenders: World Bank, Bondholders, China and the IMF

The Treasury’s June 2026 public debt bulletin lists who holds Kenya’s foreign debt. The figures are provisional and include loans the state guarantees.

Multilateral lenders such as the World Bank held 54.6% of the total, commercial creditors 27.1% and individual governments 17.1%.

China and the Railway Debt

Kenya’s debt to China is shrinking. Kenya owed Beijing about a fifth less in June 2026 than in 2021, The Star, a Nairobi daily, reported.

The best-known project China financed is the Standard Gauge Railway, which links the port of Mombasa with Nairobi. In July 2025, the Export-Import Bank of China agreed to convert three railway loans from US dollars into yuan.

Yuan debt made up 11.7% of Kenya’s foreign debt by currency in June 2026, the Treasury says.

The Missing IMF Programme

In March 2025, the IMF said the final review of Kenya’s loan programme would not go ahead. Kenya had formally asked for a new programme, the IMF added.

The old programme, worth about US$3.6 billion, had run since April 2021, Capital FM reported. Talks on a successor have been slowed by governance and corruption concerns, People Daily reported in October 2026.

CBK governor Kamau Thugge said on 8 October 2026 that the 2026/27 financing plan left out IMF money. A deal would still matter to the Treasury because IMF loans are cheap, he said.

International Development Association (IDA), the World Bank’s arm for poorer countries: KSh1.70 trillion (about US$13.1 billion), or 29.9%.

International sovereign bonds, known as Eurobonds and sold to investors abroad: KSh1.36 trillion (about US$10.5 billion), or 23.9%.

China: KSh616.9 billion (about US$4.8 billion), or 10.9%.

African Development Bank group: KSh566.6 billion (about US$4.4 billion), or 10.0%.

International Monetary Fund (IMF): KSh442.6 billion (about US$3.4 billion), or 7.8%.

Japan: KSh137.9 billion (about US$1.06 billion), counting loans the state guarantees.

France KSh101.0 billion (about US$780 million), Germany KSh54.1 billion (about US$418 million), United States KSh8.1 billion (about US$62 million).

Foreign Companies and Investors

Investors put money into Kenya’s digital economy and renewable energy in 2025, Business Daily reported. The Star named geothermal power, data centres, fintech and factories serving the region.

Vodacom and Safaricom

Safaricom runs M-Pesa, the phone-based money service used across Kenya. On 30 June 2026, Britain’s Vodafone said its African subsidiary, Vodacom Group, had raised its Safaricom stake to 55%.

Vodacom paid the Kenyan government KSh204 billion (about US$1.58 billion) for 15%, and Vodafone KSh68 billion (about US$525 million) for 5%. Vodafone said the deal gave its group control of “one of Africa’s most successful telecoms and financial services businesses.”

In September 2026, three High Court judges declared the government’s sale null and void and ordered the shares returned, Citizen Digital reported. The Treasury and Vodacom both said they would appeal, according to Capital FM.

Microsoft and G42

In May 2024, Microsoft and G42, an artificial-intelligence company from the United Arab Emirates, announced an initial US$1 billion plan for Kenya. Its centre was a data centre at Olkaria, run on geothermal power.

By May 2026 the plan had hit Kenya’s power limits, Ruto said, according to Data Center Dynamics. “To switch on that one data center, we would need to shut off power for half the country,” he said.

Gulf Oil on Credit

Since 2023, Kenya has bought fuel through a state-to-state deal with Aramco Trading Fujairah, ADNOC Global Trading and ENOC. ENOC is the Emirates National Oil Company, and the suppliers give Kenya 180 days to pay.

NTV Kenya reported in December 2024 that the deal had helped shield the shilling. In the year to June 2026, more than a quarter of its cargoes loaded in India and Europe instead.

Gulf suppliers moved loading points after the US and Israeli war with Iran disrupted the region, Business Daily reported in September 2026.

Adani and the Limits of Openness

Openness has limits. In November 2024, Ruto ordered the cancellation of a planned airport expansion and a signed power-line contract involving India’s Adani Group.

He cited information from “our investigative agencies and partner nations,” the Daily Nation reported.

Office towers and apartment blocks in Upper Hill, a district of Nairobi, Kenya’s capital (file photo, 2025). (Photo: Daniel Case, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The United States: Security Partner, Market and Donor

On 24 June 2024, President Joe Biden made Kenya a major non-NATO ally, a US status for close military partners. For Washington, the main draw is Kenya’s border with Somalia.

US forces operate from Manda Bay, an airfield on the Kenyan coast near the Somali border, and from nearby Camp Simba. Fighters from al-Shabaab, the Somali militant group, overran the Manda Bay airfield in 2020, killing a US soldier and two contractors.

Work on a 10,000-foot runway expansion there began on 29 January 2026. Stars and Stripes, the US military newspaper, said the State Department paid the US$71 million cost.

Trade is the second strand. President Donald Trump signed a law extending AGOA, the US duty-free scheme for African goods, to 31 December 2028, People Daily reported.

US goods imports from Kenya totalled US$862.2 million in 2025, the US Census Bureau says. Clothing makes up most of the AGOA trade, and accredited firms employed 82,026 people in 2025, Kenya’s statistics bureau says.

Health is the third. On 4 December 2025, Kenya signed the first health deal under the America First Global Health Strategy, the State Department says.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US would invest US$1.6 billion in health over five years. Kenya also led the UN-backed police mission against Haiti’s gangs from June 2024.

The last Kenyan contingent came home on 28 April 2026, People Daily reported. The mission handed over to a UN-mandated Gang Suppression Force, Dawan Africa reported in September 2026.

A US Marine Corps commander greets the commander of Kenya Navy Base Manda Bay, on the coast near Somalia where US forces also operate (file photo, 2025). (Photo: Cpl. Jacob Richardson, U.S. Marine Corps, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

Britain, Europe and Japan

Britain runs the British Army Training Unit Kenya (BATUK) in the Laikipia region around the town of Nanyuki. Kenya was expecting about 1,500 British soldiers for an exercise in September 2026.

In July 2026, that exercise, Haraka Storm, was moved out of Kenya after attempts to secure training licences failed. The dispute turned on legal jurisdiction over British personnel and their immunity, Citizen Digital reported.

European governments are smaller lenders. In June 2026, Kenya owed France KSh101.0 billion (about US$780 million) and Germany KSh54.1 billion (about US$418 million).

It also owed KSh27.5 billion (about US$212 million) to the European Investment Bank, the EU’s lending arm. Japan held KSh137.9 billion (about US$1.06 billion), including loans the state guarantees.

JICA, Japan’s aid agency, lists its Kenya priorities as economic infrastructure, industry, farming, universal health coverage, the environment and regional stability.

Aid, NGOs and the UN in Nairobi

Nairobi is the seat of the United Nations Office at Nairobi, which describes itself as the UN headquarters in Africa. It is home to UNEP, the UN Environment Programme, and to the headquarters of UN-Habitat, the agency for cities.

Charities and NGOs answer to the Public Benefit Organisations Regulatory Authority, under a law that took effect on 14 May 2024. In May 2026, the government moved existing NGOs onto the new framework automatically, People Daily reported.

Washington is changing how it gives. At the December 2025 signing, Rubio said the US was “not going to spend billions of dollars funding the NGO industrial complex.”

He said the new money should help Kenya’s own health system rather than outside groups. For aid groups that relied on US grants, the shift means a smaller share of US health money.

Flags of UN member states at the United Nations Office at Nairobi, the UN headquarters in Africa (file photo, 2019). (Photo: Kip254, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Diaspora: Kenyans Abroad Send More Than Investors

Remittances reached US$5.04 billion in 2025, up from US$4.95 billion in 2024, according to the CBK’s monthly data. North America accounted for 58% of the 2025 total.

The United States alone sent US$2.73 billion, or 54%, the central bank’s country breakdown shows. That ties a large part of Kenya’s foreign income to Kenyans working in America.

The flow from the US is slowing. From January to August 2026, transfers from the United States fell 12.4% from a year earlier, to US$1.59 billion.

Total remittances held almost flat at US$3.33 billion. Europe sent 16.5% more and the United Arab Emirates 53% more, while transfers from Saudi Arabia roughly halved.

Since 1 January 2026, the US has charged a 1% federal tax on remittances paid in cash, money orders or cashier’s checks. Transfers from bank accounts or US-issued cards are exempt, according to Treasury draft rules.

For the latest monthly figures, see the Kenya remittances report.

What It Means for US Readers

American money reaches Kenya through many doors: AGOA garment imports, tech firms, military spending at Manda Bay and the health deal. Kenya’s foreign policy keeps all of those doors open at once.

For investors, the Safaricom appeal is the case to watch. It will show whether a sale signed with the Kenyan state survives the country’s courts.

For Kenyan families in the US, the 1% tax applies to cash-funded transfers only. Transfers from bank accounts and US-issued cards stay tax-free.

For Washington, Kenya is a test of the shift from aid to state-to-state deals and trade. Background on the country is in Kenya Explained.

What Is Not Known

Nobody knows whether Kenya and the IMF will agree on a new programme before the August 2027 election. The Court of Appeal’s ruling on the Safaricom sale is still to come, as is a decision on the money already paid.

It is unclear whether, and at what size, the Microsoft and G42 data centre at Olkaria will go ahead. The CBK data do not show why transfers from the US fell in 2026.

Nor is it clear when large British exercises will return to Laikipia. That depends on talks over troop immunity and jurisdiction.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Kenya’s biggest foreign lender?

The World Bank’s International Development Association, which held KSh1.70 trillion (about US$13.1 billion), or 29.9% of Kenya’s foreign public debt, in June 2026. Eurobond investors came second and China third, according to the National Treasury.

How much does Kenya owe China?

KSh616.9 billion (about US$4.8 billion) at the end of June 2026, or 10.9% of Kenya’s foreign public debt. The best-known project it financed is the Standard Gauge Railway from Mombasa to Nairobi.

Does the US have troops in Kenya?

Yes. US forces operate from Manda Bay and Camp Simba on the coast near Somalia, where a US$71 million runway expansion began in January 2026. Kenya has been a major non-NATO ally of the United States since June 2024.

How much money do Kenyans abroad send home?

US$5.04 billion in 2025, according to the Central Bank of Kenya, of which US$2.73 billion came from the United States. Transfers from the US fell 12.4% in January to August 2026.

Who controls Safaricom?

Vodacom, part of Britain’s Vodafone group, raised its stake to 55% in June 2026. In September 2026 Kenya’s High Court voided the government’s 15% sale, and both the Treasury and Vodacom said they would appeal.

Does Kenya have an IMF programme in 2026?

No. Its last IMF programme, worth about US$3.6 billion, ended in 2025 after its final review was called off, and talks on a new one had not produced a deal by October 2026.

Which foreign organisations are based in Nairobi?

The United Nations Office at Nairobi, the UN headquarters in Africa, is home to UNEP and to UN-Habitat’s headquarters. UNON says it is expanding its conference facilities to give the UN a greater presence in the Global South.

World.title: Nigeria Population and Ethnic Groups Explained
World.content:
NIGERIA · POPULATION

Key Facts — The country Nigeria, a federal republic of 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory of Abuja, is Africa’s most populous country and the world’s sixth-most-populous.

— Population About 242.4 million people in mid-2026, according to the UN’s World Population Prospects 2024. The last census, in 2006, counted 140.4 million.

— Age The median age is about 18, against about 39 in the United States, according to UN estimates for 2026.

— Main groups Hausa 32.7%, Yoruba 12.8%, Igbo 11.2% and Fulani 6.6% of women aged 15 to 49 in a 2024 national survey. Ethnologue lists 520 living languages.

— Faith About 58% of women and men aged 15 to 49 in the 2024 survey were Muslim and 41% to 42% Christian. The constitution bars any state religion.

— US link 532,602 Nigerian-born people lived in the US in 2024, the largest African-born group, according to the US Census Bureau.

— Still open Nigeria has held no census since 2006. In July 2026 the census agency said only the president can set the next date.

Nigeria’s population of about 242 million is Africa’s largest, and Nigerians are the biggest African-born group in the United States. The UN expects the country to pass 350 million people by 2050.

The Hausa-Fulani, Yoruba and Igbo share it with over 200 smaller peoples, and nearly all Nigerians are Muslim or Christian.

Shoppers and traders at Balogun Market on Lagos Island, Nigeria’s largest city. File photo, 2017. (Photo: Yellowcrunchy, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

How Many People Live in Nigeria

The UN’s World Population Prospects 2024, the organisation’s official set of population estimates, puts Nigeria at about 242.4 million people in mid-2026. That makes it the sixth-most-populous country on earth, after India, China, the United States, Indonesia and Pakistan.

Growth has been fast. Nigeria had about 37 million people in 1950 and about 126 million in 2000, according to the same UN series.

In 2026 the UN expects about 7.7 million births and 2.8 million deaths in Nigeria. That adds almost 5 million people in a single year.

Nigeria’s population grew by about 2.1% a year in 2024 and 2025, according to World Bank data. At roughly that pace, a population doubles in about 34 years, by the UN’s 2026 estimate.

Looking ahead, the UN’s medium projection reaches about 359 million Nigerians by 2050. By 2100 it shows about 477 million people, more than the 421 million it projects for the United States.

The official head count is much older. Nigeria’s last census, in 2006, recorded 140,431,790 people, according to census data held by the UN Statistics Division.

In July 2026, officials of the National Population Commission, the federal census agency, put the population at 238 million to 242 million. Read more about the country on our Nigeria hub.

A Very Young Population

Nigeria’s population is very young. The UN puts the median age at about 18 in 2026, meaning half of all Nigerians are younger than that.

In the United States, the median age is about 39. About 40% of Nigerians were under 15 in 2025, according to World Bank data.

The best recent picture comes from the 2024 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey, a large household survey. The National Population Commission and the federal health ministry ran it with technical help from ICF, a US firm.

Interviewers spoke to 39,050 women and 12,204 men between December 2023 and May 2024. Of everyone living in the households they visited, 45% were under 15.

The survey measured a fertility rate of 4.8 children per woman, while the UN’s model puts the 2026 rate at about 4.2. The survey’s wanted fertility rate was 4.3, so women have about half a child more than they want.

Men want larger families than women: their ideal is 6.5 children, against 5.6 for women. Life expectancy at birth was about 55 years in 2024, according to the UN and the World Bank.

This age structure means schools, clinics and the job market must grow quickly just to keep pace.

Cities, Countryside and Moving Within Nigeria

Nigeria is now a mostly urban country. About 64% of Nigerians lived in towns and cities in 2025, according to World Bank data, up from about 59% in 2019.

Lagos, on the Atlantic coast, is the largest city, according to a Library of Congress country profile. World Bank figures, based on UN urban estimates, put Nigeria’s largest metropolitan area at about 17.2 million people in 2025.

Lagos was also the capital until 12 December 1991, when Abuja took over. The same 2008 profile listed Kano and Ibadan as the next most populous cities.

Cities of more than one million people together held about 41.8 million Nigerians in 2025. Rural areas still held about 36% of the population.

People move a lot inside the country. In the 2024 health survey, 39% of women and 40% of men did not live where they were born.

Among recent movers, the most common move was from one city to another. Among men who left the countryside for a city, 55% did so for work, while marriage was the main reason women moved.

The country is divided into six geopolitical zones. The survey found 32% of adults aged 15 to 49 living in the North West and 8% in the South East.

Traders and shoppers at Wuse Market in Abuja, the federal capital. File photo, 2026. (Photo: EsthyR, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Main Ethnic Groups of Nigeria

Nigeria has more than 250 ethnic groups, according to the US Library of Congress country profile from 2008. The Hausa and Fulani have traditionally dominated the north, the Yoruba the southwest and the Igbo the east.

The best recent figures come from the 2024 health survey, which asked adults to name their ethnic group. The answers of women aged 15 to 49 break down as follows.

Men Give Almost the Same Answers

Among men, 34.0% said Hausa, 13.2% Yoruba and 10.5% Igbo. The Ijaw, the main people of the Niger Delta on the southern coast, made up 1.2%.

These shares describe adults aged 15 to 49 rather than Nigeria’s whole population. With no census since 2006, the survey is the most recent national source.

Hausa, 32.7%: the largest group, rooted in the north.

Yoruba, 12.8%: traditionally dominant in the southwest, the zone that includes Lagos.

Igbo, 11.2%: traditionally dominant in the east; see our guide to Igbo people, language and culture.

Fulani, 6.6%: often counted together with the Hausa as the Hausa-Fulani of the north.

Tiv 2.2%, Kanuri 1.9%, Ibibio 1.6%, Igala 1.3%, Ijaw 1.1% and Ekoi 1.0%.

Other groups not listed separately: 27.6%.

Dried herbs and bark for incense and traditional medicine at Kurmi Market in Kano, northern Nigeria. File photo, 2016. (Photo: Fatima Bukar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Languages: English and Hundreds More

English is Nigeria’s official language, according to the Library of Congress profile. Section 55 of the constitution says the National Assembly works in English, and in Hausa, Ibo and Yoruba once adequate arrangements exist.

Ethnologue, a reference catalogue of world languages, lists 527 languages for Nigeria. Of these, 520 are still living and 7 are extinct.

Ethnologue classes 20 living languages as institutional, its top tier, which runs from languages taught in schools to those of government. It classes 43 as dying.

The 2024 health survey used questionnaires in English, Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo, the three big group languages plus the official one.

Religion: Islam and Christianity Side by Side

Nigeria is split between Islam and Christianity, with small numbers following traditional faiths. In the 2024 health survey, 57.6% of women and 58.2% of men said they were Muslim.

Among women, 8.2% said they were Catholic and 33.7% belonged to other Christian churches, together 41.9%. Traditional religions drew 0.4% of women and 0.9% of men.

Islam dominates the North West and North East, while Christianity dominates the South West, including Lagos, according to the US State Department. In the North Central zone, Christians and Muslims live in roughly equal numbers.

Many Nigerians mix traditional practices with Islam or Christianity, the State Department’s religious freedom report notes. Sharia courts, which apply Islamic law, function in 12 northern states and the Federal Capital Territory.

The constitution forbids the federal government and the states from adopting any religion as a state religion.

A craftsman finishes wooden writing boards used by almajiri, pupils of traditional Koranic schools, at Kurmi Market in Kano. File photo, 2019. (Photo: Yayanko, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

How the Groups Live Together

Nigeria’s constitution builds group balance into the state. Section 14(3) requires the federal government to reflect the “federal character of Nigeria”.

It aims to prevent “predominance of persons from a few States or from a few ethnic or other sectional groups”.

A Federal Character Commission enforces “proportional sharing” of public posts, from permanent secretaries to senior military officers. The president must also appoint at least one minister from each of the 36 states.

Elections follow the same logic. A winning presidential candidate needs at least a quarter of the votes in two-thirds of the states and Abuja.

Tension is real, especially over land. In its religious freedom report for 2023, the US State Department described numerous fatal clashes in the North Central region.

They pitted predominantly Christian farmers from various ethnic groups against predominantly Muslim herders. The report said many incidents were hard to classify as mainly religious, because religion, ethnicity, land and crime are closely linked.

Islamist armed groups such as Boko Haram “operate freely in certain parts of Nigeria”, a US proclamation said in December 2025. For the wider picture, see our explainer on Nigeria’s geopolitics.

Because public posts are shared among the states, every census carries political weight.

Migration and the Nigerian Diaspora

Nigerians are the largest African-born group in the United States. The Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey counted 532,602 people born in Nigeria, out of 2.97 million African-born residents.

Many more Americans trace their roots to Nigeria. In the same 2024 survey, 858,236 people reported Nigerian ancestry.

Money flows home. Personal remittances to Nigeria reached about US$22.8 billion in 2025, up from US$19.5 billion in 2023, World Bank data show.

Nigeria also hosts about 1.4 million international migrants, according to World Bank figures for 2024. In the 2024 health survey, 1% of adults were born abroad.

The UN estimates that about 35,000 more people left Nigeria than arrived in 2024. That net outflow is tiny next to the country’s natural growth of almost 5 million people a year.

What It Means for US Readers

Nigeria matters to the United States first through people. More than half a million Nigerian-born residents make it the largest African-born community in the country.

Travel has become harder. A US presidential proclamation signed on 16 December 2025 took effect on 1 January 2026.

It suspended new immigrant, visitor (B-1/B-2), student (F, M) and exchange (J) visas for Nigerians abroad, with some exceptions. Other visas now carry shorter validity.

The proclamation cited Boko Haram and Islamic State activity and overstay rates: 5.56% for visitors and 11.90% for students and exchange visitors.

Nigeria’s Guardian newspaper reported in September 2026 that the restrictions remained in force.

For investors, Nigeria’s population is a long-term story. By 2100 the UN projects Nigeria will have more people than the United States.

How Abuja manages that growth is a political question; see our profile of President Bola Tinubu.

What Is Not Known

Nobody knows Nigeria’s exact population. Every current figure is an estimate, because the census planned for 2023 was postponed on 29 April 2023 and never held.

In July 2026 the National Population Commission said only the president can set the next census date. It added that the count cannot fall in an election year.

Later that month, a Senate committee chairman said lawmakers would seek a law fixing a ten-year census cycle.

Money is another open question. The Auditor-General for the Federation, the federal spending watchdog, flagged more than N245 billion (about US$184 million) in census contracts and payments.

That dollar figure uses about 1,330 naira to the US dollar, the rate in October 2026, when the findings were reported.

Group shares are uncertain too. The survey covers adults aged 15 to 49 who describe themselves, so national shares by faith and ethnicity may differ.

The UN’s medium projection assumes the fertility rate falls to about 2.7 children per woman by 2050. A slower decline would leave Nigeria with many more people.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the population of Nigeria in 2026?

About 242.4 million people in mid-2026, according to the UN’s World Population Prospects 2024. Officials of Nigeria’s National Population Commission cited 238 million to 242 million in July 2026.

What are the largest ethnic groups in Nigeria?

The Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo. In the 2024 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey, 32.7% of women said Hausa, 12.8% Yoruba, 11.2% Igbo and 6.6% Fulani.

Is Nigeria mostly Muslim or Christian?

Both faiths are large. In the 2024 survey, about 58% of women and men aged 15 to 49 said they were Muslim and 41% to 42% Christian, with Islam dominant in the northwest and northeast.

How many languages are spoken in Nigeria?

Ethnologue lists 520 living languages in Nigeria. English is the official language, and the constitution lets the National Assembly also work in Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba.

When was Nigeria’s last census?

In 2006, when it counted 140,431,790 people. A census planned for 2023 was postponed, so every newer figure for Nigeria’s population is an estimate.

How many Nigerians live in the United States?

The US Census Bureau counted 532,602 Nigerian-born residents in 2024, the largest African-born group. Another measure, ancestry, counted 858,236 people.

Will Nigeria have more people than the United States?

The UN projects it will. Its medium projection shows about 477 million Nigerians in 2100, against about 421 million Americans.

World.title: Foreign Powers and Investors in South Africa 2026
World.content:
SOUTH AFRICA · FOREIGN POWERS

Key Facts — The country South Africa, led by President Cyril Ramaphosa, trades with the US and Europe while sitting in the BRICS club with China and Russia.

— Biggest investor The European Union, as a bloc, holds 46% of the foreign direct investment stock in South Africa, according to the EU’s diplomatic service.

— Biggest trade partner China, among single countries. South African exports to China reached US$12.4 billion in 2024, according to a trade ministry official.

— The US feud More than 600 US companies operate in South Africa, says the American Chamber of Commerce, yet Pretoria has rebuked the US ambassador three times in 2026.

— US tariff Since late July 2026, many South African goods face a 12.5% US tariff; oranges, macadamia nuts and platinum-group metals are among the exempt items.

— Trade perks AGOA, the US law granting duty-free access, was extended to December 2028 in September 2026; the list of eligible countries can change before January 2027.

— Prediction markets Polymarket bets give a 59.6% chance that South Africa’s annual inflation in December 2026 tops 5.0% (10 October 2026, 9:21 a.m. ET).

South Africa foreign relations matter to US investors: Washington is feuding with Pretoria, China leads its trade and Europe its investment.

This guide explains who brings money, warships, loans and aid to South Africa, and what each one wants back. For more country coverage, see our South Africa hub.

Container ships at the port of Durban, a gateway for South Africa’s foreign trade. File photo, 2015. (Photo: Pechristener, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Who Counts as a Foreign Player in South Africa

Foreign players come in six groups: governments, companies, lenders, aid donors, charities and South Africans abroad. Each group brings something different, and each expects something in return.

The government in Pretoria is led by President Cyril Ramaphosa, leader of the African National Congress (ANC). Our guide to who holds power in South Africa explains the parties and the people in charge.

Foreign money has become harder to win. According to World Bank balance-of-payments data, net foreign direct investment inflows fell from US$9.2 billion in 2022 to US$2.3 billion in 2024.

In 2025 the figure turned negative, at minus US$2.2 billion. In plain terms, foreign direct investors took out more money than they put in during that year.

The United States and the Trade Feud

The United States is South Africa’s most turbulent partner. More than 600 US companies operate in the country, according to the American Chamber of Commerce in South Africa, Business Day reported.

Relations broke down in 2025. On 7 February 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order ordering US agencies to halt aid to South Africa.

The same order told US agencies to promote the resettlement of Afrikaners as refugees. Afrikaners are a white, Afrikaans-speaking minority, and the order claims they face government-sponsored race-based discrimination.

The claim is widely disputed, with no evidence that the government has targeted Afrikaners, the news site IOL reported in June 2026. Washington expelled South Africa’s ambassador, Ebrahim Rasool, in March 2025 after he criticised Trump’s MAGA movement.

Pretoria’s ambassador in Washington is now Roelf Meyer, a former minister who helped negotiate South Africa’s move to democracy. He presented his credentials to Trump in May 2026, News24 reported.

In September 2026, Meyer said South Africa wanted to keep talking despite new US visa restrictions on South African officials. Washington has not named the officials concerned, Business Day reported.

Tariffs and AGOA

On 31 July 2025, a White House order set a 30% tariff on South African goods under an emergency-powers law. In February 2026, the US Supreme Court ruled that this law does not allow the president to impose tariffs.

Most South African goods then fell back to a universal 10% US rate, the business site BusinessTech reported in April 2026.

In late July 2026, the US Trade Representative imposed a 12.5% tariff on many South African goods under Section 301, a US trade law. It said South Africa does not ban imports made with forced labour, SAnews, the state news agency, reported.

Cars and car parts, which already face separate US duties, are excluded, as are items such as macadamia nuts, oranges and platinum-group metals. The trade ministry has since announced plans for its own ban on goods made with forced labour.

AGOA, the African Growth and Opportunity Act, is a US law that lets eligible African countries sell many goods to the US duty-free. In September 2026, Trump signed a funding law that extends AGOA to December 2028.

About 22% of South African exports to the US benefit from AGOA, BusinessTech reported.

Solidarity, a South African trade union, warned that the country’s place is not guaranteed. The list of eligible countries can change before January 2027.

A Combative Ambassador

Leo Brent Bozell III, a conservative media critic and Trump supporter, arrived as US ambassador in February 2026. Ramaphosa formally accepted his credentials on 8 April 2026.

By the end of September 2026, the foreign ministry had issued an unprecedented third formal rebuke, or démarche, against him in nine months. The ministry is the Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO), led by Minister Ronald Lamola.

The latest rebuke followed his public criticism of South Africa’s empowerment policies, Business Day reported. He also named farm murders as a sticking point for Washington.

Those policies, known as Black Economic Empowerment (BEE), set Black ownership targets for companies. A September 2026 US State Department report called them a significant compliance burden for US firms, Business Day reported.

The Citizen, a Johannesburg daily, quoted Bozell as saying billions of dollars from American firms are ready to go into mining. He said that money remains on hold because of the ownership rules.

Europe Is the Biggest Investor

The European Union is the quiet heavyweight. The European External Action Service (EEAS), the EU’s diplomatic service, calls the bloc South Africa’s biggest trading partner and largest foreign investor.

The EEAS puts the EU’s share of foreign direct investment stock in South Africa at 46%. In 2024, EU goods made up 23% of South Africa’s imports, and the EU took 18% of its exports.

That makes Brussels the anchor of South Africa foreign trade and investment, even as Washington and Beijing grab the headlines.

At a Cape Town summit on 13 March 2025, South Africa and the EU agreed to negotiate a Clean Trade and Investment Partnership. The EU also announced a €4.7 billion (about US$5.3 billion at October 2026 rates) Global Gateway investment package.

Global Gateway is the EU’s worldwide programme for infrastructure investment. The package mixes €303 million (about US$340 million) in EU grants with €4.4 billion (about US$4.9 billion) in loans from European lenders.

It concentrates on the just energy transition, South Africa’s planned shift away from coal, plus connectivity infrastructure and the local medicines industry.

In return, Brussels wants investment openings in clean energy, raw materials and green hydrogen. Those three areas are the focus of the partnership talks, according to the EEAS.

Office towers of Sandton, Johannesburg’s business district, above a canopy of trees and jacaranda blossom. File photo, 2015. (Photo: Aleph500Adam, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

China, Russia and the BRICS Club

China is South Africa’s largest trading partner among single countries, according to Business Unity South Africa (Busa), a national business federation. A senior official at the trade ministry put South African exports to China at US$12.4 billion in 2024.

Speaking in September 2025, the same official put China’s exports to South Africa at about US$21 billion. Mineral products made up 93% of South Africa’s exports to China, Engineering News reported.

China’s ambassador said in September 2025 that China had invested more than US$13.2 billion in direct investment in South Africa. He said that investment had created more than 26,000 jobs.

Chinese investors in South Africa include the electronics maker Hisense and the carmakers BAIC and FAW, Engineering News reported. Our guide to South Africa geopolitics covers the wider contest between the big powers.

South Africa belongs to BRICS, a club of large emerging economies with Brazil, Russia, India and China. The five countries set up the New Development Bank in 2015.

Warships in Simon’s Town

In January 2026, South Africa hosted Will for Peace, a China-led naval exercise based at Simon’s Town near Cape Town. The drill was set for 9 to 16 January.

Chinese warships and an Iranian vessel docked at Simon’s Town beforehand, and navy officials expected Russian ships, EWN reported. The Mercury, a Durban newspaper, noted that India and Brazil were not taking part.

The South African National Defence Force (SANDF) said the drill focused on the safety of shipping. Experts quoted by The Mercury warned that it could damage trade ties with Washington and Brussels.

Navy frigates at Simon’s Town, the South African Navy’s main base near Cape Town, which hosted the Will for Peace drill in January 2026. File photo, 2006. (Photo: Henri Bergius, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Lenders Behind Power, Ports and Rail

South Africa’s state companies need large sums, and lenders now tie their money to reforms around them. Eskom, the state power utility, and Transnet, which runs freight rail and ports, sit at the centre.

In July 2026, the government signed a US$1.5 billion development policy loan with the World Bank. It runs for 15 years with a three-year grace period, SAnews reported.

The money supports reforms in electricity, freight and logistics, plus water and sanitation. In return, the World Bank ties its money to agreed policy reforms rather than single projects.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF), the Washington-based lender to governments, regularly reviews South Africa’s economy. Its board last did so in an Article IV consultation on 9 February 2026.

The New Development Bank, set up by the five BRICS founders in 2015, offers another channel of loans. It funds infrastructure and sustainable development projects in member countries.

Kusile, a coal power station built by the state utility Eskom near Witbank in Mpumalanga, during construction. File photo, 2013. (Photo: Bruce Paulmac, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Aid Donors, Health Funders and NGOs

Health aid shows the cost of the rift most clearly. PEPFAR, the US anti-HIV programme, put an estimated US$400 million a year into South Africa’s HIV work for more than two decades, IOL reported.

In June 2026, the US State Department confirmed it had started a phased withdrawal of PEPFAR funding to South Africa. The country has about eight million people living with HIV, the most of any nation.

The state pays for 90% of its HIV medicines, with 10% from the Global Fund, a Geneva-based health financier, the health department said. It argued that PEPFAR mainly supported the wider HIV programme rather than the supply of medicines.

The health department said a UN high-level meeting in New York on 22-23 June 2026 would take up the funding gap.

The FW de Klerk Foundation, which carries on the legacy of the late former president, wrote to Trump in June 2026. It urged him to reverse the PEPFAR cuts.

The Diaspora and Money Sent Home

In family remittances, South Africa sends out more than it receives. World Bank data show personal remittances paid out of the country reached US$1.13 billion in 2025.

Remittances received by South Africa came to about US$1.0 billion in 2025. In other words, more money leaves South Africa through family transfers than arrives.

Our guide to South Africa and its neighbours explains its ties with Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Lesotho and other neighbours.

The order’s refugee clause for Afrikaners adds a politically charged strand to the South African diaspora in the US.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, bets give a 59.6% chance that South Africa’s annual inflation in December 2026 tops 5.0% (10 October 2026, 9:21 a.m. ET). That price moved 6.8 points lower in the previous 24 hours.

The 4.4% to 4.7% band trades at 12.5%, and 4.7% to 5.0% at 10.2%. The market has drawn about US$79,000 in total bets.

The market resolves on the Statistics South Africa report due on 20 January 2027. The statistics office put annual inflation at 4.4% in August 2026, up from 4.3% in July.

For foreign investors, higher inflation means the South African Reserve Bank, the central bank, may keep interest rates high. That moves the rand and bond returns.

Our report on the record petrol price outlook explains one pressure on prices.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

For US investors, South African mining, banking and consumer companies trade on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange. The political risk now comes as much from Washington as from Pretoria.

For US importers, AGOA decides whether many South African goods avoid normal US import duties. A separate 12.5% tariff has applied to many South African goods since July 2026.

For anyone following South Africa foreign policy, the key test is whether Pretoria can keep Washington, Beijing and Brussels on side at once. See our guide to who runs South Africa’s economy and our profile of Cyril Ramaphosa.

What Is Not Known

Washington has not said whether South Africa will stay on the AGOA list after January 2027. Nor is it known whether a South African ban on goods made with forced labour would lower the 12.5% US tariff.

The names of the South African officials hit by US visa restrictions have not been made public. The size of the US mining investment that Bozell says is on hold has not been published.

Official figures for the full impact of the PEPFAR withdrawal on HIV clinics have not been released. Nobody yet knows whether the New Development Bank or Europe will fill the gap left by US aid.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the biggest foreign investor in South Africa?

The European Union as a bloc. According to the EU’s diplomatic service, EU investors hold 46% of the foreign direct investment stock in South Africa.

Is China South Africa’s largest trading partner?

Among single countries, yes. Business Unity South Africa calls China its largest trading partner, and a trade ministry official put South African exports to China at US$12.4 billion in 2024.

What tariff does the US charge on South African goods?

Since late July 2026, many South African goods face a 12.5% US tariff under Section 301, a US trade law. An earlier 30% tariff fell after the US Supreme Court ruled against emergency-powers tariffs in February 2026.

Is South Africa still in AGOA?

Yes, as of September 2026. A US law signed that month extended AGOA to December 2028, but the list of eligible countries can change before January 2027.

Why did the US cut aid to South Africa?

A February 2025 executive order halted aid, citing South Africa’s 2024 Expropriation Act, its genocide case against Israel and its ties with Iran. PEPFAR HIV funding is being phased out.

Does South Africa hold military exercises with China and Russia?

Yes. In January 2026 it hosted the China-led Will for Peace naval drill off Simon’s Town, with Chinese and Iranian ships and expected Russian participation.

Who is the US ambassador to South Africa?

Leo Brent Bozell III, a conservative media critic, took up the post in February 2026. South Africa’s foreign ministry formally rebuked him three times in nine months, the latest at the end of September 2026.

World.title: Peru Media Landscape Explained
World.content:
PERU · MEDIA

Key Facts — The country Peru is a South American republic whose 1993 Constitution guarantees free expression without censorship and bans media monopolies in Article 61.

— Biggest owner Grupo El Comercio, long controlled by the Miró Quesada family, publishes El Comercio and Trome and co-owns América Televisión and Canal N.

— Stalled sale A deal to sell 62.95% of El Comercio to two businessmen, announced in May 2026, was frozen by a Lima court that July.

— Press freedom Peru fell to 144th of 180 countries in the 2026 RSF World Press Freedom Index, from 130th in 2025.

— Violence Peru’s national journalists’ association counted 458 attacks on the press in 2025, a year in which four journalists were killed.

— Online INEI says 82.0% of Peruvians aged six and over used the internet in late 2025, nearly nine in ten of them by phone.

— Still open Whether the El Comercio sale closes, and how courts finally rule on the 2025 APCI law on foreign-funded projects.

Peru media is concentrated in a few groups, mostly in Lima, whose ownership is shifting in ways that matter to US investors. This guide explains who owns the main outlets as of October 2026, why press freedom has slipped and where Peruvians get news.

Headquarters of the El Comercio newspaper in central Lima, decorated for Peru’s national holidays. File photo, 2015. (Photo: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Who Owns Peru Media in 2026

Peru media ownership is concentrated in a few groups based in Lima, the capital. The 1993 Constitution guarantees free expression without prior censorship, and its Article 61 bars monopolies over the press, radio and television.

In practice, one company leads the newspaper market. Grupo El Comercio, long controlled by the Miró Quesada family, publishes El Comercio, a daily founded in 1839.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

In 2013 the group bought Epensa, a rival publisher, adding titles such as Correo and Ojo. By 2016 it owned nine newspapers, says the Media Ownership Monitor, run by the Global Media Registry and Ojo Público.

The group also prints Trome, which RSF, the Paris-based press-freedom group, names as Peru’s best-selling newspaper. In 2013 and 2014 it held about 80% of newspaper circulation and 78% of readership, industry figures compiled by the monitor show.

Television ownership is shared. Two companies, Compañía Peruana de Radiodifusión and Plural TV, run América Televisión and the cable news channel Canal N.

Plural TV is a joint venture of El Comercio and Grupo La República, the Mohme family’s publisher of the daily La República. Grupo La República holds 30% of Plural TV, Perú Retail, a Lima business news site, reported in August 2026.

In 2013 La República’s director joined journalists who sued over the Epensa purchase, citing 81% of newspaper circulation, the monitor recounts.

The core business is under strain. Grupo El Comercio lost over US$19 million in 2025 as revenue fell 9.2%, says the Reuters Institute’s Digital News Report 2026.

Panamericana Televisión’s premises on Avenida Arequipa in Lima. The Schütz family sold the channel in October 2025, a sign of shifting TV ownership. File photo, January 2023. (Photo: Mayimbú, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The El Comercio Sale That Stalled

On 28 May 2026, 79 shareholders agreed to sell 62.95% of the group to two businessmen. The company reported the deal to the SMV, Peru’s securities regulator.

The buyers are Francisco Picasso Candamo and César Emilio Rodríguez Larraín Salinas. The deal is explained in more detail in this report on the original agreement.

Three minority shareholders, including Alois Miró Quesada Koechlin, then claimed a legal right to buy the shares first on the same terms. A Lima commercial court froze the transfer in late July 2026, and the three filed for arbitration on 20 August.

The dispute now sits with the arbitration centre of the Lima Chamber of Commerce. As of September 2026, the court order still kept the transfer suspended, Infobae Perú reported.

The deal also needs clearance from Indecopi, Peru’s competition authority, which reviews mergers for market concentration. Grupo La República said it would use its pre-emptive right over Plural TV if control passed to anyone but the buyers.

That means a sale could reshape ownership of América Televisión as well as the newspapers. For a market this concentrated, the outcome matters as much to readers as to investors.

The El Comercio building in central Lima. A Lima court froze the sale of 62.95% of the group in July 2026. File photo, 2017. (Photo: Felipe Restrpo Acosta, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Television and Radio Still Reach the Most People

Television remains the main medium in Peru, present in about 96% of homes, a 2025 national survey by CONCORTV found. People watched for more than four hours a day on average.

CONCORTV is an advisory council attached to the Ministry of Transport and Communications (MTC), the body that authorises radio and TV stations. It is not a regulator; its ten member institutions come from civil society, business and the state.

The survey of more than 10,000 people in 21 cities found América Televisión had the most programmes among the most-watched. Streaming and internet TV reached 52% of respondents, up from 33% in 2022.

Radio Groups and the News Hour

Radio follows television, at about three hours a day in the 2025 CONCORTV study, and music far outweighs news. RSF names Radioprogramas, known as RPP, as the leading radio news programme.

In 2016 the monitor found three radio groups with national reach: Grupo RPP, CRP Medios y Entretenimiento and Corporación Universal. Grupo RPP belongs to the Delgado Nachtigall family.

The monitor also found that three groups controlled 64% of the FM band in metropolitan Lima.

Trust is low. In the 2025 CONCORTV survey, 82% said television is run by political interests and 73% called it sensationalist.

América Televisión (Channel 4): run with Canal N by El Comercio and Grupo La República through Plural TV.

Latina (Channel 2): long controlled by the investment fund Enfoca. In March 2026 Enfoca told the SMV that a signed contract could pass control to Vytal Group, led by Argentine Tomás Yankelevich.

ATV (Channel 9): controlled in 2016 by Albavisión, the Miami-based group of Mexican businessman Ángel González, the Media Ownership Monitor found.

Panamericana Televisión (Channel 5): sold in October 2025 by the Schütz family to the mining group Grupo Paltarumi and producer Susana Umbert.

Willax Televisión: owned by businessman Erasmo Wong, Infobae reported in June 2025.

TV Perú: the state channel, run with Radio Nacional by IRTP, the national radio and television institute under the Ministry of Culture.

The historic headquarters of Radio Nacional del Perú, the state radio station run by IRTP, in Lima. File photo, 2022. (Photo: Gaboct, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Digital and Investigative Outlets

Online news was dominated by the El Comercio group, which led internet traffic in the monitor’s 2015 data. Alongside the big groups, a set of small independent newsrooms concentrates on long investigations.

Pressure on the Investigators

These outlets face legal and political pressure. On 12 June 2026, Congress approved a commission report urging prosecutors to pursue Gorriti over Peru’s 2019 deal with Brazilian builder Odebrecht.

IPYS, the Lima-based press-freedom group Instituto Prensa y Sociedad, called the charges unfounded. It said Gorriti took no part in the negotiations and only reported and commented on the agreement.

Ojo Público: an investigative site that says no millionaire shareholders or business groups stand behind it; it uses an AI tool to spot corruption in state contracts.

IDL-Reporteros: an investigative site directed by veteran journalist Gustavo Gorriti.

Convoca: a data-driven investigative outlet founded in 2014 by a team led by journalist Milagros Salazar Herrera.

Salud con Lupa: a digital newsroom covering public health.

Hildebrandt en sus trece: a weekly of news and political commentary directed by veteran journalist César Hildebrandt.

Social Media and How Peruvians Get News

Most Peruvians are now online, mainly by phone. INEI, the national statistics institute, found 82.0% of people aged six and over used the internet in the fourth quarter of 2025.

Use reached 90.3% in metropolitan Lima but only 59.6% in rural areas, and 89.2% of users went online by mobile phone. Just 60.1% of households had a home internet connection.

The phone has become a news source in its own right. The Digital News Report 2026 found social media is the main news source for 49% of Peruvians under 35.

Trust in news fell eight points to 32%, its lowest level since 2021, and 11% used AI chatbots for news each week. The survey is carried out online, so it reflects people who are already connected.

In the 2025 CONCORTV study, respondents rated social networks the most entertaining, informative and plural medium. Yet 31% also called them sensationalist.

Political campaigns increasingly rely on influencers, streamers and paid social ads, the Digital News Report notes. That lets candidates reach voters while bypassing the scrutiny of Peru media newsrooms.

Press Freedom, Violence and the APCI Law

Peru fell to 144th of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index of RSF, down from 130th in 2025. Its score dropped from 42.88 to 37.86 out of 100.

RSF says the dominant editorial line in Lima backs the coalition that took power in December 2022, which it calls authoritarian. It also reports police violence against reporters covering protests.

Violence surged in 2025. The ANP, Peru’s national journalists’ association, recorded 458 attacks and four killings that year, the deadliest for the press this century.

The dead were Gastón Medina Sotomayor in Ica, Raúl Celis López in Iquitos and Fernando Nuñez Guevara in Pacasmayo. Mitzar Castillejos died after an attack in Aguaytía.

State actors, mainly public officials and security forces, were behind more than 70% of the 2025 attacks.

On 19 September 2026, journalist Susy Aponte Polo, a candidate for governor of Áncash, was killed in Caraz, IPYS reported. Her case is covered in this report on the Caraz killing.

The 2025 reform of the APCI law has alarmed independent newsrooms. APCI, the Peruvian International Cooperation Agency, is the state body that oversees international cooperation funding.

Law 32301, signed by then-president Dina Boluarte on 14 April 2025, requires prior APCI approval for projects paid for by international cooperation. It also made using such funds to advise or finance legal action against the state a very serious offence.

Fines reach 500 tax units, or S/2.6 million (about US$755,000 at 3.44 soles per dollar), Salud con Lupa calculated. Registration can also be suspended or cancelled.

In October 2025, Salud con Lupa, IDL-Reporteros, Epicentro TV and Convoca announced constitutional amparo suits against the law in Lima courts. RSF warns that the expanded controls risk a chilling effect on independent journalism.

In January 2026, a Lima constitutional court ruled partly for the Instituto de Defensa Legal, a human-rights group. It declared both rules inapplicable to the group but upheld the fines if applied proportionately, Infobae Perú reported.

What It Means for US Readers

For US investors, Peru media is a business story as much as a political one. The El Comercio sale, an Indecopi review and the Plural TV pre-emptive right could reshape control of top newspapers and TV.

A June 2025 report by groups including Internews Europe and Free Press Unlimited studied donor funding for media. US government money made up over 75% of it in the Americas from 2020 to 2024.

The 2025 US funding cuts hit at least 60 outlets across the region, that report found. Peru’s APCI law adds a second filter, because foreign-funded projects, including media projects, now need state approval.

Diplomacy has also entered the story. On 1 October 2026, IPYS condemned US Ambassador Bernie Navarro’s repeated insults against the journalist César Hildebrandt.

Gorriti wrote that the ambassador’s attacks came through posts on his X account. For background on who holds power in Lima, see who dominates Peru and the Peru hub.

Travellers who follow local news will meet the same few brands: América TV, Canal N, RPP, El Comercio and La República. The key figures of Peruvian culture and Peru’s history add wider context.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the El Comercio sale will close, or on what terms. No decision date for the arbitration or an Indecopi review has been made public.

It is also unclear whether Vytal Group’s purchase of Latina has closed. In March 2026, Enfoca said conditions were still pending.

How the courts will finally rule on the newsrooms’ 2025 challenges to the APCI law also remains open. That leaves foreign-funded outlets planning around rules that could still change.

The motive for the killing of Susy Aponte Polo has not been established publicly, including any link to her journalism or campaign. Up-to-date audience and circulation figures are also scarce, and the Media Ownership Monitor’s ownership map dates from 2016.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who owns the biggest Peru media companies?

Grupo El Comercio, long controlled by the Miró Quesada family, is the largest. It publishes El Comercio and Trome and co-owns América Televisión and Canal N with Grupo La República through Plural TV.

What is the best-selling newspaper in Peru?

RSF names Trome, a popular daily published by Grupo El Comercio, as Peru’s best-selling newspaper in its 2026 country profile.

Is the press free in Peru?

The 1993 Constitution protects free expression, but Peru fell to 144th of 180 in the 2026 RSF index. Peru’s national journalists’ association counted 458 attacks and four journalists killed in 2025.

What happened to the sale of El Comercio?

In May 2026, 79 shareholders agreed to sell 62.95% of the group to Francisco Picasso Candamo and César Emilio Rodríguez Larraín Salinas. A Lima court froze the transfer that July, and arbitration followed in August.

What is the APCI law and why do Peru media groups oppose it?

Law 32301 of April 2025 requires prior state approval for projects funded by international cooperation and allows fines of up to 500 tax units, about US$755,000. Investigative newsrooms say it threatens independent journalism and have challenged it in court.

How do Peruvians get their news?

Television is still the most used medium, with more than four hours of viewing a day in 2025. Among Peruvians under 35, social media is now the main news source, the Digital News Report 2026 found.
