Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar. They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time. 🔴Ubili kozę na zapleczu. Wkrótce decyzja sądu, zastanawia ruch prokuratury Sąd Rejonowy w Wałbrzychu w najbliższym czasie zdecyduje o losie trójki obcokrajowców, którzy pod koniec zeszłego roku niezgodnie z polskim prawem ubili kozę. Oskarżająca Hindusa i dwójkę Bengalczyków… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 7, 2026 The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar. After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time. The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”. However, “the harmfulness of the act is relatively low, although I know that what these people did shocks many people”, he continued. “We must be realistic about the fact that the court proceedings will take some time, thus blocking the docket for other cases. A trial also entails costs for the state.” Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska. The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 Not all cases involving illegal animal slaughter have been treated as causing low social harm. Last month, a court in the town of Limanowa convicted three men for carrying out illegal halal ritual slaughter and selling unapproved meat. The main suspect, a Polish man, was found guilty of overseeing the operation, while two Azerbaijani nationals were convicted of helping distribute the illegal meat. The verdicts can still be appealed. Although it has relatively small Muslim and Jewish populations, Poland is one of Europe’s biggest producers and exporters of kosher and halal meat. Almost a third of Poland's meat exports are halal and kosher, making it one of Europe's leading producers. Having fought off attempts by the ruling party to ban ritual slaughter, the industry is now hoping to expand further to cater to a growing market https://t.co/duOJTfHoLT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2022 However, the country has itself been experiencing growing levels of migration in recent years. Most of the new arrivals are from neighbouring Ukraine and Belarus, but there are also growing numbers from outside Europe, too. Indians are now Poland’s third-largest immigrant group, numbering around 25,500, according to recent data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Among first residence permits issued by Poland last year, Indians (9,230) and Turks (7,533) were the fourth and fifth largest recipients. Poland’s current government has blamed some immigrant groups for a rise in crime and has stepped up deportations of those found to have broken the law. However, data show that, overall, immigrants are less likely to commit crimes than Poles themselves. World.title: Polish police detain more teens following school knife attacks amid fears of further incidents
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Following this week’s two knife attacks on schools in Poland, police have today carried out security checks on over 10,000 schools and detained at least 10 more people, many of them teenagers found to have made online threats or been in possession of weapons. Meanwhile, many parents decided not to send their children to school today, as rumours swirled online that this week’s attacks were somehow coordinated and that further incidents were planned on Friday. The issue has also sparked a political dispute, with the government criticising opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for previously vetoing laws intended to improve children’s safety. The opposition in turn accuses the government of failing to protect schools properly. 🚨 Ponad 10 tysięcy skontrolowanych placówek i 10 osób zatrzymanych w całym kraju. Bezpieczeństwo w szkołach priorytetem Policji ⬇️ Tragiczne zdarzenia, do których doszło w ciągu ostatnich dni na Mazowszu, wywołały w przestrzeni medialnej falę nieprawdziwych informacji,… pic.twitter.com/WVkYUdVO9C — Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) October 9, 2026 On Thursday, a 39-year-old school caretaker was killed in an attack by a 15-year-old former pupil on a primary school. Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that the assailant had been wearing a head-mounted camera intended to broadcast the attack. That came a day after a 19-year-old student carried out a knife attack on another school, leaving eight people injured. Two other teens were also detained on suspicion of planning attacks in other locations. In response, Tusk announced on Thursday that police would carry out regular checks on schools. However, on Friday, many parents in the Masovia province around Warsaw, where both of this week’s attacks took place, decided to keep their children at home. Some districts closed schools entirely. One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school by a 15-year-old former pupil. Yesterday, a knife attack by a 19-year-old at another school left eight people injured. The assailant also had a homemade explosive that failed to detonate https://t.co/xJAzhT6u3U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026 Concern was stoked by claims circulating on social media that this week’s school attacks were part of a coordinated action by a group of teenagers, who were planning further incidents on what they were calling “Bloody Friday”. Two schools in the town of Legionowo, just north of Warsaw, were closed on Friday after local authorities said they received “unconfirmed information that they were on a list” relating to the alleged group. Poland’s national police headquarters issued a statement on Friday morning saying that they were aware of the rumours but that “so far nothing indicates such an event is actually happening”. They urged people to remain calm, not share unverified information, and rely only on credible sources. At the same time, police and local authorities stepped up security in schools. At 9 a.m. on Friday, the national police headquarters announced that checks had been conducted at over 10,000 schools around the country and that ten people had been detained. Among those to be arrested was a 17-year-old in the town of Ełk, who had reportedly made online threats to attack other students, and a 13-year-old in Sochaczew who wrote in a chat that he would bring a machete to school. The boy later said it was a “silly joke”. In Bartoszyce, a school principal saw that an 11-year-old student had posted a photo of a knife alongside a statement indicating a threat. Police detained the boy and found an “imitation knife” in his backpack. In Ostrów Mazowiecka, police announced they had arrested a 15-year-old boy who had sent out images of himself in a Guy Fawkes-style mask, saying that he planned to take people’s lives. In Warsaw, police detained a 14-year-old who was found to be in possession of a concealed blade and 11 firecrackers. 🚨 Policjanci z Mokotowa niezwłocznie po otrzymaniu informacji o zagrożeniu bezpieczeństwa zatrzymali na terenie szkoły 14-latka, który posiadał nóż z ukrytym ostrzem. Nastolatek miał przy sobie także 11 petard hukowych. W sprawie prowadzone są dalsze czynności. Dokumenty… pic.twitter.com/lbQrqe2pgl — Policja Warszawa (@Policja_KSP) October 9, 2026 The situation has also taken on a political dimension. On Thursday, Tusk criticised Nawrocki for earlier this year vetoing a government bill intended to improve online safety by blocking harmful content. The president had argued that the measures were an “Orwellian” threat to free speech. In a hastily called vote in the lower-house Sejm on Thursday evening, Tusk’s ruling coalition passed a new version of the bill that will now be sent to the upper-house Senate. Once it receives final parliamentary approval, the legislation will return to Nawrocki for his signature or veto. Meanwhile, education minister Barbara Nowacka also noted that Nawrocki had vetoed a bill introducing new rights and responsibilities for school pupils, including greater powers to confiscate dangerous items. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Mieliśmy jedną z najmocniejszych propozycji zmiany prawa w Europie, która miała chronić w internecie przede wszystkim dzieci i młodzież. pic.twitter.com/dyxY6prGzB — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 8, 2026 In response, presidential spokesman Rafał Leśkiewicz criticised those who were “exploiting this issue for political purposes”, saying that “a political argument is the last thing we need right now”. Meanwhile, Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, accused the government of focusing on “political warfare” instead of ensuring security in schools. “There is no coordination or top-down directives on what to do, where it is safe, and where there is risk or threat,” he wrote on social media, calling the situation “chaos”. An overwhelming majority of MPs in the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, have voted in favour of a bill that would introduce tough new anti-alcohol measures, including a ban on all forms of advertising and on sales in shops during nighttime hours. The legislation must still pass through the upper-house Senate and will then require the signature of President Karol Nawrocki. However, given the level of support – with only two small far-right groups voting against the bill – it appears likely the measures will be approved. #PILNE | Sejm uchwalił ustawę wprowadzającą na terenie całego kraju nocną prohibicję, zakazującą reklamy alkoholu i podnoszącą opłatę za sprzedaż alkoholu. https://t.co/OawNUdtqM6 — tvn24 (@tvn24) October 8, 2026 The new restrictions were initially proposed in separate bills submitted by two junior members of Poland’s ruling coalition, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), which were combined into a single package. The measures include a ban on the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., with local authorities able to extend those hours up to 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. if they wish. Bars, clubs and restaurants would still be allowed to sell alcohol for on-premises consumption as presently. Almost 200 Polish municipalities, including large cities such as Warsaw and Kraków, have already introduced their own local bans on nighttime alcohol sales. In the first six months following the implementation of its restrictions in 2023, Kraków saw a nearly 50% decrease in nighttime police interventions, with other cities reporting similar improvements. The newly approved bill also includes a complete ban on advertising and promoting alcoholic drinks. Those who violate the prohibition can be fined up to 1 million zloty (€228,400). Packaging for alcoholic drinks will be required to include warnings about their harmful effect on pregnant women and minors. The legislation also toughens requirements for shop staff to check the age of buyers if they suspect they may be underage. The cost of licences to sell alcohol will be increased from 525 to 1,050 zloty for drinks with up to 18% alcohol content and from 2,100 to 4,200 zloty for stronger drinks. Warsaw has announced a ban on nighttime sales of alcohol in shops. The new measure will come into force on 1 June 2026 and will apply from 10 p.m to 6 a.m. across the entire city https://t.co/A7xVvJMpvU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 12, 2026 In a vote on Thursday night, the bill won support from 400 of the 433 MPs present in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. The only groups that did not vote in favour were the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). The legislation now passes to the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but only delay, not block, a bill’s passage. Once finally approved by parliament, it will reach the desk of President Karol Nawrocki, who can sign the bill, veto it, or send it to the constitutional court for assessment. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of bills. However, given the level of support for the alcohol bill in the Sejm, including from the largest opposition groups, Law and Justice (PiS) and Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), it appears likely he will sign it. Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, new data show. The average person in Poland ate 82kg of meat last year, up 7.5% from 2024 and 22.7% since 2005. They also drank 82 litres of beer, down 18.7% since 2018 https://t.co/FxFMupWLRv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 1, 2026 In June, an IBRiS poll for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 55% of Poles support some form of ban on nighttime alcohol sales while 43% are opposed. A survey by IBP for Super Express published today showed even stronger support, with 67% in favour of a ban and only 26% opposed. Recent data released by Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, showed that alcohol consumption among Poles is continuing its recent decline. In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019. However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005. World.title: Polish man suspected of helping Russian plot to assassinate Zelensky sentenced to 5.5 years
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. The sentence was handed down by the court of appeal in Lublin on Thursday, increasing by two years a jail term issued by a lower court earlier this year. The ruling is now final and binding. The 51-year-old former Polish soldier, who has been named only as Paweł K. under privacy law, was detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) in April 2024. Investigators found that the suspect had declared his willingness to collaborate with Russian intelligence and, between December 2022 and March 2024, had established contact via email and instant messaging with Russians involved in military operations against Ukraine, including army officers. Prosecutors determined that Paweł K. had been assigned tasks including gathering and transmitting information regarding security at Rzeszów airport, which is the main hub for goods and people being transported in and out of Ukraine. “These activities could have been used by Russian intelligence services, including in the context of planning a possible assassination attempt on the head of a foreign state, that is, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky,” wrote Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office earlier this year. Poland and Ukraine have revealed further details of a foiled plan to assassinate @ZelenskyyUa at Poland's Rzeszów airport. A Polish man was last month indicted in relation to the incident, which he is accused of seeking to carry out on behalf of Russia https://t.co/Lrp99vH4s2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 23, 2025 Last year, the head of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said that Paweł K. had been “recruited decades ago and firmly believed in the Soviet cause”. Polish prosecutors have not commented on that claim. However, they did find that the suspect had declared his willingness to join Russian “sabotage structures”, including the Wagner mercenary group and Unit 29155 of the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency, which is tasked with carrying out destabilisation activities. Paweł G. denied the accusations against him and claimed that he had actually been trying to help capture Russian war criminals by deceiving them into trusting him, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). His defence attorney argued that the information Paweł G. had transmitted regarding Rzeszów airport was “trivial and publicly available”, according to news website Onet. In January this year, Paweł K. was found guilty of espionage and illegal possession of ammunition by the district court in the city of Zamość, which sentenced him to three and a half years in prison. However, prosecutors appealed against that ruling, arguing that the suspect deserved a longer jail term of seven and a half years. In a judgement issued on Thursday, the Lublin appeals court agreed that Paweł G’s initial sentence had been “grossly lenient” and increased it by two years, reports PAP. “Submitting an offer to work for…the intelligence service of a country that is at war with a country directly neighboring Poland, a country that is making quite extensive unfriendly gestures towards Poland, cannot be treated leniently,” said judge Artur Achrymowicz. Poland has charged three of its own citizens with working on behalf of Russian intelligence. They are accused of spreading disinformation, conducting reconnaissance of NATO troops, and undergoing firearms training in preparation for acts of sabotage https://t.co/maYd0kb9HW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 20, 2026 Poland has become a primary target for acts of espionage, sabotage and disinformation conducted by operatives working on behalf of Russia. In many cases, they are so-called “disposable agents”: individuals already on the ground, often amateurs hired and paid through messaging apps such as Telegram, rather than professional spies or soldiers. The AWB last year launched 48 investigations related to espionage, more than twice as many as in 2024. Over those two years, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined A report published earlier this year by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026 In January, Polish prosecutors indicted five people – four Ukrainian citizens and one Russian – accused of carrying out a plot on behalf of Russia to plant explosives in packages that were then dispatched by courier services across Europe. In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops. In July this year, a Russian married couple who had been studying in Poland were jailed for spying on behalf of Moscow and involvement in a plot to send a parcel bomb. World.title: Beavers destroy sign warning about beavers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it. The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack. “We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters. “So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.” Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000. Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP. However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down. World.title: One person killed in second school knife attack in Poland in two days
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school carried out today by a 15-year-old former pupil. It comes just a day after another knife attack by a 19-year-old on a different school in Poland, which left eight people injured. The assailant was also carrying a homemade explosive device that failed to detonate. Meanwhile, police also announced today the arrest of a 17-year-old who had reportedly threatened to attack a school and was found to be in possession of knives. The developments have caused shock in Poland, a country where such violent incidents are normally rare. “We are seeing a radicalisation of young people,” warns the education minister, who has called for tougher controls on online content. W rękach Policji jest już 15-latek, który około godziny 9 wszedł do szkoły w miejscowości Leszczydół-Nowiny, w powiecie wyszkowskim i ostrym narzędziem ranił 3 pracowników placówki. Wśród rannych jest dyrektor, który ujął 15-latka. Policja była na miejscu już po kilku minutach od… pic.twitter.com/EV1RPP7LA5 — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 8, 2026 The latest attack took place in a primary school in the village of Leszczydół-Nowiny, around 60 km (37 miles) northeast of Warsaw, on Thursday morning. A 15-year-old former pupil of the school entered the facility and stabbed three members of staff, including the principal, who managed to subdue him. One of the victims, a 37-year-old female caretaker, died from her injuries. The other victim, a teacher, was hospitalised. The attacker was detained and will appear before a family court, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. The incident comes just a day after another similar tragedy only 50 km away, in the town of Ostrołęka. On Wednesday morning, a 19-year-old attacked a vocational high school, leaving four students, two teachers and two bystanders injured before being captured. The assailant, who has been named only as Jakub Z. under Polish privacy law, is a student at the school. On Wednesday evening, national prosecutor Dariusz Korneluk told broadcaster TVN that the attacker had a homemade explosive in his backpack “that almost detonated”. “The backpack was already in the computer room and, only due to the responsible actions of the teacher and the students, was it thrown out of the window” after smoke had begun to billow out of it, he said. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek pledged that “prosecutors will ensure that the perpetrator answers for every blow inflicted and faces the legal consequences…There is no tolerance for violence in Polish schools”. Policjanci z Ostrołęki w pobliżu plaży miejskiej zatrzymali 19-letniego mężczyznę podejrzewanego o zaatakowanie ostrym narzędziem osób w pobliżu i na terenie szkoły w Ostrołęce. Ze wstępnych informacji wynika, że mogło dojść do zranienia 7 osób. Policjanci na miejscu wykonują… pic.twitter.com/cRzqMs36rD — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 7, 2026 On Thursday morning, around the same time as the attack in Leszczydół-Nowiny was unfolding, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński announced that a 17-year-old boy had been detained by police after threatening to attack another school. The suspect, who resides in the same Masovia province where Wednesday and Thursday’s attacks took place, “was found with two knives”, said Kierwiński, quoted by news website Interia. His internet history also showed that “he was looking for information on how to carry out this type of bloody act”, added the minister. The potential incident was prevented after fellow pupils reported to teachers that the suspect announced he wanted to “do something bad at school”. Last week, a 13-year-old was detained by police after telling a fellow online gamer that he was planning an attack on his school in the village of Książki, north-central Poland. He reportedly confessed to having killed cats and said that he wanted to attack random people with a cleaver in the school halls. Dzięki przytomnej reakcji uczniów, nauczyciela oraz błyskawicznej akcji policjantów z Sierpca powstrzymano 17-latka, który zapowiadał, że „zrobi coś złego w szkole”. Policjanci zatrzymali nastolatka i zabezpieczyli należące do niego noże, a w jego telefonie natrafiono na historię… pic.twitter.com/oUkwKbHmNr — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 8, 2026 The Polish authorities have recently warned of growing concern over radical ideas spreading among young people. Last month, the security services detained three teenagers accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One was charged with planning an attack on a school and a mosque. Last year, a 19-year-old student was detained after it was determined he was planning an Islamic State-inspired attack on a Christmas market. In August, he was indicted to stand trial. In February, an 18-year-old was indicted over claims he planned to attack a school, also inspired by the Islamic State. Speaking on Wednesday, after the Ostrołęka incident but before today’s events, education minister Barbara Nowacka warned that “we are seeing a radicalisation of young people”, reports the Onet news website. She called for “much greater control over what happens on the internet”. Earlier this year, Poland introduced a new law banning online content depicting illegal acts or other forms of abusive and degrading behaviour. The government is also working on measures to block children from social media and has banned the use of smartphones in schools. Poland’s state-owned National Development Bank (BGK) has announced the launch of the country’s first fund to support companies developing space technologies. Vinci Space Tech Fund will be worth 500 million zloty (€114 million), investing up to 100 million zloty each in 15-20 firms in the sector. The brainchild of finance minister Andrzej Domański, the fund aims to foster the growth of Polish space technologies and bolster the country’s technological independence. Kosmos to nie tylko gospodarka i innowacje. Kosmos to także bezpieczeństwo Polski. 🇵🇱 Dziś w Krakowie uruchamiamy pierwszy w Polsce fundusz dla sektora kosmicznego – Vinci Space Tech Fund. 500 mln zł na rozwój sektora @BGK_pl Vinci. Mamy ambitne spółki, znakomitych naukowców i… pic.twitter.com/NQBy8HYOcY — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) October 6, 2026 According to the growth and technology ministry, one of the fund’s strategic partners, BGK will invest between 10 and 100 million zloty in companies with a potential for rapid growth and expansion into international markets through its Vinci investment vehicle. The fund’s other partners are the Polish Space Agency and Kraków Technology Park (KTP), where the launch took place, along with ICEYE, a world-leading Finnish microsatellite manufacturer and operator co-founded by Pole Rafał Modrzewski. Announcing the fund, Domański highlighted the space sector’s role in responding to threats, protecting critical infrastructure, strengthening energy security and monitoring Poland and its surroundings. “The money from the Vinci fund is an investment in Poland’s capacity to build its own strong companies and develop competences that will be strategically significant for our economy and security,” he said. Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Mirosław Czekaj, president of the BGK management board, also noted that the development of the space industry would help “to build Poland’s technological sovereignty”, as one of the projects that are “vital to the Polish economy”. The fund is expected to invest in 15 to 20 companies, mainly Polish, although companies from elsewhere in Europe may also qualify if they have their main business operations in Poland, the ministry said. Its key investment areas include satellites, optics and Earth observation, satellite communications, electronics and photonics, rockets and propulsion systems, and artificial intelligence. In addition to funding, companies will benefit from advice and support from the fund’s partners. KPT, the city of Kraków and the Faculty of Space Technologies at AGH University are expected to provide much of the initiative’s academic, research and technical expertise. ICEYE, meanwhile, will share its experience of growing a space company and expanding into global markets. Last month, the company opened a satellite technology centre in Warsaw, and it plans to invest more than 120 million zloty in Poland by 2028, reports industry website Space News. Modrzewski said that raising capital in Poland was difficult when the company was founded 12 years ago, but that it has become easier as space has emerged as one of the country’s “strategic domains”. “The availability of capital in Poland will allow our companies to build their position on the global market without needing to leave the country at an early stage,” Modrzewski said, quoted by financial news site Bankier.pl. Vinci has previously invested in ICEYE as part of its private equity fund. Astronaut @astro_slawosz's recent trip to the International Space Station highlighted the Polish space industry's growing importance. Once limited to making components for others, Poland is now building its own spacecraft and participating in missions https://t.co/TmQiD91IzZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 6, 2025 Poland’s space sector has expanded rapidly since the country joined the European Space Agency in 2012, moving from supplying components for foreign missions to developing its own satellites and space systems. A key milestone came in 2024 with the launch of EagleEye, Poland’s largest satellite, which was designed and built by a consortium of Polish companies and research institutions. In 2025, a Pole went to space for the second time in history, 50 years after the first Polish astronaut’s flight. The sector is now taking on larger international projects, while Russia’s war in Ukraine has highlighted the importance of domestic space capabilities for national security. In July this year, Warsaw was chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency centre focusing on civil security and resilience. World.title: Warsaw records EU’s highest employment rate
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data. The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013. Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%. The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030. At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%). After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU. In addition to topping the overall employment rate ranking, Warsaw also had the third lowest rate of youth employment (for people aged 15-29) at 3.9%, higher only than Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (3.8%) and Zeeland in the Netherlands (3.6%). And it had the third-highest rate of employment among people with tertiary education (93.5%), behind only Portugal’s Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%) and Yugozapaden (93.6%). Poland's unemployment rate of 2.6% in January is the lowest ever recorded in the country by @EU_Eurostat and was the joint-lowest that month among all EU member states For more, read our full report here: https://t.co/eP5A9JT4eg pic.twitter.com/A9oHu2zLZ6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025 The most recent Eurostat figures, from August, show that Poland’s unemployment rate (3.3%) was the second-lowest among all member states and well below the EU-wide figure of 6.2%. The strong labour market reflects years of economic growth, rising wages and increased employment. However, Poland’s ageing and shrinking population is creating labour shortages and encouraging companies to invest more heavily in automation. At the same time, job creation is slowing, while some industries – including manufacturing, automotive, furniture and construction materials – are coming under pressure, according to experts. World.title: Police Car Ends Up in Vltava River, Three People Treated for Hypothermia
World.content:
A police car plunged into the Vltava River in Prague on Saturday morning after crashing through the guardrails of Hlávkův Bridge.

The vehicle’s two occupants and a man who jumped into the water to help them were treated by emergency crews for hypothermia.

The accident was reported to police at around 8 a.m. on October 10. A man and a woman, both approximately 30 years old, were inside the car when it went into the river.



A witness jumped into the water after the vehicle fell from the bridge and helped the occupants. Emergency services subsequently treated all three people at the scene.

Prague Emergency Medical Service dispatched three ambulances, a medical inspector and a rapid response vehicle to the incident.

All three were suffering from hypothermia but were not in life-threatening condition, according to emergency responders.

“We are very grateful to the rescuer for their help,” Prague Emergency Medical Service said in a statement, confirming that all three people were in its care.

Police are investigating the circumstances of the crash, including what caused the vehicle to break through the bridge’s guardrails and fall into the Vltava.

World.title: Prague Outperforms Vienna and Berlin in Visitor Ratings
World.content:
Prague has received higher visitor satisfaction ratings than Vienna and Berlin, according to the latest Global Tourist Perception Index by Data Appeal Mabrian Intelligence.

The Czech capital scored 92.7 out of 100, compared with 85.6 for Vienna and 78.4 for Berlin, Prague City Tourism (PCT) announced on Thursday.

The results reflect six years of efforts to improve tourism services, visitor experiences and the city’s destination branding, the organization said during International Customer Service Week, held from October 5 to 9.

The Global Tourist Perception Index assesses several aspects of the visitor experience, including hotel satisfaction, safety and tourism products. Prague scored highest among the three capitals, according to PCT.



Visitor spending rises as tourism shifts upmarket

Data from Mastercard transactions indicate that spending by visitors from key foreign markets increased by 18% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, while the number of visitors rose by approximately 1%.

Social media analysis also points to Prague’s growing association with culture. More than a third of social media posts shared by visitors about the city focused on art and culture, an increase of around five percentage points year-on-year. Nightlife accounted for just 4.5% of reported reasons for visiting, according to PCT.

The Data Appeal Mabrian Intelligence Platform also gave Prague a score of 80 out of 100 for hotel service satisfaction, ahead of Vienna at 75.8 and Berlin at 71.8.

Figures from hotel data provider STR point to further growth in the market. Between January and August 2026, hotel occupancy in Prague increased by 4.9% year-on-year, while the average room rate rose by 5.1%.

Occupancy reached 84.7% in August. According to a recent overview of Prague’s tourism sector by the Czech Institute of Tourism, the average room rate was approximately €123, rising to €170 in the city center and €241 in the luxury segment.

Prague attracts hotel investors

The city is also gaining ground among hotel investors. According to the Cushman & Wakefield Hotel Investor Compass 2026, published in March, Prague ranks among the 15 most attractive European cities for hotel investment, ahead of Vienna, Zurich and Budapest.

Investor interest in Prague’s hotel market has increased for two consecutive years. In the previous edition of the study, the city recorded the largest year-on-year increase in investor interest among the markets surveyed, at 14%. The latest edition showed a further increase of 7%.

World.title: Prague 7 Turns Streets Into Outdoor Art With Designs by Local Children
World.content:
Prague 7 has transformed several streets around local schools with large-scale colorful paintings created with the help of local schoolchildren.

The new artwork can be seen on Rajská, Plynární, Jablonského and Antonínská streets, as well as part of Bubenská Street. The municipality placed the designs mainly near schools and along busy pedestrian routes.



On Antonínská Street, students from grades five through eight at Strossmayerovo Square Elementary School helped create the artwork. They produced the original drawings, which artist Jakub Karlík then combined into the final design.

Several other educational institutions are located close to the painted streets, including Bratrská Elementary School, the Holešovice Business Academy, the Higher Vocational School of Fashion Design and the Secondary Industrial School of Fashion Design.

The new designs have received mostly positive reactions from local residents. Comments on Prague 7’s Facebook page described the streets as more cheerful and said the artwork had made the area more interesting.

There has also been criticism, particularly over the cost and the practical impact of painting the asphalt. Some residents questioned whether the project was necessary and raised concerns about the roughness of the surface, pedestrian movement and whether the paint could become slippery.

Prague 7 said anti-slip paint was used, similar to materials applied to cycle paths and sports surfaces.

The project cost 755,000 CZK, covering the designs, preparation, materials and application. According to Prague 7 spokesperson Martin Vokuš, each of the two phases took around 20 days.

The municipality awarded the contract directly to Karlík. Before selecting his proposal for the Antonínská and Bubenská sections, Prague 7 compared three offers and chose his as the most advantageous.

World.title: Beer Consumption in Czech Republic Falls to Lowest Level on Record
World.content:
Czech beer consumption fell to its lowest level on record in 2025, with the average resident drinking 121 liters during the year, according to data from the Czech Association of Breweries and Malt Houses (ČSPS).

Total domestic consumption reached 14.86 million hectoliters, down 3.2% from 2024. The figure is the lowest recorded since nationwide beer consumption statistics began.

Overall beer production in the Czech Republic also declined last year. Breweries produced 19.96 million hectoliters of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beer, 4.3% less than in 2024.



The decline affected nearly every category, with non-alcoholic beer the main exception. Production of non-alcoholic and flavored non-alcoholic beer increased by 4% to 1.68 million hectoliters.

Demand for non-alcoholic beer has been rising steadily for more than a decade. Between 2019 and 2024 alone, production increased by around 50%.

Pubs lose ground as more Czechs drink at home

The shift in drinking habits is particularly visible in restaurants and pubs. Draft beer accounted for 28% of beer sold on the Czech market in 2025, down one percentage point from the previous year.

The longer-term decline is more significant. Draft beer represented 35% of sales in 2019 and 51% in 2008.

The ČSPS said the figures reflect changes in consumer behavior, including greater interest in moderation and healthier lifestyles. When Czechs do go out for beer, they are increasingly looking for quality and variety rather than simply drinking larger quantities.

Czech beer exports also decline

Exports followed the domestic market downward. Czech breweries exported 5.48 million hectoliters of beer in 2025, an 8.2% decrease compared with the previous year.

European Union countries accounted for around 90% of Czech beer exports, with Germany and Slovakia among the largest buyers.

Imports also declined, falling by 18.3% year on year. Foreign beer accounted for only 2.5% of total beer consumption in the Czech Republic, down 0.5 percentage points from 2024.

World.title: Nearly Half of Czechs Spend More Than 30% of Their Income on Housing
World.content:
Nearly half of people in the Czech Republic spend more than 30% of their net income on housing, while around one in 10 spends more than half.

Housing is generally considered financially burdensome when rent, utilities and other related costs exceed 30–40% of household income. The EU average is around 24%.



The findings come from a survey by Česká spořitelna and Evropa v datech, conducted with Ipsos among 1,000 respondents in February.

Housing affordability remains particularly difficult for young Czechs. Among people aged 18 to 29, 58% live with their parents at least part of the time, while 29% live with friends or a partner.

The survey found that 60% of people under 30 who are dissatisfied with their housing situation have postponed a major life decision because of it. For around one-third, this has happened repeatedly. Starting a family is among the decisions affected by housing conditions.

Homeowners were considerably more likely to be very satisfied than renters, with 41% of owners describing themselves as very satisfied compared with 18% of renters.

Czechia still has the least affordable housing in the EU

The Czech Republic improved by six places in this year’s housing conditions ranking, reaching 17th among the 27 EU member states. The improvement was linked to increased investment in residential construction, fewer households facing excessive housing costs or difficulties paying for heating, and relatively favorable rental conditions.

Buying a home, however, remains more difficult than elsewhere in the EU.

An average-sized Czech apartment costs 13.3 average annual gross salaries, compared with 13.6 a year earlier. The figure has improved only slightly, while other countries have made faster progress. In Hungary, the ratio fell from 13.6 to 11.9 annual salaries, while Slovakia improved from 13.2 to 11.7 and Slovenia from 13.4 to 11.4.

Ireland has the most affordable housing by this measure, with an average home costing 6.2 annual salaries, followed by Belgium and Finland.

An average apartment in Czechia costs roughly the equivalent of 29 years of average rent. In city centers, the figure is close to 31 years, compared with less than 13 years in Ireland.

High housing costs are changing household decisions

Housing expenses are also forcing some households to reduce other spending. Last year, 40% cut their budgets because of housing costs. Nearly one-quarter reduced spending on holidays, hobbies and entertainment, while 16% cut spending on essentials such as food, clothing and personal-care products.

Around 38% of Czechs see living with parents as an economic necessity caused by high property prices. Another 26% consider it a reasonable temporary solution, while 9.4% see multigenerational living as a viable long-term model.

At the same time, 46% of young people expect to inherit property from their families.

World.title: Famous Dancing House Photo Spot in Prague Is Set for a Major Makeover
World.content:
Jiráskovo Square in Prague is set for a major redesign that will change one of the city’s best-known photo spots near the Dancing House.

The project, estimated to cost around CZK 35 million, will replace part of the damaged lawn with paving, restore a historic fountain and move the monument to writer Alois Jirásek.



The Prague 2 district plans to carry out the transformation over the next two years. The redesign is based on a 2022 study prepared by archiF studio.

The square’s lawn has long been a problem. Its location directly opposite the Dancing House makes it a popular stopping point for tourists, many of whom step onto the grass to take photographs with the distinctive building in the background.

One of the most common poses involves visitors appearing to support the Dancing House with their foot or kick it. The repeated foot traffic has left the grass heavily damaged, despite attempts to restore it.

Under the new plans, part of the lawn will be replaced with a paved surface. This will create a more durable area for visitors to take photographs while reducing pressure on the remaining greenery.

Historic fountain to return to operation

The redesign will also restore the Cubist fountain created by architect Vlastislav Hofman. The area around the fountain will be repaved, while the fountain itself will be returned to its original appearance and function.

Water is expected to flow through the fountain again after decades.

Architect Soňa Formanová, one of the project’s authors, said the team was able to locate Hofman’s original documentation, including plans covering the fountain and the approaches to the nearby bridge.

The project will also introduce a raised edge around the lawn that can be used for seating. New flowerbeds and trees are planned for the northern part of the square, while existing shrubs considered unsuitable for the area will be removed.

The monument to Alois Jirásek, the Czech writer after whom the square is named, will be relocated to the center of the small park.

World.title: Queer Arts Festival PINKBUS Returns With New Performances and International Guests
World.content:
The PINKBUS Festival will return to Prague on November 3-14 with several days of theatre, dance, drag, music, visual art and performance.

This year’s edition, titled Forward March!, will focus on the need to keep moving forward amid an uncertain social and political climate.

Organised by the PINKBUS queer arts platform, the festival aims to create a space for artists and audiences to meet, experiment and share experiences. The programme combines established artists with new projects and will also mark the beginning of a new season for the platform.



One of the highlights of this year’s festival will be the premiere of two original works developed through the PINKBUS open call First Ride.

Richard Eliáš, an Academy of Arts, Architecture and Design in Prague (AVU) student, will present the interdisciplinary drag fantasy I Guess It’s Kind of My Fault, or What?. The second project, by the performative art collective Izbová teplota & Alejandra, is Štúrovci Went to Devín and Had Some Fun, offering a new and unconventional take on the group of Slovak national revival figures known as the Štúrovci.

The festival will also feature international guests. French artists Nicolas Poggi and Giselle Hauscarriaga will present SUDOR (Sweat), a Czech premiere performed with a local cast. The post-performative work explores physical exhaustion, sweat and the limits of the body.

Another premiere, Lipsync Her Name… Because It’s Precious, is being created in collaboration with the Italian festival RAINBOW.IT and Slovak organisation DRAMA QUEER. The performance focuses on three figures from European LGBTQIA+ history: Lucy Salani, Romina Cecconi and Ota Tasinata.

Directed by Tomáš “Grófka” Procházka, the production combines three monodramatic sketches exploring identity and the determination to remain true to oneself. The cast includes Italian actor Antonello Foddis and his drag alter ego La Trave Nell’Okkio, as well as Czech performer Venice, also known as Martin Talaga.

The programme will also include the PINKPANEL discussion series. This year’s edition, titled (The Tinsmith’s) Hammer Against Queerness, will examine the potential impact of current cultural policy on LGBTQIA+ artistic production and discuss possible forms of resistance.

The festival will conclude with a special BEST OF edition of the PINKBUS variety show, featuring Venice, Just Karen, La Cuntessa, Tonic Garbáge, Helena Araujo and other performers, alongside special guests.

World.title: Roger Waters Brings New Pink Floyd Show to Prague in June 2027
World.content:
Roger Waters will bring a new Pink Floyd concert production to Prague next year, with LEGACY – A Pink Floyd Show scheduled for June 8, 2027, at O2 universum.

The new production has been created under Waters’ direction and will feature a ten-piece band led by his son, Harry Waters. The Prague show will focus on music from what is widely regarded as Pink Floyd’s most influential period, spanning 1971 to 1979.



The setlist will draw from four of the band’s best-known albums: The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

The music will be accompanied by a new visual production featuring high-resolution LED screens and imagery inspired by Pink Floyd’s original artwork and stage concepts.

Harry Waters will serve as the show’s musical director, performing on Hammond B3 organ and piano while also contributing vocals. He has a long history with the band’s music and spent more than 15 years performing alongside his father on major tours, including The Dark Side of the Moon and The Wall.

His connection to Pink Floyd goes back even further. As a child, Harry’s voice appeared on “Goodbye Blue Sky” from The Wall. He also saw the original The Wall concert production at a young age.

The band includes drummer Graham Broad, guitarist Edo Scordo, bassist and backing vocalist Dahniel Knight, saxophonist and multi-instrumentalist Ryan Saranich, keyboardist Matt Riddle, lead vocalist Clifton David Broadbridge and backing vocalists Eva Avila and Genevieve Little.

Roger Waters co-founded Pink Floyd in 1965 and became the band’s principal lyricist and conceptual leader following Syd Barrett’s departure. He played a central role in the creation of albums including The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

World.title: Beyond Budapest: 15 countryside restaurants in Hungary worth travelling for in 2026
World.content:
Hungary’s food scene no longer begins and ends in Budapest. From wine-country restaurants in Tokaj and Villány to creative kitchens around Lake Balaton and destination dining in the Őrség, some of the country’s most interesting culinary experiences are now found well beyond the capital. The best countryside restaurants in Hungary:

The upcoming Dining Guide Top100 Restaurant Guide 2026 offers another indication of how widely Hungary’s gastronomic map has expanded. Four countryside restaurants made it into the national top 10, while the guide’s list of the 15 best restaurants outside Budapest stretches across almost the entire country.

For international visitors, that makes the ranking more than just a restaurant list. It can also serve as something of a gastronomic itinerary through Hungary.

As we wrote earlier, Hungary’s biggest restaurant awards 2026 announced – here are the Dining Guide winners

The 15 best countryside restaurants in Hungary in 2026

Pajta – Őriszentpéter 42 Restaurant – Esztergom Sauska Padi – Tokaj Sauska 48 – Villány Anyukám Mondta – Encs Platán Bisztró – Tata Botanica – Dánszentmiklós Kistücsök Food&Room – Balatonszemes Alkimista Kulináris Műhely – Szeged Hosszú Tányér – Hosszúhetény morzsa – Pécs Mede by Mede Ádám – Badacsonytomaj Casa Christa Agriturismo – Balatonszőlős Ikon – Debrecen Petrányi Borterasz – Csopak

Őrség: local ingredients with an international perspective

At the top of the countryside ranking is Pajta in Őriszentpéter, deep in western Hungary’s Őrség region.

Opened in 2012 by Ferenc Kvasznicza and Flóra Marjai, Pajta was created in a converted barn with the aim of bringing gastronomy, nature and culture together.

Pajta Restaurant, Hungary.

The kitchen is now led by chef duo István Akács and Yazmin Salazar. Salazar brings influences from her Mexican background, while Akács has experience in leading Scandinavian and other European restaurants.

The result is a progressive international style built firmly around local ingredients. Foraging also forms part of the restaurant’s philosophy, with forest mushrooms and the surrounding landscape providing regular inspiration.

Esztergom: a new chapter for 42 Restaurant

A short trip from Budapest, 42 Restaurant in Esztergom has undergone major changes over the past two years.

The fine-dining restaurant moved from its former ground-floor location on Széchenyi Square to an upstairs space decorated with frescoes that once served as the living room of a bourgeois family home.

42 Restaurant

Since December 2025, the kitchen has been led by Kevin Szabó, whose background includes experience with Hungary’s Bocuse d’Or team.

His cuisine starts with Hungarian ingredients but draws openly on international gastronomy. The menu changes seasonally and also includes a complete vegetarian option.

The restaurant’s owner, Sándor Varga, is also known internationally as the creator of the Alexander the Guest YouTube channel, which showcases some of the world’s leading fine-dining restaurants.

Tokaj and Villány: when Hungarian wine country meets destination dining

Two of the top restaurants are connected to one of Hungary’s best-known wine brands.

At Sauska Padi in Tokaj, traditional Hungarian flavours, local ingredients and dishes designed around Tokaj wines form the basis of the restaurant’s identity.

Sauska Padi

Executive chef Attila Bicsár developed the culinary concept, while resident chef Máté Gerák draws inspiration from the forests, gardens and gastronomic traditions of the Zemplén region.

Game, mushrooms, vegetables, fruit, poppy seed, walnuts and even aszú grapes can appear depending on the season.

Hundreds of kilometres to the southwest, Sauska 48 in Villány presents a different interpretation of the winery restaurant.

Sauska 48

Operating since 2017, it describes itself as a restaurant “in the heart of the winery”. Bicsár’s concept of “relaxed village gourmet” combines Swabian-Hungarian roots with increasingly sophisticated tasting menus.

Wine is not simply an accompaniment at either restaurant: it is part of the culinary concept.

Encs: one of Hungary’s great family restaurant stories

Anyukám Mondta in Encs celebrated its 30th anniversary in 2025.

Founded by brothers Szilárd Dudás and Szabolcs Dudás, it has developed into one of Hungary’s best-known countryside restaurants while remaining very much a family business.

The menu combines Hungarian and Italian traditions with a contemporary approach. Wood-fired pizzas and homemade pasta sit alongside Hungarian classics, reflecting a philosophy based on high-quality ingredients, precision and simplicity.

For foreign visitors travelling through northeastern Hungary or towards Tokaj, it has long been one of the region’s notable gastronomic stops.

Lake Balaton is becoming a serious food destination

The Balaton region has particularly strong representation on the list, illustrating how the country’s biggest lake has evolved far beyond its traditional summer-food image.

At Kistücsök Food&Room in Balatonszemes, more than three decades of restaurant history are now combined with accommodation, a conference space and a weekend chef’s-room concept featuring an open kitchen.

Kistücsök Restaurant, Hungary.

The cuisine remains closely tied to ingredients from the surrounding region and modern interpretations of Hungarian dishes.

On the northern shore, Mede by Mede Ádám in Badacsonytomaj takes a very different route. Chef Ádám Mede has built the restaurant around open-fire cooking, with charcoal, smoke, grills, smokers and cauldrons playing central roles.

Mede By Adam Mede

Traditional flavours appear in unexpected forms, from körömpörkölt to BBQ lecsó, alongside Balaton cheeses, sausages and other local products.

Nearby, Casa Christa Agriturismo in Balatonszőlős combines accommodation with a trattoria-style restaurant. Chef Keve Tóth has led the kitchen since 2025, supported as mentor by Michelin-starred chef Ádám Barna.

Petrányi Borterasz

And in Csopak, the Petrányi Borterasz offers perhaps the most classically Balaton experience on the list: seasonal food, estate wines and a 180-degree panorama over Lake Balaton.

From Pécs to Szeged: southern Hungary experiments with new formats

Hungary’s southern cities also show how diverse the countryside restaurant scene has become.

In Pécs, morzsa is difficult to place into a single category. It combines a Scandinavian-influenced new-wave bakery, specialty coffee, breakfast, a progressive bistro and a wine bar.

Chef Attila Kurucz, named Dining Guide’s Innovative Chef of the Year in 2018, works with a compact menu of unconventional bistro dishes and a constantly changing seasonal offer.

Morzsa

In Szeged, former journalist-turned-chef Krisztina Katkó runs Alkimista Kulináris Műhely, which describes itself not simply as a restaurant but as a “dinner place”.

It operates only three days a week and by reservation, serving an eight-course thematic tasting menu that changes every two to three weeks. The dishes revisit the traditions of the Great Hungarian Plain and the Danube–Tisza region through a contemporary lens.

If you missed it: Inside Hungary’s Dining Guide Gala 2026 – VIDEO

Smaller places, serious gastronomy

One of the most interesting characteristics of Hungary’s evolving restaurant landscape is that some of its notable destinations are located far from major tourist centres.

In Hosszúhetény, at the foot of the Zengő mountain, Hosszú Tányér builds its tasting menus around local products, regional culinary traditions and the seasons.

Hosszú Tányér

In Dánszentmiklós, Botanica operates inside a small luxury hotel inspired by the atmosphere of Provence and Tuscany. Chef Tamás Munk serves an eight-course dinner tasting menu combining contemporary countryside cuisine with fine-dining techniques.

Platán Bisztró, Tata, Hungary

Meanwhile, Platán Bisztró in Tata continues as the more relaxed member of the Platán gastronomic world following the end of Platán Gourmet’s permanent fine-dining operation in summer 2026.

Its cuisine combines Hungarian and international ingredients with refined presentation and a strong seasonal dessert programme.

Eastern Hungary also has a major player

In Debrecen, IKON remains one of eastern Hungary’s most established contemporary restaurants.

Chef Ádám Thür, who spent more than a decade gaining experience in the United Kingdom, focuses on local and Hungarian ingredients, seasonality and modern reinterpretations of familiar flavours.

Ikon Debrecen

The restaurant even maintains its own garden, producing herbs, vegetables and fruit for the kitchen while supporting its sustainability goals.

Hungary’s culinary map is getting bigger

For travellers, perhaps the most interesting message from the 2026 ranking is geographical.

Fine dining and ambitious contemporary cooking in Hungary are no longer concentrated in Budapest. Wine regions, Lake Balaton, small towns and regional centres are developing distinct culinary identities of their own.

That creates a different way of exploring the country: Tokaj through its wines and forests, Villány through its Swabian-Hungarian traditions, the Balaton through local ingredients and open-fire cooking, or the Őrség through its landscape and farm-to-table philosophy.

For international visitors prepared to travel beyond Budapest, Hungary’s countryside is increasingly becoming part of the destination — not simply the journey between destinations.

World.title: Indian community in Budapest celebrates 10th Ganesh Festival, prepares for Navratri Celebrations
World.content:
The Indian community in Budapest recently celebrated the 10th Budapest Ganesh Festival, bringing together Indian families, devotees, Hungarian friends and people from different cultural backgrounds for a colourful celebration of faith, tradition and community.

The celebrations were made possible with the valuable support of Om Vishwa Guru Deep Hindu Mandir, Budapest, which has provided the Indian community with a spiritual and cultural space to come together, celebrate Hindu festivals and keep Indian traditions alive in Hungary.

10 Years of Ganesh Celebrations in Budapest

The seven-day Ganesh Festival, held from 14 to 20 September 2026, featured traditional prayers, daily Aarti, devotional bhajans, cultural performances and Mahaprasad at Om Vishwa Guru Deep Hindu Mandir.

One of the highlights was the Ganesh Visarjan procession, featuring traditional Maharashtrian Lezim, Shivgarjana, Garba, devotional music and enthusiastic chants of “Ganpati Bappa Morya!”

The celebrations concluded with Ganesh Visarjan at Kopaszi-gát, Budapest, where families and devotees gathered to bid an emotional farewell to Lord Ganesha.

Beyond its religious significance, the festival gave children and younger generations growing up in Hungary an opportunity to experience Indian traditions and remain connected to their cultural roots.

Navratri Celebrations in Hungary

Navratri Celebrations in Budapest: 11–19 October

Following the successful Ganesh Festival, Om Vishwa Guru Deep Hindu Mandir and the Indian community in Budapest are now preparing for the nine-day Navratri celebration from 11 to 19 October 2026.

This year also marks the 10th year of Ghatsthapana celebrations in Budapest. What began as a small community initiative in 2017 has grown into an annual tradition bringing together families and devotees.

The celebrations will begin on 11 October at 10:00 AM with Ghatsthapana and Goddess Durga Puja, followed by Mahaprasad. Evening Puja, Aarti and bhajans will be held at 6:30 PM from 12–19 October. A special Kanya Pujan will take place on 18 October, followed by Vijayadashami/Dussehra on 20 October at 6:30 PM.

If you missed it: India’s Independence Day in Budapest highlights the deep Hungarian ties behind the celebration

Keeping Indian traditions alive in Hungary

Speaking on behalf of the organising team, Vinod Dhaygude said:

“The support of Om Vishwa Guru Deep Hindu Mandir has been very important for our community. Having a dedicated place where families can come together for prayers, festivals and cultural activities helps us keep our traditions alive in Hungary. It also gives our children an opportunity to experience and understand the culture we grew up with.”

The Mandir has become an important gathering place for the community, supporting religious and cultural celebrations and helping create a stronger connection between generations.

At the same time, the celebrations are open to the wider community, giving Hungarian and international friends an opportunity to experience India‘s traditions, devotional music, dance and community spirit.

The organisers warmly invite Indian families, Hungarian friends, devotees and everyone interested in Indian culture to join the upcoming Navratri celebrations.

Venue: Om Vishwa Guru Deep Hindu Mandir, Budapest

Address: Bokréta utca 29, Budapest, Hungary

Contact: Vinod Dhaygude | +36 70 226 6478

Facebook & Instagram: Indian Festival in Budapest
