World.title: Vegan powerlifter says diet change solved his health problems
World.content:
Koovit, who grew up with six brothers and a sister, all fed on good countryside fare, said his wife suggested make the change. He now eats 180–240 grams of protein a day, but plant-derived, something which is viable nowadays without getting boared.

"There were six boys and one girl of us. We usually went through eight liters of milk a day, and everything else that goes with it," he said.

"I'm fully vegan, but that doesn't mean I only eat onions and potatoes. AS I'm a powerlifter, I need to be heavy. There's a very wide choice of vegan food. My daily protein intake is between 180 and 240 grams. On top of that comes about three times as much in carbohydrates — oatmeal, rice, potato and the rest. For me it's very important to get a lot of energy from food and for my weight number to be high," Koovit said.

His wife had been vegan for longer. "I reached a point in my sport where my joints started hurting and I felt I'd taken my body so far that if I pushed a little more, health problems would start. That was nine years ago. My wife then very cleverly suggested I try vegan products. When I get stuck with something, my dear wife comes up with a solution — without her I probably wouldn't be here," Koovit explained.

Pretty much every foodstuff has a vegan alternative, he noted. "In my case, it was that after four days of eating vegan food, I realized there was no way back, as I felt so good. For an athlete, the best thing is that the recovery becomes faster."

Koovit recalled that at the time he was living in London, and in the club where he trained he was one of the smallest men. "I was a little squirt there. As things started going so well for me, and I started setting Estonian records and winning medals, burly men who I'd been afraid even to talk to at first started asking me what I was doing to do so well. One after another they started trying vegan food too."

Meat dishes tend to be highly acidic and can cause inflammation in the body, he says. "When heavy training is added to that, more and more inflammation builds up in the body. Eventually the body can't cope with it anymore — that's why more and more athletes in the sports world have been finding vegan food," went on.

"Eating vegan food is very contagious, because you feel good and get the feeling that you'd like to try more. After eating, you don't get a heavy feeling. In sporting terms, that's the charm of it — since I can eat more often, I feed my muscles and cells more often. There are more nutrients, and through that recovery is faster too," Koovit said. "Protein can be obtained from vegan food in concentrated form."

The annual Veganmess food festival takes place in Tallinn this weekend.

World.title: Estonia's central bank adds stone barrier to after multiple vehicle strikes
World.content:
After multiple instances of the building being hit by vehicles, the Bank of Estonia has installed street-side rock barriers.

The Bank of Estonia (Eesti Pank) is located on Kentmanni and Estonia pst. in central Tallinn, and has seen around 20 instances in as many years of drivers, generally those driving under the influence of alcohol, hit its exterior wall.

Part of the issue is the central bank's building lies adjacent to a left turn, if coming from Freedom Square (Vabaduse väljak) and its traffic lights, around 150 meters away. Vehicles have been known to speed along this stretch of Estonia pst. and run out of road at the turn, hitting the bank building.

The dolomite blocks being installed along Kentmanni. Source: ERR

"For the past 20 years, drivers speeding across Freedom Square have rammed the bank building's wall around twenty times. There have been accidents on the curve by Eesti Pank where a drunk driver has driven into the bank's wall. To prevent this, a stone barrier has now been brought there, " the bank said.

The Saaremaa-quarried dolomite blocks will prevent stray vehicles hitting the bank itself. The blockes are irregular shapes and will be "greened" by the next summer.

The bank's management also recalled the April 2007 "Bronze Soldier Night" riots, though the building remained adequately protected during those incidents.

The blocks are hewn from Saaremaa dolomite and placed at an intersection with Estonia pst. Source: ERR

Much of the bank's real estate is state owned, noted Rait Roosve, adviser to the Bank of Estonina board.

"We have quite a lot — or let's say, an unbelievably large amount of property in the Eesti Pank quarter, and that property doesn't belong to us, it belongs to the Republic of Estonia, or to put it more precisely, to the people of Estonia, and we have an obligation to guard and protect it at the maximum level," he said

Since the area is public urban space, the Bank of Estonia says it cannot cannot and does not want to build a wall there. At the same time, the row of blocks being installed must ensure the safety of ordinary traffic and stop cars and small trucks.

The dolomite blocks being installed along Kentmanni. Source: ERR

It is not, however, a national defense structure, ;the stones will not be sufficient to defend the building from armored vehicles such as tanks, for instance..

"This is Estonian national stone, limestone, specifically dolomite, and these have been brought from Kaarma on Saaremaa. It will certainly slow a tank, but considering the mass of these dolomite blocks and the mass of a tank, purely physically or mechanically the victory is certainly on the tank's side. But it also won't allow a tank to ram straight into our wall," Roosve continued.

The project, carried out in cooperation with Tallinn city government, will be completed by the end of next week. Grasses planted by the stones should conceal them come next summer, making the area in front of the bank on Kentmanni tänav greener, planners say.

World.title: Mari-Liis Jakobson: Are we sailing to the end with a minority government?
World.content:
Can Estonia's current minority government make it to the finish line or are we heading toward early elections, asks Mari‑Liis Jakobson.

Politics watchers have no reason to be bored. The first signs of the election campaign are already visible on the streets, the Riigikogu is processing the state budget, and the opposition is preparing yet another no‑confidence motion against the prime minister. All this in a context where the governing parties have lost their parliamentary majority and the opposition is threatening early elections.

For those who have tuned out of politics for a while: as of Thursday evening, the governing parties — Reform Party and Eesti 200 — hold 50 of the Riigikogu's 101 seats, meaning less than half. In theory, MPs not belonging to the government have a good chance of voting down coalition‑backed bills. This is loudly demanded by MPs from Isamaa, Center Party, and EKRE, while the Social Democrats have said they are willing to support the budget under certain conditions.

The budget bill currently under consideration is weightier than usual, because if the Riigikogu fails to pass it, this leads to early elections. True, the constitution says early elections must be called if the government cannot pass the budget within two months after the start of the fiscal year — meaning by February 2027. But regular elections are already scheduled for March. If a no‑confidence motion against the prime minister succeeds, it leads to forming a new government, but not necessarily early elections.

In this light, I wanted to steer the debate a bit more toward research‑based understanding and briefly introduce what political science has found about minority governments.

First, what exactly are minority governments and why are they sometimes chosen?

Generally, it is more comfortable to govern with a secure majority, allowing you to implement promises made to voters. Sometimes, however, the coalition that would form is so diverse and contradictory in its goals that it is simpler and more logical to proceed without a parliamentary majority and rely on cooperation with opposition parties on issues where views overlap.

Minority governments are quite common in the Nordic countries, where the spectrum of parties entering parliament is broad. But they have also been used elsewhere — for example in Spain, Romania, the United Kingdom, and even in Estonia, when Andrus Ansip's minority government hoped to pass certain issues with the support of the Estonian Greens. Research shows minority governments are not necessarily less effective than majority governments.

Minority governments can differ greatly in structure and effectiveness. Sometimes such cooperation is covered by formal agreements; sometimes it is more ad hoc. Some minority governments have stable partners; others change them frequently. The circle of cooperating parties also varies. Sometimes minority governments rely on small regional parties; other times on parties with more radical views.

For example, Sweden's outgoing minority government led by Ulf Kristersson relied on the so‑called Tidö Agreement with the Sweden Democrats, who were not part of the government but provided parliamentary support.

The government's interest in such cooperation is obvious. But why are partners who remain outside the government willing to cooperate?

"Sometimes minority governments rely on small regional parties; other times on parties with more radical views."

Every political move has a political cost. Entering government makes you more visible, gives your members political posts, and allows you to directly shape policy. At the same time, as a government member you are responsible for decisions your voters may dislike, and in many eyes you share blame for any blunders the state makes.

As a supporter of a minority government, you do not get political posts, but you also do not have to support all government decisions or share responsibility for them. And from time to time, in exchange for your support, you can negotiate a decision that pleases your voters.

Research shows that parties supporting minority governments generally perform better in elections than small coalition partners — though not necessarily better than parties that remain in opposition.

Parties that support the government on a case‑by‑case basis and are not tied to cooperation agreements tend to do best in elections. Minority governments also appeal to some voters because they create a sense that voter preferences are taken into account more than in majority governments. This is likely the strategy the Social Democrats and Reform Party are hoping for.

The rest of the opposition continues to beat the drum of early elections. This is a familiar tune, played mainly to highlight the government's weakness in a more dramatic light. The campaign‑covered cityscape amplifies this message: look, things are serious. But most likely election day will still be 7 March, no matter what is said.

World.title: Prime minister slams US-Russia diesel pact: Deals with dictators 'road to hell'
World.content:
Prime Minister Kristen Michal has sharply criticized the US decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia, saying agreements with dictators lead to hell.

Trump said Friday that Russia had agreed to bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the world market immediately, with more to follow, under a temporary US licence.

Ahead of next month's midterm elections, US President Donald Trump has struck a deal with Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply millions of tonnes of diesel to the world market, a move Trump said was essential to bring down fuel prices.

The US issued a temporary license for Russian diesel supplies to the world market, valid until April 7 next year.

"This is a major miscalculation, because deals with dictators are the road to hell. Innocent people are being killed for gas and fuel money. And what is very likely is that the hoped-for fuel will not come," the prime minister noted on social media.

"Such an agreement runs counter to the Western world's long-standing efforts to limit the flow of money from energy carriers to [Vladimir] Putin. The US has until now persuaded its allies to abandon Russian fuel — we have too," Michal said.

According to him, the long-term line of cutting Russia off from money is correct and must continue.

"It is worth discussing in Estonia and at the European Council next week whether we can quickly contribute more to Ukraine so they can blast Russia's oil refineries to smithereens," Michal added.

Reform MP: Trump is thinking about the midterms

MP Marko Mihkelson (Reform), chair of the Riigikogu Foreign Affairs Committee, earlier said he believes the upcoming midterm elections prompted Trump's diesel agreement with Russia, but at the same time, Russia will draw encouragement from the deal to continue its war in Ukraine.

Marko Mihkelson. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

"The Trump administration is on its back domestically over its moves and is trying to do everything to avoid a major Republican defeat in the midterm elections less than a month away," Mihkelson wrote on his social media account.

He said the hope of reducing diesel prices at US pumps with Russia's help is short-sighted and carries a much higher strategic cost for the United States.

"At the same time as the Graham sanctions bill approved in Congress would give the president the opportunity to increase economic pressure on Russia, the White House is instead lowering pressure on Russia and demanding that Ukraine stop attacking refineries," the MP went on.

"If it is true that this was accompanied by a Washington threat to Kyiv to stop sharing intelligence if the attacks continue, then this gives Moscow only one unambiguous signal — kill and destroy Ukraine, the US will not stand in the way," he added.

Mihkelson said Trump's efforts to end the war through negotiations have produced not the slightest result.

"The fighting is bloodier than at any previous moment in the entire full-scale invasion," he said. "If you give an aggressor oxygen, the war will not stop."

He stressed that Europe's allies have only one path — to ensure Russia's strategic attack goals fail and the Kremlin's imperial wars end in defeat.

"This clear strategic goal should also be in the US interest, because Russia's long-standing desire, together with China and Iran, to weaken the United States' leadership role is reaching a decisive phase," Mihkelson continued.

Ahead of next month's midterm elections, U.S. President Donald Trump has struck a deal with Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply millions of tonnes of diesel to the world market, reversing years of Western pressure on the Kremlin. Trump said the move was essential to bring down fuel prices, which have soared since Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and warned of a diesel export ban on any EU states that do not release reserves to counter the spike. The G7 agreed earlier this week to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from reserves.

World.title: Estonia condemns US sanctions on International Criminal Court
World.content:
Estonia's Foreign Ministry has publicly condemned US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), joining a growing list of countries criticizing the move.

The ministry said the ICC is a cornerstone of the rules-based international order and a key safeguard against impunity, and offered to discuss US concerns.

The U.S. announced sweeping sanctions on the ICC on Friday.

"Estonia regrets the decision by the US to impose sanctions against the ICC. The International Criminal Court is a cornerstone of the rules-based international order and a vital safeguard against impunity. Estonia remains unwavering in its support for the ICC's independence, impartiality, and integrity," the Foreign Ministry said via social media on Saturday.

The ministry stressed that the ICC is a cornerstone of the rules-based international order and an important safeguard against impunity.

"Estonia firmly supports the independence, impartiality and credibility of the International Criminal Court," the ministry said, confirming it was ready to communicate with the United States to discuss the concerns raised and find a solution.

Estonia regrets the decision by the US to impose sanctions against the ICC. The International Criminal Court is a cornerstone of the rules-based international order and a vital safeguard against impunity. Estonia remains unwavering in its support for the ICC's independence, impartiality, and integrity. We are prepared to engage with the US to further discuss its concerns, in order to resolve this situation. — Estonian MFA | #StandWithUkraine (@MFAestonia) October 10, 2026

Several other countries have hit out at the U.S. decision.

The foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the U.K. issued a joint statement expressing support for the ICC and confirming their opposition to the US decision to impose sanctions on the court.

"If implemented, these would have a significant impact on the court's work, its dedicated staff and their families. We continue to stand united in support of the ICC and consider inclusive and constructive dialogue with non-member states important," the countries said.

Spain's Foreign Ministry also condemned the sanctions. "​Spain deplores the decision by the United States Government to impose new sanctions against the International Criminal Court and reaffirms its unwavering support for the Court, which is at the forefront of the fight against impunity for the most serious international crimes," Spain's foreign ministry said.

Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said that, at Belgium's initiative, support for the ICC will be discussed with EU foreign ministers on Monday and at the upcoming European Council.

⚖️ I strongly condemn the new US sanctions against the International Criminal Court. Seeking to cripple the Court's work denies victims a path to justice and puts those responsible for the gravest crimes beyond its reach. At Belgium's initiative, support for the ICC will be discussed with my EU foreign affairs colleagues on Monday and at the forthcoming European Council. We will press for concrete protection. The Court's independence cannot depend on whom it investigates. Europe must act. Belgium is calling for the activation of the EU Blocking Statute to protect the Court and those who support its work. We must also defend our right to uphold international law without foreign sanctions dictating our choices. @BelgiumMFA @IntlCrimCourt — Maxime PREVOT (@prevotmaxime) October 9, 2026

German Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig said the U.S. move was "utterly staggering". "Historically, hardly any country has done more for international criminal law than the USA. For it was the United ​States that, after the Second World War, championed the cause of bringing the principal perpetrators of the Nazi regime to trial in Nuremberg – and thereby ​laid the foundations for international ⁠criminal law. It is utterly staggering that the US, of all countries, is now setting out to destroy this idea once and for all."

The European Commission expressed support for the ICC as well.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, expressed support for the actions of U.S. President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Netanyahu, who is on an ICC wanted list too, said that it was not a court but a political body.

The UN and several human rights organizations also condemned the sanctions.

The US has previously imposed sanctions on the court's prosecutors and judges.

The Trump administration announced sweeping sanctions on the ICC on Friday, targeting the institution itself rather than individual judges and officials, after previously sanctioning 17 ICC personnel. The U.S .says the court threatens American sovereignty, while the ICC has called the measures an assault on the rule of law; a six-month grace period allows member states to keep funding the court's operations in the meantime.

Founded in 2002, the ICC's purpose is to try war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. In March 2023 it issued an arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin, over war crimes.

World.title: Minister: We have been pressuring Silmet to cut Russian raw material reliance
World.content:
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna says an Estonian rare earth processing firm must set a deadline for ending its use of Russian raw materials, suggesting early next year as a target.

Tsahkna said Estonia has been pressuring the Sillamäe-based NPM Silmet and its owner Neo Group to find alternative suppliers, and that a deadline must now be set.

The European Commission on Friday selected Silmet 2.0 as one of 46 new strategic projects aimed at securing the EU's supply of critical raw materials; Estonia this week pushed to exclude a Russian supplier to NPM Silmet from the EU's proposed 22nd sanctions package.

Tsahkna said the project must come with a firm deadline for ending the company's reliance on Russian raw materials.

"We will work with the European Commission to set a clear deadline for NPM Silmet to stop using Russian raw materials," he told told "Aktuaalne kaamera," adding: "We cannot allow an industry critical to Europe's security to remain dependent on supplies from an aggressor state."

Asked what that deadline might be, Tsahkna said: "We're talking, I think, optimistically about the beginning of next year, next year, which is a pretty fast pace."

Tsahkna confirmed the Foreign Ministry and the government have been pressuring Silmet and Neo Group. "There has actually been pressure, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Estonian government have also been cooperating more broadly with both Silmet and Neo Group," he went on.

He said attempts had been made to find new supply sources, including in Brazil, but that so far it had not been possible to end the dependence on Russia. The supply chain runs through the Solikamsk plant, owned by the Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom.

Tsahkna said Estonia had requested an exemption for the Rosatom-linked supply chain. "We demanded that this supply chain not be interrupted and that Silmet not cease its activities and that the entire European technology industry not be put under attack through this," he said. He added that Estonia has also supported sanctioning Rosatom, but does not see appetite for it in Europe.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal has said the decision is not in line with Estonian values. Asked about this, Tsahkna said the two issues should be separated: pressure on Russia through sanctions, and standing up for Estonian industry.

"I've talked a lot with the Prime Minister about this issue, and we agree that these steps need to be taken, no matter how unpleasant it is," Tsahkna said.

Ukraine has already sanctioned the factory. Tsahkna said he would meet Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha on Monday.

Earlier this week, Estonia successfully pushed to exclude a Russian company supplying rare earth metals to NPM Silmet from the EU's proposed 22nd sanctions package.

Background:

The European Commission on Friday selected Silmet 2.0 as one of 46 new strategic projects aimed at securing the EU's supply of critical raw materials and reducing reliance on third countries. NPM Silmet processes rare earth metals at its Sillamäe plant for use in electronics, medicine, automotive, aviation and defense industries across the EU.

Earlier this week, Estonia pushed to exclude a Russian company supplying rare earth metals to NPM Silmet from the EU's proposed 22nd sanctions package, which is awaiting formal approval. Estonia's representation in Brussels confirmed the request, saying the company supplies NPM Silmet with materials of strategic importance to Europe, and that Estonia will reconsider adding the company and an individual associated with it to the sanctions list next year.

EU ambassadors agreed on October 7 to sanctions targeting 743 individuals and 826 companies linked to Russia's military-industrial complex. The package awaits final approval by member states' foreign ministers and is expected to take effect in the coming days.

World.title: Raul Eamets: Estonia is haunted by an overblown debt‑burden specter
World.content:
We forget two factors when talking about the growth of the debt burden — factors that affect the whole picture: economic growth and price growth, writes Raul Eamets.

The state budget has reached the Riigikogu, and discussions will show in what form it will ultimately be adopted. Nothing will come easily, because a minority government no longer has a voting steamroller.

Those who say (for example, the Fiscal Council) that the savings are temporary and short‑term, achieved mainly by pushing certain expenses into the future, are right. No structural changes have been made.

This is understandable, because elections are at the door, and no one will stop the indexation of social benefits or cut education costs before elections. Instead, cosmetic, symbolic‑value topics are addressed.

For example, Prime Minister Kristen Michal claimed that the salary increase for senior state officials will not come in the amount prescribed by the formula (law). In real life, this means that in 2023 the coefficient determining salary growth was reduced for some officials. The lowered coefficient was initially supposed to apply until 2028, but now it has been decided to extend it until 2031. The financial impact is symbolic; as a message, it is an important step to gain a bit of support. Simply put, pure political technology.

One negative aspect of the entire budget and budget strategy, constantly emphasized by critics, is the rapid growth of the debt burden and the interest costs that must be paid starting in 2030.

If our public‑sector debt burden is roughly 26 percent of GDP, then according to current plans and forecasts it will grow to 38.6 percent of GDP by 2030. Interest payments will grow from €205 million to €650 million. To solve the situation even somewhat, the budget should be brought into balance as quickly as possible.

"Everyone wants economic growth, and price growth — at least to some extent — is unavoidable."

One must agree that paying current expenses — especially those indexed to price increases — with borrowed money is not very wise. Current expenses should be covered by current revenues. That seems logical. If investments are needed — expenses that will bring revenue back in the future — then borrowing is practically unavoidable.

It must be kept in mind that investment is not only pouring money into concrete or railways, but also investing in human capital. Whether it is for increasing birth rates, improving healthcare, or improving education. All these expenses bring greater returns in the future, whether in the form of more taxpayers or healthier and smarter workers.

But let's return to those three claims and look at each separately. The first is simple. What happens if the debt burden grows to 39 percent of GDP by 2030? The honest answer is: nothing happens. We will certainly still be among the last three in the EU in terms of debt burden, perhaps among the last four, but that does not change the big picture.

According to the EU's founding principles, a 60‑percent debt‑to‑GDP ratio is acceptable; the EU average is 90 percent. Finland's national debt is moving toward that 90 percent, and Finland can borrow on financial markets at very normal interest rates. Scare tactics claiming that "no one will lend to us then" simply do not work in real life.

The second claim — that interest costs in four years will be as large as current spending on science and higher education combined — does not hold for a very simple reason. Carrying current costs into the future requires accounting for price increases; inflation reduces the value of money in the future.

A cost of €650 million will be worth €589 million in four years if we assume a modest 2.5‑percent price increase. Considering what is happening in the world, one can assume that the impact of the oil crisis on prices will be longer and deeper, meaning that a 3‑percent annual inflation rate could easily be used. In that case, the value of €650 million in four years would be €578 million.

"Finland's national debt is moving toward that 90 percent, and Finland can borrow on financial markets at very normal interest rates."

Now the other side of the equation. Our higher‑education costs will certainly not be €650 million in four years. If we assume that higher‑education costs grow by roughly five percent annually, then in four years they will be €790 million. Compare the two numbers: 578 and 790 are not exactly in the same magnitude. A five‑percent annual growth rate is more than modest; looking back in time, the growth number could be much, much higher.

The third claim — that we must achieve a balanced budget at any cost, and only then will happiness arrive — also does not withstand much criticism. We forget two factors when talking about the growth of the debt burden: economic growth and price growth.

Everyone wants economic growth, and price growth — at least to some extent — is unavoidable. Has anyone ever thought why the EU has a three‑percent deficit rule, a 60‑percent debt limit, and a two‑percent inflation target?

If we put these numbers into a formula and calculate how the debt burden changes in a year when the economy grows three percent, inflation is two percent, and the budget deficit is three percent, we get a surprising result. Under these conditions, the debt burden does not grow in a year — it stays the same.

If we continue the thought experiment, the current average EU debt burden of 90 percent of GDP would decrease by 0.8 percentage points in a year if we use a forecasted three‑percent inflation rate, a 3.3‑percent consolidated budget deficit, and assume 1.5‑percent economic growth. These are indicators that could characterize the euro‑area economy in 2026. All this happens while the budget is 3.3 percent in deficit, not balanced. For the debt burden not to grow under certain conditions, the budget does not need to be balanced.

Of course, no one knows what our economic growth, inflation, or actual borrowing needs will be in four years. It is impossible to predict because global uncertainty is too great. Therefore, all kinds of model calculations are made, which in turn rely on various assumptions.

Economic forecasting has become mathematics. All the more important is to talk about nominal and real indicators, about how inflation reduces the purchasing power of money in the future, and how economic growth changes ratios relative to GDP. Life is a bit more complicated than simply waving around numbers whose magnitudes are incomprehensible to ordinary people anyway. The specter in the room is much smaller than it is being painted. About the size of a matchbox.

World.title: Feature: Spanish jets leave Ämari — but the Baltic mission goes on
World.content:
NATO's Baltic air mission is now over 20 years old and was recently upgraded to a defense posture — making it high time to visit Ämari Air Base to catch up on developments.

The mission is held on a rotational basis and planes from Turkey's Air Force were joined from late August to early October by those of Spain's Air Force.

Four Spanish EF-18M Hornets left Ämari Air Base on October 9, five weeks after arriving, and the crews gathered on the apron to see them off.

If you had told me previously there were Spanish Hornets in Estonia, I would likely have thought you were talking about the effects of climate change. However, these are state-of-the-art multirole fighter planes we are talking about here, and they are leaving that very morning ERR News visits.

This provides the last chance to see the Spanish contingent, but the first chance to understand what a five-week rotation actually means.

Maj. Antonio Mancebo Marín stands at the edge of the apron and watches his aircraft leave. The four EF-18M Hornets have been parked at Ämari for some weeks, but unlike many military ground vehicles they do not require being transported back home by road, rail or sea, and the pilots can fly them back themselves.

On the morning they are due to fly home to Spain, personnel gather on the tarmac to see them off in suitably enthusiastic manner. Some carry national and unit flags. This is a mood that is closer to celebration than it is to routine. Around three crew members support every aircraft too. The jets are heading back home to sunny Zaragoza, a journey of around four hours including a mid-air refuel over Germany.

Next the jets begin to taxi. While on civilian flights you are kept well away from jet exhaust, on a military base you get much closer, enough to feel the heat coming off the engines as well as the noise, despite being issued ear defenders. There is a smell of burnt aviation fuel that lingers in the air after they have passed by, the pilots giving their own signature farewells through the closed canopies.

Most of the Spanish Air Force contingent's personnel are from Wing 15, based in Zaragoza. Source: mil.ee

One of the planes is held up — a hydraulics issue which would affect control surfaces, the Spanish Air Force's helpful press officer tells me. It, too, is soon on its way once this gets fixed. The base at Ämari is not small — about twice the land area of nearby Keila. A car is needed to get from the entrance to the apron. Fortunately the weather is fittingly glorious and sunny too. Liaison and flight plan filing with civilian air traffic control takes place well before the take-off, so we can be sure the flights won't interfere with anything.

The takeoff itself is not something you can prepare for. Four fighters going up in pairs make a sound you feel in your body as much as hear, and the length required to take off is considerably shorter than with civilian airliners. But soon the last plane is on its way — they are flying direct to Spain from Estonia.

The pilots are gone but many of the personnel remain until at least the next day, sometimes more, packing up equipment, and making sure everything is in good order for the next arriving deployment.

The EF-18M is Spain's modified variant of the McDonnell Douglas F/A-18 Hornet. Source: Triin Musting/mil.ee

The mission

The Spanish detachment had arrived at Ämari in late August and left by or on October 9 — joining a Turkish Air Force deployment already there. Around 110 personnel came with the aircraft, most of them from Zaragoza, particularly from Wing 15 and the Air Deployment Support Squadron of the Ejército del Aire y del Espacio, the Spanish Air Force.

"The detachment comprises around 110 personnel, and the pilots are only its most visible element," the air force had said in a written statement. "Behind every flight are specialists in maintenance, weapons, operations, logistics, communications, force protection, medical support and administration. Without them, no aircraft would take off."

The Spanish and Turkish detachments share the base but retain their own national command structures. Daily coordination covers flying schedules, airspace, flight safety, alert duties and joint training.

"We use the same procedures and command-and-control structure," the press officer tells me. "Sharing the base has made that cooperation very natural and has allowed us to learn from each other."

Baltic Air Defense has changed much since Spain's first deployment here over a decade ago. What was once primarily peacetime surveillance, identification and interception is now integrated into a broader defensive posture — a posture designed to address both manned and unmanned threats, with closer links between fighters, surveillance systems, command-and-control centers and ground-based air defenses.

Drones are the clearest example of that shift. Maj. Mancebo, the unit's commander, says roughly 20 percent of training in the Baltics now relates to drones, including seek-and-destroy drills.

One of the four EF-18M pilots giving a wave before heading home. Source: Triin Musting/mil.ee

With their small size, around 2 meters maximum, these naturally present a different target which must be adapted to.

"The message is that no one without authorization may fly in NATO airspace," Maj. Mancebo says.

This is not an abstract matter either. In August this year, a Spanish Hornet just like the ones departing Ämari downed a Russian-made drone, this time in the skies over Romania.

As for Baltic airspace, the mission here has long conducted interception missions of foreign aircraft too, if they stray too near to, or occasionally briefly even inside, Estonian airspace.

Scrambling to identify and intercept is "a professional and highly controlled task" the press officer said. "In the cockpit, we focus on the behavior of the aircraft and on carrying out the instructions received, rather than on its nationality."

"When directed, we approach safely, identify the aircraft visually, report what we observe and monitor or escort it as required. Operating close to national borders demands discipline, situational awareness and strict adherence to established procedures. An interception is a defensive measure intended to maintain safety and awareness, not a provocation," he went on.

As for what a typical day might look like, this "depends on whether you are assigned to Quick Reaction Alert, a training mission or mission planning. A normal day includes intelligence and weather briefings, checking the status of the aircraft, reviewing the tasking and coordinating with operations, maintenance and the control agencies.

"Alert crews remain ready to respond when directed. At the same time, we regularly fly air-defense and Close Air Support training missions with our Allies, both by day and at night. These activities allow us to practise identification, interception, air-to-air refueling, support to forces on the ground and coordination among aircraft and control agencies."

Vapor trails follow the EF-18Ms as they take off from Ämari. Source: Triin Musting/mil.ee

Quick Reaction Alert (QRA) is maintained around the clock. The Air Force could not give exact readiness times for operational-security reasons, but from being roused from sleep by the alarm in a QRA scramble to being airborne is about 15 minutes, meaning pilots and ground personnel alike have to have everything well drilled. The actual order to launch comes from the Combined Air Operations Center at Uedem in western Germany.

"Every mission begins with detailed planning and ends with a debrief, where we review its execution and identify ways to continue improving," the press officer notes.

As of the end of the rotation, the detachment had flown over 200 hours without incident — something the commander describes as one of the mission's main successes.

Including the recently departed contingent, Spain has now deployed fighters to Ämari five times: in 2015, 2017, 2022 (combined with the German Air Force), 2023 and then this year.

Comandante (Major) Antonio Mancebo Marín is the unit's commander. Source: Triin Musting/mil.ee

The host nation

For all its state of the art equipment and trained personnel, the detachment could not have operated from Ämari without Estonian support, the Air Force was explicit about that.

"Estonian host-nation support is fundamental," the officers tell me. "It includes airfield infrastructure and services, air traffic coordination, fire and rescue capabilities, security and daily logistical support."

Estonian personnel also provide local knowledge and can help the Spanish integrate into the base and the wider NATO command-and-control system.

"We could not sustain our operations from Ämari without their continuous support and close cooperation."

The plane

The Spanish Air Force deployment consisted of four EF-18Ms. This is the Spanish version of the McDonnell Douglas F/A-18 Hornet.

The air force describes it as a mature, reliable and highly capable aircraft, well suited to air-defense missions, with sensors and communications that allow it to integrate into NATO's command-and-control system.

The plane designation follows the U.S. F-for-Fighter, B-for-Bomber format, regardless of manufacturer. In the Spanish variant the designation is EF-18M: originally an F/A-18, when sold to Spain it became EF-18, with the M subsequently added to stand for "Modernized (MLU)." The "E" stands for España.

There are usually 3 ground crew per plane on the apron when awaiting taxiing and take-off. Source: Triin Musting/mil.ee

Spain's Hornets are also unusual in one further specific respect. When the aircraft were purchased, Spain was the only user nation granted permission in the contract to modify the planes itself. Most of those modifications were software-related, and over time they produced this distinct EF-18M version.

Also unusually, the Spanish Hornets carry European weapons on an American airframe, which means integration work has to go through the relevant defense industries.

As for operating in Estonia, the regional environment puts specific demands on the aircraft. The press officer cited rapidly changing weather, reduced visibility, dense airspace and the proximity of several borders — conditions the crews train for regularly, while Maj. Mancebo notes that colder conditions bring challenges too. "Planes suffer in the cold," he said.

Maj. Mancebo would have no other plane than the EF-18M, which he describes as superb and his favorite jet to fly. Past experience includes time on a more vintage plane, the F-5, which comes in as a worthy second favorite. As for planes he would like to fly but has not yet, the F-22 Raptor figures highly.

The people

As noted, around 110 personnel came from Zaragoza, particularly from Wing 15 and the Air Deployment Support Squadron, though several other units contributed.

"The pilots are only the most visible element," the press officer says. "Behind every flight are specialists in maintenance, weapons, operations, logistics, communications, force protection, medical support and administration."

Many of the gound staff, soon heading back themselves, turnout for the big sendoff. Source: Triin Musting/mil.ee

Life on deployment means long working days and time away from families. The air force says morale is maintained through a sense of purpose, team cohesion, physical training, shared activities and regular contact with home. "Knowing that every member of the detachment contributes directly to the mission also brings the team together."

Not all of the time is spent on base. The commander mentions Tallinn's Old Town and Patarei Prison among the highlights of places personnel visited during what free time they had during the deployment.

As to what he would say to those back home, the press officer points to the families as much as the crews. "Every sortie represents the effort of a large team and the support of our families, who also make this mission possible," he said.

And a message to Estonia: "Spain's commitment is real and practical. We are here with our personnel and aircraft, ready to contribute to the protection of Allied airspace because Estonia's security is also Spain's security."

The goodbye

Maj. Mancebo was clear about how he felt.

"We are happy to go back to our families, but sad to leave," he said. "I would have loved to stay another month."

The plans will refuel mid-air over Germany on the way home to Zaragoza. Source: Triin Musting/mil.ee

The EF-18Ms have gone now. Life at the base at Ämari goes on, however.

The walk back away from the base brings a curious blend of state-of-the-art and traditional, too: I spot an old woman out mushrooming in the copious forest that surrounds the base. Along the public road leading up to the gate lies a Soviet-era cemetery where pilots from another epoch lie buried below headstones shaped like the vertical stabilizer from a MiG-17.

The Spanish crews have packed up, their planes long gone, and the Turks are still at Ämari. That is how the Baltic air mission works: it does not stop, it just changes flags.

With thanks to Staff Sergeant Siim Verner Teder and Junior Sergeant Triin Musting of the Estonian Air Force (Õhuvägi) for facilitating the visit.

Maj. Mancebo Marín also discusses his career, the Hornet and the Baltic mission in an interview on the Fighter Pilot X podcast here.

World.title: Taiwan’s leader says increasing defence spending to ‘deter war’
World.content:
Taipei – Taiwan aims to “deter war” by increasing its defence spending, the democratic island’s leader said on Saturday, as China uses military pressure to assert its territorial claims.

Taiwan’s 23 million people live under the constant threat of an attack by China, which insists the island is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to annex it.

“Our aim by increasing investment in national defence is not to provoke, rather, it is to deter war,” President Lai Ching-te said in a speech to celebrate Taiwan’s National Day.

Successive administrations have ramped up military spending as Taiwan improves its fighting abilities to avoid a potential Chinese invasion — and to show the United States it is serious about its own defence.

Lai’s government has earmarked a record NT$1.1 trillion (US$34.5 billion) in defence spending for 2027, which accounts for more than three percent of GDP.

“We do not seek hegemony, nor do we seek to dominate others,” Lai said in his annual address in front of the Presidential Office in Taipei, where thousands of people, including foreign diplomats, were gathered.

“However, peace cannot rely solely on wishes, and tolerance cannot become a pretext for aggressors to encroach ever further,” Lai said, noting that China continued to “apply pressure through military and grey-zone activities in an attempt to alter the status quo across the Taiwan Strait”.

Lai welcomed talks between the United States and China, but insisted “there must be respect for the right of the people of Taiwan to exist”.

Government officials in Washington and Taipei have said repeatedly that US policy on Taiwan has not changed under President Donald Trump, whose remarks have jangled nerves at times.

– ‘US support is extremely important’ –

The United States switched official diplomatic relations from Taipei to Beijing nearly 50 years ago, but Washington is Taipei’s most important security backer.

Trump’s suggestion in May, following a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing, that US arms sales to Taiwan could be a bargaining chip with China set off alarm bells across the world.

Taiwan is waiting for Trump’s signature on $14 billion worth of weapons, including the US-made Patriot air defence system.

Taiwanese fighter jets and two Chinook helicopters carrying giant Taiwan flags flew over the capital ahead of Lai’s wide-ranging speech, which also covered housing pressure and the declining population.

“You can really feel the warmth in Taiwanese society,” said Feng Jing-heng, 70, who was in the crowd watching the military parade and dance performances.

Tao Yi-feng, a political scientist at National Taiwan University, said Lai’s speech was “relatively moderate” and unlikely to be met with “overt reaction from Beijing”.

Saturday’s celebrations mark the 115th anniversary of the toppling of China’s Qing dynasty and the subsequent founding of the Republic of China.

The current dispute between China and Taiwan dates to a civil war between the nationalist forces of Chiang Kai-shek, who retreated to the island in 1949 after being defeated by Mao Zedong’s communist fighters.

Parliamentary speaker Han Kuo-yu, who is a senior member of the main opposition party that favours closer ties with China, said “US support is extremely important to Taiwan’s security”, but he noted the historical and cultural links with China.

“The overwhelming majority of Taiwanese compatriots do not want war; they wish to live their lives in peace and hope for peaceful cross-strait exchanges,” Han said at the National Day event.

World.title: Year later, Gaza ceasefire promises mostly unfulfilled
World.content:
Jerusalem – One year after US President Donald Trump declared the war in Gaza to be over, few of the long-term promises of the ceasefire have come to fruition.

Here is a list of some of the key points of the October 10, 2025 ceasefire and where things stand:

– Hostages released, calm in Israel –

Three days after the agreement was announced, Hamas freed the 20 remaining living hostages seized during the group’s October 7, 2023 attack, the deadliest day in Israel’s history.

The captives’ return was a key priority for Israel, whose public had agonised over their fate.

The ceasefire anniversary also marks one year of quiet for Israel from the Gaza front, with no rocket attacks by Hamas.

The group’s missile inventory was depleted by near-constant Israeli bombardment, which damaged or destroyed the vast majority of buildings in the Palestinian territory.

The US military set up a command post with foreign allies near the Gaza border to monitor the truce.

– No Israeli withdrawal or let-up –

Israel has reduced its level of attacks but has kept striking Gaza on a near-daily basis.

Israeli strikes have killed some 1,450 Palestinians since the ceasefire, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which operates under Hamas and whose figures are considered accurate by the United Nations.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is in a tight election race, has vowed to kill everyone involved in the October 7 attack.

Netanyahu said on the attack’s anniversary that 4,000 out of 6,000 “Hamas monsters” had been killed.

Israeli forces were allowed to stay in 53 percent of Gaza under the terms of the ceasefire, but a year later they control about 70 percent of it, according to official accounts.

– Hamas remains, with weapons –

The second phase of the agreement was supposed to include a political transition away from Hamas, and technocrat Ali Shaath was appointed head of a new National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).

Hamas announced in July that it was disbanding its governing body and handing over Gaza’s administration to the US-blessed NCAG.

But Hamas effectively remains in charge of security in Gaza, and Shaath has taken a low profile.

The Palestinian Islamist movement elected a new leader, Khalil al-Hayya, in July. Shortly afterwards, the group announced it would give up its weapons, a step hailed by Trump as a breakthrough.

But Israel has been sceptical, with Netanyahu demanding verifiable decommissioning of all weapons down to individual guns.

Hamas has not gone ahead with disarmament, and Israel has refused to reciprocate by starting to withdraw forces.

– Reconstruction just talk –

Trump set up a new global body for the deal dubbed the “Board of Peace”, tapping as key figures former British prime minister Tony Blair and Bulgarian diplomat Nickolay Mladenov, who serves as “Gaza high representative”.

Trump, a critic of foreign aid, in January promised $10 billion in US funding to the board he controls, and Gulf allies have pledged more, but no money is known to have made its way to Gaza reconstruction.

In September, the board proposed a $2.45 billion Gaza recovery plan at a meeting of its members and stakeholders, in an effort meant to span over six months.

World.title: Hunger and malnutrition stalk Gazans, a year on from ceasefire
World.content:
Khan Yunis – Every day, Gazan mother Niyaha al-Masri spends six exhausting hours or more queueing at a community kitchen in the hope of getting some food for her family.

It has been a year since a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel was supposed to allow food to flood into the ruined territory, yet widespread hunger persists there.

Masri has little choice. Without the kitchen run by humanitarian groups, she and her eight children would have “nothing at all”, the 35-year-old told AFP.

Each day she sets out early in the morning and returns in the afternoon, this time bringing four containers of rice, lentils and a little chicken, which the family throws itself at.

Among them is her husband, wounded in both legs by an airstrike, meaning he “cannot go and fight with the others” to get food.

This will be the only meal of the day for the family of 10, living in a tent in Khan Yunis. There was no breakfast and they will have no dinner.

What little flour they have, Masri explained, has to be rationed.

In August 2025, a United Nations-backed body, the IPC, declared a state of famine in Gaza, though Israel quickly denounced it as a lie.

By December, the UN had lifted that declaration, saying that the ceasefire had allowed in enough supplies over the course of two months to ease conditions.

COGAT, the Israeli defence ministry organisation responsible for civilian affairs in the Palestinian territories, told AFP that the humanitarian situation in Gaza was stable.

But Shaun Hughes, of the UN’s World Food Programme, was less sanguine.

The food security situation, he said, “is still extremely serious”.

The most recent figures, from July, show that “1.4 million out of the population of about 2.1 million people are acutely food insecure”, he said, with 200,000 of them “just one step below famine”.

– ‘Shameful’ –

While some food is getting in, a lack of sufficient nutritional variety continues to pose a health threat.

“Dietary diversity is a major food security issue in Gaza,” said Hughes.

“You cannot survive on dry goods and wheat flour and bread alone. Particularly children, particularly pregnant and breastfeeding mothers, they need the micronutrients that come with high protein foods, fresh vegetables, fresh fruits,” he explained.

Masri said that her children, aged between three and 14, “dream of eating fruit” but the family doesn’t have the means to buy any.

She said one of her sons suffered from malnutrition during the 2025 famine, although “little by little, his condition is improving”.

Malnutrition isn’t only caused by a lack of food, but also essential nutrients. It weakens the immune system of children, making them vulnerable to illnesses and stunting their growth.

“Repeated bouts of acute malnutrition amongst children is something that human beings just don’t recover from,” said Hughes.

Cognitive and physical impairments “continue into later life”, he added.

At Khan Yunis’s Nasser hospital, the head of the malnutrition unit, Israa al-Najjar, told AFP she had “observed an increase in syndromes and conditions” linked to malnutrition that affect the immune system.

In a report published on Thursday, the day after the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attack that sparked the Gaza war, Medecins du Monde published a study that found 93 percent of pregnant or breastfeeding women had symptoms of anaemia, which is closely linked to malnutrition.

Just 17 percent had a sufficiently varied diet to meet their nutritional needs, the group found.

All the while, Masri has kept visiting the community kitchen, despite asthma leaving her exhausted.

Her children spend their days collecting “pieces of nylon, bits of cardboard and chunks of foam” to try and reinforce their tent, which is in a poor state.

She said it was “shameful” that her children had to do so.

“I swear to God, this isn’t normal.”

World.title: Three Mexicans convicted in murders of Australian, US surfers
World.content:
Ensenada – A Mexican judge on Friday convicted three men in the 2024 murders of two Australian surfers and their American friend, who were killed during a botched robbery that sparked international outrage.

Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in a suspected robbery.

They were camping in a remote beachside area near the coastal city of Ensenada when they were attacked on April 27, 2024.

Their bodies were found days later, dumped in a cliff-top shaft, with gunshot wounds to their heads.

The judge ruled that the three Mexican defendants acted with premeditation. They have yet to be sentenced.

The Robinsons’ parents traveled from Australia for the month-long trial.

Debra Robinson burst into tears when the guilty verdict was pronounced.

In a statement on behalf of the family Martin Robinson said that “while no verdict can ever bring back our boys or ease the heartbreak of losing them” the convictions marked “an important step towards justice and accountability.”

The prosecution has requested 210 years imprisonment for each of the accused, though the maximum sentence in Baja California is 60 years.

– Victim begged for mercy –

In its closing arguments on Thursday, the prosecution described the cold-blooded killings of the three surfers, who were caught off guard at their campsite.

A 9mm and a .45 caliber pistol were used in the attack.

The prosecutors recalled the testimony of the girlfriend of the main suspect, identified only as Jesus Gerardo, at her trial last November.

She said that Rhoad had begged for his life and that her boyfriend, who is nicknamed “El Kekas,” had bragged about “how beautifully” the victims cried and about items he robbed from them.

The girlfriend was sentenced to two decades in prison after admitting that she instigated the robbery in order to steal the pickup’s tires.

Testifying on the final day of the trial, Debra Robinson said what hurt herself and her husband the most was that “in their final hours” their sons “were treated with such cruelty.”

Rhoad’s fiancee Natalie Weirtz told the court by video call that the accused “must be punished so that no other family suffers the same pain.”

Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organized crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity doesn’t usually affect tourists.

Other foreign visitors have been targeted in attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.

Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were murdered in 2015 while traveling through the northwestern state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

World.title: Trump hails Russia deal to release diesel as midterms loom
World.content:
Washington – US President Donald Trump said Friday that he had secured Russia’s agreement for a major release of diesel, as he eased war sanctions on Moscow in a push to lower energy costs ahead of midterm elections.

Moscow has been hit with waves of sanctions by the United States and partners since its 2022 invasion of neighboring Ukraine, and President Volodymyr Zelensky criticized Trump for an “unworthy” and “weak” move.

The deal comes weeks before key US elections where Trump’s Republican Party risks losing its grip on Congress as voters express frustration over the mounting cost of living.

Prices at US gasoline and diesel pumps have surged since late February, when US-Israel strikes targeting Iran triggered Tehran’s blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for energy transit.

“Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace,” Trump said on social media after talks with Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

The Kremin said Russia “reaffirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and world markets.”

Trump added Moscow would supply 500,000 tons in November, followed by one million tons, with further larger releases promised.

Zelensky told reporters: “It is certainly not honest, it is certainly unworthy of our partners, and it is, in my view, a weak decision.”

The US Treasury issued a temporary license Friday to enable Russian diesel to flow to global markets through April 2027.

“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” Trump posted on social media.

– Conflict stalemate –

The average cost of regular US gasoline has jumped more than 46 percent since late February to $4.37 per gallon, while that of diesel rocketed 67 percent over the same period to $6.28 per gallon.

Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for surging fuel prices, although the US-Israeli war with Iran has been the principal disruptor of global energy supplies.

News of the deal came as Ukrainian and US negotiators met on Friday in Miami in a fresh attempt to break the conflict’s stalemate.

The sides “held constructive discussions on potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter,” said US envoy Steve Witkoff.

The Miami meeting follows visits to Moscow and Kyiv last month by Witkoff, a longtime Trump confidant, and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, as Washington seeks to revive negotiations that have yielded little progress.

With winter approaching, the prospect of continued fighting and attacks on vital infrastructure has added urgency to the search for a settlement against a backdrop of deadly Russian attacks.

On Thursday a Russian strike on buses in the frontline Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed 30 people.

Trump’s repeated attempts to broker an end to the war have foundered over Moscow’s sweeping territorial demands, particularly its insistence on controlling all of Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, including areas still held by Kyiv.

Zelensky has rejected surrendering Ukrainian-held territory, warning that Russia could use it as a springboard for another attack.

Russia now occupies roughly one-fifth of Ukrainian territory.

The Miami discussions covered “security guarantees, as well as longer-term arrangements for Ukraine’s and Europe’s security to prevent future conflicts, and support Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction,” Witkoff said.

Officials from Britain, France and Germany were at the talks, along with representatives of NATO and the European Union.

World.title: Anthropic AI model sent fake murder tip to Philadelphia police
World.content:
San Francisco – An artificial intelligence model developed by Anthropic submitted a fabricated tip about an unsolved homicide to Philadelphia police, authorities said Friday, criticizing the company for taking two months to report the incident.

The Philadelphia Police Department said the false submission was made in July through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a public website where people can share information about unsolved killings.

According to Anthropic’s account, as relayed by police, the model was running a test that involved interacting with randomly selected websites when it reached the site and filed false information about an unsolved murder.

The AI model presented itself as someone who might have knowledge of the case.

The department said it was going public with the incident ahead of a report that Anthropic was planning to release Friday describing this and other instances of unintended behavior by its models.

The case echoed other recent cases, including one where an OpenAI agent undergoing a security evaluation broke out of its testing environment and breached systems at AI platform Hugging Face.

The episode heightened concerns about the AI industry’s increased use of AI agents, systems programmed to take multi-step actions without human supervision.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request from AFP for comment.

Police said the tip, dated July 18, was flagged as spam and never reached the department’s Real-Time Crime Center for vetting.

They added that there was no sign that police systems had been breached or department data compromised.

Anthropic discovered the incident on September 28, shut down the automated testing process responsible and added a new validation step for future tests, police said.

The company alerted the department on October 7, and the two sides met the following day.

“The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable,” the department said.

Police said their safeguards had limited the impact, but that these “do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide.”

“Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the statement added.

World.title: Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Tel Aviv airport: UAE prosecutor
World.content:
Dubai – The co-pilot who attacked the captain of a flydubai jet last month had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv’s international airport, the United Arab Emirates’ top prosecutor said on Friday.

The unnamed Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from Al-Qaeda’s September 11, 2001 suicide attacks on the United States, and carried out his attempt “with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”, according to the prosecutor’s findings published by state media.

“The findings showed that he had met the professional and security requirements for employment, including holding a pilot’s licence, providing a certificate of good conduct and completing the required checks.”

“However, none of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot.”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu previously said that the co-pilot must have got around restrictions preventing individuals from nations that do not recognise Israel operating flights to the country.

According to the UAE prosecutor, the co-pilot — identified in reports as Hamam al-Hammami — had previously worked for Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc.

– ‘Extremist literature’ –

Last week, Emirati investigators said the co-pilot was planning a terrorist attack and revealed that he had used the cockpit’s emergency axe to attack the captain, but did not at the time reveal his motivations.

Netanyahu told the media last week that the suspect had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination”.

According to the Emirati prosecutor, the co-pilot was radicalised while studying in Australia “through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks”.

He said this was the co-pilot’s third flight to Tel Aviv, following two earlier trips he had used to plan the attack.

During the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, the Omani co-pilot assaulted the plane’s Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, but he managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the attacker and force an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

In the immediate aftermath, passengers described rushing the cockpit and a fight for control after the plane suddenly plunged by around 5,000 metres (17,000 feet).

An off-duty pilot travelling on the plane was then able to take the controls and land the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia.

The passengers on board the aircraft were overwhelmingly Israeli, with Netanyahu hailing them and the pilot for their bravery after the foiled attack.

He later ordered a “thorough review of all security aspects of foreign civil aviation to Israel” in response to the incident.

World.title: Mike Ditka: Chicago Bears icon as player and coach
World.content:
Los Angeles – Mike Ditka was already an NFL champion and Chicago icon when he guided the celebrated 1985 Bears to the Super Bowl crown.

With Ditka’s death on Friday at age 86, his legendary role on one of the most overwhelming teams in NFL history was recalled fondly by American football fans.

Coached by Ditka, led by quarterback Jim McMahon and featuring legendary running back Walter Payton and unlikely superstar William “Refrigerator” Perry,” the 1985 Bears also boasted one of the best defenses in NFL history. They lost just one game before pounding the New England Patriots 46-10 in Super Bowl 20.

Their on-field dominance was matched by an off-field swagger that earned them pop-culture fame reaching far beyond traditional NFL supporters.

“They changed the laws of football,” former US President Barack Obama — who calls Chicago home — said of the team. “They were gritty. They were gutsy. They were hard-working. They were fun-loving.”

For Ditka, born Michael Dyczko in the Pittsburgh-area town of Carnegie, Pennsylvania, on October 18, 1939, grit, guts and hard work had long been the keys to gridiron success.

“There’s more to winning than just wanting to,” Ditka once said. “You have to prove yourself every Sunday. “Just throwing your helmet on the field doesn’t scare anyone.

“There’s no more empty feeling in the world than losing.”

Drafted fifth overall by the Bears in 1961, Ditka introduced a new dimension to the tight end position long the preserve of talented blockers.

He was among the first tight ends to emerge as a significant pass receiving threat, punishing opposing defenses with 56 catches for 1,076 yards and 12 touchdowns in his Rookie of the Year ’61 season.

In 1964, he caught 75 passes — a season record for tight ends that lasted until 1980.

He earned All-NFL honors four straight seasons from 1961 through 1964 and was a Pro Bowl choice after each of his first five seasons.

Ditka finished his 12-year playing career with 427 receptions for 5,812 yards and 43 touchdowns and was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame as a player in 1988.

By then, he had left Chicago and returned in triumph.

After a falling out with Chicago owner-coach George Halas, Ditka was traded to the Eagles in 1967, and finished his playing career with Dallas.

His best campaign with the Cowboys came in 1971, when they won their first Super Bowl title.

Ditka had 30 receptions that year and he scored the final touchdown in the Cowboys’ 24-3 win over the Miami Dolphins in Super Bowl Six.

Ditka was an assistant coach for the Cowboys when they won the Super Bowl in 1978.

– Folk hero –

In 1982, Halas brought Ditka back to Chicago. His tenure as coach included 127 victories and spawned a legendary “Saturday Night Live” comedy sketch in which “Bill Swerski’s Superfans” laud all things to do with “Da Bears” and Ditka.

He parlayed his popularity into a wealth of ventures: restaurant owner, TV personality, co-owner of an Arena Football League team.

He once promoted his own brand of sausages and a line of wine and cigars.

Ditka’s folk-hero status belied a ruthless streak. Tough as nails, he was back on the sidelines a week after suffering a heart attack in 1988 — and he expected the same resolve from players.

Dave Duerson, a standout safety on the ’85 Bears team who was found to have the concussion-related brain disease CTE after he committed suicide in 2011, once said that Ditka “was not one who gave a damn about the players or their injuries when he was coaching.”

Ditka sparked controversy in 2017 when he weighed in against the national anthem protests led by quarterback Colin Kaepernick.

He never shied away from the spotlight, continuing to follow — and comment on — the Bears after a stroke in 2012 and another heart attack in 2018.

“I’m a Bears fan,” he said in December 2018. “Always will be.”

World.title: Entire Delhi shut down; police, BJP's 'goondas' beat up students: Rahul Gandhi at Chhatron Ki Goonj
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in Lok Sabha

on Saturday accused Prime Minister

and the

of silencing dissent, alleging that the internet was shut down in Delhi and students were beaten up during protests in the national capital.

âThey are silencing voices as you saw in Delhi. The entire city was shutdown, internet was shutdown. Police was beating students. BJP released their own 'goodas' who were beating and thrashing students,â Rahul said while addressing students at the 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' event in Chennai.

Slamming the Prime Minister over the alleged police action on student protesters Rahul said, "Modi is destroying India's democracy".

The Congress leader's remarks came as protests rocked Delhi over demands for Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar's resignation and allegations of irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Protesters were prevented from reaching Jantar Mantar, the designated venue, amid heavy security deployment, with groups attempting to assemble at different locations across the city.





Delhi Police had deployed around 25,000 personnel, including police and paramilitary forces, ahead of the demonstration. Restrictions were also imposed at several metro stations, while protesters were detained as they attempted to regroup and raise slogans.

Rahul, meanwhile, linked the importance of dissent and questioning to the role of students in a democracy, arguing that curiosity was essential for progress and innovation.

âWe said that curiosity comes from your culture, your history, and your land. It is the basis with which you ask questions. Curiosity is also the foundation of your progress. Anything that you ever do, any business that has built, any country that has built, any innovation, any art, dance or music. Anything that you do well will always begin as a question that you ask. So, questioning is the foundation of curiosity, questioning is also the foundation of progress,â he said.

World.title: ‘Is peacefully raising your voice a crime?’ CJP alleges Delhi Police dragged, forcibly detained protesters
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Saturday accused Delhi Police of forcibly detaining its activists and dragging protesters attempting to reach Jantar Mantar for a demonstration demanding Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumarâs resignation over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls.

More than 7,000 people were detained across the national capital, while six police personnel were injured after stones were allegedly hurled at two locations. Police are also set to register an FIR in connection with the alleged assault on personnel.

In a post accompanying a video purportedly showing police detaining activists and taking them away, CJP said: âCJPâS TEAM FORCEFULLY DETAINED!â

âDelhi Police is pushing, dragging and detaining people for peacefully protesting!â the party wrote, adding, âIs peacefully raising your voice a crime now?â

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, co-convener Saurav Das and leader Ashutosh Ranka were detained aboard their flight after it landed at Delhi airport, according to the party.

Legal affairs head Ratna Singh was also reportedly detained earlier outside her residence in New Delhi.

A video from the aircraft showed Dipke challenging the officers. âI have come to be arrested, arrest me ... I am not afraid of you guys,â he said. An officer responded, âNo, this is not an arrest. Please cooperate.â

Delhi Police had denied permission for the proposed demonstration, with reports citing the late submission of the request as the reason.





The authorities imposed extensive security restrictions, with barricades and personnel deployed to prevent protesters from reaching the designated venue.

The protest was called over alleged electoral-roll irregularities and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise, with demonstrators demanding Kumarâs resignation. Several INDIA bloc leaders and activists were also detained, including Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) national convenor Arvind Kejriwal and former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee.

In a post on X, Kejriwal said, "This is worse than the Emergency. Itâs official.. we are living under an absolute dictatorship ruled by Modi. Arresting cockroaches straight off their flight shows an unprecedented level of fear. PM Modi clearly knows he only won the election through vote chori and now he is hell-bent on protecting his fraud by completely crushing democracy. Gyanesh must go, but so must Modi.."

Banerjee, detained with Trinamool Congress leaders after staging a sit-in, also echoed: âThis has gone beyond an Emergency; it has become a Super Emergency.â

Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi expressed solidarity with the protesters and challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to detain all those participating. âArrest all the leaders. Arrest all the young people. Arrest us all,â Gandhi said.

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), meanwhile, criticised the protest. Party leader Sambit Patra described it as a âflop showâ and called the detentions a victory of democracy over âmob ruleâ.

A police officer said six personnel were injured, with stones allegedly thrown at security personnel at two locations. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals, and the circumstances surrounding their injuries were being ascertained.

World.title: From mass detentions to political war of words: How Delhi protests unfolded
World.content:
As the detentions mounted, opposition leaders accused the government of suppressing dissent. BJP defended the police action and the SIR process, accusing the protesters of attempting to create unrest.

Early morning: Delhi tightens security, detentions begin

Morning: CJP leaders and Dhruv Rathee detained

Late morning: Students, lawyers and activists detained

Afternoon: Kejriwal and Mamata detained

BJP defends SIR, criticises opposition
