World.title: Doha diary: A historian amid the Iran war
World.content:
(Renowned historian and author, Rila Mukherjee, was scheduled to fly from the USA to India by Qatar Airways [QA] on February 25, 2026. Her route—Shreveport–Dallas Fort Worth–Doha–Kolkata—was expected to bring her to Kolkata on the night of February 26 or in the early hours of February 27. However, as of March 8, she was still stranded in Doha. Qatar’s skies were closed due to the US-Israeli attack on Iran. QA’s commercial flights were suspended. At the time of writing, evacuation flights to India were scheduled to start soon. She reached home on 12 March.)

Today is 8 March. I am now camping out in Doha for the ninth day since 28 February. The Qatar airspace is shut and padlocked. The authorities have thrown away the key. Limited numbers of passengers are being flown to Europe and the Americas on evacuation flights (they are called ‘relief flights’) organised by QA, and relief flights to Africa and Asia will start from tomorrow. But for the time being, I am effectively marooned in Doha.

Doha is one of the largest airplane hubs in the world, and a cosmopolitan group of transit passengers has been put up by QA in the 4-star The Royal Riviera Hotel. The hotel is situated on Doha’s Corniche. It is an ageing hotel; not terribly posh, and the plumbing is a bit iffy. But it is well located, with comfortable rooms, and it is a clean and friendly hotel. I feel safe here. Its staff is composed of Asians (from Bangladesh, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Nepal), North Africans (Algerians and Moroccans mostly) and some West Asians. All of them are helpful despite the pressures they are facing. They deal gracefully with the diverse demands and complaints of the passengers.

My room faces the Corniche and I can see the Persian Gulf from my window. As a maritime historian, this makes me very happy.

This country and its national airline are looking after us very well and, really, I have no complaints. QA’s representatives visit the hotel twice daily. There is no information forthcoming on my evacuation to Kolkata, and the greater part of passenger bags are still to arrive at the hotel. My South African neighbour says one of their bags has not been delivered; perhaps it is lost.

We are largely dependent on the clothes we have on our backs and those we had in our carry-on. Most of us are washing and drying them overnight. We have to use the hair dryer if they are still not dry.

My bags came in today, i.e., 8 March.

There are some elderly travellers. Many of them say that their medicines are running out. Mine will last another week.

Will I be able to get out by then?

We are told that a limited air corridor may open today; alternatively, we may be evacuated by the land route through Saudi Arabia to Riyadh (this would take around seven hours), where a leased QA aircraft may take us to India. But we have to make our own arrangements for the Saudi e-visa and overland travel. This seems a risky enterprise. And whether this potential leased aircraft would fly me direct to Kolkata is not known. There is no clarity to date.

***

But if I was scheduled to arrive in Kolkata on 27 February (and the war broke out a day later, on 28 February), how is it that I am still in Doha

Ah, thereby hangs a tale!

It is a cautionary tale on buying air tickets with multiple connections, and what ensues when the first connection does not take off as per schedule.

***

I had spent nine weeks in Shreveport with my son and daughter-in-law and was scheduled to leave on 25 February. Unfortunately, my flight from Shreveport to Dallas Fort Worth (DFW) by QA’s codeshare partner American Airlines (AA) did not take off. We were told that the incoming flight had nose gear problems and therefore could not land. Ultimately it made an emergency landing. Fire engines, firefighters, EMTs and ambulances were standing by. Luckily, there was no fireball and there were no casualties. The vice-chair of my daughter-in-law’s department was on that flight; I bumped into him in the terminal as he deplaned, and he said that the landing had been really scary.

There were no more AA flights to DFW that day. Roo and Stephanie came back to the airport and took me home. I spent a restless night. I hate flying at the best of times.

I was put on the same AA flight the next day, on 26 February, but when I reached DFW I was told that my connection flight to Doha was full. Apparently, the AA staff at Shreveport Regional Airport knew there were no seats on that flight; nevertheless they sent me on to DFW hoping I would ‘sort out’ the matter with AA’s customer care there. The only ‘sorting out’ that AA did at DFW was to put me on a later QA flight to Doha on the same day, that is, late evening on 26 February. It was a smaller aircraft (not the Airbus 350 on which I was ticketed), the flight was cramped and some of my co-passengers were not very well behaved. One lady kept on drinking; she skipped the meal service and was quite abusive. Another one, African American, told me that as an ‘American’ she was superior to Asians. Right, I thought, we all know how you as a Black person got there!!!

In all my years of travelling I have never encountered such blatant racism.

When we reached Doha very late on the night of 27 February (almost 24 hours later due to the time difference with DFW), I had missed that evening’s flight to Kolkata!

No problem, QA’s customer care said, we’ll talk with AA as it is their problem. This took a while, so I went off to buy myself a snack at Brioche Dorée in the airport’s food court.

By then it was early morning on 28 February.

Readers, note the date!

***

AA agreed to comp me a room for the remainder of the night at The Royal Riviera Hotel. I was granted a 48-hour emergency visa by Qatar Immigration and I was shifted to the hotel on 28 February at 2 AM. QA’s ground staff helped me throughout. The room was comfortable, the bed looked inviting, and I went to sleep, confident that my Kolkata flight would take off as scheduled at 18.45 hours on that day itself (that is, 28 February). At that point, I was going to reach only 24 hours behind my original schedule.

I informed Kolkata and asked my driver to collect me from the airport accordingly.

***

On 28 February, I was woken around 8 AM by a strange sound from my cell phone. It was a very loud, continuous screech. I don’t have international roaming and I wondered who was calling me and what was happening. I saw a ‘Security Alert’ on my screen but the text was in Arabic. I started hearing thuds and bangs. Another alert, still in Arabic, came in.

What was going on? I was mystified.

I was now getting alerts in English. It said the US and Israel had jointly attacked Iran. US bases and embassies and consulates across the Gulf were vulnerable. Qatar was in this critical area. Sirens were going off. I started watching Al Jazeera and Richard Engel on NBC.

This was Day 1.

Smoke rises following an explosion, after Israel and the US launched strikes on Iran, in Tehran, Iran, February 28, 2026. PHOTO: REUTERS

By Day 2, the Gulf was not just lying in a war zone; it had been converted into a theatre of war. Doha was undergoing regular drone strikes and missile attacks.

Day 3 was relatively quiet. Apparently, Qatar and Iran had a phone conversation, and Qatar urged Iran to stop the strikes. But our temporary visas were extended by Qatar. This was an indication that the phone call was not conclusive. This war was not going to end anytime soon.

The Qatar–Iran conversation does not seem to have yielded the desired result. There is no relief from Iranian attacks. These now form the backdrop to our daily life at The Royal Riviera. Drone attacks and missile strikes re-started from Day 4. None of them target the downtown area; they target only the US base and industrial areas in Qatar. Most of the drones and missiles are successfully intercepted; the few that are not cause localised fires. The attacks usually happen around breakfast and lunch, and sometimes they occur very late at night or in the early morning hours. This means we are always in a state of extreme alert. It is jarring on the nerves. We can neither eat properly nor rest. We are getting stressed out.

But I must also mention that the attacks and interceptions sound more like Diwali patakas than the very loud explosions that one expects.

*** Days 4 till 9 (that is, till date) have seen this regional war extending from land to sea: from the Hormuz Strait to the Indian Ocean. This is now becoming very serious. Critical choke points like this strait have become a curse. Ports across the Gulf are lying idle; almost no cargo is getting through. But we have had no alerts today. Does this mean that Iran will not strike Qatar for the time being? Is this a temporary reprieve? Will relief flights be able to take off? ***

Some bags arrived at the hotel on Day 5. Mine were not among them.

By Days 6 and 7 we have more or less settled into what is turning out to be our semi-permanent home. The hotel is no longer very ‘royal’; it has taken on the character of a London bedsit. Or a council housing estate in one of the UK’s inner cities! Children play noisy games in the corridors, an oddly comforting sound among the explosions, security alerts and sirens that go on regularly.

I see an enormous solidarity among the travellers, both on my floor and when we meet up at meal times. I have a very nice South African couple next door who check on me each morning, always asking how I am faring (‘please don’t hesitate to knock if you face any difficulties’). They have even offered to take me out to buy clothes (this was before my bags arrived). Elegant MENA (Middle East North Africa) people greet me each day at breakfast, a young Pakistani financial analyst from Toronto shares his insights with me at the breakfast table, and a British couple advise me to carry my passport with me at all times (especially when I leave my room in case of an attack and subsequent fire). They kindly offered to buy me my medicines, although they are at least a decade older than me. A young school teacher from Geneva shares my table at dinner. I have not seen her lately; perhaps she has already been repatriated on one of the relief flights to Europe which started operating from Day 7. The British couple and the South Africans are still here; the Pakistani man left for Toronto early this morning. He was given only two hours’ notice and he phoned my room to say goodbye at 1.15 AM this morning.

***

What does my daily schedule look like?

It is like what I imagine a day at boarding school would be. Because it is Ramadan, the hotel starts the breakfast buffet from 3 AM, lunch is from 12 noon, and dinner is over by 7.30. The food served (although mild in taste and quasi-institutional as regards the daily menu, which does not rotate much in terms of items), is nevertheless amazingly varied as regards the cuisine: Arabic, Turkish, Italian, Spanish and South Asian (the last is not good at all). A lot of lemon is used in the preparations, but practically no onions. This may be due to the fact that there was an onion shortage; onions came in from India only on Day 5. There are loads of different kinds of salads, some bland European cheeses and diverse types of hummus. In addition, there is feta cheese, stuffed vine leaves, green and black olives, veg and non-veg samosas and spring rolls, koftas, and baba ghanoush or baingan bharta. Good cappuccinos and lattes. Flaky croissants and brioches, pastries and amazing Arabian/Persian/Yemeni sweets. A decadent baked (and often caramelised) bread pudding called Umm Ali is served at dinner. Obviously, the Qatari supermarkets are still well-stocked with FMCG. The Indian-origin Lulu supermarket chain has flown in a whole lot of perishable and non-perishable food items.

Strangely, no fresh fruit!

***

Gas prices have shot up.

I have given up watching the death and destruction on TV, and watch Looney Tunes, Anthony Bourdain, Fawlty Towers and Mr Bean instead. Priyam Paul, my editor at The Daily Star, has sent me some e-books which help to pass the time.

When I am not reading, or watching sitcoms, cartoons and travel and food documentaries, I reflect on what brought us to this war. I see the Persian Gulf from my room; it is still a brilliant blue. But it is also desolate since the Hormuz Strait was closed off. I see no cargo ships or container vessels; there are no cruise ships or tankers. For a maritime historian like me, this is not the Persian Gulf I know. After all, it has been a crossroads since recorded history! My India in the Indian Ocean World (2022) documents this history of two thousand years at the very least. Now, mobility is severely constrained.

Persian Gulf. Photo: Collected

We are living now in a world of fragmented geopolitics, of accelerated climate degradation, and of critical demographic shifts. The world is undergoing these changes along with increasingly disaffected groups of peoples, perhaps terrorists, some of them. We are seeing the rise of AI which, to my mind, is linked, along with the toxicity of social media, with the increasing authoritarianism that we see worldwide. It horrifies me when I see a young nation declare it will bring ‘civilisation’ to Iran. It disregards the fact that Iran-as-Persia predates Arab culture and is one of the world’s oldest culture areas. Not just the glory of Shi’ite Safavid Persia (1501–1736), which political theorists and analysts invoke when describing this civilisational space and whose heritage modern Iran draws on: think of the period from c. 550 BCE to 651 CE (Muslim conquest and start of Islamisation by the Rashidun Caliphate), when four mighty Persian empires ruled a large portion of the then-known world: Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian and Sassanian. Persia challenged Egypt, Greece and Rome, and then it faced up to the Ottoman and Russian empires. This memory of resistance of 2500 years will not be easily erased.

However, the total disregard of international law and the collapse of the rules-based order will usher in a new regional order in West Asia. This will impact on the Gulf states. Once-biblical Lebanon is almost destroyed by a rampant Israel. Syria has closed its borders. As a rogue USA intimidates Persia and trains its eye on the Caucasus and Azerbaijan, it also destabilises Iraq. Iranian Kurds based in Iraq have been reactivated. How will this impact on the Turkish Kurds? Turkey, a NATO country, is already feeling threatened.

The relatively young post-WW1 statelets in the Gulf will lose out in the violent reshuffle in the greater region. The Dubai story was already over. And Oman had lost its sheen even earlier. Financial and service centres will shift eastward—to Singapore or perhaps to KL. As will global airline hubs. The Gulf states will see their importance in location, business and finance diminish. They will have to reconsider their dependence on the USA which has now become a double-edged sword. Iran will endure, but perhaps in a new form. But it will not be erased from the map of the world.

World.title: André Béteille: A sociologist Bangladesh should read
World.content:
My first encounter with the ideas of Professor André Béteille was in July 1966 in an introductory sociology course at the University of Dhaka (at that time in East Pakistan) through Professor Tom Bottomore’s book, Sociology: A Guide to Problems and Literature (1962). The emphasis on general theory of social stratification for an explanation of the Indian caste system found its empirical reflection, as Bottomore refers to, in the work of Béteille, especially in Caste, Class and Power: Changing Patterns of Stratification in a Tanjore Village (1965).

My second encounter with him was in the Fall of 1975 at Dalhousie University, Halifax where I was writing my Master’s thesis under Professor Bottomore, and he referred to read me Béteille’s “Closed and open social stratification” (1966). Reading Béteille after nine years under the Maple tree, I began to admire his empirical depth, comparative methodology, and theoretical clarity, which reshaped my understanding of social hierarchies in India.

In the Christmas of 1976, I had an occasion to share some of my understanding of Béteille’s work. At that time, I was at York University, Toronto where I was doing my PhD. Professor K. Ishwaran, one of our faculty members, who wrote Tradition and Economy in Village India (1966), invited me for Christmas dinner-- Turkey with cranberry sauce, cooked by his Dutch wife. There we talked about the contribution of both Béteille and his supervisor M. N. Srinivas towards understanding the impact of social change on Indian social stratification.

In order to realistically understand contemporary caste hierarchy, Béteille emphasised the “other factors such as class and power” that “have to be considered as independent variables” (1966). It appeared to me highly useful for comparative empirical research. It creates a distance from traditional essentialist and ideological perspective of inequality.

Borrowed from Max Weber, he focused on multidimensionality of stratification and examined how status, economic resources, and political control interact to shape multifarious social order. This was a tremendous contribution in the field of stratification studies. Though he focused on rural stratification, the model is also applicable to the study of urban social stratification.

It is puzzling that in Bangladesh universities, both sociology and anthropology disciplines overlooked and neglected the Weberian model of multidimensional stratification system: anthropology remained spell-bound under the dichotomous model of rural “ashraf-atraf”; and sociology was locked in the iron cage of simplistic Marxist model of “land ownership” under the name of peasant studies. In spite of teaching Weber’s “Class, Status, Party” (1922/1946) in the universities, there is a marked absence of the application of Weberian model in the study of rural and urban complex social hierarchy. Probably in Bangladesh, this shows the intellectual bankruptcy of these disciplines, which are suffering from morbidity.

In fact, in order to understand contemporary social change in Bangladesh, especially its regime of accumulation under crony capitalism, it is essential to understand the nexus between power and class. The determining power of traditional property ownership in the formation of classes and consequent class consciousness has diminished in Bangladesh.

The notion of political capitalism advanced by Max Weber is also useful in understanding Bangladesh social stratification, especially class formation. The party consciousness along with ruling party affiliation, may give legitimate or illegitimate access to economic resources, thereby determining class position in terms of life opportunities and life style. This in turn, heavily influence commodification of prestige and honour; and becomes marker of status.

André Beteille (1934 - 2026). Photo: Collected

The rural and urban dispossession, which is an integral part of neoliberal and crony capitalism’s regime of accumulation, is also the progenitor of emergent lumpen bourgeoisie, whose class position do not correspond with their demeaning status position. Again, the traditional status group in Bangladesh, as Béteille found in his Tanjore village study with respect to traditional caste, suffer from status dislocation, having less access to power and economic resources. The ontology of inequality and hierarchy can best be understood by the Weberian epistemology.

I think study of this process of social change, and its impact on inequality in Bangladesh, is vital towards understanding Bangladesh society. The internationally acclaimed Indian empirical model provided by Béteille can be one of the best guides to study the intersectionality of class, status and power in both urban and rural Bangladesh. It is unfortunate that social sciences in Bangladesh have neglected such a significant social dynamic that affects all our lives.

In March 1989, Professor Abhijit Dasgupta, a colleague of Professor Béteille, facilitated my direct meeting with him. Professor Dasgupta was kind enough to arrange a seminar talk by me in the sociology department of Delhi School of Economics. After the seminar, I paid a visit to Professor Béteille’s office room. He was very warm and hospitable to offer tea to me and my wife. He spoke in Bangla and affirmed his Bangali origin. I felt very comfortable to have a vibe of Bengal. I mentioned to him how I came to know of his work à la Bottomore and Ishwaran. I was so surprised to experience his stock of knowledge mediated by modesty and simplicity. The meeting with professor Béteille during the short-lived spring of Delhi was one of the most memorable events of my life. I wish his conceptual and methodological clarity inspire the young Bangladeshi sociologists to break the chain of ignorance, myopic framework, and the hegemony of intellectual infantilism.

A.I. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed is a professor in the Department of Sociology at the University of Dhaka.

World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Germany eyes joining GCAP fighter jet project with U.K, Italy and Japan
World.content:
Germany is considering joining Japan, Britain and Italy in their joint project to develop a next-generation fighter jet, a government official suggested Friday.

This came after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday that Britain is positive on Germany’s participation in the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP).

Steffen Meyer, first deputy spokesperson for the German government, said at a regular news conference Friday that the country took Burnham’s view very favorably.

Meanwhile, Meyer noted that Germany intends to pursue a European way of finding a solution to the development of a next-generation fighter jet, indicating that the country plans to assert its national interest during various discussions.

There has been mounting speculation that the founding GCAP countries could open the door to Germany after a rival Franco-German fighter program collapsed in June.

Burnham said the idea “is something that we seek to progress in the coming period, working with our other partners, Italy and Japan.”

GCAP has been set up to allow differing levels of involvement and it expanded for the first time in July, when Canada signed on as an observer, which could pave the way for deeper engagement in the future. Saudi Arabia has long been touted as another country interested in joining.

Germany is viewed by some defense experts as a suitable partner given its growing military budget and the fact that it already works on the Eurofighter Typhoon with the U.K. and Italy.

From Britain’s point of view, adding another country at a time when its military budget is under strain would help share the cost burden, but Japan may need convincing. Italy has also said in the past it would be open to new countries joining to help share the cost.

Japan is particularly focused on the 2035 target for the program given the security threat from China and the fact that it is due to start retiring its F-2 fighters in the middle of the next decade.

Some executives have warned that adding new partners could lead to delays. The GCAP is being led by BAE Systems, Leonardo and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries.

Asked Friday if Germany had inquired about joining GCAP, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi declined to comment, but noted the group’s thinking on the issue.

“To begin with, GCAP itself was developed with a view to fostering cooperation among Japan, the United Kingdom and Italy, as well as allies and partner nations,” Koizumi told a news conference. “Regarding cooperation with third countries, we intend to work in coordination with the U.K. and Italy to ensure that GCAP becomes an even better program.”

World.title: Taiwan’s leader says increasing defense spending to ‘deter war’
World.content:
Taiwan aims to “deter war” by increasing its defense spending, the democratic island’s leader said on Saturday, as China uses military pressure to assert its territorial claims.

Taiwan’s 23 million people live under the constant threat of an attack by China, which insists the island is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to annex it.

“Our aim by increasing investment in national defence is not to provoke, rather, it is to deter war,” President Lai Ching-te said in speech to celebrate Taiwan’s National Day.

World.title: Takaichi again in a bind as U.S. threatens to ‘end’ ICC
World.content:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has again found herself in a tough spot after the U.S., Tokyo’s key security ally, slapped the International Criminal Court with fresh sanctions, months after it targeted the Japanese head of the court with similar measures.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration on Friday ordered the Treasury Department to add the entire court to its Specially Designated Nationals list, a move that would impose financial punishment on any entity that does business with the ICC.

The announcement was a step beyond his administration’s targeted sanctions against top court officials, including ICC President Tomoko Akane, a Japanese national.

World.title: Anthropic cites new AI misbehavior, some on government sites
World.content:
Anthropic said its Claude AI model carried out additional unintended actions on the digital systems of outside organizations, including some U.S. government agencies’ websites, prompting a warning from U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration for artificial intelligence companies to secure their systems.

In a report outlining previously undisclosed incidents, Anthropic listed four types of unintended behaviors that the AI has demonstrated, including exploiting basic flaws in software to run commands, submitting forms it should not have and bypassing restrictions to access certain public data.

The company said that some of the cases involved websites run by government agencies at the federal, state and local levels, without specifying the agencies. The report did not name the outside entities involved, which Anthropic said was at the request of some of the affected parties.

World.title: U.S. Treasury chief Scott Bessent to skip IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok
World.content:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will skip next week’s annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok, Thailand, due to domestic engagements, a U.S. official said on Friday.

The Treasury Department confirmed that Deputy Treasury Secretary Francis Brooke and Under Secretary for International Affairs Erin Browne will lead the U.S. delegation for the department, with many pressing economic issues on the agenda.

Treasury said U.S. officials would work with partners at the meetings to address policies and structural imbalances that have held back growth, while pushing for “more transparency and more effective approaches to sovereign debt.”

Bessent’s absence from the high-profile financial event comes at a critical moment when benchmark Treasury yields have surged to their highest levels in nearly 25 years and the ongoing energy shock caused by the war in the Middle East has set back global growth.

It was not immediately clear what domestic engagements are keeping Bessent at home, but he has been a key spokesman for domestic economic policies as the midterm U.S. elections approach.

The U.S. also leads the Group of 20 major economies this year, and the Treasury chief would normally have chaired a meeting of finance ministers and central bankers from around the world. Bessent is expected to attend the G20 leaders summit in Miami, Florida, in December.

It is not unprecedented for top officials to miss occasional meetings due to scheduling issues or other factors, but Bessent’s decision may frustrate top officials from other countries, who generally use the meetings to secure formal and informal bilateral meetings with their U.S. counterpart.

Bessent skipped the G20 meetings in South Africa last year amid objections by U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration to the country’s land reforms and other issues.

Treasury said the U.S. delegation would focus on the debt issues so that countries facing debt distress could restore stability and return to growth, while creditors and borrowers are “held to clear and consistent standards.”

The U.S. would also continue to press the International Monetary Fund and World Bank — where it is the biggest shareholder — to focus on their core mandates, operate efficiently, and support policies that promote economic stability, productivity and growth.

“Our engagement in Bangkok will be guided by a clear objective: ensuring that the international financial institutions and the broader international economic system advance U.S. economic and national security interests,” Treasury said in a statement.

World.title: More Japanese firms hit by large-scale data breaches
World.content:
More Japanese companies have revealed that they have experienced major customer data breaches due to cyberattacks.

JR East said that about 6.09 million customer accounts may have been compromised, while JR Kyushu said about 1.3 million customer accounts may have been compromised. Both were a result of a ransomware attack on IDC Frontier, a cloud services subsidiary of SoftBank, they said Friday.

Bookoff Group Holdings, a secondhand goods retailer, reported that its subsidiary responsible for managing membership data had suffered unauthorized access, possibly resulting in a data breach affecting up to 6.43 million customers.

Daiichikosho, the operator of the Big Echo karaoke chain, also said personal information on about 8.72 million customers may have been compromised due to unauthorized access to a system managed by an external contractor.

Adventure Inc., the operator of the Skyticket travel booking website, reported a potential breach involving about 14.64 million sets of personal information, following a cyberattack on its servers and the business management system for its booking website.

The potentially affected information includes email addresses at JR East and customer names, dates of birth and telephone numbers at the other three companies. Adventure said it had confirmed that credit card and passport numbers had not leaked.

The companies respectively said that they had found no evidence of unauthorized use of the affected information by third parties. They are urging customers to watch out for suspicious emails and phone calls.

World.title: Tax cut to bring ¥36,000 benefit per citizen, Takaichi says
World.content:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Friday that the planned consumption tax cut for food is expected to reduce household financial burdens by about ¥36,000 per citizen.

“The tax rate cut will basically be reflected in prices,” Takaichi said at a plenary meeting of the Senate, the upper chamber of parliament.

She explained that the ¥36,000 figure was calculated by dividing the total tax revenue loss to the central and local governments from the tax cut by the country’s population.

During the Upper House meeting, Yasue Funayama of the Democratic Party for the People asked the prime minister how her administration will make up for local government revenue losses.

Takaichi vowed to fully cover these revenue losses with state funds, saying, “We’ll properly secure necessary local tax grants.”

The prime minister also said the government is considering measures to support agricultural and fishery businesses, as well as food companies and restaurants whose operations could be affected by the tax cut. “It is necessary to assess circumstances on the ground and respond according to the impact on each sector,” she said.

Meanwhile, Komeito Secretary-General Makoto Nishida called on the government to clarify who would be eligible for a financial aid program for workers that will be introduced alongside the consumption tax cut.

Takaichi indicated that the government will explain the matter during parliamentary deliberations, based on discussions by the suprapartisan National Council on Social Security.

Sanseito leader Sohei Kamiya argued that the consumption tax reduction should apply across the board, not only to food.

Takaichi countered that such a move could affect public services, including pensions, medical care, nursing care and measures to address the declining birthrate.

World.title: Beer maker leaders may have been aware of price cartel
World.content:
Top management officials of some of the four major beer makers suspected of a price cartel are believed to have been informed of details of shipping price hikes negotiated among the companies, informed sources have said.

The Japan Fair Trade Commission is investigating whether these top officials recognized that the information was a result of negotiations, the sources said Friday.

According to the sources, some officials of the companies — Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Sapporo Breweries and Suntory Holdings — have admitted to the cartel during the commission’s investigation.

Officials from the companies are believed to have held unofficial talks after industry group meetings to exchange information on the timing and scale of shipping price increases and compile price tables.

On Wednesday, the commission conducted compulsory inspections of the headquarters of the four companies on suspicion of violating the Antimonopoly Act.

Under the act, companies found to have engaged in illegal price fixing can face penalties, including financial surcharges and orders to prevent further violations. Unlike routine administrative inspections, compulsory investigations allow authorities to search premises and seize evidence under court warrants, typically in cases considered particularly serious or damaging to consumers.

The four companies, which collectively control more than 90% of Japan’s beer market, are suspected of coordinating the timing and scale of price increases for beer, low-malt beer and other beer-like beverages over several years.

World.title: 127 arrested as Hong Kong police bust Vietnamese-led loan-sharking syndicate
World.content:
Hong Kong police have arrested 127 people in a six-month undercover operation against a Vietnamese-led crime syndicate accused of running loan-sharking rackets charging interest rates of up to 3,700 per cent, as well as illegal gambling and unlicensed bars in West Kowloon.

The syndicate is also alleged to have helped illegal immigrants find shelter and work, with police raiding eight premises on October 8 and 9.

Among those arrested were 10 alleged core members, including the suspected leader, a Vietnamese woman holding a Hong Kong identity card.

World.title: Senior civil servants could face disciplinary action over Tai Po fire if named in report
World.content:
Senior public servants found accountable for last year’s deadly Tai Po fire could face disciplinary action if named in an investigation report that a government-appointed panel is expected to submit this month, Hong Kong’s civil service chief has said.

Secretary for the Civil Service Ingrid Yeung Ho Poi-yan also said on Saturday that a support unit was being set up to assist the Public Service Commission if investigations into officials’ “administrative responsibilities” were eventually launched.

“If the [investigation] report clearly pinpoints an individual [official] and points out what he or she has done inadequately, or there is prima facie evidence established, I would not rule out the possibility of launching disciplinary action directly,” she told a radio programme.

“Otherwise, if system failure is said to be a main issue, the Public Service Commission could also probe the officials’ administrative responsibilities.”

World.title: Hong Kong records 21 mpox cases since August, high-risk groups urged to get jabs
World.content:
Hong Kong has recorded 21 cases of mpox since August, accounting for 70 per cent of this year’s total, prompting health authorities to urge people who engage in high-risk sexual contact to take protective measures and get vaccinated to reduce their risk of infection.

The latest case, involving a 29-year-old man, brought the total number recorded in Hong Kong this year to 30, comprising 23 local cases and seven imported ones, the Centre for Health Protection (CHP) said on Saturday. Twenty-one cases, or 70 per cent of the total, were recorded since August.

Epidemiological investigations showed that all 21 patients reported engaging in high-risk sexual behaviour during the incubation period, including having sex with male strangers or multiple partners, and having sex without a condom, the centre said.

World.title: Hong Kong police smash alleged Thai prostitution ring, seize HK$13 million cash
World.content:
Hong Kong police have dismantled a local syndicate allegedly running a vice ring involving Thai women, seizing HK$13 million in cash (US$1.66 million) and freezing HK$5 million in suspected crime proceeds.

The force said on Saturday that it arrested five local men and two foreign men, aged between 44 and 54, for allegedly running a prostitution ring in the Tsim Sha Tsui district by luring Southeast Asian women to work as sex workers in Hong Kong.

Four core members, including three brothers and one Thai national, were arrested on suspicion of human trafficking, living off the earnings of prostitution of others, causing prostitution and money laundering.

Nine sex workers from Thailand, aged between 19 and 33, were also arrested on Friday during an undercover operation for allegedly breaching their conditions of stay.

World.title: Guangdong yachts to sail into Hong Kong from Friday under southbound scheme
World.content:
Guangdong-registered yachts will be allowed to sail into Hong Kong waters from next Friday under a new travel scheme, the city’s transport minister has confirmed.

Writing in her weekly blog on Saturday, Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said the maiden voyage ceremony for the Southbound Yacht Travel Scheme would be held on launch day.

“Building on the groundwork laid by the Northbound Yacht Travel Scheme, the maiden voyage ceremony for the Southbound Yacht Travel Scheme marks a two-way journey of maritime connectivity,” she said.

Chan made the announcement after the Marine Department and the Guangdong Maritime Safety Administration signed work arrangements last month to establish a framework for cross-boundary yacht travel between the two places.

World.title: New mechanism to strengthen oversight of renovations after Tai Po fire: minister
World.content:
A three-tier dispute resolution mechanism could help Hong Kong homeowners strengthen oversight of major renovation projects and prevent exploitation by “unscrupulous traders”, according to the home affairs minister.

The city’s building management challenges came under the spotlight after the deadly blaze at Tai Po’s Wang Fuk Court in November 2025. The estate was undergoing a HK$330 million (US$42.3 million) renovation when the fire broke out, killing 168 people and displacing nearly 5,000 residents.

An independent committee investigating the blaze earlier uncovered evidence pointing to suspected bid-rigging and connected bidding companies, among other concerns.

Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak Mei-kuen told a radio programme on Saturday that the proposed mechanism could better handle disputes among property owners and foster a more constructive environment for building management.

World.title: A fortune, a HK$72m flat and a family feud: inside the Abby Choi murder trial
World.content:
A bitter family dispute over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million flat allegedly led a retired police officer and his two sons to murder socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung three years ago, a Hong Kong court has heard.

The trial over the 28-year-old model’s killing, which shocked Hong Kong and attracted international attention, started after a one-week delay caused by unresolved preliminary issues and jury selection

Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, told the High Court how her relationship with her daughter’s former in-laws deteriorated, accusing them of clinging to her family’s fortune and having “bitten the hand that fed them”.

Giving evidence for the prosecution, Cheung became emotional at times as she accused Choi’s former in-laws of living in luxury without contributing to the upbringing of the two children her daughter had with her ex-husband.

World.title: Hong Kong to expand community recycling after shelving waste-charging scheme
World.content:
Hong Kong will strengthen its community recycling network with measures such as round-the-clock automated collection points after scrapping its waste-charging scheme due to strong public opposition, the environmental chief has said.

Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan on Saturday also pledged to review the permitted profit levels of the city’s two power companies when their control agreements with the government expire in 2033. He added that the government would boost clean energy imports from mainland China.

Tse expressed confidence that Hong Kong would achieve the four binding goals on environmental protection outlined in the city’s first five-year plan, unveiled last month.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019103/Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.title: Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019103/Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.content:
Two books translated into English from Chinese have been shortlisted for the 2026 U.S. National Translation Awards, which recognize excellence in both original and translated literary works.

The shortlist, announced Tuesday by the American Literary Translators Association, includes two originally written in Chinese: Chinese author Shuang Xuetao’s short story collection “Hunter,” translated by Jeremy Tiang, and Hong Kong writer Hon Lai Chu’s “Mending Bodies,” translated by Jacqueline Leung, among a total of 11 poetry and prose works translated from nine languages.

“The Ruins,” an anthology by Chinese poet Ye Hui and translated by Li Dong, was longlisted among 23 works across prose and poetry on Sept. 3 but did not make the shortlist. Ye is known for his spare, understated poems that draw on everyday life and nature and explore questions of time, memory, and existence.

Established in 1998, the awards rank among the world’s top professional accolades for literary translation. Winning translators in both categories — poetry and prose — each receive a $4,000 prize. Translations of Chinese works have previously been listed for the prize, including works by contemporary writers Xu Zechen and Yan Lianke, as well as Qing dynasty (1644–1911) novelist and playwright Li Yu.

Shuang Xuetao, author of “Hunter,” one of the two shortlisted Chinese works, was born in 1983 in Shenyang, capital of the northeastern Liaoning province. He is widely considered a leading figure in the “Dongbei Renaissance,” a cultural movement emerging from northeast China, or Dongbei. Known for his use of local dialect, Shuang often portrays the lives of ordinary people in the region, long dismissed as a cultural backwater and rust belt. Several of his works have been adapted into films.

“Hunter” features 11 standalone stories, some of which were originally written in Dongbei dialect: from provincial ambulance drivers searching for a hospital in the middle of the night, to a legendary knife fighter working in a factory. In a note about their selection published alongside the announcement, the competition’s judges wrote that Shuang’s stories “paint a portrait of a region marked by gritty pragmatism, dark humor, and magical realism.”

The work was translated by Shuang’s long-term collaborator Jeremy Tiang — a novelist in his own right. The judges wrote that Tiang “expertly translated Shuang’s often inventive, utterly unique description; his English texts are layered and witty.”

The second book nominated for the prize, “Mending Bodies” by Hong Kong writer Hon Lai Chu, is a work of speculative fiction and follows a young woman adjusting to life after surgically binding her body to a partner, in a future where people are encouraged to do so. Hon has previously drawn praise for her surreal, introspective fiction, which often explores the fragility of the body, memory, and human relationships.

According to the judges, Jacqueline Leung, the book’s Hong Kong-based translator, “flawlessly translates the between-the-lines subtleties of the languages.”

“The shortlisting of these works carries substantial significance for the overseas circulation of Sinophone literature and its greater visibility within global professional literary circuits, representing, in a sense, a multifaceted retelling of Chinese stories across fiction and poetry,” Shao Dong, an assistant professor of creative writing at Hong Kong Metropolitan University, told Sixth Tone.

The overall award winners will be announced on Oct. 23 as part of the American Literary Translators Association’s annual conference.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Covers of “Hunter,” “Mending Bodies,” and “The Ruins,” by Shuang Xuetao, Hon Lai Chu, and Ye Hui, respectively. Reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019087/‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.title: ‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019087/‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.content:
The thieves came in the dead of night in late August — seven ghostly figures illuminated only by the glow of their flashlights and burning cigarettes. When they left, tucked under their arms were 10 chickens and two geese.

The next day, watching footage of the theft recorded by a security camera, Xu Lingni’s heart sank. It was the end of a dream.

The poultry had been kept overnight in a hilltop coop at the bucolic Huxi campus of the Sichuan Fine Arts Institute (SCFAI), in the southwestern megacity of Chongqing, and belonged to the Happy Chick Feeding Cooperative, a student-led club aimed at rebuilding the bonds between humans and nature.

The group had intended to use the project to promote interest across campus and beyond in food-waste conversion, community-supported agriculture, plastics consumption, and other sustainability issues.

For Xu, the club’s leader, those plans vanished along with those 12 birds. Yet worse was to come.

After a brief investigation, the Chongqing police discovered that several workers hired by SCFAI for a summer construction project had taken the poultry and eaten them. Their crew manager agreed to pay 7,000 yuan ($1,040) to compensate for the financial loss and the students’ emotional distress.

However, the theft drew widespread attention and sparked fresh criticism over raising animals on campus. Facing mounting pressure, the school’s leadership decided to ban the practice. The cooperative was over.

Hatching a plan

The Happy Chick Feeding Cooperative was a key part of the Healing Garden Project, which inhabits a patch of land on campus once piled high with construction waste. Seven years ago, Jin Lipeng, an associate professor in SCFAI’s School of Experimental Art, led students in repurposing the debris to pave paths and build planting beds. He envisioned an area that could restore nature and nurture people.

At the time, the campus cafeteria was sending hundreds of kilograms of food scraps — often mixed with unsorted plastic waste — to an incinerator dozens of kilometers away. Jin and his students began to use these leftovers as compost, converting roughly 40 tons of food waste into fertilizer over the years.

The idea for the cooperative stemmed from a graduate student’s thesis project in spring 2025 that looked at permaculture and the role of foraging chickens in loosening soil, eating pests, clearing weeds, and providing eggs. To test a theory, the student purchased five chickens of a local breed with red combs and black skin. They were allowed to roam freely through campus and returned at night to their hilltop coop.

Xu, an undergraduate majoring in sculpture, was already involved in the garden project and began informally caring for the chickens, buying them grain and taking them to the veterinarian.

In summer last year, as temperatures soared above 40 degrees Celsius, one bird died of heatstroke, and three others disappeared. Fearing that the sole survivor would get lonely, Xu bought a new one from the market. Then one of the escapees returned.

A few days later, Xu found six new adolescent chickens in the coop. A school janitor, who had bought them to raise for their meat, agreed to sell the birds to the students. These were soon joined by a common chicken brought from a roadside stall, a Plymouth Rock chicken, a new hatchling, and a wuhei black-boned chicken. (Two birds died before the theft — one from hypothermia, the other from a wild animal attack. The wuhei chicken was the only one left behind by the thieves; its dark plumage likely made it hard to spot at night.)

As the flock grew, the birds began producing more eggs than the students could eat. Jin, whose research area includes labor issues, proposed creating the cooperative as a student club and asked Xu to lead it. Soon, the students were dividing up their responsibilities: caring for the animals, sourcing and selling merchandise, writing articles, and managing social media channels. In June this year, several attended an international conference to introduce the cooperative’s work.

Those who joined the project felt that caring for the chickens brought them “healing energy.” Xu recalls one classmate who would often hold the birds and cry. “The theft this summer hit her especially hard, and she wasn’t the only one,” Xu says, adding that the cooperative not only fostered friendships but also helped some members find meaning.

While she doesn’t exactly share Jin’s grand ideals, Xu believes that through her work she came to understand seemingly distant but deeply personal issues such as permaculture and climate change.

“Most university students have no idea where eggs come from, what happens to food waste, or why rubbish gets incinerated,” she said in a speech at a climate change forum in May. “Dorm rooms are piled with takeout plastic. Delivery workers risk heatstroke in extreme temperatures. Yet few students have enough awareness to connect these to drought, heat, and carbon emissions.

“Our work lets people feel the pressure and causes of climate change firsthand,” she added, “and shows that through campus community-supported agriculture we can mount a small resistance.”

Making a mess

The cooperative began selling eggs for about 2 yuan each to residents on and around campus this March. The chickens laid two to eight eggs a day. Xu stored them in her apartment’s refrigerator, took orders through an online group chat, and delivered them to customers on her electric bike. She calculates that this brought in just over 500 yuan in total.

Fans of the project were kept up to date through the club’s channel on the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, which has more than 6,300 followers. In addition, the cooperative sold themed merchandise including fridge magnets, tote bags, and silk scarves, which brought in about 2,000 yuan.

Not everyone was supportive, though. The most common complaint was that the free-roaming chickens often defecated on the pathways and at the entrance to the student dormitories. To prevent this, this summer the birds were fenced in on the hillside.

In 2022, Chongqing introduced regulations prohibiting the raising of livestock and poultry in urban areas. However, the restrictions apply only to commercial-scale farming, while exceptions can be made for educational purposes and scientific research.

While the number of chickens at SCFAI was far below commercial scale, the activity fell outside the definition of “backyard rearing,” putting it in a gray area. As such, the school took an open-minded approach, requiring only proper fencing and separation, despite repeated objections from others in the campus community.

The cooperative used old bamboo posts and tall netting to enclose the poultry on the hilltop. But the gate was never locked. “This is a public welfare project. Anyone was welcome to come in to spend time with the chickens,” Xu explains.

For security, the group installed an infrared camera to watch the flock at night and raised two goslings to guard the coop. “Geese bite hard. Once I went up the hill in a raincoat, and they didn’t recognize me, so they bit me,” Xu adds. “We’d thought the intruders would be stray cats or weasels — never thieves.”

Ruffling feathers

The theft sparked an outpouring of grief online. “Come home, little ones” and “My babies are gone” were typical comments posted by students in the aftermath.

In the coming weeks and months, Xu and her classmates had planned to step up marketing and sales, offer egg-based food delivery services, and write a handbook on community supported agriculture that could inspire other schools and universities.

That’s now all been scrapped. This fall, the school’s leadership announced a ban on keeping poultry on campus.

In a statement, it also said that officials had learned during mediation that the maintenance workers who took the birds had endured long hours of intense labor in hot weather, with limited food and lodging. Some students strongly objected to this version of events, arguing that chicken meat is cheap and widely available — and that the workers weren’t “desperate,” they just wanted to taste free-range birds.

“Pioneering ecological practice is inherently accompanied by trial and error and waiting,” the statement read. “We will review and consolidate, continue deepening our existing work, and wait for the right conditions to restart explorations.”

The cooperative maintained that its activities “filled a gap” in the school’s labor education by giving students hands-on experience as well as teaching responsibility and empathy. But there was no overturning the decision.

The sole survivor of the theft, the wuhei chicken, was moved to a student’s home for safekeeping and has quickly adapted to her new environment. Xu says the bird is even laying eggs again.

(Due to privacy concerns, Xu Lingni is a pseudonym.)

Reported by Kong Lingyu.

A version of this article originally appeared in FoodThink. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.
