World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019100/China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.title: China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019100/China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.content:
DeepZang, China’s first Tibetan-language large language model, is being upgraded to better adapt to Tibetan dialects, enable real-time translation between Tibetan and Mandarin Chinese, and support offline use.

At a Monday seminar in Hohhot, capital of northern China’s Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, the model’s developer unveiled a series of upgrades scheduled between October and December. The seminar featured representatives from companies, research institutions, and universities.

DeepZang, developed by local technology company Choknor, was launched in March in Lhasa, capital of the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region. Its app supports AI-powered conversations, translation, and speech transcription in Tibetan, Mandarin Chinese, and English.

At the model’s launch, organizations including the Xizang branches of China Mobile and the People’s Insurance Company of China, as well as Sichuan Minzu Publishing House, signed agreements with Choknor to promote its adoption.

According to Choknor, DeepZang has attracted nearly 400,000 users across Xizang, the northwestern Qinghai and Gansu provinces, and southwestern Sichuan province, where most of China’s Tibetan speakers reside.

The company has said the model has cut the time needed for some Tibetan-Chinese translation tasks involving two or three people from 40 minutes to just over 10 minutes for one person. It also reported that the model has been used in such varied settings as helping non-Tibetan-speaking doctors communicate with local patients, generating Tibetan-language contracts for yak sales, and assisting grassroots officials in drafting Tibetan work reports.

The model has been trained on nearly 70 million pairs of standardized Tibetan and Chinese texts, along with more than 30,500 hours of Tibetan speech covering its three major dialect groups — Ü-Tsang, Kham, and Amdo. The team collected the data from libraries, medical institutions, and monasteries, among other settings.

At Monday’s seminar, Choknor unveiled plans to develop offline language packages for Tibetan, Chinese, and English, allowing the app to function with limited or no internet access. The company also plans to pilot 50 simultaneous interpretation devices among at least 300 participants in Lhasa this December.

Tenzin Norbu, Choknor’s founder, said the company aims to bring DeepZang into “pastoral tents, tourist service counters, and grassroots hospitals,” enabling Tibetan speakers to “enjoy the benefits of artificial intelligence on an equal footing.”

Choknor said on Sunday that beyond fostering exchanges and integration among ethnic groups, DeepZang could help ensure the accuracy of Tibetan-language information and contribute to social stability and long-term security.

Founded in 2016, Choknor specializes in Tibetan-Chinese bilingual speech technology, scanning and translation tools, and optical character recognition. Its products include smart computer mice, scanning and translation pens, and an AI-powered Tibetan subtitling system.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019096/The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.title: The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019096/The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.content:
With hundreds of concerts scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, some fans found the cheapest way to upgrade a seat was to rent a better camera phone.

For about 100 to 200 yuan ($15 to $30) a day, concertgoers can rent flagship smartphones with powerful telephoto cameras that pull distant performers into clearer view, a useful option when high demand leaves fans seated far from the stage and professional cameras and long lenses are often barred from venues.

On Chinese rental platform Renrenzu and Xianyu, a secondhand marketplace owned by Chinese tech giant Alibaba, some flagship phones are listed as “concert essentials.”

One Renrenzu ad touted a “200-megapixel telephoto, crystal clear — even the nosebleed seats feel VIP,” while the platform has also offered concert ticket reimbursements through prize draws.

The phones on offer are among the latest flagships from Chinese smartphone makers such as vivo and OPPO, with high-resolution telephoto cameras, image stabilization, and, in some cases, detachable lens kits that extend their reach.

A vivo X300 Ultra bundled with a telephoto lens, for example, rents for about 215 yuan for one day, while a two-day rental brings the average daily cost down to about 125 yuan. Other popular models include OPPO’s Find X10 Pro Max, which packs three 200-megapixel rear cameras and is advertised as supporting up to “20x lossless zoom” with its official telephoto kit.

Such high-end models typically sell for about 5,000 to 8,000 yuan, while official telephoto lens kits can add another 1,000 to 2,000 yuan, making a short rental far cheaper for fans who only want the extra reach for one concert.

Online, concertgoers are comparing phones and lens attachments, posting photos from the stands, and swapping tips on which setups work best from distant seats.

Liu Hang, who attended Taiwan singer Steve Chou’s concert at Beijing Workers’ Stadium, told Time Finance that he brought a Ruiying Z10 camera module and telephoto attachment made by Chinese tech giant Huawei into the venue. “I had a 580-yuan ticket, but with the ‘Huawei cannon,’ it felt like a 1,680-yuan seat,” he said.

Another social media user, who said he had attended nearly 100 concerts, compared several phones and camera setups for live shows. He said such phones were easy to carry, worked well for close-up shots, and had a dedicated stage mode that automatically adjusted exposure, though adding a telephoto attachment made it tiring to hold through an entire concert.

Renrenzu said orders for concert-related equipment jumped 388% year on year over the summer, far outpacing a 67% rise in short-term rentals overall. A total of 257 concerts were scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, according to Alibaba’s entertainment data platform Lighthouse.

Chen Shenyu, a manager at consulting firm China Insights Consultancy, told Time Finance that smartphone photography was becoming less about simply recording daily life and more about performing well in specific situations. Concerts are especially challenging because fans may be seated far from the stage, lighting changes constantly, and they are often shooting handheld photos and video.

That also makes concerts a natural showcase for smartphone makers, Chen said. If consumers increasingly reach for telephoto cameras at sporting events, on trips, and during family activities, demand for the same high-end imaging features could extend well beyond concerts.

(Header image: Posts show concertgoers using flagship camera phones with telephoto attachments to capture performers from the stands. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.title: China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.content:
Chinese travelers are increasingly stringing together multiple destinations during the weeklong National Day holiday, boosting mid-holiday air travel and drawing more visitors to smaller cities and counties.

More than 20% of air travelers booked flights to two or more destinations during the holiday, which runs from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, according to online travel platform Tongcheng Travel. Demand for flights in the middle of the holiday rose 35% from a year earlier.

Smaller destinations were among the biggest beneficiaries of the holiday travel boom, with data from travel platform Qunar showing that its 10 top trending scenic spots were all in county-level destinations.

In Qilian County in northwestern Qinghai province, which has a population of about 50,000, more than 100,000 tourists arrived on Oct. 3, filling local hotels and prompting authorities to house nearly 500 stranded visitors in school dormitories as temperatures fell to minus 4 degrees Celsius and snow covered nearby mountaintops.

The county’s culture and tourism department received more than 400 calls for help in seven hours, according to local authorities. Posts on Xiaohongshu, the lifestyle app also known as RedNote, showed tourists searching for rooms as hotels across the county filled up.

One traveler told domestic outlet Jimu News that he spent the afternoon and evening searching major booking platforms after arriving in Qilian from Xi’an but could not find a room. After seeing a notice from local tourism authorities, he called for help and was assigned a school dormitory room shared by four people, with new bedding provided.

Wansui Mountain Martial Arts City in central Henan province also struggled with heavy crowds, repeatedly capping admissions and suspending same-day ticket sales after interest surged 22-fold from a year earlier.

Many travelers were also going farther and staying away longer. According to Tongcheng Travel, people on multi-city trips visited an average of 1.2 more cities than in 2025, with Chengdu, Suzhou, and Wuhan among the busiest transfer hubs.

More than 70% of multi-city travelers booked both natural and cultural attractions, suggesting that many were combining different types of destinations within a single itinerary.

Interest in six- to 10-day groups and customized tours to destinations including Xinjiang, Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guizhou rose more than 60% on Tongcheng from a year earlier. Couples and families accounted for more than half of those bookings.

(Header image: Tourists visit the Zhuo’er Mountain Scenic Area in Qilian County, Qinghai province, Oct. 1, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.title: Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.content:
Researchers have identified a new species of feathered dinosaur from northeastern China whose anatomy suggests that birds and their close dinosaur relatives developed flight-related features along separate evolutionary paths.

The fossil — a nearly complete 57-centimeter skeleton with some feathers preserved — dates to the Early Cretaceous, more than 100 million years ago. Discovered by a local farmer in Liaoning province’s Jianchang County, it was donated to Hebei Geo University’s museum in 2023.

Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences and Hebei Geo University, working with colleagues from around the world, named the species Norellraptor barsboldi in a study published Sept. 29 in the journal Nature Communications.

The fossil adds evidence to a long-running debate over whether birds and their close dinosaur relatives inherited flight-related anatomy from a common ancestor or developed it separately.

Norellraptor belongs to the microraptorines, a group of small, feathered predators closely related to birds. Fossils of some members show long feathers on both their forelimbs and hindlimbs, suggesting they were adapted to move through the air.

The researchers compared Norellraptor with other fossils and found that roughly 30% of the anatomical changes they traced through microraptorine evolution also appeared in the bird lineage. In microraptorines, finger bones shortened before wrist and hand bones fused and the breastbone lengthened. In the bird lineage, those changes appeared in the opposite order.

Growth marks in Norellraptor’s forearm bone suggest it was at least 3 years old and still growing when it died, an age estimate the researchers factored into their comparisons with other fossils.

The different sequences challenge the idea that microraptorines and birds inherited the same flight apparatus or followed a shared pattern of development, the researchers said. They argue that the similar features arose independently in the two lineages.

(Header image: Left and right: Fossilized limb bones of Norellraptor barsboldi. Center: An artist’s reconstruction of the species by Zhang Chuang. From Nature)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.title: The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.content:
Few people in China have heard of Transsion Holdings, but hundreds of millions of people across the Global South use its phones.

The firm, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, has risen from obscurity to become a dominant player in Africa, where it makes nearly half of all phones bought on the continent every year, beating competition from Samsung, Apple, and domestic Chinese giants like Xiaomi and Huawei Technologies. It also holds more than a 10% share of the Southeast Asian and Middle Eastern markets.

Transsion’s rise has been all the more impressive given its humble origins: unlike many of its rivals, it hasn’t benefited from massive funding or market-leading technology.

Instead, it has built a global business almost from scratch — a decades-long journey spanning Shenzhen’s knock-off electronics markets, scrappy networks of African “suitcase entrepreneurs,” and years of careful, locally targeted innovation.

Lu Miao, a media anthropologist and assistant professor at Hong Kong’s Lingnan University, charts this fascinating tale in her book “The Transsion Approach: Translating Chinese Mobile Technology in Africa.”

Based on years of research, it explores the secrets to the company’s success in the Global South — and how its strategy offers an alternative to the “blitzscaling” model favored by many tech startups in both Silicon Valley and China.

In this interview, Lu talks to Sixth Tone and Zhang Lin, an associate professor at the University of New Hampshire whose research focuses on tech innovation, about the Transsion story and what it teaches us about global technology flows. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: Your book explores how Transsion grew from the informal global phone market that emerged during the 1990s and early 2000s, when African and Arab traders began traveling to southern China to buy cheap knock-off — or shanzhai — handsets. What is the company’s connection to that era?

Lu Miao: Shanzhai phones were extremely common in the early 2000s. The Huaqiangbei electronics market in Shenzhen was a major hub, while Chungking Mansions in Hong Kong was an important gateway for knock-off phones going overseas.

The main buyers were small traders from Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Some scholars call them “suitcase entrepreneurs” because they would arrive with a few suitcases, buy phones, take them home, and distribute them to smaller towns.

By the time Transsion was founded in 2006, shanzhai phones had already swept through many African countries. On the one hand, they met the basic communication needs of many low-income users; on the other, they damaged the reputation of Chinese phones, which African consumers came to associate with cheapness and poor quality.

When I went to Ghana in 2019, I found that many of Transsion’s national distributors had started out-selling secondhand and shanzhai phones bought from traders in Chungking Mansions. After partnering with Transsion, they gradually became formal agents for a multinational company.

These local African distributors linked the shanzhai era to the Transsion era. The personal connections and distribution networks they had built up played a major role in helping Transsion establish itself.

There is also continuity in design. Features such as dual-SIM support and large batteries originated in the shanzhai phone ecosystem and were later adapted for African markets. Dual SIMs, for example, help users avoid costly cross-network calls in countries with patchy network coverage.

But Transsion also represented a break from that era. First, the phone business became more formalized and institutionalized. These distributors set up trading companies of their own, and their relationships with Transsion became governed by more formal contracts.

Second, Transsion did not want to make quick money and leave, as sellers had done in the shanzhai era; it wanted to build a brand and stay for the long term. That is why it invested heavily in its after-sales service network.

Shanzhai wasn’t simply about one manufacturer producing copycat phones. It was an ecosystem: factories, supply chains, designers, distributors ... Transsion grew out of that ecosystem, but also moved beyond the shanzhai model of the time.

Sixth Tone: Looking at the bigger picture, how has Africa’s digital communications sector evolved over time, and how has that affected Chinese companies like Transsion?

Lu: Take Ghana as an example. The country’s telecommunications companies were originally state-owned. But in the 1980s and 1990s, the country had to turn to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund for loans to deal with ongoing economic and debt crises. One condition of these loans was structural adjustment, which meant privatizing the telecom sector.

After the reforms, one common outcome was a widening urban-rural gap. Commercial operators were reluctant to serve low-margin rural areas, where costs were high and consumer spending was low, so infrastructure such as base stations remained concentrated in cities.

The needs of rural and low-income communities were overlooked during the reforms, and after the state retreated, it did not step back in to meet those needs. That meant many people could only afford cheap Chinese shanzhai phones.

Transsion stepped into this market, offering affordable feature — or “dumb” — phones that were tailored to African users’ needs. It optimized its models for areas with sparse base-station coverage, making them better at picking up weak signals than many other phones. Electricity supply could also be unreliable in rural areas, so the long battery life of both shanzhai and Transsion phones was another important advantage.

Zhang Lin: Against this backdrop, you argue that we should understand global technology flows in terms of “technology translation” rather than “technology transfer.” What does this framework help us understand about how technology moves between countries?

Lu: I don’t really like the concept of “technology transfer” because it frames the process as one-way: advanced Western societies export technology to less-developed non-Western societies in order to help them develop. But the endpoint of development in this model is always Western modernity.

It also assumes that technology is neutral and fixed, as if transferring technology alone will solve social problems and generate economic growth. Yet many aid projects failed precisely because they transferred equipment without transferring the knowledge, skills, and institutional environment around it.

That is why I used the concept of “technology translation.” When a technology enters a new context, it is often reinterpreted, adjusted, and transformed. Examining the context and process of how technology is translated allows us to see how knowledge moves, and the politics embedded in the process.

Transsion did not simply take phones made in China and move them unchanged to Africa; its products were continually redesigned through their encounter with local markets. Chinese engineers and product managers, Ghanaian promoters, distributors, and repair workers all became “translators” in this process.

For example, Transsion’s dual- and multi-SIM functions were not simply extra hardware features; they responded to high communications costs, uneven network coverage, and users’ need to switch between operators. Cameras optimized for darker skin tones respond to the fact that imaging technologies have historically treated white skin as the default.

These features were not simply invented by an individual designer. They emerged through interactions among the company, users, distribution channels, and repair networks.

Zhang: You describe Transsion’s business strategy as “deep plowing” and contrast it with Silicon Valley’s “blitzscaling” model. How are they different?

Lu: “Blitzscaling” was a widely celebrated model in Silicon Valley from the mid-2010s onward. Popularized by (American internet entrepreneur) Reid Hoffman, it relies on large amounts of capital to expand rapidly, prioritizing speed over efficiency.

The idea is to capture the market first and then achieve winner-takes-all dominance. Facebook, Uber, and Airbnb are typical examples, as are Chinese companies such as ride-hailing firm Didi.

At its core, blitzscaling involves a deliberately inefficient use of capital. Companies sustain themselves through venture capital, and much of that money is wasted. It is a game only a small number of players can afford. Most fail; the few that survive can end up monopolizing the market.

“Deep plowing” is more commonly seen in the Global South. It is slower and depends much more on local knowledge and relationship networks. The term originally comes from agriculture, referring to a labor-intensive mode of production that requires long-term investment and continual care.

In business and technology, I use it to describe a market-driven, labor-intensive approach in which a company continuously interacts with local markets and adjusts its products and business strategies in response to feedback.

In many cases, this model is adopted out of necessity. Transsion chose to work deeply in rural markets overlooked by Western capital largely because it lacked large pools of capital and core technologies. It often had to create room for itself by understanding markets in much finer detail.

(Header image: An entrance to the Circle Market in Accra, Ghana, 2019. Courtesy of Lu Miao)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.title: China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.content:
As the esports competition at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, came to a close Friday, China finished atop the medal table with three golds and one silver after entering four of the 11 events. Its final gold came in Identity V, where victory over host Japan made 20-year-old Mu Xinyue the first woman to win an Asian Games esports title.

China won gold in Naraka: Bladepoint and Honor of Kings, took silver in Game for Peace, the Chinese version of PUBG Mobile, and closed its campaign with the Identity V gold. All four games were developed by Chinese companies.

Mu was one of only 14 women among more than 500 esports athletes registered for the Games, where competitions are not divided by gender. She was the only woman on China’s 23-member esports squad.

Mu competes under the name Tao Wan’an as a survivor in Identity V, an asymmetrical multiplayer game developed by Chinese tech giant NetEase that made its Asian Games debut this year. In each round, teams play two halves, taking turns as four survivors trying to escape and one hunter trying to catch them. Points are awarded based on how many survivors escape or are caught.

China and Japan were level after the first two rounds. China pulled ahead in the third and, after another draw in the fourth, secured the title during the first half of the fifth round.

Mu joined professional esports club Beijing Weibo Gaming at 18 and is now the only woman with a starting role in Identity V’s professional league.

According to domestic media reports, she decided to pursue professional gaming at 16 but could not win her family’s support. She moved out of her family home in the eastern province of Shandong and supported herself while practicing with Mechanic, her signature character, eventually becoming the server’s top-ranked player in that role.

“I had never even dared to imagine this scene,” Mu wrote on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo on Oct. 1, after winning gold.

South Korea won the final esports gold Friday by defeating Chinese Taipei in League of Legends. Japan and South Korea each finished with two golds, with Japan taking second place in the esports medal table because it won more silvers.

Esports first appeared at the Asian Games as a demonstration sport in Jakarta in 2018, then became a medal sport in Hangzhou in 2023. China won four golds and one bronze at those Games, which featured seven esports events.

China had collected 155 golds, 71 silvers, and 64 bronzes across the Games by the end of Oct. 1, with three days of competition remaining. It led both the gold-medal and overall medal counts and was on course to top the standings for the 12th consecutive edition, extending a run that began in 1982.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Mu Xinyue at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. From Weibo)

World.title: With power bills already high, Meralco wins approval to raise own fees after 15 years
World.content:
After its first rate review in 15 years, Meralco has won regulatory approval to raise its distribution charges even after already posting a record P51.13 billion in profits in 2025

MANILA, Philippines – Meralco customers will face higher electricity bills after regulators approved the utility’s first distribution rate increase in 15 years, pushing up already-high energy costs and further tightening household budgets strained by rising food, fuel, and other living expenses.

The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) approved a new average distribution rate of P1.48 per kilowatt-hour (kWh), up from the existing P1.35 per kWh, an increase of around 13 centavos. The actual increase will depend on the final residential rate, though Meralco has yet to clarify how exactly this will raise consumer bills.

The regulator and Meralco has also not mentioned when the new rate will reflect in consumer electricity bills.

Meralco’s overall residential electricity rate already stood at P14.7424 per kWh in September, meaning a household consuming 200 kWh already paid nearly P2,950 monthly. This is before the latest rate hike was factored in.

The distribution charge accounts for only one portion of the electricity bill, alongside generation, transmission, taxes, and other charges. However, it is the portion that actually goes to Meralco to cover its distribution operations and earn a profit.

Meralco’s distribution rates were last reviewed in 2011 and have effectively been frozen since 2015, as successive ERC administrations did not complete regular rate reviews. The prolonged delays kept the utility from raising its distribution charges.

Meralco originally asked for P532 billion in revenue requirement over four years, but the ERC cut this to P342 billion, 36% less than what the energy giant asked for. Even with this reduction, the approved distribution rate is still higher than what customers currently pay.

“We trimmed capital projects that were not yet justified, disallowed excessive operating costs and bad debt provisions, removed contingencies and duplicated assets from the asset base, and used a lower return on capital than what Meralco proposed,” ERC Chairperson Francis Juan said in a statement.

“The approved revenue gives Meralco a clear path to operate more efficiently and to roll out the capital projects needed for a more reliable network, including new substations and lines, modernized metering, and measures to bring down system loss. Meralco will be held to delivering these results,” he added.

Meralco, in a statement on Saturday, October 10, said it had yet to receive the full decision and would need to review it before determining its implications for the company and customers.

“We believe that this will allow Meralco to move forward with greater clarity as we pursue investments and initiatives to modernize our distribution network and enhance service delivery,” Jose Ronald Valles, Meralco’s head of regulatory management, said in a statement, pointing to investments in advanced metering infrastructure, cybersecurity, and other network modernization projects.

The increase comes as inflation soared to 7.2% in September, with faster price increases in food, transportation, electricity, and other household expenses.

Record profits even before latest hike

The higher distribution rate also comes as Meralco continues to earn record profits.

The company reported a record P50.6 billion in core profit in 2025. In the first half of 2026, its consolidated core net income reached P26.5 billion, up 3.8% from a year earlier.

The rate approval also comes just days after Manuel Pangilinan-led Metro Pacific Investments Corporation (MPIC) completed its P12.4-billion acquisition of additional Meralco shares from San Miguel Global Power on Thursday, October 8, raising the holding company’s stake in the power utility to 49.4%.

The shares were purchased at P580.99 each, about 40% above Meralco’s market price that day. Meralco shares subsequently climbed 5.3% to P437 on Friday, October 9, the same day regulators approved the rate reset, although the decision was only publicly announced the following day.

So much for Marcos’ push to lower electricity bills

There is also a twist of irony in the increase, as it comes just as President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has been pushing to bring down electricity costs by removing system loss charges that consumers have long been forced to shoulder.

During his July State of the Nation Address, Marcos explicitly called for lawmakers and government officials to focus on lowering energy costs.

“Malinaw din sa pamahalaan ang hinaing ng taumbayan na pababain ang presyo ng kuryente sa bansa,” Marcos said then. (The plea of the public to lower the price of electricity in the country is clear to the government.)

Among the reforms he pushed for was the removal of system loss on consumer energy bills. Shortly after Marcos made the proposal, Pangilinan, who also serves as Meralco’s longtime chairman, criticized this, warning that the power industry “may not survive” if companies were forced to absorb the cost of system losses themselves.

The government has made limited progress on this front. Beginning with the October billing, Meralco customers will no longer pay the 12% value-added tax on allowable system loss charges, but the underlying charge itself remains firmly in place.

For now, energy agencies are still drawing up plans to reduce these losses. This means consumers will likely continue paying system loss charges for years to come, even as Meralco prepares to collect higher distribution rates. – Rappler.com

World.title: #CourageON: A river in Cebu remembers
World.content:
The river has wisdom. If you walk slow enough to listen, then you learn that water always finds a way.

Hello, I am Chris L. Villarino. I am a tree hugger, having survived Super Typhoon Yolanda by hugging a tree in Tacloban. Since then, I have dedicated my life around advocacy for the environment by engaging individuals, organizations and communities through forest and watershed walk, wellness and regenerative activities in Cebu.



Over the weekend, the Cebu Citizens Initiative organized a river walk together with Rappler’s Cebu-based multimedia reporter John Sitchon, Rappler’s head of civic engagement Jene Pangue, and some friends in preparation for the MovePH roadshow in Cebu. We walked in one of Cebu’s rivers — not the Cebu of malls and traffic, but the old Sugbo, the Sugbo that still whispers.

We followed the water upstream; narrow, overgrown, stones covered in moss, plastic in some corners. But the river is still alive, still flowing. At some point, the water was knee deep.

They say that Cebu used to have a river like this. But now, the rivers are buried in culverts and flood control projects. Easily, we forgot the rivers. But as they say, the river never forgot us.

The river has wisdom. If you walk slow enough to listen, then you learn that water always finds a way. Even when choked with trash, blocked by concrete, the water still finds its way down to the sea. Just like life.

But during this walk, the river taught us its hardest lesson.

On a slippery stretch, our dear team leader had a bad fall; hard, face-first onto stones and sand. In a second, the laughter turned to blood, shock, and silence. He was hurt badly — needed stitches and emergency care.

We cared for him. Good thing we had an emergency kit (thanks Agence France!). We could not call for help. We were deep in the river ravine having walked more than an hour. At that moment, the leisurely walk became real.

And I realized: this is exactly what we did to our rivers.

We walked fast, distracted, taking a lot of pictures, looking at our phones, at the view. We forgot the river is not a backdrop. It is alive. It has sharp stones. It demands respect, presence, and slowness.

We also learned what community means. No one was left behind. Hands reached out. Someone held his head. Someone cleaned the blood. Someone prayed. Someone acted as buddy and walked the way back with him (thank you to our friend Karsten!).

The forest that felt so quiet suddenly felt like family.

He is okay now — stitched, resting, healing (driving around the city doing his work). We are grateful it wasn’t worse but the whole experience gave me an important life lesson.

He fell for all of us, in a way. A reminder that rewilding and re-rivering — whether through watershed walks, building urban pocket forests inspired by Laudate Deum, or carrying out the Handuraw Panaw project — is not just a nice workshop concept. It’s real terrain. It will wound you if you don’t walk with humility, much like surviving nature’s wildest forces as a tree hugger clinging to hope and life during Super Typhoon Yolanda.

Going for a river walk is not just going to a waterfall for Instagram or Facebook. It’s not for the faint of heart. It’s going back to our source.

Thank you Rappler, Jene Pangue, and John Sitchon for walking with us, for being brave, for teaching us courage and walking the talk. Thank you everyone for not leaving when it got hard.

I look forward to carrying this spirit forward into our upcoming partnership with Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH for #MoveCebu: Sugbo alang sa mga Sugboanon event this October 14–16, where fellow advocates, community leaders, and storytellers will gather to move together towards environmental resilience and civic action.

The river remembers. – Rappler.com

World.title: Who is Jeus Yape and what is virtual taekwondo?
World.content:
CHAMPION. Jeus Yape of the Philippines wins the gold medal in mixed individual virtual taekwondo in the 2026 Asian Games.

Reaping the fruits of nearly two decades spent honing his craft in taekwondo, Jeus Yape becomes the first Filipino to win a gold medal in the sport in the Asian Games

Few knew Jeus Yape before the Asian Games.

But that changed overnight as the 22-year-old became the first Filipino to win a taekwondo gold medal in the quadrennial showpiece following his triumph in the mixed individual virtual taekwondo.

Yape helped the Philippines equal its four-gold tally in the 2018 and 2023 stagings as he delivered the last mint after Carlos Yulo claimed the floor exercise and vault titles in men’s artistic gymnastics and EJ Obiena defended his crown in men’s pole vault.

On top of his gold, Yape also bagged bronze in the men’s individual poomsae, joining Yulo as the only Filipino athletes to win multiple medals in the 20th edition held in Nagoya, Japan.

The medals are the fruits of nearly two decades Yape spent honing his craft in the sport.

Runs in the blood

Hailing from Kananga, Leyte, Yape comes from a taekwondo family, with both his father, Roderick, and mother, Joyce, holding black belts and serving as taekwondo instructors. His older sister, Stella Nicole, has also represented the country in the sport.

He first took up taekwondo at just four years old and has not looked back since.

“Back then, I just tagged along whenever my father taught classes and I spent my time playing. Eventually, he started having me join sparring sessions, and over time, I grew to like the sport,” Yape said in Filipino.

Yape started as a kyorugi (full-contact sparring) athlete before switching to poomsae (non-contact form) when he reached high school.

“I was quite small back then, so I was moved to poomsae because my size was a disadvantage in kyorugi. From then on, I became more focused on poomsae,” Yape said.

That shift paid dividends as Yape earned a taekwondo scholarship from the University of Sto. Tomas and became a member of the national team, representing the country in the 2024 World Poomsae Championships and 2025 Southeast Asian Games, where he both won bronzes as part of the mixed team.

Little did Yape know that perhaps the biggest achievement of his career would come in virtual taekwondo, an event that debuted in the Asian Games.

What is virtual taekwondo?

Yape likens virtual taekwondo or VTKD to Tekken, the popular fighting game where players aim to deplete their opponents’ health bars through a combination of attacks and strategic moves.

But instead of controllers, VTKD competitors wear virtual reality headsets to enter a digital arena, while motion-tracking nodes attached to their backs, thighs, and shins capture their movements in real time.

Attacks are measured by acceleration, with faster kicks inflicting greater damage. Competitors, though, can negate damage with successful blocks.

VTKD also borrows elements from video games, including a stun meter that renders opponents temporarily defenseless once filled. While punches do not deal damage, they help charge the stun bar.

Although VTKD requires no physical contact, Yape said the sport presents its own challenges.

“It’s difficult because you’re not hitting anything, so there’s more strain on the hamstrings since nothing absorbs the impact of your kick, especially when you kick with full force,” he said.

Play Video

VTKD also demands stamina, with players delivering a steady stream of kicks in each fast-paced, one-minute round.

“I can say it’s hard because there’s luck involved. It’s anybody’s game,” Yape said.

New star

Yape’s landmark Asian Games victory has thrust him into the same spotlight as Yulo and Obiena, two established stars he only once looked up to from afar.

For Yape, being mentioned in the same breath as the two Olympians is a tremendous honor.

“We watched kuya EJ compete in the Tokyo Olympics on TV at home. I never expected that I’d get to talk to him and be here with him,” Yape said during the heroes’ welcome for Asian Games medalists.

“I also really admire kuya Caloy. Our sport, freestyle taekwondo, has some similarities to gymnastics, so I’m really amazed by what kuya Caloy can do. He’s so good at sticking his landings and that’s one of the things I want to learn too. I’m inspired by him.”

While still riding high on his breakthrough triumph, Yape has returned to the familiar demands of student life as he continues his studies in fitness and sports management at UST’s Institute of Physical Education and Athletics.

“Things are back to normal now. I still have to catch up on the assignments and works I missed,” Yape said. – Rappler.com

World.title: When history comes to life again through a fiction novel
World.content:
ALIVE AGAIN. Darwin De Jesus Mariano holds his novel beside the Laguna Copperplate at the National Museum of Anthropology.

Inspired by a 1,000-year-old museum artifact, author Darwin de Jesus Mariano breathes life into the names engraved on the Laguna Copperplate with his debut fantasy novel, ‘Namwaran and the Golden Tara’

MANILA, Philippines – In the late 1990s, when the National Museum of Anthropology was still called the Museum of the Filipino People, a younger Darwin de Jesus Mariano first saw the Laguna Copperplate. It sits on a podium inside a glass case, fairly simple: a thin, hammered sheet of copper engraved with words from an ancient script.

Translated, it bears a thousand-year-old legal text recording the acquittal of a debt in gold for a man named Namwaran and his relatives.

More than two decades later, Mariano — now a Filipino author, corporate leader, tech entrepreneur, and lawyer — returned to the same museum with those names no longer confined to an inscription. He debuted his historical fantasy novel, Namwaran and the Golden Tara, on September 13, a day after its official launch at the Manila International Book Fair.

The novel is mainly inspired by the Laguna Copperplate and the Golden Tara of Agusan, following the story of three siblings: Namwaran, Angkatan, and Bukah, whose lives change after their mother disappears and the golden statue is stolen.

Mariano wove real artifacts and documented periods of Southeast Asian history into his imagination to revive the people on the copperplate.

“It all started with the scribbles on my notebook from my museum visits that fueled my fascination for ancestral history. I wondered — what if these people were on a journey and along the way, they discover the other artifacts in the Philippines and Southeast Asia?” said Mariano, explaining how he came up with the idea that bore his first novel.

Bringing adventure to history

Imagining these people living their lives in the past wasn’t the hard part in creating the novel. For Mariano, this was the base. It was the historical backdrop that tied it all together. The real challenge was to build an adventure out of fragments of the past.

He took the three names of relatives in the Laguna Copperplate and turned them into siblings and gave them the magic of eternal life, which they use to search for their missing mother across different eras in the novel.

“There was no mother mentioned in the artifact, so I had the freedom to create that character,” he said during the book launch.

But beneath the fiction and magic were real incidents, such as the civil wars and major eras mentioned. Specifically, Mariano lets the siblings journey through the rise and decline of regional powers such as Srivijaya and Majapahit, as well as conflicts surrounding Manila centuries later. The book also carries real historical figures from these time periods.

“I first heard about these Southeast Asian empires from an early mentor, the late senator Raul Roco. Combined with my museum notes, these learnings made me realize that the people, places, and things in our history can make for a great story,” he explained.

On the same note, Mariano said that he wants to share his appreciation for history with other Filipinos.

But Mariano had a question that followed him through years of museum visits and research: how can he make people curious about a history that can feel impossibly distant?

His answer is to create a world that is more understandable and relatable, something more familiar and easier to consume: an ancestral fantasy novel.

“We don’t have a lot of ancestral fantasy books and it’s not a common genre. Novels like this inspire curiosity and in turn, you’d want to learn more. Hopefully, this book’s readers will be interested in revisiting our history and culture,” he said.

When ‘them’ becomes ‘us’

Apart from reading historical textbooks and novels, another way to revisit the past is by going to museums. Mariano chose to hold the book launch at the National Museum of Anthropology, not just to match the theme of his novel, but also to invite the attendees to a guided tour.

The tour, guided by museum staff, featured five artifacts: the Kulaman limestone burial jars, the Maradika Qur’an, the Manunggul Jar, the Banton Burial Cloth, and finally, the Laguna Copperplate itself.

At the last stop, Mariano took over from the guide to give a short speech to explain the story of the copperplate.

“Imagine what would have been required for this document to exist in 900 AD,” he pointed out. “The society behind it would have needed systems for writing and keeping time, as well as laws, governance, and a means of recognizing when an obligation had already been settled.”

He explained that because of the contents of the copperplate, historians were able to say that this artifact is evidence of an organized society having regional connections.

However, museum pieces like this don’t fully describe the lives of those who once held them.

For National Museum of the Philippines director-general Jeremy Barns, this way of looking at the past can also change the distance Filipinos place between themselves and their ancestors.

“When we speak about our precolonial ancestors, we tend to speak about ‘them,’ when we are really talking about ‘us’,” he said in his opening remarks.

Ultimately, Mariano’s idea to fictionalize the lives of these historical characters aimed to address this issue. He created a world where these people can exist again and gave them concerns that readers could recognize: family, loss, survival, and the search for someone they love.

“We realize that they are regular people like us. They experience love, hope, fear, and sadness. In reality, they are not very different from who we are today,” he said, referring to the main characters of his novel.

During his discussion at the launch, he pointed out that there may be differences in language, place, and identity across communities, but there were also things people had in common.

For Mariano, a huge part of being interested in our history comes from the sense of connection that we have with the past. He noted that most Filipinos learn about history in school, but books, museums, and personal research made him more inclined to learn about our own culture.

He also admitted that his decade-long research and writing brought him new learnings, and that he hopes he can share these with the readers of Namwaran and the Golden Tara.

It is this sense of connection that Mariano hopes readers take with them after the adventure ends.

Telling our own stories

While Mariano’s novel aims to reconnect people with Philippine and Southeast Asian history, he admits it’s only one way to preserve our past.

The launch also came at a time when the Laguna Copperplate is being considered for inclusion in the UNESCO Memory of the World Committee for Asia and the Pacific Regional Register, a program concerned with safeguarding and widening access to documentary heritage.

During the event, UNESCO National Commission of the Philippines secretary-general Ivan Anthony Henares similarly described heritage as something that lives not only in artifacts, but also in documents, manuscripts, films, and other records.

In his remarks, he said Namwaran brings a part of the shared past “back to life, retold and made accessible to the new generation.”

For Mariano, accessibility does not have to come only from academics or cultural institutions either.

“You can be an ordinary Filipino and still be interested and spreading the word about history,” he said during the discussion.

Mariano believes Filipinos should take part in telling these stories themselves, “before other people start writing down what we should’ve been writing on our own.”

Standing once more before the artifact that had sparked his curiosity decades earlier, he left guests with another question.

“What kind of debt do we owe people like Namwaran and this family?” Mariano asked. “…the people who came before us, who lived in these islands that we now call the Philippines, that we don’t remember.”

For Mariano, remembering does not necessarily mean knowing everything about them. Much of their lives may never be recovered from the fragments that remain.

But perhaps a museum visit, a story, or an adventure can make someone curious enough to begin looking. – Rappler.com

World.title: DICT chief Henry Aguda has resigned, says Ombudsman Remulla
World.content:
DICT. Department of Information and Communications Technology Secretary Henry Aguda on September 7, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines – Ombusdman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday, October 10, said

Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) chief Henry Aguda has resigned.

Remulla mentioned Aguda’s alleged resignation on the show Executive Session on DZRH.

Play Video

Asked about Aguda’s status, Remulla said “Nag-resign. Tinanggap na ‘yung resignation.” (He resigned. The resignation was accepted.)

Aguda denied resignation rumors last Wednesday, October 7. He said, “I am aware of the reports circulating regarding my position as Secretary of the Department of Information and Communications Technology” and that he continued to serve as the DICT chief.

Aguda and the DICT faced a controversy in the past weeks over the government’s efforts to regulate and block online platforms, including a decision to ban Discord, which was met with a severe backlash from users of the platform, including workers.

Rappler has reached out to Henry Aguda for confirmation. – Rappler.com

World.title: ‘Chiz with his cheese’: Squishy hype reaches Senate impeachment trial
World.content:
(1st UPDATE) Escudero has been spotted fiddling with a squishy toy during the impeachment trial

Participating in an impeachment trial is stressful, but presiding over one? A totally different story.

Senate Impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero appears to have found a way to manage courtroom pressure of overseeing the proceedings: a bright yellow, cheese-shaped squishy toy.

Much to its name, squishies are soft, squeezable toys designed to slowly return to their original shape after being compressed. They come in various shapes, sizes, and textures, with some offering a crunchy or resistant feel. The toys have been trending on social media, with some content creators making hauls or autonomous sensory meridian response (ASMR) videos.

During the impeachment trial, Escudero was repeatedly seen fiddling with a bright yellow, rectangular squishy resembling a cheese. At one point, he even delivered a ruling on a prosecution slide that had briefly appeared on the screen while playing with his squishy.

“Can the clerk kindly check with the tech what was flashed and upon whose authority it was flashed,” Escudero said.

Squishies may be marketed as toys for children, but they can also be great stress-relievers for adults.

And with Escudero celebrating his birthday on Saturday, October 10, a great gift idea, perhaps, could be another squishy! – Rappler.com

World.title: Why Congress should think twice about banning under-18s from social media
World.content:
SOCIAL MEDIA. TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, Snapchat, X, Reddit app icons are seen in this illustration taken June 15, 2026

Australia's experience and a more nuanced House proposal raise questions about the effectiveness, proportionality, and unintended consequences of a blanket social media ban

MANILA, Philippines – Protecting children from the dangers of social media is an increasingly urgent concern for governments worldwide. But does keeping young people off these platforms necessarily make them safer?

This is a question Philippine lawmakers must confront as Congress deliberates on legislation prohibiting anyone below 18 from accessing social media and other high-risk digital services.

On Thursday, October 8, the Senate approved Senate Bill No. 2424, or the Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) Act, by a vote of 16-1.

The measure comes amid concerns about cyberbullying, online sexual exploitation, violent content, grooming and manipulation, and addictive algorithms.

But an outright ban covering everyone under 18 — the widest-reaching age threshold in the world if enacted — is arguably a draconian response to a serious problem. It raises questions about proportionality, enforcement, and whether restricting access addresses the underlying causes of online harm, or just delays regulation that deals with the addictive and harmful features of social media platform.

What Australia tells us

Australia implemented a nationwide social media minimum-age restriction in December 2025, prohibiting those under 16 from holding accounts on covered platforms.

Its experience offers lessons for Philippine lawmakers: implementing it is a challenging matter.

According to Australia’s eSafety Commissioner, social media usage among children under 16 only declined from 85.9% before the restrictions to 81.5% three months after.

In other words, roughly eight in ten children continued using social media despite the ban.

A CNA Talking Point documentary showed teenagers circumventing age-verification measures. Some passed facial age-estimation checks because the technology incorrectly identified them as older than 16. Conversely, some adults were denied access after being mistakenly classified as minors.

Teenagers also described creating new accounts, using alternative devices, and seeking help from adults.

An expert involved in Australia’s age-assurance technology trial attributed some failures to inconsistent implementation by platforms.

Australia’s experience illustrates the limitations of what may be a stopgap measure, particularly when enforcement remains inconsistent. If young people can readily circumvent restrictions, how much protection does the law actually provide?

Are we addressing the source of harm?

A blanket ban doesn’t address the harmful platform features, including algorithms that amplify disturbing content, infinite scrolling, autoplay, and notifications designed to keep users engaged.

Such features do not disappear when minors are prohibited from accessing platforms.

Ian Russell, a British online safety campaigner whose 14-year-old daughter Molly died by suicide in 2017, has questioned blanket restrictions. An inquest concluded that harmful online content contributed to Molly’s death.

Despite campaigning for stronger protections, Russell argued in a BBC Newscast interview that banning children does not address the source of harm, and believes governments should hold technology companies accountable for algorithms and design features that expose users to dangerous content.

Restrictions and more targeted regulation against dangerous features are not mutually exclusive. But we must recognize what the proposal of a ban for under-18s: a stopgap solution that doesn’t go at the root of the issue.

Not all minors are the same

The Senate raised the age threshold from the original under-16 proposal to under 18.

The increase comes amid recent school shootings and other violent incidents involving young people in the Philippines. But lawmakers must establish whether sufficient evidence connects these incidents to social media and whether a blanket ban would prevent similar tragedies.

A policy driven primarily by fear rather than scientific evidence risks unintended consequences. This concern is central to Senator Risa Hontiveros’ dissenting vote.

“Eighteen is the legal threshold for adulthood. But it is certainly not a developmental threshold,” Hontiveros said.

She argued that a 13-year-old and a 17-year-old are not developmentally equivalent simply because both are minors.

Hontiveros cited the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, which recognizes children’s evolving capacities as they mature.

She also emphasized that social media provides livelihoods through online selling and content creation, helps children connect with OFW parents, and allows them to report abuse and participate in public discussions.

At 15, Filipinos can already vote in Sangguniang Kabataan elections and legally work, subject to labor regulations. Yet the proposed ban would restrict access to platforms used for political participation and economic opportunities.

Beyond these consequences, a blanket ban could also be viewed as a repressive restriction on young people’s freedom of expression. Digital platforms have become common avenues for teenagers to voice opinions, exchange ideas, and participate in public discourse.

A more nuanced House proposal

The House of Representatives has taken a different approach.

On October 6, it approved on second reading House Bill No. 11566, or the Safe and Friendly Environment for Kids in Digital Spaces Act.

According to INQUIRER.net, the House measure proposes a complete social media ban for children 13 and younger, while allowing older teenagers restricted access.

The legislation would shield teenagers from harmful advertising, livestreaming, algorithm-driven short-video feeds, and gambling-like mechanisms. It would also restrict contact with unknown adults and certain artificial intelligence features.

Pasig Representative Roman Romulo, who sponsored the measure, said the distinction was deliberate.

“Younger children require a clear minimum age boundary, while adolescents require a framework that recognizes their growing capacity for independence without disregarding the risks to which they remain exposed,” Romulo said.

The House approach resembles the age-appropriate framework advocated by Hontiveros, recognizing that older teenagers can gain greater independence while retaining safeguards.

Preparing children for a digital world

A blanket ban could also undermine digital literacy. Young people need to understand algorithms, misinformation, online predators, scams, and exploitation.

Would an 18-year-old encountering social media for the first time necessarily be better equipped than a younger teenager who gradually learned under parental guidance?

Supporters may argue that digital literacy can be taught without social media access. But supervised exposure offers another approach.

Social media companies have also advocated age-appropriate frameworks, including teen accounts and parental controls. Their position warrants scrutiny, given their commercial incentives to retain users.

Again, governments could instead impose enforceable standards addressing harmful algorithms, addictive design, and inadequate child protections.

As the House reviews SB 2424, it has an opportunity to examine which restrictions are proportionate, enforceable, and supported by evidence. The goal should not simply be to keep children off social media, but to make the digital environments they encounter safer. – Rappler.com

World.title: The Regime Is Laying a Trap for the US. Will Washington Fall for It?
World.content:
Myanmar has become increasingly salient in Washington’s economic and national security calculus.

However, the country is far from simple. Its military and political power is dispersed across multiple centers, demanding deft handling and nuanced thinking.

In the absence of a single like-minded counterpart, Washington may be tempted to look for a shortcut and treat the military regime as the easiest channel through which to advance U.S. interests. Doing so would risk falling into the trap laid by Naypyitaw: mistaking access to the military regime for access to Myanmar itself.

Will Washington take the bait? Or will Washington resist this temptation and build a strategy around navigating Myanmar’s intricate and decentralized landscape?

Washington’s calculus

For Washington, the central question will be how to address two particular interests that converge in Myanmar as cost-effectively and reliably as possible. Washington is seeking to reduce dependence on China-dominated rare earth supply chains while confronting a rapidly expanding form of transnational organized crime that directly harms Americans. The country borders India and China, links mainland Southeast Asia to the Indian Ocean and is the world’s fourth-largest producer of rare earths. Myanmar also serves as one of the primary hubs for scam compounds that directly defraud Americans of billions of dollars.

Under the Trump administration, Washington’s foreign policy has fundamentally changed. Longstanding traditions of promoting human rights and democracy have now been deprioritized in favor of an “America First” approach interpreted narrowly as protecting core national interests. The 2025 National Security Strategy (NSS) signed by Trump last November identifies “flexible realism” as one of its guiding principles. Under this approach, Washington seeks good relations and peaceful commercial ties with countries without requiring them to adopt democratic principles.

This change may have significant ramifications for Myanmar, where the U.S.’ concerns over democracy and human rights have historically been prioritized, constraining diplomatic engagement with the country’s military rulers and business deals that could benefit them.

Equally important, the NSS also recognized the Indo-Pacific as “among the next century’s key economic and geopolitical battlegrounds” and emphasized that successful competition in the region is essential to American prosperity. As Washington seeks to rebalance its economic relationship with China and reduce its dependence on China-dominated supply chains, Myanmar’s strategic importance could grow.

Washington’s calculus is also shaped by regional governments, including U.S. partners, and by its own private sector. Global volatility and geopolitical shocks have exposed vulnerabilities in regional supply chains and energy security. The added threat of economic coercion has placed greater pressure on governments, including the U.S., to seek stability and secure critical supply chains. To this end, regional governments have started high-level engagements with the regime to explore possibilities. These engagements may increase the appeal of normalizing relations with the military regime in Naypyitaw for Washington.

American businesses, whose voices carry weight, are watching these shifts as well. As regional governments signal openness to normalization with the regime, Myanmar may appear to become a viable market for foreign investment. These businesses may perceive that U.S. sanctions and other regulations could leave them at a competitive disadvantage to regional competitors. The first entrants into uncertain and unstable markets often absorb the greatest risks, but the willingness of American businesses to pursue investment despite uncertainty may make the prospect of securing an early foothold difficult to dismiss.

Washington’s blind spot

For Washington, this renewed attention on Myanmar has revived an older policy problem that it had tried to work around, as it struggled to develop a coherent approach to the country. For much of the 1990s and 2000s, Washington tended to work through a small number of central political actors, even though political authority and armed power were far more dispersed. Myanmar’s ethnic armed organizations, despite being political and military stakeholders, did not fit neatly into the U.S.’ engagement model. In practice, Washington’s political focus remained on Aung San Suu Kyi and the military regime, and its engagement with ethnic armed organizations was largely reduced to a national reconciliation framework, excluding powerful groups that did not participate in the ceasefire process.

Today, Myanmar’s political landscape has changed. For decades, Aung San Suu Kyi served as Washington’s principal democratic interlocutor in Myanmar, but she remains under detention today. The opposition is dispersed among the National Unity Government, ethnic armed organizations and other resistance actors. Intensified war since the 2021 coup has further shifted political and military power toward ethnic armed organizations. No single actor represents the opposition as a whole. Engaging Myanmar today therefore requires moving beyond an approach built around a select few central political actors, and Washington has yet to adapt to a decentralized political landscape, as Beijing has.

Understanding this blind spot, the military regime in Naypyitaw has positioned itself to exploit an intensifying geopolitical competition and unresolved gap in Washington’s approach to Myanmar. The military regime has paid millions of dollars to influential lobbying firms to help tailor its message to current U.S. priorities, pitching itself as a partner capable of advancing them. What remains uncertain this time, however, is whether Washington will take the bait.

A familiar bargain

Under sanctions and growing isolation, the regime has repeatedly staged political openings with pitches for engagement to the U.S. throughout its history. This history, however, offers a clear lesson: the military will act in bad faith and abandon its agreements whenever it sees fit.

In May 2002, the military released Aung San Suu Kyi from house arrest. One week later, it registered a firm in Washington to lobby for normalizing relations with the U.S. The regime pitched cooperation on issues prioritized by the Bush administration, including counternarcotics, terrorism, trade and public health. The opening did not last. In May 2003, regime-paid attackers assaulted Aung San Suu Kyi’s convoy near Depayin, and the military detained her again.

Another opening came under President Thein Sein in March 2011. That August, he met with Aung San Suu Kyi in Naypyitaw. Subsequently, his government released political prisoners, relaxed censorship, allowed the National League for Democracy to reenter electoral politics and pursued ceasefires with ethnic armed groups. Washington responded by sending Secretary of State Hillary Clinton to Burma in December 2011, restoring ambassador-level diplomatic relations and easing restrictions on investment and financial services. The political opening lasted nearly a decade before the military, under Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, seized power in February 2021 and detained Aung San Suu Kyi again.

The 2011 opening, notably, was different. Thein Sein and other reform-minded officials made significant concessions and pursued genuine, if imperfect, political reforms. The changes allowed political freedoms and economic opportunities that had been unimaginable under previous military governments. Myanmar experts and analysts will continue to debate what could have been done differently to preserve that opening, but for Washington, dwelling on the past or trying to recreate it would only distract from addressing Myanmar’s present realities and building a better future.

The 2011 opening, and any hope of returning to it, was shattered by the 2021 coup and the military’s subsequent campaign of violence against its own people. The present reality is that the military leadership now ruling in Naypyitaw is not the one that pursued those reforms, but the one that overturned them.

The price of a shortcut

Normalizing relations with the regime is highly unlikely to secure access to rare earths or curb the scam compounds it supports. Instead, normalization would exacerbate these issues by giving a lifeline to the Min Aung Hlaing regime as it faces growing internal tensions, a new round of military defeats and economic pressures.

The military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party recently postponed its congress, reportedly due to leadership disputes. At the same time, the elevation of Min Aung Hlaing’s loyalists over more senior generals has raised questions about tensions within the armed forces. While exaggerating its success on the battlefield, the military now relies heavily on conscripts. Reportedly, more than 70 percent of its frontline troops are conscripts. While these developments do not necessarily indicate an imminent collapse, they contextualize the growing strains within the regime at a time when it is seeking international engagement.

The regime is also struggling militarily. In Kachin State, the military has failed to break the Kachin Independence Army’s resistance around Bhamo, while losing additional positions to resistance forces. In Rakhine State, a major offensive launched in September to retake territory from the Arakan Army has failed to achieve significant gains despite the deployment of thousands of troops backed by air and naval support. In Karen State, the Karen National Liberation Army and allied forces have continued to contest the military’s attempts to regain lost positions around Kawkareik.

Economic pressures are also adding to the regime’s mounting difficulties. Even Min Aung Hlaing, who has long presented an optimistic picture of Myanmar’s economy, recently acknowledged the regime’s failure to make meaningful progress. The regime’s pursuit of a loan arrangement with Belarus with high interest rates further suggests growing financial pressures and a need to secure alternative sources of financing. The regime’s efforts to circumvent international jet fuel sanctions also suggest that these measures are imposing constraints. With technical and material support from Chinese companies, the regime is developing its own aviation fuel production capacity at the Thanlyin refinery near Yangon to reduce its dependence on imported jet fuel. The project underscores the lengths to which the regime is going to secure a reliable fuel supply for its air force.

Will Washington take the bait?

The trap is laid. Washington’s recent actions indicate a trajectory towards normalization, but these three key drivers will shape what happens next in U.S. policy toward Myanmar.

Will Congress take a strong bipartisan stand? Although members of Congress have expressed concerns about engagement with the military regime, statements alone may do little to influence the administration’s calculations. The more consequential test will be whether Congress will press the Trump administration to implement the BURMA Act and pass the BRAVE Burma Act, which would “ turn the screws

Although members of Congress have expressed concerns about engagement with the military regime, statements alone may do little to influence the administration’s calculations. The more consequential test will be whether Congress will press the Trump administration to implement the BURMA Act and pass the BRAVE Burma Act, which would “ How will U.S.-China relations develop? The outcome of negotiations between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping for the remainder of this year

The outcome of negotiations between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping for the Can Myanmar’s resistance forces present a credible alternative? World.title: Over Two-Thirds of Myanmar’s Population Poor or at Risk of Poverty: UN
World.content:
More than 37 million people—over two-thirds of Myanmar’s population of more than 54 million—are experiencing or at risk of “multidimensional poverty,” according to the latest report from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) released on Thursday.

Drawing data from a nationwide household survey of nearly 7,500 people in 2025, the UNDP’s latest analysis examines what it calls multidimensional poverty, which looks beyond income and also covers non-financial deprivation, including access to education and healthcare, and other basic needs, amid economic and political crisis and natural hazards.

It said nearly 18 million people (32.6 percent) in Myanmar are multidimensionally poor, while more than 19 million (35.5 percent) others are vulnerable. That brings the total figure to more than 37 million people (68 percent) who either face poverty or are at risk of falling into it.

“Myanmar may no longer dominate international headlines, but the hardships facing millions of people continue to deepen,” said Kanni Wignaraja, UN assistant secretary-general and UNDP regional director for Asia and the Pacific. “We are seeing a depth of poverty in Myanmar that is eroding human development itself. This is a no-win war. Everyone is losing. The core muscle of the country is being systematically eroded.”

The survey found that people in rural areas are poorer than those in urban areas.

In terms of both severity and scale, the UNDP report highlights Rakhine State as the worst-affected area, with approximately 1.66 million residents enduring the most intense multidimensional poverty. Sagaing Region followed with a larger total of approximately 2.38 million people experiencing less severe poverty. Ayeyarwady Region ranked third.

The UNDP’s analysis indicated that poverty is driven by a combination of long-standing household vulnerabilities, including low education levels, insecure jobs and limited income, and wider pressures such as rising prices, natural hazards and armed conflict.

In war-torn Rakhine and Karenni (Kayah) states, poverty has been compounded by conflict, displacement and restrictions on movement.

To address poverty effectively, the report concluded that aid must provide intensive support to hard-hit conflict zones while reaching larger numbers of poor residents elsewhere, with assistance tailored to local needs.

World.title: Regime Shuts Down Myanmar’s Surging Online Gold Market
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime has moved to ban online sales of gold and jewelry, citing the risk of flawed products and market destabilization.

On Wednesday, the Commerce Ministry announced it has suspended issuance of licenses for selling gold, raw gold, jewelry, art objects, and household items via online platforms. It threatened unlicensed traders with prosecution under the 2013 Essential Commodities and Services Law, which carries six months to three years in prison and fines up to 500,000 kyats (roughly US$ 240).

Under existing rules, online sellers must obtain a Commerce Ministry license, while those dealing in gold and gemstones must also secure a permit from the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environmental Conservation.

Industry insiders told The Irrawaddy that more than 700 businesses have applied for licenses to sell gold and jewelry online in recent years. However, the ministry has now refused to extend expired permits, with inspections and enforcement expected to begin at the end of this month.

Online gold and jewelry shopping has become popular in Myanmar over the past few years, with internet outlets hiring actors and celebrities to promote their livestream sales.

Traders say the clampdown follows growing complaints from buyers that jewelry purchased via livestream “flash sales” was later rejected by pawnshops or gold shops.

“Online customers have no way of verifying the weight, quality, or reference price of their purchases. That leads to disputes and losses,” one Yangon jeweler explained.

Last month, Mandalay police announced the arrest of 11 foreign nationals and 17 Myanmar citizens accused of running online gemstone scams. Authorities said the suspects were using fake jade to defraud buyers in livestream sales.

Online gemstone sales remain permitted provided merchants hold a license from the Myanma Gems Enterprise and refrain from selling gold.

While the Yangon Region Gold Entrepreneurs Association has set the domestic reference price for 24K gold at 7.1 million kyats per tical, the market price exceeds 10 million kyats — a gap of 3 million kyats. Before the 2021 coup, a tical sold for under 1.4 million kyats.

Business owners warn that banning online sales will hurt digital commerce and marketing, which had surged during the pandemic. “Shops that relied on livestream promotions will struggle. Now we can only depend on walk-in customers,” one trader said.

World.title: China Takes Top Investor Crown in Myanmar, and More
World.content:
China now Myanmar’s top investor, trade partner

China is now officially the top foreign investor and trading partner in Myanmar, consolidating its economic grip as others retreat, according to a report by Japan External Trade Organization.

In fiscal year 2025 ending this March, Myanmar approved US$472.6 million in foreign direct investment, down another one-third or 31.5 percent from a year earlier. But inflow from China rose 2.1‑fold to $201.1 million, meaning it now accounts for 42.6 percent of the total.

The previous leader due to long-standing commitments, Singapore, dropped to second place with $155 million, while Hong Kong contributed $54.9 million, the report said citing data from Directorate of Investment and Company Administration.

Much of the Chinese and Hong Kong capital is in light industry, particularly garment and shoe factories.

Myanmar’s exports to China also climbed 24.7 percent to $4.312 billion over the period, while imports surged 42.6 percent to $5.952 billion. That means China now accounts for over one-third of of Myanmar’s total trade or 35 percent, up from 27.8 percent the previous year.

With the border disruptions, trade has shifted to alternative routes, says the report. The figures did not count China’s trade with territories controlled by the Brotherhood Alliance in northern Shan State bordering Yunnan.

Chinese documentary maps scam empires in lesser-known Shan hubs

A docuseries aired this week by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV has shed light on scam syndicates that thrived in four areas along Myanmar’s northern border. While Kokang’s scam empires have long made international headlines, the documentary focuses on three lesser‑known hubs—Wa, Mongla and Muse—as it boasts of Beijing’s “achievements” in cracking down on them.

The show identifies quasi-autonomous Wa territory as the incubator of regional scam economy. At the height of the boom, Mong Pawk alone hosted 265 scam centers involving nearly 60,000 people. But unlike the Kokang clans, who resisted Beijing’s demand to halt operations, the long- ruling United Wa State Army (UWSA) cooperated after one leader was arrested in Kunming and warrants were issued for others.

In October 2023, Wa authorities launched large‑scale sweeps of scam compounds, the documentary reveals. Since then, the UWSA has reported regular transfers of Chinese suspects and illegal immigrants, introducing procedures for voluntary return. More than 1,400 Chinese nationals have been reportedly handed back this year.

But it was in Mongla, controlled by the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA), where Beijing started its crackdown in September 2023, and the group cooperated with Chinese authorities. A second strike in July 2024 led to a border law enforcement cooperation agreement between Yunnan police and Mongla authorities, establishing monitoring and repatriation mechanisms.

The crackdown proved most difficult in Muse, where Beijing identified 33 distinct local armed groups and militias, each with over 100 members, alongside Myanmar military‑aligned forces. Unlike the fortified scam parks in Kokang, Muse syndicates operated out of ordinary hotels, apartments, and villas. Despite joint raids in April 2024, scam sites keep popping up like a game of Whac-a-Mole, with arrests continuing this year.

Scam arrests in junta-aligned territory

This week Naypyitaw reported the arrest of 87 scammers—75 Chinese nationals and 12 Myanmar—in the remote valley of Hopong in the Pa-O Self-Administered Zone in southern Shan. They were reportedly operating in makeshift huts, with dozens of computers, more than 500 phones and Star Link satellite dishes.
