World.title: AFLW round nine: Dal Santo jokes he ‘should have quit earlier’ after equal record low one week, win the next
World.content:
Departing St Kilda AFLW coach Nick Dal Santo has accepted responsibility for his side’s poor season, but denied there were issues around the club’s treatment of the women’s team as an independent review into the program looms.

After eight consecutive losses, the Saints galvanised on Saturday to defeat Collingwood by two points and snatch their first win of the season, 5.9 (39) to 5.7 (37). The long-awaited victory came 24 hours after St Kilda announced they had parted ways with Dal Santo and confirmed they would initiate an independent review of their AFLW program, led by former Blues footy boss Brad Lloyd.

Nick Dal Santo sings the Saints’ song after his final game as the club’s AFLW coach. Getty Images

The 1-8 Magpies, meanwhile, are doing their own soul searching, with coach Sam Wright saying it’s clear the club didn’t “have our own backyard in order right now”.

After the game, Dal Santo joked with his players that he “should have quit earlier”, referencing their third-quarter comeback.

“It looked a little different, didn’t it? And what I just said to the group is, ‘That’s actually what it takes – but it’s every single week, and it’s every day of your whole football life’.”

Dal Santo started his press conference with a brief but emotional speech with his family and children watching on.

The 42-year-old ex-St Kilda AFL star acknowledged the season had been challenging and accepted responsibility for the Saints’ AFLW situation. They last week equalled the lowest score in competition history – 0.1 (1) – in their loss to the Western Bulldogs.

“There’s no hiding the fact that it hasn’t been great, but that’s part of our journey, unfortunately,” he said. “There will be a time that this whole club is really successful, and our women’s program in particular.”

Dal Santo said the independent review would uncover parts of St Kilda’s program that need to change, and said the club had identified “a month or so ago” that they wanted some “fresh eyes on the program”.

In a column for this masthead, football media figure and commentator Kelli Underwood reported several sources close to St Kilda said women’s players at the club feel like second-class citizens, with one source saying the club chef cooks for the men’s players whenever they’re in the building, and only once a week for the women’s team – and only when the men’s team is also there.

Underwood said some players were told they’d benefit from extra tackling sessions, but that they’d have to pay for them out of their own pocket.

This masthead asked Dal Santo if there was discrepancy between how the men’s team and women’s team were treated, and if players had voiced their concerns to him.

He replied that he had not read the paper.

“I would hate to think that anyone in our women’s program doesn’t feel like we’re fed well. Like, the way that we are treated, this is my assessment, and I’ve never heard any of our players speak about that in particular,” he said.

“If you’re talking about food … there’s bigger issues in the world as well.

“But no, we are very fortunate. We get cooked meals, we get takeaway meals, we have snacks ... so I’m not quite sure what that story is.”

Dal Santo referenced the group of Saints men’s players who had attended the match, noting “every club is trying to build a one-club feel”.

“There’s some challenges within that, like the size of the facility, or one oval, but as sort of the representative of the women’s program, there’s things that we would love to do more of, but there’s also some restrictions around that.

“So hopefully, this [the review] uncovers a little bit of that, where everybody, and I’m sure the men feel the same at certain times. But that’s my stance on that.”

When asked if St Kilda AFL coach Ross Lyon – Dal Santo’s own former coach in his time as a Saints player – had shown enough support to the women’s program, Dal Santo said he “got along with Ross really well”.

“I think the bit that the group wouldn’t see is the amount of chats that Ross has, particularly with me. Coach to coach, I know he supports me heavily, and I know he supports our program, but maybe that fits into that same bucket of, ‘How do you just make it better?’”

At one point during the press conference, a St Kilda media officer interrupted and told journalists to ask “questions about the game”.

Dal Santo said his decision to not have social media was not about avoiding scrutiny, adding it was to be “more present” with his family and friends.

“I don’t read the paper because they’re probably not as available as they once were,” he said. “But the beauty about living in Melbourne is people are happy to tell you about it anyway. So when you’re grabbing your coffee, someone checks in.

“I understand that my surname probably gives it a little bit of extra oomph when you’re writing articles or talking about it, but I’m OK with that – I truly am.”

World.title: The All Blacks dominated the Wallabies. Their struggle in South Africa made it possible
World.content:
It appears the All Blacks did learn a thing or two in South Africa after all - their 50-19 victory over the Wallabies at Eden Park on Saturday night which allowed them to retain the Bledisloe Cup for another year contained all sorts of improvements, most notably their ability to catch a high ball.

Their aerial prowess was just one aspect of a victory which helped them break a three-test losing streak and take their unbeaten record at their fortress to 54 tests.

Their ability to finish opportunities - a major issue in South Africa - was also vastly improved.

They scored seven tries to Australia's three and may have scored one or two more had Will Jordan not looked to create opportunities for others rather than seek them himself. Naturally, he made the most of a very late one to put an exclamation mark on the win.

A rare try for replacement prop Pasilio Tosi was also scrubbed out for an earlier knock-on.

So, the drought for the poor old Aussies goes on - they lost the big trophy in 2003 and have not held it since - and, while they were in this test at halftime with the score 17-14 to the home side, they were blown away in the second half.

They could not deal with the speed of thought and action of men such as Damian McKenzie, who looked sharp at No.10, or the almost supernatural workrate of Jordie Barrett, the man outside him in the No.12 jersey.

Tupou Vaa'i scores against Australia at Eden Park. www.photosport.nz

Barrett was everywhere, with his midfield partner Quinn Tupaea not far behind, and, with Leroy Carter and Barrett having a vastly improved night under the high ball, the All Blacks got all the possession they needed and more.

Former skipper Scott Barrett got through a mountain of work and loose forwards Peter Lakai, Tupou Vaa'i and Wallace Sititi had the better of their vaunted opposites.

There were still issues, of course.

The All Blacks' lineout maul defence began shakily, and it was a big reason for Tom Wright's early converted try, but the response was impressive and built on a lightning quick ball against which the Wallabies had no answer.

The two tries in just over two minutes for Lakai and fellow loose forward Vaa'i were based both on lightning-fast ruck speed and the All Blacks' aerial superiority.

Jordie Barrett snaffled the first for the attack set alight by McKenzie and finished nicely by Lakai and there was another high ball win before the little No.10 cut capers again for Vaa'i's try.

At 14-7 up, the All Blacks had well and truly wrested momentum away from the visitors who needed to do something to slow the opposition's ball and succeeded only in giving away penalties.

All Blacks halfback Cam Roigard celebrates his try. Brett Phibbs / www.photosport.nz

McKenzie kicked the second one to push the All Blacks out to a 17-7 lead but back came the Wallabies through skipper Harry Wilson, the big No.8 scoring under the posts after the home side's defence was caught short up the middle.

It created an unsatisfactory end to the first half for the All Blacks, who passed with accuracy in the excellent conditions and looked like dynamite when attacking from depth (as did the Wallabies), but who too often misfired at lineout time.

It was end to end stuff early in the second half with Beauden Barrett twice getting into good positions to save the All Blacks.

Jordan was again probably overly generous in trying to pass to the supporting Sititi only to see it intercepted, but the pressure stayed on the Wallabies and Cam Roigard was the beneficiary from close range.

Tries for Codie Taylor, Leroy Carter and replacement outside back Josh Moorby followed as the score got into ugly territory for the Australians.

The defeat broke a six-game unbeaten streak for the Wallabies who arrived in Auckland confident of making history after their recent victory over a weakened Springboks but they came up against an All Black team determined to right a few wrongs.

They did it in style.

All Blacks 50 (Peter Lakai, Tupou Vaa'i, Cam Roigard, Codie Taylor, Leroy Carter, Josh Moorby, Will Jordan tries; Damian McKenzie 6 cons, pen)

Australia 19 (Tom Wright, Harry Wilson, Josh Nasser tries; Ryan Lonergan 2 cons)

World.title: Opponents label National's fishing policy 'desperate' and a 'flip-flop'
World.content:
New Zealand First says National's fishing policy is desperate and unresearched, and would have huge impacts on employment and the costs of fish.

Meanwhile, environmental groups and parties to National's left say National cannot be trusted on the issue, given the party's track record this term.

After a spearfishing trip departing from Auckland's Takapuna Beach on Saturday, National leader Christopher Luxon announced the policy to ban ring-net fishing in the Hauraki Gulf, establish a new Waiheke Island marine reserve, ban commercial sales of marlin, and review bottom trawling on sea mounts with a view to reducing use of the technique over time.

'Desperate and unresearched' - Peters

NZ First's Shane Jones has been championing the fishing industry this term of government, so the policy would appear to be a shot across his bow - and Luxon said he did not care what Jones might think of it.

NZ First leader Winston Peters, after what he said was a "wall to wall" public meeting in Invercargill, suggested the consequences had not been thought through.

"It's rather desperate and it's rather unresearched as to the consequences of what they propose to do, both with respect to the workers and the fishermen and fisherwomen, and everybody's involved in the market, but also the customers and the cost of fish going forward," Peters said.

"I don't understand why he's actually making that announcement because there's been a lot of work and a lot of research going into the total consequences of such decisions, and it's premature to arrive at that because the work in its totality hasn't been done."

However, he would not commit to opposing the policy in coalition negotiations.

"Look, we just heard about it today so we're not going to rush to judgement on it, but ... when you're forced to check out what you've just heard - to its authenticity and its veracity, and its utility and its workability - it's not going to survive that test.

"We'd be opposed to it but we need the time to work on that - but I was actually quite surprised that they would make such a premature announcement."

He said the policy went against what the government had been trying to do over the past term.

"We've tried to keep in mind two things: there are thousands of workers involved, and there are also hundreds of thousands of customers involved - and within a cost of living crisis like we have, those sorts of costs are significant."

'Really disappointing' - Forest and Bird

Forest and Bird spokesperson Bianca Ranson said Labour and the Greens had offered support to National on a ring-net ban for Hauraki, so there was "no need to compromise those high protection areas by allowing fishing in them".

She said the Waiheke Marine Reserve proposal had been "sitting on their desk" for nearly two years, and the decision could have been made already.

"It's great to see some energy around protection for the gulf, but it is very much a case of why did they not act on it this term?"

National seemed to be using the issue's popularity to score points, she said.

"It's very clear that bottom trawling on the Hauraki Gulf is an election issue, we've been campaigning hard on it. There's overwhelming social licence; people want to see action in the gulf ... what has been announced today could have been done this term. It feels quite unfair to hear they're announcing these things when they've literally had the power to be able to enact them."

National can't be trusted on oceans policy - Labour, Greens

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said National's time in government suggested it would do the opposite of what it campaigned on, and the party could not be trusted.

"When we announced protections around the Hauraki Gulf when we were in government, the National Party said that they didn't go far enough and they supported them, and then in government, undid much of the work that we were doing."

Hipkins said Labour was committed to banning bottom trawling in the Hauraki Gulf, but in terms of scaling up a ban in New Zealand's EEZ, there was more work to do.

"It can't be done immediately. There's a need for us still to fish. There's jobs associated with that. As new technology emerges, and we've invested as a country in quite a lot of research and development in this area, we need to do more of that so that we can work out how to do fishing more sustainably and with less environmental impact."

Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick also said the policy showed National could not be trusted on oceans policy.

"When we were going through the amendment to the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act ... we ended up with a proposal for these high protection areas, and then at the 11th hour ministers of this government had a backroom meeting and decided to create carve-outs in those so-called high protection areas to allow ring-net commercial fishers to continue fishing.

"Now they're turning around, understanding how deeply unpopular this is and saying they're going to campaign on undoing it. You cannot trust the National Party when it comes to conservation."

Opportunity Party welcomes shift

The Opportunity Party also noted much of the policy could have been progressed in the last three years, but welcomed the new approach.

Oceans and fisheries spokesperson Kayla Kingdon-Bebb said National did not need to rely on New Zealand First in the first place to get the legislation that created the high protection areas - including the exemptions - over the line.

"Parties on the other side of the House would have supported it. There was absolutely no need to exempt commercial fishing from those two areas in the first place. So I think it's pretty interesting to see that National's now campaigning on reversing a decision it didn't actually have to make in the last term."

One of Opportunity's five bottom lines is an immediate end to bottom trawling in inshore areas such as the Hauraki Gulf, followed by a complete phase-out.

Leader Qiulae Wong said National had "clearly been led astray by some of their coalition partners" this term and wanted to see the party go further.

World.title: Youth homelessness a 'growing reality' as Aotearoa marks World Homeless Day
World.content:
Youth homelessness is "getting younger", with support workers warning more rangatahi are going without basic necessities and safe places to stay.

Rangatahi, youth advocates and housing providers gathered in West Auckland on Saturday to mark World Homeless Day, calling for better support for young people experiencing homelessness.

The event was organised by Manaaki Rangatahi, a kaupapa Māori-led collective working to address youth housing insecurity and homelessness in Aotearoa.

Te Kou o Rehua Panapa, from Mā Te Huruhuru Charitable Trust, works with the organisation's Manukura outreach team, connecting with taitamariki experiencing homelessness across Tāmaki Makaurau.

He said the situation was changing, with younger children increasingly needing support. The night before the event, his team had connected with a 12-year-old who had been homeless for more than nine months.

"I've not seen homelessness like this before. It's a different homelessness now. It's getting younger.

"The need is more, and there's not a hell of a lot of support out there for them."

He said many young people lacked access to basic necessities, while the proportion of rangatahi Māori and Pacific young people experiencing homelessness was particularly concerning.

"I would say 90 percent are of Māori whakapapa or are from Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa," he said.

"It hurts. It shouldn't be a reality for us as people of the land, as tangata whenua. We shouldn't be experiencing this.

"It is really hard to swallow sometimes to see our own people out there."

Te Kou o Rehua Panapa says homeless youth are getting younger and needing more support. RNZ / Coco Lance

Mā Te Huruhuru's Manukura outreach vehicle, or 'waka', allows kaimahi to go directly to young people rather than requiring them to find their way to a service.

The team provides food, hygiene products, phone-charging equipment and a safe space for rangatahi to sit down and talk.

Raising awareness was an important first step towards finding lasting solutions, Panapa said.

"We need to normalise the conversation and have more kōrero, and work collectively to come up with sustainable solutions for our taitamariki and our whānau who are currently homeless."

As Aotearoa marks World Homeless Day, Panapa wants New Zealanders to understand that homelessness and youth homeless is "a reality".

"Homelessness is not our future. It should not be our future, for our taitamariki, for our mokopuna and for our whānau."

Te Aroha Humarie Morgan-Neal, 18, says finding support helped her work towards a safer future for herself and her baby Kaos. RNZ / Coco Lance

'Change can happen'

18-year-old Te Aroha Humarie Morgan-Neal knows what it is like to experience homelessness and the importance of having somewhere safe to turn.

Morgan-Neal said she experienced "deep addiction" and an abusive relationship before seeking support from Grace Foundation, a charitable trust providing accommodation and rehabilitation services.

She said she had been sober for five months and was working towards a better future for herself and her baby.

Before seeking help, she had spent time sleeping in stolen cars and abandoned houses when she was only 12 years old up until she was 16.

"I felt neglected and broken. I didn't grow up with my parents."

A key kaupapa of this year's World Homeless Day was 'What does Home mean or look like to you?' RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

Morgan-Neal said losing touch with her Māori culture while growing up had also affected her, but reconnecting through pōwhiri, wānanga and kapa haka at Grace Foundation had been an important part of her journey.

She said the support helped her rebuild trust and focus on herself and her child.

"I didn't want to give my baby the life that I had. I wanted to give him better."

For her, a safe home had "healthy connections, love, caring ... and respecting and loving one another".

"Connecting with one another. That's what I think home is."

Her message to others experiencing similar challenges and addiction was to reach out for support.

"Change can happen. Change is worth it. Reach out for help. Speaking up is not wrong."

Manaaki Rangatahi chief executive Bianca Johanson is calling for more youth housing and a national strategy to address youth homelessness. RNZ / Coco Lance

Home is more than a roof

Community Housing Aotearoa's most recent report on severe housing deprivation found Māori made up 28.8 percent of people

experiencing homelessness, despite accounting for 17.1 percent of the population.

Pacific people accounted for 22.6 percent of those experiencing homelessness, despite making up about 8 percent of the population.

The report also highlighted the scale of youth homelessness, with more than half of people experiencing homelessness under the age of 24.

It warned youth homelessness could become a pathway into adult homelessness without early, age-appropriate support and changes to barriers that prevent young people accessing housing.

The World Homeless Day art exhibition by Kākano Youth Arts Collective reflects the lived experiences of rangatahi, capturing journeys from a “trap house to a home”. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

21-year-old Georgia, a member of Kākano Youth Arts Collective, said youth homelessness could be difficult to recognise because many young people were not sleeping on the street.

She had supported someone close to her who moved between homes, including a period when they slept together on a mattress in a garage.

"Just because you don't see youth on the street begging for change or sleeping in a blanket on the street doesn't mean it doesn't exist," she said.

"Youth homelessness is quite often jumping from couch to couch, staying at friends' houses, sleeping on horrible mattresses in people's garages."

Georgia said young people could end up staying in unsafe environments because they had nowhere else to go.

"It's quite a dangerous situation to be in, but you're so desperate to be somewhere that's not your own home because you don't want to be in your own home."

She said the lack of visibility meant youth homelessness could be pushed aside, even when young people were experiencing significant housing insecurity.

"Just because they're in a house doesn't mean they're actually safe, and that still classes as homeless because if you're couch surfing, it's not stable."

20-year-old youth advocate Platinum says homelessness goes beyond sleeping rough, with many rangatahi couch surfing or living in unsafe homes. RNZ / Coco Lance

Platinum, a 20-year-old rangatahi MC at the event, reiterated that homelessness was much broader than sleeping rough, with many young people moving between houses or living in unsafe environments.

"Homelessness is just an umbrella word for so many things. Homelessness is when you live in a house that has way too many people. Homelessness is when you are couch surfing, going from home to home," she said.

"People aren't choosing to be homeless."

Platinum said a home should be a safe place where people felt protected, heard and seen.

"Home isn't just a place, it's a life."

Manaaki Rangatahi is calling for greater investment in youth housing and a coordinated national response to homelessness.

World.title: Otago dominate Hawke's Bay on home turf, earning spot in NPC semifinals
World.content:
Otago got their revenge over Hawke's Bay and continued to defend their home ground fortress with a 50-14 win in their NPC quarter-final in Dunedin.

Earlier this season, Hawke's Bay pulled off a come from behind victory over the southerners but could not do the same on Saturday with a place in the semifinals on the line.

Otago made their intentions clear early with no.8 Christian Lio-Willie powering over from the back of a scrum to open the scoring in the seventh minute.

The home side had doubled their lead when halfback Kieran McClea marked his return to the starting lineup with a try in the 16th minute.

Hawke's Bay replied through their halfback Folau Fakatava, when he finished off a break from winger Nic Benn, but Otago restored their lead through tighthead prop Saula Ma'u who crashed over after some strong work from his forwards and took a 24-7 lead into halftime.

After the break Henry Bell extended the lead when he also scored off the back of a maul.

The visitors were awarded a penalty try and Joseva Tamani was sent to the sinbin for playing the ball on the ground and preventing Fakatava scoring his second in the 50th minute.

However, the home side could not be slowed down as Sam Nemec-Vial sprinted in to score, even though his team were still down to 14 men.

Replacement back Joel Lam scored his first try of the season as Otago kept piling on the points.

Hawke's Bay made mass changes on the hour mark but could not turn around their fortunes.

Otago's final try came after a couple of players came close but it was Harry Irving who got the ball down over the line.

The win also reinforced Otago's strength on their home ground, with a record of one loss in their last 12 games at Forsyth Barr Stadium.

World.title: Ruthless Taranaki clinch NPC semifinal spot after Bradley Slater hat-trick against North Harbour
World.content:
Taranaki have continued their high-scoring late season form and secured a place in the NPC semifinals with a 50-31 win over North Harbour on the North Shore.

In the first meeting between these teams this season, Taranaki hooker Bradley Slater was once again the star with a hat-trick of tries in his side's eight-try rout.

Slater had also scored three tries against Harbour last season.

In a tit for tat first half, Harbour winger Rory Taylor scored in the second minute of the match when he was on the end of a move that began at a lineout, went through several sets of hands, and was sealed with him crossing the try line in the corner to give the home side a dream start.

However, 10 minutes later Taranaki struck back on the counter when pacy winger Kini Naholo outran the defenders to score in the left corner. The try was not converted and Harbour held on to the lead.

Just after the half-hour mark, Taranaki were temporarily reduced to 14 men when centre Meihana Grindlay got a yellow card for no clear release at the breakdown.

While Harbour had the numerical advantage, Taylor ran in his second try, but again Taranaki hit back minutes later through Slater, who scored off the back of a maul.

Taranaki then took the lead for the first time in the match while still a man down - flanker Michael Loft went over in the corner after the hooter in the first half to go into the sheds ahead 17-14.

After a back and forth first half, Taranaki unleashed in the second.

Naholo scored his second try four minutes after halftime, off some solid work by the forwards.

Slater then scored twice in six minutes after getting driven over the line both times before getting subbed at the 60-minute mark.

Jacob Ratumaitavuki-Kneepkens got in on the try scoring action, as did Vereniki Tikoisolomone.

Back Sam Wye came off the bench and scored for the home side in the 65th minute.

There was a delay in play when Harbour's Zinzan Hansen was stretchered off with a leg injury after playing just over 15 minutes.

Fullback Hunter Rice scored two late tries but it would be too little too late.

In further late drama, Taranaki also played out the final minutes of the game with 14 men as Kaylum Boshier was sinbinned.

World.title: Two dead, two seriously injured as homicide investigation launched in Christchurch
World.content:
A 58-year-old man has been charged after two people died and another two were seriously injured in Christchurch.

Police were called to an address on Olliviers Road, in the suburb of Phillipstown, overnight.

Detective Inspector Greg Murton said two people died at the scene, while two others were taken to hospital with serious injuries.

"The man will face two charges of murder, one charge of attempted murder and one for wounding with intent.

"He will appear in the Christchurch District Court on Monday 12 October."

Murton said police believed this was an isolated incident and are not seeking anyone else.

Police are wanting to reassure the public that there is no risk to their safety. Louis Dunham/RNZ

"Police want to reassure the public there is no risk to their safety but also appreciate this incident will be deeply upsetting and unsettling for those who reside in the area."

Police said people should expect an increased police presence in the coming days and appreciate their co-operation as scene examinations continue.

Patricia Grant, who lives in the street, said the incident came as a surprise.

"I couldn't believe it when I got up this morning. There was a cop here, a cop there, a cop over the road and I thought, what the hell's going on?

"My grandson rung me and said where are you Nana and I said inside, why? And he said there have been murders in your street! And I said, come on Karl! No Mum, it's true! And I had a look out and oh my god, there were cars everywhere, I couldn't believe it!'

Louis Dunham/RNZ

She said the neighbourhood had become increasingly unsettled, with people she didn't know coming to the door and asking for cigarettes or money.

Another neighbour said it sounded like an argument broke out at the east Christchurch house.

He said the street was rowdier than usual.

"It sounded like it was a bit of a party going on, someone was pissed off or whatever. I heard a little bit yelling and doors constantly being slammed, banging on cars.

"I feel a bit shocked, but times are tough. Drugs are always an issue."

Detective Inspector Nicola Reeves is asking anyone who may have seen anything, or may have CCTV of the area, to contact 105.

World.title: Samoa looks for power from pain in World Cup tilt
World.content:
Junior Paulo knows what it feels like to pull yourself from the depths of grand final misery and glowingly represent your country at a Rugby League World Cup weeks later.

So he is happy to lend a helping hand to his Samoa teammates who are suffering similar heartache.

Parramatta's Paulo had big dreams of winning the NRL grand final in 2022, but they shattered when the forward's side suffered a 28-12 loss to Penrith in the decider.

He had to forge on, and weeks later found himself leading Samoa in a historic World Cup final against Australia.

Paulo will lead Samoa for the second tournament in a row. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

Paulo will be looking to repeat the dose this time around after the tournament was officially launched at the Sydney Football Stadium on Saturday.

Samoa are one of 10 men's teams vying for glory, beginning when Australia face New Zealand on Thursday night, while eight teams will make up the women's tournament that starts with the Jillaroos taking on Samoa in Parramatta the following evening.

This year, four of Samoa's players — Newcastle winger Greg Marzhew, prop Pasami Saulo, and second-rowers Francis Manuleleua and Jermaine McEwen — will be feeling a similar pain to Paulo's back in 2022.

The Knights quartet lost to the Sydney Roosters in the grand final last Sunday.

"I was in the same shoes, losing to Penrith and then [having to play in the] World Cup," Samoa co-captain Paulo said.

"All you want to do is … be able to turn it around.

"So for them [Manuleleua and McEwen], they're eager to get back out and play some footy. Hopefully it means they bring the physicality that they do.

"It's time for us to bring them up to being ready to represent Samoa, but also making it enjoyable for them."

Regardless, Paulo cannot wait to lead a star-studded Samoan side when they begin their campaign next Friday against France before facing Papua New Guinea and Tonga.

The men's and women's tournaments will kick off next week. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

All eyes are sure to be fixed on star half Jarome Luai after a headline-riddled season where he was announced as the first official signing for the PNG Chiefs from 2028 before later being released by Wests Tigers to join Parramatta for 2027.

"He's [been] just a bit misunderstood by many towards the back end of the year. People were very opinionated about him," said Paulo of his co-captain.

"He's locked in, putting his best foot forward and representing Samoa. He enjoys being in these camps, and you can just tell how locked in he is by the first day we got into camp.

"[I] just want to see him evolve as a leader, and grow into the leader he is now. All the boys will be backing him, and luckily, nothing fazes Romey [Luai] too much."

In the lead-up to the tournament, some members of the team also spent some time in Samoa, which Paulo said was an "indescribable" feeling as it reminded the players they are embarking on something for more than themselves.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Wallabies humiliated by All Blacks 50-19 as Eden Park curse continues
World.content:
The Wallabies have been humiliated by the All Blacks via a 50-19 thumping in the opening Bledisloe Cup Test at Eden Park.

The victory means the All Blacks retain the Bledisloe Cup for yet another year, having held the precious silverware since 2003.

They also pushed their winning streak over the Wallabies out to 12 Tests and gave coach Dave Rennie a triumph in his first meeting with his former side.

Despite arriving in Auckland in a buoyant mood, the Les Kiss-coached Wallabies will return to Australia with their tail between their legs.

Their hopes of ending a 40-year losing streak against the All Blacks at Eden Park were dashed after the home side ran rampant in the second half.

Holding a slender 17-14 lead at the break, the All Blacks scored five tries to one in the second term to record a deserved victory at their spiritual home.

The All Blacks hold the Bledisloe Cup aloft after their convincing victory. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

The All Blacks scored seven tries in total, with Damian McKenzie adding six conversions and a penalty goal.

The Wallabies began strongly, scoring a brilliant try from Tom Wright in the seventh minute of play.

Ryan Lonergan added the extras to make the score 7-0, but the All Blacks replied with converted tries from back-rowers Peter Lakai and Tupou Vaa'i.

McKenzie's 32nd-minute penalty goal extended the All Blacks' lead to 17-7, but Wallabies captain Harry Wilson scored under the posts in the shadows of half-time to keep his side in touch on the scoreboard.

Once All Blacks scrum half Cam Roigard scored eight minutes after half-time, however, the floodgates opened.

All Blacks captain Codie Taylor (right) celebrates his try against the Wallabies. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Tries from captain Codie Taylor, Leroy Carter and Josh Moorby followed, before the Wallabies managed a consolation five-pointer from reserve hooker Josh Nasser.

Will Jordan touched down for the final All Blacks' try only moments before full-time, icing the convincing win.

The Wallabies' six-match unbeaten run came to an abrupt end, with the defeat serving as a bitter reality check.

Adding to the Wallabies' woes was the loss of star centre Len Ikitau, who failed an HIA in the first half.

The result gave Kiss his first defeat since taking over as Wallabies coach from Joe Schmidt.

Kiss and his players will have to re-group quickly as both sides meet again next Saturday at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: SA starts Shield defence with innings win over Victoria
World.content:
South Australia has started its Sheffield Shield campaign in the same way it ended the last one, beating Victoria at Junction Oval.

The two-time defending champions wrapped up their dominating start today, beating the home side by an innings and 40 runs.

Fittingly, debutant Noah McFadyen took the last wicket of the game when he had David Moody caught and bowled, after top-scoring with 134 in SA's innings.

McFadyen had hit two sixes to go from 88 to 100, finished with 16 fours and five maximums.

The 23-year-old all-rounder had match figures of 3-65, including Moody's wicket to clinch the game.

Resuming at 7-175 and needing another 89 to bat again, Victoria was dismissed for 224.

Victoria made 244 in its first innings and SA took the game away from them with 508.

Fergus O'Neill top-scored in Victoria's second innings with 62, while Nathan McAndrew and Henry Thornton took three wickets apiece.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Oldest Wallaby remembers historic Eden Park win over All Blacks
World.content:
Don Strachan has accomplished a feat that only a handful of Wallabies still living have achieved — defeating the All Blacks at Eden Park.

In his second test match in 1955, the then-26-year-old prop started in Australia's 8–3 defeat of New Zealand at the iconic ground in Auckland.

The Wallabies have only tasted success against the All Blacks there on three other occasions, the last 40 years ago.

"We were determined to win that [1955] game," Strachan said.

" It was something that everyone on that team was proud of … A lot of them are not here anymore. "

An excerpt from a local newspaper following the game detailed the win as "one of the finest" the Wallabies had produced.

"The Australians gave a magnificent exhibition to outplay the All Blacks," the article said.

Don Strachan featured in the Wallabies 8–3 win over the All Blacks at Eden Park in 1955. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

Despite the victory, New Zealand retained the Bledisloe Cup following wins in the first and second test matches in Wellington and Dunedin.

The series loss still haunts Strachan all these years later.

He was disallowed a try in his debut game at Carisbrook on the South Island, which the All Blacks won 8–0.

"We were cheated," Strachan said.

Lucky to be alive

Hailing from Orange in the New South Wales Central West, the 97-year-old is the oldest living Australian rugby union player.

"I'm Wallaby number 413, and that means there are 412 of them who are no longer here anymore," he said.

"I wouldn't have wished for anything else. I've been lucky … I've had a great time."

Don Strachan is Wallaby number 413 after making his debut against the All Blacks in Dunedin in 1955. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

His international rugby career almost ended before it began following a motorbike crash in the Blue Mountains while returning from a game in Sydney.

"I had a terrific motor accident. A truck came over the hill on the wrong side of the road," Strachan said.

"[It] hit me head-on. Threw me almost into the front yard of the house next door."

After suffering a compound fracture to his leg, Strachan narrowly avoided having it amputated and spent several months in hospital.

"Their advice was that I would never be able to play rugby again because I could lose my leg," he said.

Returning to rugby

Back on his dad's potato farm near Orange, Strachan began building his strength to return to the footy field.

"I used to lift 1,000 bags of potatoes a day," he said.

"I had a very strong back, legs and shoulders … That stood me in good stead because I had the muscles to support everything else."

As a front rower, Strachan "loved the game" and the physicality that came with it.

Don Strachan remembers his time with the Wallabies fondly. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

"I never got pushed out of a scrum in my life … If they played fair, I played fair," he said.

"If they wanted to do something else, I'd accommodate them.

"I accommodated a few of them."

That love of rugby ultimately saw Strachan captain the Combined NSW Country side for five years, represent the NSW Waratahs and play twice for Australia.

Don Strachan captained the Combined NSW Country side for five years. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

It could have been more after being selected for a seven-month tour of the United Kingdom, Ireland, Canada and the United States in 1955, but with a baby on the way with wife Wendy and a farm to help run, he declined the opportunity.

Orange Emus founded

In 1947, the Orange Rugby Club had been travelling to Sydney most winter weekends to take on lifesaving clubs and agricultural schools.

From that team spawned the idea to create a four-team local competition in Orange that would become the Central West Rugby Union tournament in 1956.

The Orange Emus have won 17 first-grade premierships in the Central West Rugby Union competition, winning the Blowes Cup in 2025. (Supplied: Orange Emus)

Given that macropods had been adopted by many clubs across the country, Strachan and his friends turned to the other side of the Australian coat of arms for inspiration. And thus, the Orange Emus Rugby Club was born.

"We had a collection of some of the nicest people you could ever meet," he said.

To fund the construction of an oval and grandstand, the club had to get creative.

"We used to do these rabbit drives," Strachan said.

"We were catching 1,200 rabbits at a time and taking them into the abattoirs and selling them.

"The whole club got together and worked and made this money … eventually we were able to put it together."

The Orange Emus became one of the most successful clubs in the Central West Rugby Union competition, winning 17 first-grade titles.

The Wallabies will play NZ on Saturday afternoon.

World.title: Verstappen pips Russell to sprint pole at Singapore F1 grand prix
World.content:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen will take pole position for the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race ​on Friday, having pipped Mercedes driver George Russell, who will join him on the front row at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

Verstappen, who had never previously taken pole or won a race in Singapore, set the fastest time of one minute 31.156 seconds, 0.120 seconds quicker than Russell.

Australia's Oscar Piastri qualified fourth-fastest, just ahead of McLaren teammate Lando Norris.

"It's closer in Singapore. Your lap itself, you're pushing as hard as you think is possible, close ​to the walls in places," Verstappen said.

"Once we ‌bolted on the soft tyres, it felt like the car was coming alive a little bit more. But I did not expect this, so, of course, very happy to be first.

"The last few races we've been a lot stronger, but of course this track still highlights a few little weaknesses in the car. But we ‌managed to drive with them as well as possible."

Verstappen was investigated by the stewards for overtaking Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton under the yellow flags in SQ1. ⁠However, they accepted the Dutchman's explanation that braking could have created an unsafe situation and he had reduced his speed by lifting off the throttle afterwards.

Ferrari's ​Charles Leclerc was third fastest, while Mercedes ‌championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who leads Russell by 84 points, was only seventh quickest.

Piastri hoping for better in Singapore Oscar Piastri is hoping McLaren will be more competitive during the Singapore Grand Prix weekend after a disappointing round last time in Malaysia.

Russell was the fastest in the only practice session earlier on Friday, but his power unit penalty will not affect his position on the grid for Saturday's sprint.

However, the FIA handed the Briton a 40-place grid penalty for Sunday after he incurred a 10-place penalty for each of four additional elements, effectively consigning him to the back of ​the ‌pack.

"We've been competitive all day, from the first laps in FP1. We obviously topped the time sheets there," Russell said.

"We knew Max was fast and he went on a slightly different strategy from us in Q3, just doing the one lap. Who knows what was best, but pretty ⁠satisfied with the P2.

"It's going to be very challenging. The grip left to ‌right here is a big difference. The drivers ‌on the pole side last year had a big advantage, so it's probably going to be trying to maintain P2."

Sergio Perez brought an end to the first sprint qualifying session when he hit a barrier. (Getty Images: Clive Rose)

The first sprint qualifying session was ‌red flagged when Cadillac's Sergio Perez crashed into a barrier and attempted to nurse his car back into the pits, leaving behind debris from his front wing that marshals needed to remove.

That effectively gave drivers one lap to ‌advance to SQ2, ​and Verstappen was one of the ⁠last drivers to set a lap time, with the Dutchman topping the time sheets.

A glitch in the systems delayed the start of SQ2, with the FIA saying some lap times had not been registered. But the FIA added that the issue had been resolved and the "current timings are considered correct".

Moreover, "overtake mode" was not available after the red flag period during SQ1. It was then activated for a period ⁠of 27 seconds before being deactivated again.

"The FIA acknowledges that this unfortunate human error had an impact on the performance of certain cars based on the timing of their run and their position ‌around the lap," it said.

"The ‌second and third periods of Sprint Qualifying were not affected."

A software bug also caused chaos last weekend. Cars slowed to a crawl on two formation laps that were held after heavy rain at Sepang forced the original start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to be aborted.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Bulldogs dominant in win over Bombers to start Pride Round
World.content:
The Western Bulldogs have brought a ruthless mentality to Pride Round in thrashing Essendon by 43 points.

Friday night's 10.5 (65) to 2.10 (22) result was the Bulldogs' seventh win for the season and sent a warning to the top eight sides on the cusp of finals.

It came despite their shaky start in front of a home crowd at Whitten Oval.

Essendon came out firing and Emily Gough kicked the first goal inside the first two minutes, spurring the Dons, who played with high pressure and repeatedly locked the ball in their forward half.

The Bulldogs responded with five unanswered goals with the help of an unstoppable Isabelle Pritchard, who had 30 disposals and 10 clearances.

"We weren't playing the style of game that we came to play," Dogs midfielder Jess Fitzgerald said after quarter time.

"We wanted to come into the game with a bit of a ruthless mentality, and we felt like we didn't bring that in the first.

"So, yeah, we turned that on."

Essendon were down by 25 points at half-time but hopes of repeating last week's win over the Giants, a comeback from 24 points down at half-time, were cut short by their inability to find the goals.

After Gough's early major, the Bombers kicked nine points until Sophie Alexander found their second just before three-quarter time.

The Bombers managed one more point in the final term, while the Dogs slotted another three goals.

Star forward Sarah Hartwig had a career-high four goals and helped the Western Bulldogs surpass the 60-point mark for the fifth time since 2025.

"Honestly, it's just that work rate and the pressure that we bring, especially in the forward line. That's what we pride ourselves on," she said.

Despite the win, the Bulldogs still have work to do in the season's run home, Hartwig said.

"We're not looking to finals yet. We've got three tough games coming up, so we're going to focus on that first," she said.

The Dogs will face Carlton, Melbourne and Geelong — all premiership contenders — in the final three games of the season.

Essendon will play North Melbourne, before facing Hawthorn and Collingwood.

AAP

World.title: Australia's Test start no disaster, but order issues hint at troubles ahead
World.content:
It was Steve Waugh — Mr Mental Disintegration himself — who once said the most emotionally taxing aspect of his time as the most important man in Australian cricket was not the burden of captaincy, nor the concurrent need to keep making big runs, but his role as a national selector.

How long to wait for a treasured teammate's form to come right, when the axe might end his career? Should he be replaced with fresh blood or someone on a second or third chance, as Waugh himself had once been? What was the right balance of talent and personalities?

Overnight in Durban, Waugh's man-management issues seemed trifling compared to the self-inflicted problems of Australia's current selectors. But you'd need a very specific combination of tarot cards and crystals to work out which question of George Bailey's led to the answer "Nic Maddinson".

The final analysis on day one was not entirely disastrous. Australia stumbled to 6-187 before bad light stopped play and there were at least positive signs in a few problematic areas.

One was a solid start from Marnus Labuschagne, whose momentary lapse on the brink of lunch ended a sparkling partnership with Steve Smith. The other was a steady hand from Matt Renshaw, who was undefeated on 46 at the day's premature end.

Renshaw renaissance rescues Aussies Matt Renshaw is stranded four runs short of his first Test half-century in nine years as bad light halts play on the first day of the opening Test against South Africa.

There were deeper currents, though. Troubling ones. What stood out was not just the sense of a well-drilled bowling attack reminding the world why South Africa was the reigning world champion, but of Australia, with its makeshift batting order and selection on the fly, presenting as an increasingly confused rabble.

Maddinson's mere selection was contentious enough; he had not played a first-class match in 19 months. The corollary was throwing him to the wolves as opener on a pitch offering lateral movement. That second part was so surprising to most onlookers that the host broadcaster initially had him down as batting at five.

But then, how else could it have played out? Had Cooper Connolly got the nod instead, he probably would have slotted in at five and Renshaw would have moved up to open with Travis Head, himself a world-class number five whose impact in Tests is now being blunted by his ongoing hostage ordeal at the top of the order. Further problems flow from there.

You had to feel for Maddinson. Mark Waugh, who was among the selectors who picked the left-hander for his first three Tests in 2016, has since admitted he had been discarded too quickly. Now he's been brought back almost at random and given this thankless task.

Maddinson's 33-ball duck was awful to watch, but one would hope he's backed to make a slightly better fist of whatever follows.

Another thing Steve Waugh used to do was make it clear to each player in his team what was expected of them in their specific role. It's hard to imagine things being phrased so plainly now. Aside from Labuschagne and Smith, could any current Australian batsman say he's in the right spot for the right reason?

Another cheap dismissal for Travis Head raises questions about his experimental role as opener. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

At 32, Head's identity crisis should, on current evidence, be considered a serious matter for the future of this team.

Right now, we are being asked to accept that Renshaw — an undoubtedly tough and capable player whose Test record is nevertheless modest — needs to bat where he is most comfortable, and that as a result, Head, now in his prime years, needs to play an essentially experimental role that is clearly not suited to him.

It is true that Bailey's job has been made harder by injuries to Cameron Green and Josh Inglis, and a dearth of irresistible opening candidates in the Sheffield Shield. But the strangest aspect of all the pre-tour kvetching over selection was how much of it centered on Labuschagne, who was and remains the logical choice at three.

Far more baffling, in hindsight, was the lack of focus on Bailey's claim that the number-three slot could be just as easily filled by Connolly, who has never made a first-class century, or the since-injured Inglis, neither of whom have batted higher than five for their state.

Even in this era of "false threes" and result pitches, the linchpin positions in the top order should surely not be devalued so casually. Australia is now approaching double digits for opening combinations of the post-Warner era.

Anyway, that is what Australia could have controlled. What it still can't, it seems, is the sideways movement of medium pacers. When this tour was merely on the horizon, Kagiso Rabada and Lungi Ngidi loomed as the destroyers.

Both are missing in Durban, yet Marco Jansen and Wiaan Mulder caused Australia just as many problems without Jansen ever really hitting their stride.

It made for an absorbing battle, but for Australia things could actually have been far worse. We must now accept a world order in which the combination of the words "Ollie Robinson" and "Ashes hero" are not just plausible but a distinct possibility.

The consolation is that a Test series is never decided on its opening day and can therefore often be taken with a grain of salt, per Merv Hughes's tinder-dry diary entry following the first day of another Test series, three decades ago:

"Back to hotel. Few beers downstairs, then up to room … Have room service. Watch Cape Fear. Quiet night." Thus ended the day Shane Warne bowled the ball of the century.

Nothing so dramatic transpired this time around but, for Australia, you sense the road ahead will be trying.

World.title: Quick hits: Maddinson makes historic 33-ball duck as Aussie batters flounder
World.content:
Nic Maddinson's unlikely Test return has ended with a historic duck as Australia's battered floundered despite a South African DRS debacle.

Here are the quick hits from the opening day of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Maddinson makes historic duck on return

Maddinson was unable to make the most of an early reprieve on day one. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

With almost a decade having passed since the last of his three Test appearances, veteran opener Nic Maddinson could have been forgiven for thinking his days in Australian whites were over.

But after being parachuted into the squad earlier this week, the 34-year-old's sensational return to the Test arena was cemented at the toss in Durban, with Pat Cummins confirming Maddinson would be the replacement for the injured Cameron Green.

In an even bigger surprise, he was in line to open his side's innings, with the also recently recalled Matt Renshaw dropping down the order.

Maddinson did not play at all in the last Sheffield Shield season, with his last First Class appearance having come back in March 2025.

And with Australia winning the toss and batting, he was put to the test immediately.

Maddinson looked both nervy and underdone in his drought-breaking Test knock, unable to get off the mark during his first 32 balls before being dismissed by his 33rd, the New South Welshman chopping onto his stumps off the bowling of Marco Jansen.

Unfortunately for Maddinson, it was a historic return as well as a miserable one, his 33-ball effort setting a new record for the longest duck by an Aussie opener in Test cricket.

Overall, it was the second-longest no score by an Australian in the history of the format, only behind Mike Whitney's 42-ball 0 in 1981.

2. South Africa in DRS debacle

Nic Maddinson was unable to make the most of an early reprieve. (Fox Cricket)

Only minutes earlier, Maddinson had been gifted a huge slice of luck.

With the opener swinging across the line wildly, a Wiaan Mulder delivery thudded into his front pad. There was a big appeal, but umpire Richard Kettlebrough was unmoved.

South African captain Temba Bavuma indicated Maddinson had gotten some bat on ball and opted against the first review of the series.

And there certainly were two noises but replays showed Maddinson's willow had gotten nowhere near the ball, instead clipping his pad.

The South Africans watched the big screen ruefully as it showed the three reds that would have sent Maddinson back to the pavilion.

It was an unconvincing start for the South Africans as far DRS was concerned, with Bavuma also burning two reviews on appeals that didn't have a whole lot going for them.

First, Marnus Labuschagne survived a referral on a ball that swung too sharply and was projected to be missing leg stump.

Then, the hosts wasted a second review when a steepling Marco Jansen delivery caught Renshaw on the arm. The ball had looped up to wicketkeeper Kyle Verreynne, who took a simple catch, and the South Africans were convinced it had brushed the Australian's glove.

It hadn't.

The replays showed Jansen had found nothing but arm guard and the hosts had just one review remaining.

3. Labuschagne departs on stroke of lunch

Labuschagne's innings came to an end on the stroke of lunch. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

It was a gut-wrenching end to an innings of serious promise for Labuschagne.

The Queenslander, so desperately in need of a score to get his Test career back on track, reached the final over of the morning session on 37 and with one eye on kicking on after the first break.

He was able to see off the first five balls of the set, but fell on its last.

Angling into the right-hander, Mulder was able to sneak one past Labuschagne's outside edge and into the front pad.

It looked touch and go whether the ball made impact in-line with the stumps, but the umpire's finger was up.

Labuschagne didn't look overly hopeful sending the decision upstairs, but DRS showed how close he was to getting outside the line of off stump, with the Australian only having to leave the field because of the umpire's original call.

It is not the kind of luck you need when you've gone more than three years without a Test century.

4. Smith makes anticlimactic entrance

Smith couldn't make the most of his start. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

With all that had been made of Steve Smith's return to the country his Test career had so shockingly unravelled eight years earlier, the understated reception he received when entering the game felt at least a little anticlimactic.

There was no chorus of boos from the few spectators in place for the morning session as Smith joined Labuschagne at the crease, tasked with steadying the Australian innings with both Maddinson and Head back in the sheds.

And Smith began his innings like he had so often in the past: fidgety, idiosyncratic and paranoid, but set on getting himself into the game.

After seeing off the opening pace barrage, Smith stamped his authority on the morning with two big sixes back over the head of spinner Keshav Maharaj in the space of four balls.

Smith made it to lunch, but only lasted three balls after the first break.

He was struck on the finger by a rearing Marco Jansen length ball, before edging the very next delivery through to the slips.

Smith was out for 25 and Australia had lost two wickets in four balls either side of the lunch break.

5. Bad light robs Renshaw of drought-breaking milestone

Matt Renshaw was Australia's best on day one. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Coming in at number five, Renshaw was a bright spot in an otherwise dark day for the Australian batters.

The southpaw watched on as South African spearhead Anrich Nortje removed Alex Carey and Beau Webster in the space of three balls, and looked supremely confident in his new home in the middle order.

He made his way to 46 before bad light ended the day with over an hour left of scheduled play and just 65.2 overs bowled.

Renshaw will begin day two four runs away from his first Test 50 in more than 3,500 days, tasked with continuing to rebuild Australia's innings alongside Cummins.

Tech.title: Will Warner Bros. kill Skydance — or will David Ellison kill Warner Bros?
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Today, I’m talking with Peter Kafka, chief correspondent at Business Insider and host of the Channels podcast, about the gigantic Warner Bros.-Paramount merger and the future of the company now simply called Skydance.

Skydance is owned by David Ellison, son of Oracle CEO Larry Ellison, and its deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery officially closed the day Peter and I spoke.

There are some grand ambitions here, but the reality is that acquiring Warner never goes well for anyone. AOL failed, AT&T failed, and Discovery failed — although it did succeed in flipping these assets to Skydance. So I wanted to ask Peter if he thinks the Ellisons and Skydance have a real shot at succeeding where so many companies before them have hit the rocks.

Okay: Peter Kafka on Warner Bros. and Skydance. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Peter Kafka, you’re the chief correspondent at Business Insider, and you’re the host of the Channels podcast, our sister podcast here on the Vox Media Podcast Network. Welcome back to Decoder.

Thanks for having me. It’s big media day again!

A big media day. It’s an auspicious day, as my parents would say. It is the day that the Warner-Paramount merger closes. We’ve all been calling it Warner Mount, but I’m told this company will instead just be called Skydance.

Skydance!

Every time I see the word Skydance, I assume it is foreign-owned, which is maybe true in some way.

Another way to think of it is that there are iconic names in Hollywood. Paramount is such an iconic name that Viacom turned itself into Paramount years ago. Warner Bros. is a legendary studio. Let’s get rid of those names. Let’s add Skydance, which no one’s ever heard of.

Let’s just start at the start. There was Paramount. There’s Warner Bros. The deal closes today. That is all going to be a new company called Skydance. Is Skydance just a holding company? Are we as consumers meant to know that this thing exists?

I think for the near term, you’re still gonna think of companies like Paramount, Warner Bros., and HBO as brands you know, but this is going to be one company. They’re going to merge everything. They’re likely going to merge the streaming services, Paramount and HBO, into a thing, not right away, but eventually. So I do think Skydance will be a name that consumers will probably know at some point.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

I just have to ask, what are the chances that HBO Max will be rebranded yet again into Skydance?

There’s probably gonna be some branding stuff. Not again. In the near term, because this is still a cable TV company, there are actually some limits on what these guys can do with their brands and their services. And they won’t come out and say, “We’re gonna mush this stuff together.”

But there’s likely to be one mega streaming service, and maybe you can get HBO separately, or maybe you can only get HBO or only Paramount. Still, it’s gonna be one thing, and one movie studio. It’s all gonna get mushed together, and it’s all gonna be run by David Ellison.

David Ellison is just the latest to believe that he can buy Warner Bros. and make something good happen. I have joked many times on this show that maybe the only antitrust policy this country needs is to make it illegal to buy Warner Bros., and that would just solve a lot of problems. Why does he think he will be successful?

Well, his dad’s the eighth richest man in the world, so that’s not nothing.

That Oracle stock is tied up in a bunch of AI stuff. It’s moving up and down.

We can talk about that. But one, that means that he literally has the money to buy this, and two, that this is a public company kind of in name only. David Ellison and Larry Ellison, his father, control this company effectively. They don’t really need to worry that much about equity shareholders. Debt’s a different issue.

And he’s 43. He’s got a long run backed by tens of billions of dollars of his father’s money to take a stab at this. And as you said, he will not be the first person to do this. There’s a long list of failures. I think maybe that’s appealing to guys like him. It’s like, “Everyone else is dumb. I’m the smart guy who’s gonna figure it out.”

“Everyone else is dumb, and I’m smarter than everyone else is,” is very appealing. But that long list of failures, if you just look at it — they’re all shaped like this idea. We’re gonna take iconic Warner Bros. content, we’re gonna marry it to new distribution, we’re gonna reduce the overhead and costs and decadence of Hollywood. Where does new revenue come from?

There’s no plan for new revenue. There’s no announced plan for new revenue. Right now it’s shrinking; it’s cutting costs. It’s when we merge these two companies together, we’re gonna save $6 billion over the next three years. We promise that most of that’s not gonna come from layoffs, but a lot of it’s gonna come from layoffs.

These are companies that have had many, many rounds of layoffs prior to this. And you could argue, well, there’s probably not that much more to cut. I think reasonably you could say, look, if you combine two big streaming operations, two big studio operations, there probably is stuff [to cut]. You can probably sell off some real estate. You probably don’t need all the executives you currently have. There’s some savings there. But how do you grow? No idea. And no one’s really articulated that.

Growth is required for a couple of reasons here. One, yes, there are going to be shareholders; people will be looking at it. There’s David Ellison’s ego. Then there’s debt. This deal is levered to the max, right?

Eighty billion dollars [in debt]. Eight zero. More important than the number is the reason that David Ellison was able to buy Warner Bros. was that the last owner couldn’t deal with the debt that he took on to buy the company. And that was a mere $43 or $50 billion, depending on who was counting. This is David Zaslav, the former CEO of Warner Bros. Discovery, who spent his entire tenure running that company telling Wall Street that, yes, he was gonna get the debt down, and that was his main focus, and debt, debt, debt, reduce, reduce, reduce.

I mean, he did reduce some debt, but he never convinced Wall Street that he had a plan to grow. Wall Street gave up on this company years ago, which is why when David Ellison decided he wanted to buy it, the stock was, like, seven bucks or something like that. Eventually bought it for, you know, many, many times that.

And now David Zaslav is considered — or he considers himself — a genius for selling the company at such a high price. You could also argue, as someone told me yesterday, that a unicorn sort of manifested itself and allowed David Zaslav to exit the situation he had put himself into.

I don’t know who the next unicorn will be for this company if David Ellison at some point decides, “Ugh, actually this is a lot of debt and a lot of pain. I don’t wanna do this anymore.”

I want to come back to that because I have a little bit of a conspiracy theory. It’s a little bit supported by the attitudes of some of the players here, but we’ll come back around. Even the previous owner, AT&T, which is remarkable that AT&T was the... Somewhere in this chain of ownership, AT&T owned Warner.

Yes.

They could not deal with these assets. Their plan was to distribute Warner content on AT&T phones, which never made any sense. But they were a more aggressive owner.

It also wasn’t really their plan. Their plan was, “Hey, Netflix is a really valuable company. The stock is very high. We’re this boring telecoms company. Our stock is not moving. What if we owned a [version of] Netflix? I bet Wall Street would reward us as a high-flying tech company all of a sudden.” And Wall Street didn’t.

Within a couple of years, AT&T said, “Uh, oh yeah, no, we’re out of this.” And yes, they had said a bunch of stuff about mobile, connectivity, ads, and targeting, and none of that ever went anywhere

I will never forget covering their antitrust case when they had to get approval for that deal. They convinced the judge that they had a vision of the future.
